| 15.7 | Shulgi X: Šulgi sails to Unug, Inana's love song and her decree of his fate ↔ Ur-Ninurta's foes struck down, An's unchangeable fate for him; the Anuna say 'so be it'; Inana, Suen's daughter, and the king go joyfully to the palace (Ur-Ninurta A 44-95) | The god's utterance cannot be changed or overturned (5.5), The king, as the goddess's bridegroom (Dumuzid), lies with Inana, who then decrees his fate (5.3), A god formally decrees (nam tar) a good destiny for the king: heroism, long reign, splendour (4.9) |
| 15.7 | EA 325: Yidya of Ashkelon prepares bread, beer, oxen, goats, grain and straw ↔ A ruler, servant, dust and ground under the king's feet, to the Sun from heaven: as the king wrote, I guard the city (EA 231) | The overlord's letter orders a vassal to guard the king's place, obey the royal official and have bread, wine and supplies ready for the arriving troops (4.8), A vassal calls himself the dust (or clay, or trodden ground) under the overlord king's feet (4.1), A vassal addresses the Egyptian king as 'my god(s), my Sun (god)' (3.7), Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior (3.1) |
| 15.7 | A vassal, dust of the king's feet and groom of his horses, to the Sun from heaven: I guard the king's city (EA 311) ↔ A ruler, servant, dust and ground under the king's feet, to the Sun from heaven: as the king wrote, I guard the city (EA 231) | The overlord's letter orders a vassal to guard the king's place, obey the royal official and have bread, wine and supplies ready for the arriving troops (4.8), A vassal calls himself the dust (or clay, or trodden ground) under the overlord king's feet (4.1), A vassal addresses the Egyptian king as 'my god(s), my Sun (god)' (3.7), Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior (3.1) |

Abdi-Ashirta the dog has taken the king's land (EA 071) ↔ Rib-Addi to Amanappa: may Amun and the Lady of Byblos give you honour; I have no copper or ivory; if no archers this year all lands go to the Habiru (EA 077) | A vassal writing to an Egyptian official wishes that Amun, the king's god, give him honour before the king, and urges him to speak to the king (7.3), Bandits or brigands called sa-gaz (Akkadian ḫabbātu, the Ḫabiru/ʿapiru) (4.2), A vassal begs the overlord to send archers (piṭṭātu) quickly, or the city and land will be lost (4.1) |

(7.7), A hero's prized object falls into the netherworld beyond his reach (7.7) |

| 15.5 | Proverbs collection 3, nos. 111-147: the goat and the wasteland, mouth and tongue, false witness, offerings, the aching heart, the personal god as shepherd ↔ Proverbs from Urim 24-33: good and evil in the hands, the palace a forest, the unruly tongue, a man's god his shepherd | A man's personal god is a shepherd who finds pasture for him and leads him like sheep to the food they can eat (7.7), Saying: my tongue, like a runaway donkey, does not turn back (7.7) |

| 15.5 | The young gods' noise; Apsu plots and is slain by Ea (Enuma elish I 21-78) ↔ Enūma eliš I (STT 1, 1-2): Apsû plots against the gods; Ea kills him; Marduk born; Tiāmat roused | The victorious god founds his dwelling on top of the slain enemy (the Apsu) (7.7), The wise god puts the primeval father to sleep with a spell, strips his crown and radiance and kills him (7.7) |
| 15.5 | Erra in Esagil; Marduk recalls the flood when he left his throne (Erra I 124-162) ↔ Marduk warns of chaos if he leaves; Erra offers to govern meanwhile (Erra I 163-191) | When the supreme god rises from his throne the seams of heaven and earth come apart: a flood follows, stars leave their places (7.7), The god's image is tarnished and must be cleansed by the fire god before the god returns to his seat (7.7) |

| 15.5 | A year passes and it worsens; diviners fail; treated like one who neglected the gods though he was pious; the unknowable will of the gods; human fickleness (Ludlul II 1-48) ↔ Demons from the netherworld attack; the body broken limb by limb; wallowing in dung; wasting; exorcist baffled; the tomb readied; enemies rejoice (Ludlul II 49-120) | The sufferer calls to his god, who does not show his face; he prays to his goddess, who does not raise her head (7.7), The exorcist recoils from the symptoms and cannot diagnose them; the diviner gives no time limit to the illness (7.7) |
| 15.5 | Babylon stele: Ištar of Uruk departs in anger and her image is restored (Nabonidus 3 col. iii) ↔ Babylon stele: Anunītu restored by Neriglissar; the child-king Lābāši-Marduk (Nabonidus 3 col. iv) | An improper image is set in the god's shrine; a later king removes it and restores the god's rightful image and emblems (7.7), A goddess, stripped of her proper rites and emblems, leaves her temple in anger and dwells in a place not her own (7.7) |
| 15.5 | Harran stele: hymn to Sîn, lord of the gods (Nabonidus 47 ii 3-42) ↔ Harran stele: return from Tema, homage of kings, Ehulhul completed, charge to future king (Nabonidus 47 iii) | The high god's command is never turned back and his word is not spoken twice (7.7), When the year is full and the god's appointed time has come the exile returns home, as a frightening night dream had foretold (7.7) |

| 15.5 | Udug-ḫul rituals: the sick man wiped with dough, sheep's heart and clay lumps (SpTU 5, 235) ↔ Lunar eclipse ritual: temples purified, drums set by the dais, lamentation priests in torn linen, eršemmas sung by phase (BRM 4, 6 reverse) | The patient is ritually 'wiped' (kuppuru) with dough, flour, clay lumps or a sheep's heart, and the materials carry off the evil (7.7), Exorcistic adjuration 'be sworn by the life of the Anunnaki, the great gods' (zi Anunnakene ... ḫe-pà) (7.7) |

| 12.1 | Šuʾila to Ištar 13: ritual for a slandered man and the prayer 'I implore you' (an eršahunga) ↔ Šuʾila to Ištar 31: 'O Ištar, lady of the cities, creator of the peoples' with its sickbed ritual | The high gods (Anu, Enlil, Ea) exalt the goddess in the divine assembly, fix her fate and give her kingship of heaven and earth (7.3), A prayer is labelled a lifted-hand prayer (šuʾila) and followed by its ritual: roof swept, pure water sprinkled, portable altar, censer of juniper, libation, recitation three times, prostration (4.8) |

| 11.4 | Ishme-Dagan Q: adab to Nuska, Enlil's minister, who is to speak good words for the king ↔ A prayer for Samsu-iluna (Samsu-iluna E) | The chief god's minister (Nuska) leads the king with his offerings into the temple and before the god's shining face (7.1), Prayer that the king's days be prolonged for generations and he be enthroned forever before God (4.4) |
| 11.4 | Lipit-Eshtar E: Enlil and Ninisina in dialogue decree an unalterable fate for the king ↔ Rim-Sîn A: a servant's prayer that Enlil and the gods of Nibru grant the king throne, reign and life | A protective deity is asked to take hold of the king's head and pronounce a good fate unalterable by command of An and Enlil (7.1), Prayer that the king's days be prolonged for generations and he be enthroned forever before God (4.4) |
| 11.4 | Rim-Sîn G: blessing that Nanna and Ningal accept the king's offerings and words, save him from famine and give abundance ↔ A song of Inana and Dumuzid - the couch, the sacred marriage and the blessing of the king (Dumuzid-Inana D1) | Prayer that under the king there be flax, barley, fish, birds, reeds, wild herds, syrup, wine and long life in the palace (6.4), The god sets the crown on the king's head and puts the holy sceptre, staff, shepherd's crook and nose-rope in his hand (5.1) |

| 11.4 | Psalm 106, national confession of sins from Egypt to exile ↔ Psalm 147, builder of Jerusalem, counter of stars, giver of snow | The cultic cry 'Hallelu-Yah' (praise Yah) closes or opens a psalm (5.7), God will gather the exiles even from the end of heaven and restore them (5.7) |
| 11.4 | Defeat of Og of Bashan and allotment of Transjordan ↔ Battle of Gibeon, hailstones, sun and moon stand still, five kings in the cave, southern campaign | Ban (herem): total destruction of a conquered population (6.0), God celebrated as a warrior ('YHWH is a man of war') (5.3) |
| 11.4 | Rules of war: exemptions, peace terms, fruit trees ↔ Battle of Gibeon, hailstones, sun and moon stand still, five kings in the cave, southern campaign | Ban (herem): total destruction of a conquered population (6.0), God celebrated as a warrior ('YHWH is a man of war') (5.3) |
| 11.4 | Iddin-Dagan B: praise of Iddin-Dagan as shepherd, lawgiver and patron of the scribal school ↔ Šulgi as provisioner of E-kur; Urim with its holy chest of the abzu; Enlil's good day for Šulgi's reign (Šulgi G 35-70) | The people and lands relax under the king's broad protection (an-dul3, 'shade') (6.5), A god formally decrees (nam tar) a good destiny for the king: heroism, long reign, splendour (4.9) |
| 11.4 | Iddin-Dagan B: praise of Iddin-Dagan as shepherd, lawgiver and patron of the scribal school ↔ Hymn to Asarluḫi (Marduk), firstborn of Enki: the river ordeal refines the just like gold; the god of incantation, pure hands and pure feet; settled in Kuara | A god (Enki) gives the king broad understanding and knowledge of everything (6.5), A god formally decrees (nam tar) a good destiny for the king: heroism, long reign, splendour (4.9) |
| 11.4 | Lipit-Eshtar C: adab of An, who chooses the king and blesses him in direct speech ↔ Lipit-Eshtar D: adab to Ninurta, suckled by Nintur and presented to Enlil for his fate, asked to arm the king | The warrior god falls on the rebel lands like the south wind or a storm (6.8), A Sumerian song divided into numbered kirugu sections, each followed by a ĝišgiĝal antiphon (4.5) |
| 11.4 | Lipit-Eshtar C: adab of An, who chooses the king and blesses him in direct speech ↔ Ur-Ninurta C: adab of Ninurta, right arm of Enlil, who entrusts the four quarters to Ur-Ninurta | Among the black-headed people, numerous as ewes, the deity singles out the king to be their shepherd (6.8), A Sumerian song divided into numbered kirugu sections, each followed by a ĝišgiĝal antiphon (4.5) |
| 11.4 | Lipit-Eshtar E: Enlil and Ninisina in dialogue decree an unalterable fate for the king ↔ Kirugu 6: the city made ruin mounds; corpses in gates and streets; families torn apart; Elam sacks Ekišnuĝal (Lament for Urim 207-253) | The slain are piled up in heaps like grain stacks or sheaves (6.8), A Sumerian song divided into numbered kirugu sections, each followed by a ĝišgiĝal antiphon (4.5) |
| 11.4 | Ur-Ninurta D: adab of Inana, equal of An, who chose Ur-Ninurta as en and lover ↔ Bur-Sîn B: adab to Enlil, whose word none can interpret, who promises the king days like Utu's | The god's intricate judgments cannot be fathomed or revealed by anyone (6.8), A Sumerian song divided into numbered kirugu sections, each followed by a ĝišgiĝal antiphon (4.5) |
| 11.4 | Ur-Ninurta E: adab of An, who gives the king throne, crook and sceptre and addresses him: 'trust in my name' ↔ Praise poem of Anam of Unug: god-fearing en of Inana, rebuilder of E-me-urur, who released the people of Nibru | The king combines the priestly office of en with kingship and dwells in the goddess's ĝipar (6.5), A god formally decrees (nam tar) a good destiny for the king: heroism, long reign, splendour (4.9) |
| 11.4 | Praise poem of Anam of Unug: god-fearing en of Inana, rebuilder of E-me-urur, who released the people of Nibru ↔ Šulgi as provisioner of E-kur; Urim with its holy chest of the abzu; Enlil's good day for Šulgi's reign (Šulgi G 35-70) | The king combines the priestly office of en with kingship and dwells in the goddess's ĝipar (6.5), A god formally decrees (nam tar) a good destiny for the king: heroism, long reign, splendour (4.9) |
| 11.4 | A tigi to Nergal, sa-ĝara - Mešlamta-ea, the Enlil of his land and avenger of his father (Nergal C) ↔ Tigi to Ninurta, hero of the fifty divine powers of E-kur, for Išme-Dagan (Išme-Dagan O, first version) | The god gives the king a mighty mace that heaps up enemy heads like dust and smashes rebel lands (6.8), A Sumerian song divided into numbered kirugu sections, each followed by a ĝišgiĝal antiphon (4.5) |
| 11.4 | Kirugu 1: god after god abandons stall and sheepfold to the wind (Lament for Urim 1-38) ↔ Kirugu 3: Ningal cannot sleep; she wails day and night for the doom of her city (Lament for Urim 76-135) | The city's goddess weeps bitterly: 'Alas, the destroyed city, my destroyed house' (6.8), A Sumerian song divided into numbered kirugu sections, each followed by a ĝišgiĝal antiphon (4.5) |
| 11.4 | Mursili II, great king of Hatti, gives Niqmepa of Ugarit the border towns of Mukish named in Suppiluliuma's treaty, town by town and mountain by mountain, for ever; whoever contests or changes these words, may the thousand gods, the Storm god of Mount Hazzi and the others know it (RS 17.0062 + RS 17.0237) ↔ Šuppiluliuma I's tribute treaty for Niqmaddu: Ugarit refused to join Nuhašše and Mukiš against Hatti; tribute to king, queen, crown prince and court; the thousand gods know (RS 17.0227) | The treaty tablet ends: whoever changes this treaty, may the named gods (storm god, sun god, city goddesses) be the lords of his oath (avenge it) (5.9), The 'thousand gods' (līm ilānī) of Hatti are summoned to assemble and hear the oath, or invoked in a greeting (5.5) |
| 11.4 | Treaty of Muršili II of Hatti with Niqmepa of Ugarit: loyalty, mutual help, fugitives, secrecy; the thousand gods as witnesses; curse and blessing (RS 17.0079+) ↔ The case against Mita, the neighbours' oath and duties (CTH 146 §15-19) | When an enemy rises or a revolt breaks out against the overlord, the vassal must go at once with his troops and chariots (or send his son or brother) to help (5.9), The vassal must love the king and his friends and hate his enemy (5.5) |
| 11.4 | Ḫuqqana treaty (CTH 42) §9-26: oath gods destroy the oath-breaker, blessing for the loyal, enemy of the king, no excuse of neutrality ↔ The case against Mita, the neighbours' oath and duties (CTH 146 §15-19) | When an enemy rises or a revolt breaks out against the overlord, the vassal must go at once with his troops and chariots (or send his son or brother) to help (5.9), The vassal must love the king and his friends and hate his enemy (5.5) |
| 11.4 | Friend and enemy, half-hearted war, mutual aid (CTH 92 §§10-16) ↔ The case against Mita, the neighbours' oath and duties (CTH 146 §15-19) | When an enemy rises or a revolt breaks out against the overlord, the vassal must go at once with his troops and chariots (or send his son or brother) to help (5.9), The vassal must love the king and his friends and hate his enemy (5.5) |
| 11.4 | Psalm 104, the great creation hymn (cf. the Great Hymn to the Aten) ↔ Qaf: wonder at the warner, the earth that consumes the dead, the sky without rifts and the destroyed peoples | Human comes from dust and returns to dust (5.9), Rain from the sky gives life to the earth after its death, a sign of resurrection (5.5) |
| 11.4 | Treaty of Muršili II of Hatti with Niqmepa of Ugarit: loyalty, mutual help, fugitives, secrecy; the thousand gods as witnesses; curse and blessing (RS 17.0079+) ↔ Captives, instigators, Nuḫašše folk in Hatti, refugees and requests (CTH 53 §§10-14) | The vassal may not excuse inaction by saying 'I am bound by oath and treaty; whether the enemy kills them or they kill him, I do not know' (6.4), Fugitives who flee from one realm to the other must be handed back (5.0) |
| 11.4 | Captives, instigators, Nuḫašše folk in Hatti, refugees and requests (CTH 53 §§10-14) ↔ Calling for troops, runaway soldiers, Arzawa captives (CTH 67 §§12-14) | The vassal may not excuse inaction by saying 'I am bound by oath and treaty; whether the enemy kills them or they kill him, I do not know' (6.4), Fugitives who flee from one realm to the other must be handed back (5.0) |
| 11.4 | Captives, instigators, Nuḫašše folk in Hatti, refugees and requests (CTH 53 §§10-14) ↔ Mankind is corrupt; the four kings of Arzawa; borders; fugitives (CTH 76 §§15-18) | The vassal may not excuse inaction by saying 'I am bound by oath and treaty; whether the enemy kills them or they kill him, I do not know' (6.4), Fugitives who flee from one realm to the other must be handed back (5.0) |
| 11.4 | Calling for troops, runaway soldiers, Arzawa captives (CTH 67 §§12-14) ↔ Mankind is corrupt; the four kings of Arzawa; borders; fugitives (CTH 76 §§15-18) | The vassal may not excuse inaction by saying 'I am bound by oath and treaty; whether the enemy kills them or they kill him, I do not know' (6.4), Fugitives who flee from one realm to the other must be handed back (5.0) |
| 11.4 | Prophecy for Assurbanipal: vision of a golden star (SAA 9 11) ↔ Oracles to Esarhaddon 1.2: through Sinqīša-āmur (SAA 9 1 i-ii) | The god makes the king's throne firm so that no one can remove it (6.1), God addresses the hero with 'Fear not' in a vision (5.2) |
| 11.4 | Prophecy for Assurbanipal: vision of a golden star (SAA 9 11) ↔ Oracles to Esarhaddon 2.1: Bānītu speaks to the queen mother, through Nabû-hussanni (SAA 9 2 i) | The god makes the king's throne firm so that no one can remove it (6.1), God addresses the hero with 'Fear not' in a vision (5.2) |
| 11.3 | Shulgi D: opening praise of the king and the refrain 'who rivals you?' ↔ Enlil-bani A: kings bow and bring tribute; the gods' gifts; praise in the scribal academy | The high god names the king with a good name at his birth or accession (5.8), Formula: there was none like him among all the kings before or after (5.5) |
| 11.3 | Ibbi-Suen A: tigi to Suen, who makes Ibbi-Suen canal inspector of the Land ↔ Dedication of a statue: Išme-Dagan the tireless runner sets up his running statue in Eniguru; curse on whoever erases its inscription (Išme-Dagan S) | The high god names the king with a good name at his birth or accession (5.8), The god's utterance cannot be changed or overturned (5.5) |
| 11.3 | The woken Storm god's complaint, washing with the water of turning, the iron sky, and the return to the house (mugawar fragment 2, CTH 332.2) ↔ Offerings to the Sun god, 'as the ewe recognises her lamb' (CTH 403.3.1) | On the god's return the mother recognises her son again, the ewe her lamb and the cow her calf (6.5), The ritualist sets food and drink before the angry god and invokes him (mugai-): eat, drink, still your hunger and thirst, come back and be at peace (4.9) |
| 11.3 | Fragrant woods burned; Anzili and Zukki return; the household set right; Anzili eats everything; the salt-lick analogy for the patron's life (CTH 333) ↔ Invocation; as (the cow takes back) the calf, the deity cares for him again in goodwill, with life and vigour; gold (CTH 335.12) | On the god's return the mother recognises her son again, the ewe her lamb and the cow her calf (6.5), The ritualist sets food and drink before the angry god and invokes him (mugai-): eat, drink, still your hunger and thirst, come back and be at peace (4.9) |

| 11.3 | The Storm god's body purged limb by limb; restored, he goes up to heaven; the eagle's wing, the sieve of a thousand holes, Kamrusepa's rams; go to Zalpa by the sea (CTH 335.17) ↔ Hallara's cloud window; the mother goddess brings the souls out of the river into the cloud; Kamrusepa, Telipinu; the oven; Sulinkatti kills a pig; the vessel with lid of lead whence nothing returns; sweet bread (CTH 335.17) | The healer or goddess takes from the god's body his anger, wrath, sin, sullenness, the evil tongue and the evil sole (6.5), The ritualist sets food and drink before the angry god and invokes him (mugai-): eat, drink, still your hunger and thirst, come back and be at peace (4.9) |

| 11.0 | Lugal-e: triumphal return by boat, hymn of the boatmen, Enlil's blessing, Nisaba and doxology ↔ Rim-Sîn B: hymn to Ḫaia, scribe of the tablets of destiny, archivist of heaven and earth, who hears prayer | A goddess of writing (Nisaba) keeps the tablets, measures and accounts and is entrusted with the harvests (6.0), 'Who is like you among the gods, YHWH?' (5.0) |
| 11.0 | Lifted-hand prayer to Bēlet-ilī, with Šamaš-šuma-ukīn's eclipse insertion (šuʾila Bēlet-ilī 1) ↔ Šuʾila to Ištar 2: 'I beseech you, lady of ladies' (the great prayer to Ištar) | At the healing goddess's look the dying revives and at her word the feeble rises; she brings the dead back from the netherworld (6.2), A prayer is labelled a lifted-hand prayer (šuʾila) and followed by its ritual: roof swept, pure water sprinkled, portable altar, censer of juniper, libation, recitation three times, prostration (4.8) |
| 11.0 | Šuʾila to Šamaš 6: 'King of heaven and earth', against a curse seizing the chest, with an effigy rite ↔ Šuʾilas to Ea and to Marduk (SpTU 3 78): sorcery turned back on the sorcerers; 'Mighty, resplendent, lord of Eridu', Marduk's epithets | Talionic formula: bewitch the witch with the witchcraft with which she bewitched me (6.2), A prayer is labelled a lifted-hand prayer (šuʾila) and followed by its ritual: roof swept, pure water sprinkled, portable altar, censer of juniper, libation, recitation three times, prostration (4.8) |
| 11.0 | Ur-Ninurta D: adab of Inana, equal of An, who chose Ur-Ninurta as en and lover ↔ Ur-Ninurta E: adab of An, who gives the king throne, crook and sceptre and addresses him: 'trust in my name' | The king combines the priestly office of en with kingship and dwells in the goddess's ĝipar (6.5), A Sumerian song divided into numbered kirugu sections, each followed by a ĝišgiĝal antiphon (4.5) |
| 11.0 | Ur-Ninurta D: adab of Inana, equal of An, who chose Ur-Ninurta as en and lover ↔ Šulgi as provisioner of E-kur; Urim with its holy chest of the abzu; Enlil's good day for Šulgi's reign (Šulgi G 35-70) | The king combines the priestly office of en with kingship and dwells in the goddess's ĝipar (6.5), A Sumerian song divided into numbered kirugu sections, each followed by a ĝišgiĝal antiphon (4.5) |

| 11.0 | Kirugu 1: god after god abandons stall and sheepfold to the wind (Lament for Urim 1-38) ↔ Kirugu 8: 'Lady, how can your heart endure?': priests, festivals and music gone; return to your city (Lament for Urim 331-389) | Destruction undoes fertility: brackish water in rivers, weeds in fields, no lambs in the fold, no churning song (6.5), A Sumerian song divided into numbered kirugu sections, each followed by a ĝišgiĝal antiphon (4.5) |

| 10.1 | Abi-Milku: you are the Sun, the sweet breath; I guard Tyre awaiting the king's breath; Zimreddi gives us no water (EA 146) ↔ A ruler (fragment): dust of your feet, charioteer of your horses; the city is taken; may the king give his breath (EA 312) | A vassal calls the overlord 'the breath of my life', or awaits the breath (wind) of the king's mouth that revives him (6.0), A vassal calls himself the dust (or clay, or trodden ground) under the overlord king's feet (4.1) |
| 10.1 | Rib-Addi: like a bird in a cage; Abdi-Ashirta tells Ammiya 'kill your lord and be like us'; children sold for food (EA 074) ↔ Ili-rapih and Byblos, the king's maidservant: Byblos is to the king like Memphis; Aziru killed the kings of Ammiya, Ardata, Irqata and the commissioner (EA 139) | A rebel leader urges the townsmen to kill their ruler and become like the rebels, so that they too may have peace (7.1), Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior (3.1) |
| 10.1 | Aziru defends himself: do not listen to the false men who slander me; I was in Tunip, may your gods and the Sun know it (EA 161) ↔ Abdi-Heba: what have I done? they slander me; not my father or mother but the king's strong arm set me here; why do you love the Habiru and hate the mayors? (EA 286) | Slanderers 'eat the pieces' (akālu karṣī) of the writer, maligning him before the king (7.1), Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior (3.1) |
| 10.1 | Ili-rapih and Byblos, the king's maidservant: Byblos is to the king like Memphis; Aziru killed the kings of Ammiya, Ardata, Irqata and the commissioner (EA 139) ↔ Rib-Addi: Abdi-Ashirta incited my murder; the peasants sold their children for food; like a bird in a cage; send archers in two months (EA 081) | A rebel leader urges the townsmen to kill their ruler and become like the rebels, so that they too may have peace (7.1), Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior (3.1) |
| 10.1 | EA 323: Yidya sends thirty pieces of glass to the son of the Sun whom the Sun loves ↔ EA 148: Abimilki of Tyre asks for Usu for water; the king of Hazor has joined the Habiru; the land of Canaan | A vassal sends raw glass (eḫlipakku, mekku) to the king at his request (7.1), Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior (3.1) |
| 10.1 | EA 104: Rib-Addi: the sons of Abdi-Aširta, slave and dog, take Ullaza and act like great kings ↔ EA 124: Rib-Addi: Aziru has taken all my cities; Byblos alone remains | A rival ruler is denounced to the overlord as a mere slave and dog who seizes the king's land (7.1), Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior (3.1) |
| 10.1 | EA 148: Abimilki of Tyre asks for Usu for water; the king of Hazor has joined the Habiru; the land of Canaan ↔ EA 331: Šipṭi-Baʿlu sends the glass he has | A vassal sends raw glass (eḫlipakku, mekku) to the king at his request (7.1), Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior (3.1) |
| 10.1 | Aziru of Amurru: I have done all the king commanded; I will build Sumur this year; do not listen to slanderers (EA 160) ↔ Abdi-Heba: what have I done? they slander me; not my father or mother but the king's strong arm set me here; why do you love the Habiru and hate the mayors? | 10.1 | Adab to Nergal: storm-warrior, dragon drinking blood, junior Enlil of the netherworld; Nergal plucks the king's enemy like a swallow (Šu-ilīšu A) ↔ Adab for Šu-ilīšu: final lines only, a prayer for long days | Catalogue of song genres (adab, tigi, šir-gida, balbale, zamzam ...) composed in praise of the king (5.7), Prayer that the king's days be prolonged for generations and he be enthroned forever before God (4.4) |

| 8.9 | Ishme-Dagan B: adab to Bau the healer, who presents the king to Enlil to have his fate decreed ↔ Lipit-Eshtar C: adab of An, who chooses the king and blesses him in direct speech | A Sumerian song divided into numbered kirugu sections, each followed by a ĝišgiĝal antiphon (4.5), Prayer that the king's days be prolonged for generations and he be enthroned forever before God (4.4) |
| 8.9 | Ishme-Dagan B: adab to Bau the healer, who presents the king to Enlil to have his fate decreed ↔ Lipit-Eshtar E: Enlil and Ninisina in dialogue decree an unalterable fate for the king | A Sumerian song divided into numbered kirugu sections, each followed by a ĝišgiĝal antiphon (4.5), Prayer that the king's days be prolonged for generations and he be enthroned forever before God (4.4) |

| 8.0 | Rib-Addi of Byblos: send archers or we die; the land is not plagued; the commissioner Piwuri killed (EA 362) ↔ Shuwardata: I killed the Habiru the king's god gave me; Abdi-Heba and I alone fight; Akko and Akshapa came with fifty chariots (EA 366) | A vassal claims he alone still serves the king loyally while all other rulers have gone over to the enemy (4.9), Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior (3.1) |
| 8.0 | Rib-Addi of Byblos: send archers or we die; the land is not plagued; the commissioner Piwuri killed (EA 362) ↔ Biridiya of Megiddo: I alone plough at Shunem and bring corvée workers; the other mayors do not (EA 365) | A vassal claims he alone still serves the king loyally while all other rulers have gone over to the enemy (4.9), Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior (3.1) |
| 8.0 | Rib-Addi of Byblos: send archers or we die; the land is not plagued; the commissioner Piwuri killed (EA 362) ↔ Ammunira of Beirut to the king, 'my Sun, my gods, breath of my life': I am the footstool of his feet; I am ready with horses and chariots (EA 141) | A vassal claims he alone still serves the king loyally while all other rulers have gone over to the enemy (4.9), Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior (3.1) |
| 8.0 | Rib-Addi of Byblos: send archers or we die; the land is not plagued; the commissioner Piwuri killed (EA 362) ↔ Rib-Addi: the sons of Abdi-Ashirta, slave and dog, take the king's cities; once Canaan's kings fled from an Egyptian, now they treat Egyptians like dogs; death is good for me (EA 109) | A vassal claims he alone still serves the king loyally while all other rulers have gone over to the enemy (4.9), Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior (3.1) |
| 8.0 | Rib-Addi of Byblos: send archers or we die; the land is not plagued; the commissioner Piwuri killed (EA 362) ↔ Rib-Addi in exile in Beirut: my brother swore to the city and gave it to the sons of Abdi-Ashirta; half the city loves them, half my lord; they say 'Rib-Addi is dead'; I sit in Beirut like a dog (EA 138) | A vassal claims he alone still serves the king loyally while all other rulers have gone over to the enemy (4.9), Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior (3.1) |
| 8.0 | Shuwardata: I killed the Habiru the king's god gave me; Abdi-Heba and I alone fight; Akko and Akshapa came with fifty chariots (EA 366) ↔ Biridiya of Megiddo: I alone plough at Shunem and bring corvée workers; the other mayors do not (EA 365) | A vassal claims he alone still serves the king loyally while all other rulers have gone over to the enemy (4.9), Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior (3.1) |
| 8.0 | Shuwardata: I killed the Habiru the king's god gave me; Abdi-Heba and I alone fight; Akko and Akshapa came with fifty chariots (EA 366) ↔ Rib-Addi: Aziru seized twelve of my men for a ransom of fifty silver; my ships taken; who will love me if I die? (EA 114) | A vassal claims he alone still serves the king loyally while all other rulers have gone over to the enemy (4.9), Bowing to the ground seven times before a superior (3.1) |

| 7.7 | No bill of divorce; third servant song ↔ Look to the rock you were hewn from | Enemies or the world wear out like a garment that the moth devours (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Look to the rock you were hewn from ↔ The parable of the fly; messengers from angels and men; the religion of Abraham | The religion of 'your father Abraham', who named you Muslims before (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Look to the rock you were hewn from ↔ Ha-Mim Fussilat: the veil between; creation in days; heaven as smoke | Heaven likened to or made from smoke [contrast between the texts] (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Blind watchmen, mute dogs; the righteous taken away ↔ Pack your bundle; my tent is destroyed; a man cannot direct his steps | Israel's watchmen are blind and its leaders mute dogs that cannot bark, lovers of slumber and greedy (7.7) |

| 7.7 | Your sins have separated you; God arms himself ↔ The slave and the free, the mute man, the woman who unravels her yarn (Surah 16:71-100) | Do not be like the woman who unravels her yarn into strands after spinning it strong (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Arise, shine - the nations come to Zion's light ↔ The prophet was not there; the two books; believing People of the Book | Produce and wealth of every land brought to a sacred city [divergence between the texts] (7.7) |
| 7.7 | The spirit of the Lord is upon me ↔ Who is this coming from Edom? The winepress of wrath | Proclamation of a year of God's favor and a day of vengeance of our God (7.7) |
| 7.7 | The spirit of the Lord is upon me ↔ A new exodus from the north; fishers and hunters | Instead of shame the people receive a double portion in their land (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Hephzibah and Beulah - Zion's new name ↔ Found by those who did not seek; rebels and servants | Zion or God's people receive a new name from God's mouth (Hephzibah, Beulah, 'Sought-out', 'not forsaken') (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Remembering the days of Moses - O that you would rend the heavens ↔ The parable of the fly; messengers from angels and men; the religion of Abraham | Whether Abraham is the father of the community addressed [contrast between the texts] (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Remembering the days of Moses - O that you would rend the heavens ↔ Raging hell, the disowning of false gods, the split sky and the regretful wrongdoer | The sky torn open for a descent from heaven [divergence between the texts] (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Remembering the days of Moses - O that you would rend the heavens ↔ Al-Sajda: creation, the angel of death, and the two fates | No soul knows what delight of the eyes is hidden in store for the righteous (7.7) |

| 7.7 | New heavens and a new earth ↔ Judgment by fire, ingathering of nations, the undying worm | God creates new heavens and a new earth; the former things will not be remembered (7.7) |

| 7.7 | The circle of kindness, misers, and the atom's weight ↔ Articles of faith; hypocrites wavering between two sides | Good works (spending, prayer) done to be seen by people (riyāʾ) (7.7) |
| 7.7 | The circle of kindness, misers, and the atom's weight ↔ Tenfold reward; my life and death for God; no bearer bears another's burden | God multiplies a good deed (tenfold) while an evil deed is requited only by its like (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Shifted words, 'we hear and disobey', and the people of the Sabbath ↔ Trusts, obedience to authority, and the hypocrites who seek other judges | Some of the People of the Book believe in al-jibt and al-ṭāghūt (idols, false powers) (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Female deities, Satan's vow, slit cattle ears, and Abraham the friend ↔ The slave and the free, the mute man, the woman who unravels her yarn (Surah 16:71-100) | Whoever does good, male or female, and believes, enters paradise (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Orphan girls, reconciliation, the suspended wife, and justice against oneself ↔ The final ruling on kalāla | Form: 'They ask you for a ruling (yastaftūnaka); say: God gives you a ruling' (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Articles of faith; hypocrites wavering between two sides ↔ Allies, apostates replaced, the mocked call to prayer, apes and swine | Do not take Jews and Christians (or mockers of your religion) as allies (7.7) |
| 7.7 | The indictment of Israel; the Messiah not crucified but raised ↔ Jesus' miracles, the table from heaven, and Jesus questioned at judgment | God raised Jesus up to himself (7.7) |
| 7.7 | The indictment of Israel; the Messiah not crucified but raised ↔ Near compromise, prayer times, the praised station, the spirit, the challenge and the demanded signs (Surah 17:73-100) | Opponents demand a written book brought down from heaven (7.7) |
| 7.7 | The chain of revelation; Jesus, word and spirit; 'say not three' ↔ Abraham's line of eighteen prophets; Torah in sheets; the false claimant | Catalogue of prophets who received revelation, from Noah to Jesus (7.7) |
| 7.7 | The chain of revelation; Jesus, word and spirit; 'say not three' ↔ Dragged in chains; messengers told and untold; faith on seeing punishment | Of the messengers before you, some we have related to you and some we have not (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Israel's covenant and twelve chiefs; the Christians' forgotten portion ↔ 'God's hand is fettered'; the blessings of observing the Torah | God cast enmity and hatred among them until the day of resurrection (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Israel's covenant and twelve chiefs; the Christians' forgotten portion ↔ Against the deification of Jesus; the weeping Christians | Those who say 'God is the Messiah son of Mary' have disbelieved (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Judging by the Torah, the Gospel and the Quran; eye for eye ↔ Life like withering plants; the Garden as wide as heaven and earth; every calamity written; iron sent down; Jesus' followers and invented monasticism | Jesus was given the Gospel (Injīl), confirming the Torah before it (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Against the deification of Jesus; the weeping Christians ↔ Life like withering plants; the Garden as wide as heaven and earth; every calamity written; iron sent down; Jesus' followers and invented monasticism | Christians are nearest in affection to the believers because they have priests and monks and are not proud (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Questions not to ask; the freed camels of the pagans ↔ The hanif creed and patience | Whoever is guided is guided for his own good; whoever strays strays against himself (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Jesus' miracles, the table from heaven, and Jesus questioned at judgment ↔ Al-Mujadila: the woman who disputed, the zihar formula and its expiation; God the fourth of three; the party of God | God is well pleased with them and they with him (radiya llahu 'anhum wa-radu 'anhu) (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Darkness and light, clay and two terms, and those who would not believe ↔ The Book made firm, the Throne on the water, the challenge of ten surahs | Deniers demand that a treasure be sent down to the prophet or an angel come with him (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Mercy written on himself; the idolaters' denial at the gathering ↔ Tenfold reward; my life and death for God; no bearer bears another's burden | The Prophet is commanded to be the first of those who submit (awwal al-muslimīn) (7.7) |
| 7.7 | The Prophet consoled; a ladder to the sky; animals as communities ↔ Noah, the boiling oven, the lost son and al-Judi | The prophet disclaims having God's treasuries, knowing the unseen, or being an angel (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Splitter of seed and dawn; stars for navigation; do not revile their gods ↔ The command has come; cattle, rain, sea and stars as blessings (Surah 16:1-23) | God made the stars for guidance in the darknesses of land and sea (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Splitter of seed and dawn; stars for navigation; do not revile their gods ↔ The jinn hear the recitation | God has taken neither consort (sahiba) nor child (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Sworn oaths for a sign; even the dead speaking would not convince ↔ Eat what God's name is spoken over; the opened breast; jinn and humans judged | Every prophet has enemies: devils of humans and jinn inspiring one another with gilded speech (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Eat what God's name is spoken over; the opened breast; jinn and humans judged ↔ Life like a crop, the abode of peace, darkened faces | Paradise as the abode of peace (dār al-salām) (7.7) |
| 7.7 | The prostration to Adam, Iblis' refusal and the fall ↔ Stand firm; prayer times; good deeds remove bad | God vows to fill hell with the devil and all who follow him (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Hell's quarrels, the camel and the needle, the people of the Heights ↔ Man from black mud, jinn from scorching fire, and Iblis's refusal (Surah 15:26-50) | God removes all rancor from the hearts of those in paradise (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Hell's quarrels, the camel and the needle, the people of the Heights ↔ The son of Mary as an example and sign of the Hour; the Garden with golden dishes; Malik of hell | Paradise is given to the blessed as an inheritance for what they did (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Hud and the people of Ad ↔ Badr - angels, slumber, rain and God's throw | God cuts off the last remnant (root, dabir) of a people who denied (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Salih, Thamud and the she-camel ↔ Deaf and dumb beasts, heart and trial | The arrogant elite confront the weak (mustad'afun) who believed the prophet (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Shu'ayb and Midian ↔ Messengers in their people's tongue; Moses and the days of God; the threatened messengers (Surah 14:1-17) | The elite threaten the prophet and believers: expulsion unless they return to the old religion (7.7) |
| 7.7 | The unlettered prophet foretold in Torah and Gospel ↔ Recite the Book; dispute with the People of the Book; the unlettered prophet | The awaited messenger is 'the unlettered prophet' (al-nabi al-ummi) (7.7) |
| 7.7 | The unlettered prophet foretold in Torah and Gospel ↔ Al-Saff: ranks like a solid structure; Moses hurt by his people; Jesus foretells Ahmad; the disciples as God's helpers | The coming prophet is found written in the Torah and the Gospel (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Twelve tribes, twelve springs, and the word changed at the gate ↔ Made for hell, the beautiful names, the unknown Hour | Among Moses' people is a community that guides by the truth and acts justly by it (7.7) |

| 7.7 | The disavowal - treaties, sacred months and asylum ↔ Twelve months and the ban on intercalation | Four of the twelve months are sacred (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Who maintains the mosques; God above family ↔ Hypocrites who mock and the destroyed peoples | God's good pleasure (ridwan) is greater than the gardens of Eden (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Those who stayed behind, the exempt, and the Bedouin ↔ The bargain of lives for paradise; Abraham's prayer for his father | Catalogue of believers: repenting, worshiping, praising, wandering/fasting (sa'ihun), bowing, prostrating, enjoining right (7.7) |
| 7.7 | The wise Book, creation, sun and moon, the prayer of paradise ↔ Ashes in the wind, Satan disowns his followers, the good and bad tree (Surah 14:18-34) | The blessed in paradise cry 'Glory to you, O God', greet with 'Peace' and end with 'Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds' (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Prayer in distress, a changed Quran, the storm at sea ↔ The Book made firm, the Throne on the water, the challenge of ten surahs | Man calls on God lying, sitting or standing in distress, then passes on as if he had never prayed once relieved (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Prayer in distress, a changed Quran, the storm at sea ↔ Stand firm; prayer times; good deeds remove bad | Humankind was originally one community, then they differed (7.7) |
| 7.7 | A messenger for every nation; no ransom ↔ Legends of the ancients, the fallen roof, the angels who take souls (Surah 16:24-50) | Every nation has a messenger, and it is judged justly when he comes (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Ask the readers of scripture; the people of Jonah ↔ Lot's old woman; Jonah and the fish | Jonah's people is the one town whose belief benefited it, lifting the punishment (7.7) |
| 7.7 | The Book made firm, the Throne on the water, the challenge of ten surahs ↔ Al-Mulk: death and life as test, seven flawless heavens, stars as missiles against devils, hell nearly bursting with rage | God created heaven and earth to test which of you is best in deeds (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Joseph and his brothers (Surah 12, full read) ↔ Abraham's guests and the destruction of Lot's people (Surah 15:51-77) | Do not despair of God's mercy (rawh / rahma); only unbelievers or the astray despair (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Joseph and his brothers (Surah 12, full read) ↔ Daughters of God, all things glorify him, bones and dust, the cursed tree (Surah 17:40-60) | Satan stirs up enmity (nazagha) between brothers or among people (7.7) |
| 7.7 | The signs of creation, thunder and the parable of the foam (Surah 13:1-17) ↔ Legends of the ancients, the fallen roof, the angels who take souls (Surah 16:24-50) | All in heaven and earth prostrate to God, willingly or unwillingly, even their shadows morning and evening (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Messengers, the Mother of the Book and the witness of scripture (Surah 13:30-43) ↔ The split heavens, water of life, orbits, mortality and the scales | God comes to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Ashes in the wind, Satan disowns his followers, the good and bad tree (Surah 14:18-34) ↔ The command has come; cattle, rain, sea and stars as blessings (Surah 16:1-23) | If you counted God's blessings you could never number them (7.7) |
| 7.7 | The guarded reminder, the guarded heaven and the fertilizing winds (Surah 15:1-25) ↔ The jinn hear the recitation | Jinn or devils who used to sit listening at heaven's gates now find it full of stern guards and shooting stars (shuhub) lying in wait (7.7) |

| 7.7 | The command has come; cattle, rain, sea and stars as blessings (Surah 16:1-23) ↔ Those whose works are weightless; the sea as ink (Surah 18:102-110) | Your God is one God (ilahukum ilahun wahid) (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Not two gods; daughters ascribed to God and buried alive; milk, wine and the bee (Surah 16:51-70) ↔ Iblis's threat to bridle Adam's offspring; sea peril; the honored children of Adam (Surah 17:61-72) | In distress, at sea or otherwise, people call on God alone, then return to polytheism once rescued (7.7) |

| 7.7 | Near compromise, prayer times, the praised station, the spirit, the challenge and the demanded signs (Surah 17:73-100) ↔ Those whose works are weightless; the sea as ink (Surah 18:102-110) | The prophet declares he is only a human messenger, a mortal like his hearers (7.7) |

| 7.7 | Moses, Ishmael and Idris remembered; the later generation that neglected prayer (Surah 19:51-65) ↔ Job, Ishmael, Idris, Dhul-Kifl, Dhul-Nun, Zechariah and Mary | A prophet named Idrīs is mentioned among the righteous (7.7) |

| 7.7 | One community, Gog and Magog, the rolled heaven and the Zabur's promise ↔ One community split into sects; the heedless rich and the God-fearing | Humanity was one community (umma) but split its affair into sects (7.7) |

| 7.7 | Abraham preaches against idols, is saved from the fire, and Lot believes ↔ Abraham's dream and the near-sacrifice of his son | Lot believes in Abraham, who declares 'I am emigrating to my Lord' (7.7) |

| 7.7 | Midian, Ad, Thamud, Korah, Pharaoh and Haman punished ↔ The Hour, the times of praise, and the signs of God | God did not wrong them; they wronged themselves (refrain) (7.7) |

| 7.7 | Recite the Book; dispute with the People of the Book; the unlettered prophet ↔ The first of those who submit; canopies of fire; chambers above chambers | The punishment of hell envelops the damned from above them and from beneath their feet (7.7) |

| 7.7 | Praise, the atom's weight, and mockery of resurrection ↔ The ranks, the guarded heaven and the shooting stars | Scoffers ridicule the claim that after being torn to pieces utterly they will be created anew (7.7) |

| 7.7 | The damned questioned; the blessed on facing couches; the tree of Zaqqum ↔ Al-Waqi'a: the Event that abases and exalts; the three classes; the Foremost, the Companions of the Right and their Garden | Paradise drink from which they suffer no headache nor intoxication (7.7) |

| 7.7 | Do not despair of mercy; the earth in God's grip; the throngs to hell and Garden ↔ Ha-Mim 'Ayn-Sin-Qaf: revelation, the angels' intercession and the one religion of the prophets | To God belong the keys (maqalid) of the heavens and the earth (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Ha-Mim 'Ayn-Sin-Qaf: revelation, the angels' intercession and the one religion of the prophets ↔ Abraham disowns his father's worship; the great man of the two towns; silver roofs; the devil-companion | God expands provision (rizq) for whom he wills and restricts it (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Ha-Mim 'Ayn-Sin-Qaf: revelation, the angels' intercession and the one religion of the prophets ↔ Life like withering plants; the Garden as wide as heaven and earth; every calamity written; iron sent down; Jesus' followers and invented monasticism | God sent down the Book with the truth and the Balance (al-mizan) (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Provision in measure, rain, ships like mountains and the ethics of consultation and pardon ↔ Abraham disowns his father's worship; the great man of the two towns; silver roofs; the devil-companion | What is given in this life is passing enjoyment (mata'); what is with God is better and more lasting (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Provision in measure, rain, ships like mountains and the ethics of consultation and pardon ↔ Al-Rahman: the Merciful taught the Quran; sun and moon by reckoning; clay and smokeless fire; the two seas and the barrier | Ships running on the sea like landmarks/mountains are a sign; God could still the wind and leave them motionless or wreck them (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Ha-Mim: the Mother of the Book, the riding prayer and the 'daughters' of God ↔ The Companions of the Left in smoke and samum; who creates semen, crops, rain and fire?; the hidden Book; the soul at the throat | The scripture exists with God in the 'Mother of the Book' (umm al-kitab), a heavenly archetype (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Abraham disowns his father's worship; the great man of the two towns; silver roofs; the devil-companion ↔ Al-Mumtahana: no affection for God's enemies, Abraham's excellent example, examining emigrant women, and the women's pledge | Abraham declares to his father and people that he is free of what they worship, except the one who created him (7.7) |
| 7.7 | The son of Mary as an example and sign of the Hour; the Garden with golden dishes; Malik of hell ↔ Muhammad: deeds nullified, striking necks and freeing captives, and the four rivers of the Garden | The Hour will come upon them suddenly while they are unaware (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Deniers demand their fathers; the people of Tubba'; the tree of Zaqqum; silk, brocade and the houris ↔ Qaf: wonder at the warner, the earth that consumes the dead, the sky without rifts and the destroyed peoples | The people of Tubba' (the Himyarite kings of Yemen) as a destroyed people (7.7) |
| 7.7 | Kindness to parents, thirty months of bearing and weaning, the prayer at forty and the son who says 'Uff' ↔ Al-Mujadila: the woman who disputed, the zihar formula and its expiation; God the fourth of three; the party of God | For all there are degrees (darajat) according to what they did (7.7) |

| 7.1 | The Flood (full read) ↔ Noah remains a thousand years less fifty among his people | Why God destroyed a generation or a people [divergence between the texts] (7.1) |
| 7.1 | The Table of Nations ↔ The Hour, the times of praise, and the signs of God | Nations distinguished by land, language and clan (7.1) |
| 7.1 | Lot's guests and the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah ↔ Hypocrites who mock and the destroyed peoples | The 'overturned cities' (al-mu'tafikat), Lot's towns (7.1) |
| 7.1 | Pharaoh's dreams and Joseph's elevation ↔ Moses before Pharaoh: the laughing courtiers, the rivers beneath Pharaoh and the drowning | King invests the hero with ring, linen and chariot (7.1) |
| 7.1 | The burning bush and the divine name ↔ Who revives rotten bones? Fire from the green tree; Be and it is | God made fire for you from the green tree, from which you kindle (7.1) |
| 7.1 | Signs for Moses, Aaron as mouthpiece, return to Egypt, the bridegroom of blood ↔ Moses and Aaron, Noah, Ad, Thamud, the People of the Rass and the rained-upon town | Aaron's role beside Moses and how he is appointed [divergence between the texts] (7.1) |
| 7.1 | Manna and quail; the first Sabbath ↔ Twelve tribes, twelve springs, and the word changed at the gate | Quail come up in the evening and cover the camp (7.1) |
| 7.1 | Covenant Code - homicide, injury and the goring ox ↔ Abrogation, the foreign teacher, coerced unbelief, food law, Abraham the hanif and the Sabbath (Surah 16:101-128) | Eye for an eye, tooth for a tooth (lex talionis) [divergence between the texts] (7.1) |
| 7.1 | Covenant ratified in blood; the elders see God ↔ Closing confession and prayer | Believers' confession 'we hear and we obey' (sami'na wa-ata'na) (7.1) |
| 7.1 | Mourning, the tent outside the camp, and Moses sees God's back ↔ The chain of revelation; Jesus, word and spirit; 'say not three' | God speaks to the prophet face to face, as a man speaks to his friend (7.1) |
| 7.1 | The eighth day - Aaron's first offerings and the divine fire ↔ Misers, those who called God poor, and the fire-consumed offering | Fire comes out from before God and consumes the offering on the altar (7.1) |
| 7.1 | Forbidden sexual unions; the land vomits out its inhabitants ↔ Wine, gambling, orphans, mixed marriage and menstruation | Intercourse with a menstruating woman is forbidden (7.1) |
| 7.1 | Be holy - ethical laws and love of neighbor ↔ Times of privacy, elderly women, eating in kin houses, leave from the messenger | Do not curse the deaf or put a stumbling block before the blind (7.1) |
| 7.1 | The appointed times - sabbath and annual festivals ↔ Al-Dhariyat: the oath by the winds, the conjecturers, the night-wakeful righteous and the beggar's due | Corners of the field, gleanings and fallen grapes left for the poor and the stranger (7.1) |
| 7.1 | Covenant blessings for obedience ↔ 'God's hand is fettered'; the blessings of observing the Torah | Had they observed the Torah and Gospel they would have eaten from above them and beneath their feet (7.1) |
| 7.1 | Rebellion after the spies' report and the forty-year sentence ↔ Noah, the lowly followers and the laden ark | The people are about to stone their leader (7.1) |
| 7.1 | The Sabbath wood-gatherer; the law of tassels ↔ Covenant at the mountain and the Sabbath-breakers | Punishment of those who break the Sabbath [divergence between the texts] (7.1) |
| 7.1 | The Sabbath wood-gatherer; the law of tassels ↔ The Sabbath-breaking seaside town turned into apes | Punishment of those who break the Sabbath [divergence between the texts] (7.1) |
| 7.1 | The Sabbath wood-gatherer; the law of tassels ↔ Desire as god, 'only Time destroys us', and every nation kneeling before its book | Whoever takes his own desire (hawā) as his god (7.1) |
| 7.1 | Censers as altar plating, Aaron stops the plague, Aaron's rod blossoms ↔ The family of Imran, Mary and Zechariah | Lots, rods or reeds decide who will be the child's guardian (7.1) |
| 7.1 | Defeat of Sihon king of Heshbon ↔ The ratio of the steadfast, captives and ransom | Livestock and spoil taken as booty after the ban (7.1) |
| 7.1 | Exhortation at Horeb's memory; no image; exile and return ↔ Polemic with the People of the Book | Israel's position at the mountain when the covenant is made [divergence between the texts] (7.1) |
| 7.1 | The Decalogue restated and the people's fear at Horeb ↔ Closing confession and prayer | Believers' confession 'we hear and we obey' (sami'na wa-ata'na) (7.1) |
| 7.1 | The Shema and the instruction to teach ↔ Signs for people of understanding; closing prayer | Those who remember God standing, sitting and on their sides and reflect on creation (7.1) |
| 7.1 | The Shema and the instruction to teach ↔ Shortened prayer and prayer in shifts under arms | Those who remember God standing, sitting and on their sides and reflect on creation (7.1) |
| 7.1 | The Shema and the instruction to teach ↔ Moses and Pharaoh disputing; the magicians; the sea split like mountains | Israel will inherit cities, houses, cisterns, vineyards and olives they did not build or plant (7.1) |

## Unmatched motifs: search targets

Motifs found in only one unit. For units read from their original text, these are the details no other tagged text shares yet, so they are the places to look next (rabbinic, Syriac, apocryphal and other literature).

**Pure Dilmun, where the lion did not kill and no one grew old (Enki and Ninhursaga)**
- In a primeval or ideal land there is no disease, no old age and no one says 'I am old' (ETCSL 1.1.1 20-23)
- In a primeval or ideal land no wailing or lament is heard (ETCSL 1.1.1 27-28)

**Ninsikila asks for water; Enki makes fresh water rise and Dilmun an emporium**
- A god turns salt or bitter water into fresh, drinkable water (ETCSL 1.1.1 47, ETCSL 1.1.1 58)

**Enki impregnates Ninhursaga and then each daughter in turn (Ninnisig, Ninkura, Ninimma)**
- A divine pregnancy lasts nine days instead of nine months (ETCSL 1.1.1 75-83, ETCSL 1.1.1 102-104, ETCSL 1.1.1 126R-126Z)
- A god lies with his daughter, then with the daughter born of her, and so on down the generations (ETCSL 1.1.1 97-107, ETCSL 1.1.1 117-126, ETCSL 1.1.1 126L-126CC)

**Uttu is warned, Enki comes as a gardener with fruit, and Ninhursaga takes his seed**
- A suitor wins a woman's consent with gifts of fruit (cucumbers, apples, grapes) (ETCSL 1.1.1 147-151, ETCSL 1.1.1 171-177)

**Eight plants spring up; Enki asks what they are and eats them**
- A god asks 'what is this?', learns each plant and determines its destiny (ETCSL 1.1.1 200-201, ETCSL 1.1.1 219)
- A god eats plants whose nature has not been fixed, bringing a curse and illness on himself (ETCSL 1.1.1 202-218)

**Ninhursaga curses Enki; the fox brings her back; eight healing deities born, Ninti from the rib**
- A goddess curses a god's name and vows not to look on him with the eye of life until he dies (ETCSL 1.1.1 220-221)
- The gods sit down in the dust in grief or helplessness at a cosmic crisis (ETCSL 1.1.1 222)
- An animal (fox) offers to bring back an estranged deity in return for a reward (ETCSL 1.1.1 223-227)
- An animal (fox) offers to bring back an estranged deity in return for a reward (ETCSL 1.1.1 228-230, ETCSL 1.1.1 235-239)
- A goddess heals a sick god by giving birth to a deity for each of his aching body parts (ETCSL 1.1.1 252-271)
- A goddess named Nin-ti ('Lady of the rib' / 'Lady who gives life') is born from a god's rib (ti) (ETCSL 1.1.1 268-269, ETCSL 1.1.1 279)
- Each newborn deity's name puns on the body part from which it came (ETCSL 1.1.1 254-271)

**Namma wakes the sleeping Enki, who plans humankind from the clay of the abzu**
- The wise creator god lies asleep in the subterranean waters and must be woken to act (ETCSL 1.1.2 13-14)

**Drunk on beer, Ninmah makes six flawed humans and Enki decrees a fate for each**
- A deity deliberately fashions a woman who cannot give birth (ETCSL 1.1.2 72-74)
- A human without sex organs (eunuch) is destined to stand before the king (ETCSL 1.1.2 75-78)

**Enki fashions Umul, a frail creature Ninmah cannot help**
- A god fashions Umul ('my day is far off'), a frail being who cannot stand, eat or speak - the first old man or newborn (ETCSL 1.1.2 88-91, ETCSL 1.1.2 96-99)
- A being is described as 'neither alive nor dead' (ETCSL 1.1.2 101)

**Enki's cult in the abzu, his barge, the ships of Dilmun, Magan and Meluḫa, and gifts to the Martu**
- Ships of distant lands (Dilmun, Magan, Meluḫa) bring timber, gold and silver to the god's city (ETCSL 1.1.3 123-130)

**Marshes, fisheries and the sea shrine; Nanše placed over the sea**
- A god builds a holy shrine in the sea whose interior is a tangle beyond human understanding, aligned with constellations (ETCSL 1.1.3 285-291)

**Enki builds his silver and lapis temple in Eridug; Isimud praises the speaking temple (Enki's journey to Nibru)**
- Musical instruments in a god's temple sound of their own accord (ETCSL 1.1.4 62-67)

**Enki's boat sails of itself to Nibru, where he feasts An, Enlil and the gods; Enlil praises his temple**
- A god's boat casts off and moves of its own accord, its tow-rope held by itself (ETCSL 1.1.4 88-89)

**Nibru, its holy river, and Nun-bar-še-gunu's warning to Ninlil; Ninlil refuses Enlil (Enlil and Ninlil)**
- A young woman is told not to bathe in a holy river, where a god will see her (ETCSL 1.2.1 15-16, ETCSL 1.2.1 23)
- A maiden refuses a god's advances: she is too young and her parents will punish her (ETCSL 1.2.1 28-34)

**Enlil takes Ninlil by boat, she conceives Suen; the gods seize Enlil as impure and he leaves the city**
- The council of gods seizes a god as ritually impure for a sexual offence and expels him from the city (ETCSL 1.2.1 54-62)
- A woman pregnant by a god follows him into exile (ETCSL 1.2.1 63-64)

**Enlil as gatekeeper, man of the man-eating river and ferryman fathers Nergal, Ninazu and Enbilulu**
- Children are begotten as substitutes so that a firstborn may be released from the underworld (ETCSL 1.2.1 85-86, ETCSL 1.2.1 111-112, ETCSL 1.2.1 137-138)

**Sud of Ereš; Enlil, without a wife, finds her, is rebuffed, and sends Nuska with a proposal (Enlil and Sud)**
- A god or king without a wife travels through the land searching for a bride and chooses one for her beauty (ETCSL 1.2.2 1.A:9-13)
- A suitor's first, impertinent approach is rebuffed by the young woman, who goes into her house (ETCSL 1.2.2 1.A:15-26)

**Nuska at Ereš; Nanibgal accepts the proposal, Sud serves the envoy, Nuska reports to Enlil**
- On her mother's instruction the bride washes the envoy's hands and gives him drink, and receives jewellery (ETCSL 1.2.2 1.A:77-85)

**Inana delights in herself and goes to Enki in Eridug; Enki knows her purpose (Inana and Enki)**
- A wise god knows from his own dwelling what a visitor intends before she arrives (ETCSL 1.3.1 B:9-12)

**Enki, in his cups, gives Inana the divine powers one group after another**
- A god, drunk at a banquet, gives away his divine powers (me) to a guest (ETCSL 1.3.1 D:1-5)

**Inana sails off with the powers; Enki sobers and asks where each power is**
- When the effects of drink wear off, the god asks where his gifts are and tries to take them back (ETCSL 1.3.1 F:9-13, ETCSL 1.3.1 F:17-34)

**Seven times Enki sends Isimud and monsters to seize the Boat of Heaven; Ninšubur saves it each time**
- A goddess accuses her father of lying and swearing falsely by his name when he revokes his gift (ETCSL 1.3.1 H:20-26, ETCSL 1.3.1 H:54-60)

**The powers brought to Unug are recited; Inana names the quays; Enki makes peace**
- A goddess names quays and places in her city after what happened at each (ETCSL 1.3.1 I:115-125)

**Inana storms and kills Ebih, mocks it for its height, and builds her palace**
- A deity declares the enemy destroyed because of its height, beauty and reaching up to heaven (ETCSL 1.3.2 152-159)
- Birds of sorrow build nests on the flanks of the destroyed land (ETCSL 1.3.2 163-165)

**Inana goes up into the mountains; Enki's raven plants the first date palm (Inana and Šu-kale-tuda 1-90)**
- A god gives instructions to a bird (the raven), which then performs the work of a man (ETCSL 1.3.3 49-55, ETCSL 1.3.3 59, ETCSL 1.3.3 69-71)
- The raven plants, climbs and pollinates the first date palm and works the shadouf, an origin of date cultivation (ETCSL 1.3.3 63-77, ETCSL 1.3.3 85-87)

**Šu-kale-tuda violates the sleeping Inana; the wells turn to blood (Inana and Šu-kale-tuda 91-138)**
- An incompetent gardener destroys every plant he was meant to water, pulling them out by the roots (ETCSL 1.3.3 93-96)
- A mortal looks east and west and sees the gods of sunrise and sunset, and a lone goddess (ETCSL 1.3.3 97-106)
- A single shade tree whose broad shade does not change from morning to evening (ETCSL 1.3.3 107-111)
- A goddess wearied by travelling around heaven and earth lies down to sleep under a tree (ETCSL 1.3.3 112-116)
- A whole land is struck with a plague because of one man's hidden crime (ETCSL 1.3.3 129-135)

**Šu-kale-tuda hides in the city; second and third plagues (Inana and Šu-kale-tuda 139-238)**
- A father tells his guilty son to go and live among his brothers in the city so that the avenging deity will not find him (ETCSL 1.3.3 177-184, ETCSL 1.3.3 206-213, ETCSL 1.3.3 231-238)
- Three successive plagues (blood, storm, blocked roads) are sent while the culprit stays hidden (ETCSL 1.3.3 168-176, ETCSL 1.3.3 185-193, ETCSL 1.3.3 214-220)
- Seven times seven helpers attend a deity (ETCSL 1.3.3 191)
- A deity blocks the highways of the land so the people cannot travel (ETCSL 1.3.3 216-218)

**Inana appeals to Enki, finds Šu-kale-tuda and decrees his death and lasting name (Inana and Šu-kale-tuda 239-310)**
- A wronged goddess prostrates herself before her father god and demands that he hand over the culprit (ETCSL 1.3.3 242-250)
- A condemned man is told he will die, but his name will not be forgotten: it will be sung in songs by singers and shepherds (ETCSL 1.3.3 295-301)

**The tale of Gudam**
- Many armed men follow an upstart in the streets of the city and sit before him (ETCSL 1.3.4 B:4-7, ETCSL 1.3.4 C:1-6)
- A rampaging warrior wrecks the temple beams and kills many in the city until a humble man (a junior fisherman) strikes him down (ETCSL 1.3.4 C:20-28)

**Inana plans to seize E-ana from An, with Utu's oath and the fisherman Adagbir (A mythic narrative about Inana, A-C)**
- A goddess sets her mind on seizing the great heaven (An's temple E-ana) from the sky god (ETCSL 1.3.5 B:3-6, ETCSL 1.3.5 B:19-20)
- A god swears by the life of heaven and by the life of his own throne (ETCSL 1.3.5 B:10-15)

**Inana captures E-ana from An; daylight is shortened (A mythic narrative about Inana, D)**
- A goddess stamps on a scorpion and cuts off its tail; it roars like a lion then falls silent (ETCSL 1.3.5 D:29-31)
- The sky god slaps his thigh and sighs: 'What has my child done? She has become greater than me!' (ETCSL 1.3.5 D:41-42)
- A cosmic change in the length of day and night is fixed from that day on (day equal to night) (ETCSL 1.3.5 D:43-45)
- A temple brought down from heaven is made firm as heaven, given a name, and all people bow at its feet (ETCSL 1.3.5 D:50-54, ETCSL 1.3.5 D:56-60)

**Inana abandons her temples, adorns herself and instructs Ninšubur (Inana's descent 1-67)**
- Cosmetics and jewels carry seductive names ('Let a man come', 'Come, man, come') (ETCSL 1.4.1 22-23)

**Inana spares her mourners and hands Dumuzid to the demons (Inana's descent 306-358)**
- Those who mourned the goddess in dust and filthy garments are refused to the demons as her substitute (ETCSL 1.4.1 311-328, ETCSL 1.4.1 334-338, ETCSL 1.4.1 344-347)
- The goddess finds her husband not mourning but enthroned in magnificent garments (ETCSL 1.4.1 348-349)

**Dumuzid's flight as a snake, Inana's grief, the fly, and the half-year decree (Inana's descent 359-412)**
- An animal (a fly) reveals where the hidden man is and is rewarded by the deity with a decreed destiny (ETCSL 1.4.1 394-403)
- Two siblings each spend half the year in the underworld, one released when the other is taken (ETCSL 1.4.1 404-410)

**Dumuzid and Ĝeštin-ana**
- A sister refuses, under torture, to reveal where her brother is hiding (ETCSL 1.4.1.1 57-64)

**Inana's lament; she goes to the sheepfold and finds Dumuzid slain (Inana and Bilulu 1-80)**
- A goddess composes and fashions a song of lament for her slain husband (ETCSL 1.4.4 74-80)

**Inana curses Bilulu and Ĝirĝire, avenges Dumuzid, and Ĝeštin-ana laments (Inana and Bilulu 81-177)**
- A goddess proves her husband's equal by avenging his death on his killer (ETCSL 1.4.4 90-94, ETCSL 1.4.4 162-165, ETCSL 1.4.4 174-176)
- The killer is cursed and turned into an object (a waterskin) that serves travellers (ETCSL 1.4.4 101, ETCSL 1.4.4 112)

**Nanna-Suen resolves to go to Nibru; the praise of Nibru (Nanna-Suen's journey 1-36)**
- A god sets his mind on travelling to the city of his father and mother (ETCSL 1.5.1 1-16)
- Boast that a city's palms grew 'before Dilmun existed', i.e. the city is older than another land (ETCSL 1.5.1 34-36)

**Nanna-Suen builds his barge from materials of many lands (Nanna-Suen's journey 37-144)**
- A god's boat is built from materials fetched from named distant lands (reeds, pitch from the abzu, cedar, timber from Ebla) (ETCSL 1.5.1 37-78)
- A boatmen's work chant (a-u3-a) is repeated with the god's names as his barge sets out (ETCSL 1.5.1 103-139)

**The cargo for Enlil and the goddesses' welcomes along the way (Nanna-Suen's journey 147-252)**
- At each city a goddess welcomes the passing boat with offerings, but the boat refuses to unload: 'I am going to Nibru' (ETCSL 1.5.1 198-252)
- A boat or traveller is greeted with the repeated welcome 'Be well! Be well!' (silim-ma he2-me-en) (ETCSL 1.5.1 201-202, ETCSL 1.5.1 212-213, ETCSL 1.5.1 223-224A, ETCSL 1.5.1 234-235, ETCSL 1.5.1 245-246)

**Arrival at Nibru; the porter opens; Enlil feasts and blesses Nanna (Nanna-Suen's journey 253-352)**
- Before leaving, the son asks the father god for fish, barley, reeds, game, syrup, wine and long life, and receives each (ETCSL 1.5.1 331-348)

**Ninurta's might, his slain monsters hung on his chariot (The return of Ninurta to Nibru 1-75)**
- A divine warrior's slain monsters (six-headed ram, dragon, bison, Anzud bird, seven-headed serpent ...) are listed as his trophies (ETCSL 1.6.1 30-40)
- The victor hangs his captured beasts and slain monsters on the parts of his chariot (ETCSL 1.6.1 52-63)

**Nuska meets Ninurta; he enters E-kur, boasts of his weapons and exalts Nibru (The return of Ninurta to Nibru 76-174)**
- The chief minister meets the returning warrior and begs him not to frighten his father in his dwelling (ETCSL 1.6.1 79-97)
- The victor asks that his arms be washed with holy water, his chariot set on a pedestal, and captive kings bow to him (ETCSL 1.6.1 152-158)
- The god's city is to raise its head to heaven, be the freshwater well of the land, with birds nesting in it and refugees cool in its shade (ETCSL 1.6.1 168-174)

**Lugal-e: Šar-ur reports the birth and kingship of the Asag**
- Named stones and minerals form the army of the mountain monster and raid the cities (ETCSL 1.6.2 37-39)

**Lugal-e: Ninurta's war-cry, cosmic convulsion and first march; Šar-ur scouts**
- The divine battle-storm ruins the birds of the sky, the fish of the waters and the wild animals (ETCSL 1.6.2 92-94)

**Lugal-e: Ninmah comes to her son and is renamed Ninhursag, lady of the stone-pile**
- The mountain is blessed to yield herbs, honey, wine, cedars, gold, silver, copper, tin and wild animals (ETCSL 1.6.2 397-405)

**Lugal-e: Aruru reminds Ninurta; he curses and blesses the stones (u, šu, gasura, saĝkal, esi, na, elel, kagena)**
- The god's ordinances are to be inscribed in lines on a stone set up on a pedestal in his courtyard (ETCSL 1.6.2 493-495)

**Lugal-e: triumphal return by boat, hymn of the boatmen, Enlil's blessing, Nisaba and doxology**
- The victorious god returns home in his sacred barge while boatmen sing his praise (ETCSL 1.6.2 647-651, ETCSL 1.6.2 672-674)

**How grain came to Sumer**
- The high god stores the barley inside a mountain and bars it shut (ETCSL 1.7.6 7-11)
- Younger gods plan to bring the hidden grain down from the mountain to the land (ETCSL 1.7.6 13-27)

**The šumunda grass: born of Heaven and Earth after the flood, it burns the E-ana and is cursed by Inana**
- A goddess seizes a raven and sets it over a bound offender (ETCSL 1.7.7 29-34)

**Pabilsaĝ's journey to Nibru B-D: Enlil's blessing of the watercourse, the marriage, Pabilsaĝ refuses food**
- The high god addresses a watercourse and blesses the land's flax and grain (ETCSL 1.7.8 B:1-3, ETCSL 1.7.8 C:8-11)

**Gilgamesh and Aga: Kiš's envoys; Gilgamesh consults the elders, then the young men**
- The ruler puts the question of war first to the council of elders, then to the assembly of young men (ETCSL 1.8.1.1 3-14, ETCSL 1.8.1.1 18-29)
- The unfinished wells and hoisting gear of the land are the refrain argument in a council on war or submission (ETCSL 1.8.1.1 5-7)

**Gilgamesh and Aga: the siege, Birḫar-tura, 'Is that man your king?', Aga released**
- The besieger, seeing a man on the wall, asks the captive 'Is that man your king?' (ETCSL 1.8.1.1 67-70, ETCSL 1.8.1.1 90-92)
- The victor releases the captured enemy king in repayment of an earlier kindness (ETCSL 1.8.1.1 112-113)
- The hero recalls that the enemy once gave him refuge as a fugitive and fed 'the fleeing bird' (ETCSL 1.8.1.1 102-106)

**Gilgamesh and the Bull of Heaven (version 2): Inana's refusal to release him, the giant weapons, the Bull slain**
- The hero hurls a haunch of the slain bull at the goddess, who flees (ETCSL 1.8.1.2 2.D:50)

- The king holds the importance of the humble to be of special value (ETCSL 2.4.2.02 239)
- By command of An and Enlil the king never lets the prayers for the life of the Land and the foreign lands be interrupted (ETCSL 2.4.2.02 241, ETCSL 2.4.2.02 242, ETCSL 2.4.2.02 243)

**Šulgi's service to the gods, preservation of old hymns, and charge to a future king (Šulgi B)**
- The king claims never to have done violence to another king, Akkadian, Sumerian or Gutian (ETCSL 2.4.2.02 265-269)
- The king collected and preserved old hymns from ancient times, never declaring them false, and added them to the singers' repertoire (ETCSL 2.4.2.02 270-280)

**Curse on a hostile successor; the academies of Urim and Nibru; no lies in his inscriptions (Šulgi B)**
- The king founds 'Houses of Wisdom of Nisaba' (academies) in Urim and Nibru where scribes copy and singers perform his hymns; the academies shall never cease (ETCSL 2.4.2.02 308-315)
- From the origins of mankind to its full flourishing no king will ever equal the speaker's achievements (ETCSL 2.4.2.02 332-336)

**Lions culled like weeds; oath by Utu; Šulgi chosen by Nanna; praise of Nisaba (Šulgi B)**
- The king's shadow lies over the mountain lands (ETCSL 2.4.2.02 355)
- The king swears that even in far lands without roads or writing his songs will be recited as heavenly writings (ETCSL 2.4.2.02 358-365)
- The king calls himself the steward of the god's temple and the house-born slave of the sky god (ETCSL 2.4.2.02 376)
- The king's palace is 'the palace of palaces', towering like a lapis-lazuli mountain (ETCSL 2.4.2.02 377, ETCSL 2.4.2.02 379)

**Šulgi the wild bull, calf of a divine cow, purified at Eridug (Šulgi C)**
- The king calls himself a great storm let loose from heaven, his splendour spreading far (ETCSL 2.4.2.03 A:3)
- The king performs royal hand-washing and purifies himself with the water of Eridug; the seven wisdoms attend him (ETCSL 2.4.2.03 A:28, ETCSL 2.4.2.03 A:29, ETCSL 2.4.2.03 A:30)

**Šulgi in the house of wisdom: stylus, measuring line, plans and assembly (Šulgi C)**
- The king is expert in the pickaxe and brick-mould, drawing plans, laying foundations and writing inscriptions (ETCSL 2.4.2.03 A:42-49)

**Šulgi, extispicer, dream-interpreter and discerner of hearts (Šulgi C)**
- The king is the dream-interpreter of the Land and the divine judge (Ištaran) of the foreign lands, reading omens from extispicy and censers (ETCSL 2.4.2.03 A:102, ETCSL 2.4.2.03 A:103, ETCSL 2.4.2.03 A:104)

**Šulgi destroys the rebel lands; ruins never to be rebuilt (Šulgi C)**
- The king's radiance covers the cities and his battle-cry terrifies the lands like a storm in the heavens (ETCSL 2.4.2.03 B:7, ETCSL 2.4.2.03 B:8, ETCSL 2.4.2.03 B:9)
- The city the king smashes shall not be restored; its houses shall be counted as ruin mounds (ETCSL 2.4.2.03 B:20, ETCSL 2.4.2.03 B:21, ETCSL 2.4.2.03 B:32, ETCSL 2.4.2.03 B:33, ETCSL 2.4.2.03 B:34)

**Šulgi plays the seven instruments; fragments mentioning Ĝeštin-ana and Gilgameš (Šulgi C)**
- The king names a goddess (Ĝeštin-ana) as his sister and Ninsumun as his mother (ETCSL 2.4.2.03 B:93, ETCSL 2.4.2.03 B:94)

**Shulgi D: the king's own boast of how he crushes the foreign lands**
- The conqueror kills the enemy on the roofs and walls where they lie; those who can stand he sets on their feet (ETCSL 2.4.2.04 211-214)
- The king's weapons gnash their teeth like a beast and pour venom like a serpent into the enemy (ETCSL 2.4.2.04 158, ETCSL 2.4.2.04 161, ETCSL 2.4.2.04 171)

**Shulgi D: the king vows to avenge Sumer on the foreign lands; the gods turn against the enemy**
- A god of dreams (Zaqar) appears as protective spirit in a dream to the king (ETCSL 2.4.2.04 252-254)

**Shulgi D: the hero's revenge, the booty, the royal barge, and the entry before Enlil**
- The king invokes the names of the gods over captured fattened cattle and sheep (ETCSL 2.4.2.04 351-353)
- The king's sacred barge is caulked with bitumen from the abzu, adorned with horns and decorated with stars like the sky (ETCSL 2.4.2.04 354-360)

**Shulgi E: the king swears his hymns contain no lies, and commands their performance**
- Whom the moon god curses is struck with skin disease; the city he curses never rises again (ETCSL 2.4.2.05 41-42)

**Shulgi E: the great musician; a negligent king of old; Ninurta's weapons and the unique sceptre**
- A former king who in arrogance neglected canals, offerings and temples is held up as the anti-model (ETCSL 2.4.2.05 175-185)

**Shulgi E: the campaign against Gutium, the king alone ahead of his troops**
- The king's warfare is a horizon covered with storm clouds and flames cast on the mountains (ETCSL 2.4.2.05 219-221)

**Shulgi O: litany of Urim and its shrines, each 'well established'**
- The walled city is a mace and its assembly a shield; its army an irresistible flood (ETCSL 2.4.2.15 A:17-18, ETCSL 2.4.2.15 A:22-24)

**Shulgi O: Šulgi meets Gilgameš and praises his victory over Kiš**
- Narrative opens 'on the day when the destiny of the Land was fixed, when the seed of living beings came forth' (ETCSL 2.4.2.15 A:38-39)
- The hero captures the seven heroes (champions) of the enemy city (ETCSL 2.4.2.15 A:57)
- Kingship is carried from one city to another by conquest (from Kiš to Unug) (ETCSL 2.4.2.15 A:60)

**Shulgi O: further praises of Gilgameš (Huwawa, the seven terrors) and of Šulgi**
- Seven gods stand beside a statue or hero wielding battle-axes (ETCSL 2.4.2.15 A:81-82)
- The hero lets the mother of a sick (or captured) man take her son back into her embrace (ETCSL 2.4.2.15 A:101)

**Shulgi Q: adab to Utu, who gives Šulgi kingship and chooses him in his heart**
- The king or god is like a mace with three lion heads that makes the mountains tremble (ETCSL 2.4.2.17 A:12)

**Shulgi R: Ninlil's barge, built by Šulgi, described part by part**
- A deity commands the construction of a sacred object or house and entrusts the work to the king (ETCSL 2.4.2.18 A:1-5)
- Each part of a sacred boat is likened to a cosmic or animal image (dragons, stars, sky, the sun and moon at prow and stern) (ETCSL 2.4.2.18 A:11-27, ETCSL 2.4.2.18 A:34-38)
- Little birds chirping in the reeds delight the gods like the sound of the churn (ETCSL 2.4.2.18 A:28-31)

**Shulgi R: the festival voyage of Enlil and Ninlil to Tummal and back, and their blessing on Šulgi**
- The great gods bathe in holy water at the festival (ETCSL 2.4.2.18 B:43)
- The sacred boat plunges like a goring ox and frightens the fish of the deep (ETCSL 2.4.2.18 B:60-63)
- Different kinds of fish playing in the water each give joy to a different god (ETCSL 2.4.2.18 B:74-78)
- A goddess wishes the king's life to be covered as with her holy garment (ETCSL 2.4.2.18 B:90)

**Shulgi U: hymn to Nergal (Mešlamta-ea) for Šulgi**
- The father god loves his heroic son and makes his heroism known among the people (ETCSL 2.4.2.21 C:17-20)
- Wherever the god strides the enemy troops (named peoples) suffer (ETCSL 2.4.2.21 C:24-26)

**Shulgi V: Enlil's favour, Šulgi's run from Nibru to Urim, and his statue**
- The king is called the creation of the god's hands (ETCSL 2.4.2.22 4)
- A violent storm or whirlwind breaks out while the king is on the road, but he completes his journey (ETCSL 2.4.2.22 27-28)

**Shulgi X: Šulgi sails to Unug, Inana's love song and her decree of his fate**
- Litany: the king is worthy of the dais, throne, crown, robe, sceptre, sandals and weapons (ETCSL 2.4.2.24 56-69)

**Shulgi X: Utu, Ninazu and Nanna-Ašimbabbar decree fates for Šulgi; the just king**
- A goddess spreads her lap for the king (ETCSL 2.4.2.24 139)

**Shulgi Z: love song, 'My sister, I would go with you to my fields and my garden'**
- The lover laments that because of the beloved the date clusters and harvest do not come to hand (ETCSL 2.4.2.26 A:6-9)

**Amar-Suena A: the temple of Enki left in ruins year after year, rebuilt only when Enki speaks**
- The people turn against (revolt from) the king during his building or reign (ETCSL 2.4.3.1 A:8)
- The king exchanges his royal garments for mourning clothes (ETCSL 2.4.3.1 A:12)
- The king searches for the god's plan (ĝiš-ḫur) for the temple and cannot find it until the god speaks (ETCSL 2.4.3.1 A:16, ETCSL 2.4.3.1 A:20, ETCSL 2.4.3.1 A:22)
- 'At that time' humanity had no wisdom or wise words and evil was thought good (ETCSL 2.4.3.1 B:5-8)

**Shu-Suen A: balbale of Bau, the queen's song of her lord's gifts and sweetness**
- The king's mother is praised for having given birth to the holy king (ETCSL 2.4.4.1 1-4)
- May the king's city stretch out its hands to him and lie at his feet like a lion cub (ETCSL 2.4.4.1 17-18)

**Shu-Suen B: balbale of Inana, 'Man of my heart, your allure is sweet as honey'**
- The woman says she will come of her own will and flee with the man into the bedroom (ETCSL 2.4.4.2 5-8)
- The woman tells the lover to speak to her mother and father, who will give her to him (ETCSL 2.4.4.2 15-17)

**Shu-Suen C: balbale of Inana, 'My hair is lettuce'**
- The woman's hair is likened to well-watered lettuce (ETCSL 2.4.4.3 1-8)

**Shu-Suen D: tigi to Ninurta, the king's great wall**
- The god is asked to be the king's great wall and look on him favourably (ETCSL 2.4.4.4 D:27-28)
- The god is a yellow evening light and a dragon raising a terrible torch that casts fear over the land (ETCSL 2.4.4.4 F:45-49)
