**Proverbs collection 2+6, the ox, the lamentation priest, the dog, finding and losing (A.2.83-126)**
- Saying: the ox walking round the threshing-floor is not sowing; who eats at harvest is not breaking clods (ETCSL 6.1.02 A.2.86:147-A.2.88:150)
- Saying: the ox that kicks up dust gets flour in its own eyes (ETCSL 6.1.02 A.2.90:152)
- Satire: the lamentation priest throws his son into the water saying 'may the city be built like me, may the land live like me' (ETCSL 6.1.02 A.2.99:163-164)
- Saying: for his pleasure he married, on reflection he divorced (ETCSL 6.1.02 A.2.124:203)

**Proverbs collection 2+6, on work, the house and the palace (B.2.131-165)**
- Saying: gathering firewood is for the strong man; the weak man waits on dry land (ETCSL 6.1.02 B.2.133:4-B.2.134:7)
- Saying: hand added to hand builds a man's house; stomach added to stomach destroys it (ETCSL 6.1.02 B.2.138:14-15)
- Saying: the house built by the upright man is destroyed by the treacherous man (ETCSL 6.1.02 B.2.142:19)
- No rest in a house where the wife does not speak and the father utters no joyful word (ETCSL 6.1.02 B.2.146:25-27)
- Saying: the palace is a forest, the king a lion, and the goddess Nungal covers men with her battle-net (ETCSL 6.1.02 B.2.155:40-42)

**Proverbs collection 2+6, birds, fish and Enlil's offering table (C.2.c1-D.2.d18)**
- Saying: a bird in the sky is as good as an um bird; a fish in the deep as good as a carp in the reeds (ETCSL 6.1.02 C.2.c2:2-C.2.c4:4)
- Saying: all the birds flew away and their mother alone stayed (ETCSL 6.1.02 C.2.c5:5)
- Saying: he who lives from birds and fish cannot sleep (ETCSL 6.1.02 C.2.c8:8)
- Saying: the pigeon's voice is the glory of the garden, the francolin's of the field (ETCSL 6.1.02 C.2.c13:13-C.2.c15:15)
- Saying: offerings are the glory of the gods (ETCSL 6.1.02 D.2.d1:1)
- A list of birds and fish (carp, sea fish) is set on Enlil's offering table (ETCSL 6.1.02 D.2.d13:17-D.2.d14:21)

**Proverbs collection 3, nos. 1-17: the outcast son, procrastination, taboos of Utu, shepherds, friendship**
- A parent goes on feeding and giving drink to a son who is an outcast and whose personal god has turned against him: 'you are still my son' (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.5)
- Saying: a weary shepherd-boy does not recognise his own mother (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.12)
- Saying: while a man lives his friend is his friend; once he is dead the friend becomes his worst demon (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.16)

**Proverbs collection 3, nos. 18-35: quarrel and slander, tears, reciprocity, Enlil's chaff, Nanni's old age**
- Saying: on a journey a man does not tire of eating; he gathers food all day long (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.19)
- Saying: there are bitter tears (a gig) in human flesh (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.20)
- A mote or straw (u2) in the eye that is, or is not, removed, in a saying about petty faults (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.21)

**Proverbs collection 3, nos. 36-66: slave girls, lies, Unug cursed, the boss, the merchant**
- Saying: the joy of a daughter-in-law is anger (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.44)
- Saying: it is because you are the boss (nam-ugula) that you bully me (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.62)
- Wish or saying that the arrogant man's head be bowed to his neck like a damp reed (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.63)

**Proverbs collection 3, nos. 67-110: the strong and the weak, the insulter, Iškur's oath, sunrise and kingship, trades, the fool**
- Saying about our own smell: let it be of leeks, not turnips; our own smell is pulled-up turnips, sweet things are brought by strangers (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.68, ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.85)
- Saying: the fool (ḫu-ru-um) is garrulous; who can rival a garrulous man? (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.97, ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.103)
- Saying: where someone is lame, the emissary of the goddess Bau comes to help (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.105)
- Saying: the two of them are like one man (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.109)
- Saying: something offered is not offered, something finished is not finished: nothing changes (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.107)

**Proverbs collection 3, nos. 111-147: the goat and the wasteland, mouth and tongue, false witness, offerings, the aching heart, the personal god as shepherd**
- Saying: punishment is assigned to the swaggerer (sun7-na) and he is afflicted with diseases (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.121)
- Saying: my aching finger is held, my aching foot has its sandal, but who will find my aching heart? May Inana pour oil on it (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.127, ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.128)
- Saying: the heavens were destroyed and the earth shaken, yet the people still stood there by themselves (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.136)
- Saying: he who entered Elam has his lips sealed; he who has to live in Elam does not have a good life (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.138, ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.139)
- Saying: for one rejected by Inana, his dream is to forget (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.145)

**Proverbs collection 3, nos. 148-190: priests and craftsmen, drought, abominations to Suen, Inana and Ninurta, Fate, the leader in the fire, righteousness cut off**
- Saying: in Eridu built in abundance, the monkey sits in the singer's house with longing eyes (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.150)
- Saying: let the solitary one remain alone; he is forever treacherous (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.152)
- Saying: the goat spoke like a wise old woman but acted like an unclean woman (words and deeds differ) (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.153)
- Saying: a good word is a friend to many people; a destructive word is four yoked oxen (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.159, ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.160)
- Coveting (igi-tum3 la2) and grasping (or spying) are an abomination to Ninurta (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.175)
- Saying: the speaker confronts Fate (nam-tar), to whom it makes no difference whether one speaks as a just man or as a wicked man (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.176)
- Saying: when righteousness (si sa2) is cut off, injustice (niĝ2-erim2) increases (ETCSL 6.1.03 A.3.190)

**Proverbs collection 4, source A: the shouting statue, the sky-holder, the four winds, the knower who conceals**
- Saying: why should someone who knows something conceal it? (ETCSL 6.1.04 A.4.10)

**Proverbs collection 4, source B: the witness like a fruit tree, each to his task, the man on the roof, the thief and the honest man**
- Saying: a witness should be like the prosopis tree, from which fruit pods come forth (ETCSL 6.1.04 B.4.45)
- Saying: a heart that does not know accounting, is that a wise heart? (ETCSL 6.1.04 B.4.46)
- Saying: he who ploughs should plough, he who harvests should harvest (each to his own task) (ETCSL 6.1.04 B.4.47)
- Saying: after the snake has been caught for him, he himself recites the incantation (taking credit too late) (ETCSL 6.1.04 B.4.49)
- Saying: what are the dreams of a slave girl, what are the prayers of a toiling slave? (ETCSL 6.1.04 B.4.51)
- Saying: to value the earth is for the gods; I am merely covered in dust (ETCSL 6.1.04 B.4.59)
- Saying on body and speech: bitterness that afflicts the anus entered by the mouth; the anus breaks wind, talking produces excess words (ETCSL 6.1.04 B.4.61, ETCSL 6.1.04 B.4.62)

**Proverbs collection 5 (animal fables), sources A-B: the elephant and the wren, wild bull, ox, cow, horse and donkey**
- Fable: the elephant boasts that no creature of Šakkan is like him; the small wren answers that it too was created just as he was (ETCSL 6.1.05 A.5.1)
- Sayings on the wild bull: taboo for the plough, free of the plough, wandering in the rushes, doing only what pleases it (ETCSL 6.1.05 A.5.3, ETCSL 6.1.05 A.5.4, ETCSL 6.1.05 A.5.5, ETCSL 6.1.05 A.5.6)
- Saying: like a cow that has never calved, you look for a calf of yours that does not exist (ETCSL 6.1.05 B.5.34)

**Proverbs collection 5, source D: the lion fables (the clever goat, the boar, the trapped lion and the fox)**
- Fable: when the lion falls into a trap, the fox comes and offers to carry his sandals home for him (ETCSL 6.1.05 D.5.58)
- Saying: no one walks a second time where a lion has eaten a man (ETCSL 6.1.05 D.5.67)

**Proverbs collection 5, source D: wolf fables (the fox's share, the wolf's oath to Utu, the lonely wolf)**
- Fable: nine wolves catch ten sheep and cannot share them; the fox gives the nine wolves one sheep and takes nine for himself (the lion's share) (ETCSL 6.1.05 D.5.x5)
- Fable: the wolf caught in a trap swears to Utu by a righteous oath to eat no more sheep, then asks what he can eat now (ETCSL 6.1.05 D.5.x10)
- Fable: the wolf weeps before Utu that the animals frisk together while he is all alone (ETCSL 6.1.05 D.5.x11)
- Saying: where the wolf takes sheep the shepherd cannot increase his flock (ETCSL 6.1.05 D.5.x13)

**Proverbs collection 5, source D: dog sayings and fables (the dog and the door-bolt)**
- Saying: the dog recognises a man who loves him (ETCSL 6.1.05 D.5.83)
- Fable: a dog beaten with a door-bolt in a warehouse goes back the same night for more and has its leg broken again (ETCSL 6.1.05 D.5.102)

**Proverbs collection 5, source D: more dog sayings (the snarling dog, the dog at the party, the bitch and her puppies)**
- Fable: the bitches tell their young not to eat the food of a funeral offering (ninda ki-sig10-ga) (ETCSL 6.1.05 D.5.119)
- Fable: the bitch tells the kid that whether yellow or mottled she still loves her own little ones (ETCSL 6.1.05 D.5.123)

**Proverbs collection 7, sources A-B: the curse on the destroyed place, the sinking boat, verdict and curse, flea and fly, borrowed bread**
- Saying-curse: where places are destroyed let more be destroyed, where not, let a breach be made, let his place be like chopped turnips (ETCSL 6.1.07 A.7.1)
- Saying: a verdict (di) can be accepted, a curse (aš2) cannot (ETCSL 6.1.07 B.7.28)
- Saying: linen is stretched out for the flea, a reed mat woven for the fly, a storehouse built for the gecko (even vermin are provided for) (ETCSL 6.1.07 B.7.29)
- Saying: he gathered everything for himself but had to slaughter his pig, used up his wood (ETCSL 6.1.07 B.7.31, ETCSL 6.1.07 B.7.32)

**Proverbs collection 7, source C: Fate a biting dog, the boat that reached port, the stranger's ox, the fatherless reed, the songs of a city**
- Saying: Fate (nam-tar) is a dog well able to bite; it clings like dirty rags (ETCSL 6.1.07 C.7.70)
- Saying: one cried 'Woe!' and his boat sank, another 'Alas!' and the rudder broke, the young man said 'Ah, god!' and the boat reached its destination (ETCSL 6.1.07 C.7.77)
- Riddle-saying: conceived by no father, conceived by no mother, the reed came out of the breast of the storm (ETCSL 6.1.07 C.7.93)
- Saying: the songs of a city are its omen diviners (what is sung shows the city's fate) (ETCSL 6.1.07 C.7.121)

**Proverbs collection 8, sources A-B: pig, goat, bear and fox fables**
- Saying: having lost the sow, they sit and strengthen the pigsty (locking the stable after the horse has gone) (ETCSL 6.1.08 B.8.b2)
- Fable: the fox asks Enlil for the wild bull's horns; caught in rain, unable to enter its burrow, it vows to return the feature to its rightful owner (ETCSL 6.1.08 B.8.b20)
- Fox sayings: the fox is full of lies, plots treachery, boasts that no one sees its bent behind, and talks its way out of traps (ETCSL 6.1.08 B.8.b22, ETCSL 6.1.08 B.8.b30, ETCSL 6.1.08 B.8.b33, ETCSL 6.1.08 B.8.b35)
- Fable: the fox wants to leave its shoes in the goat's house but will not stay the night once it hears a dog lives there (ETCSL 6.1.08 B.8.b28)

**Proverbs collection 8, sources C-E: birds, the raven and the fox, trees and furniture that speak**
- Fable: a raven with a porous jar tells the fox it sprinkles the water into the Tigris and the Euphrates (ETCSL 6.1.08 D.8.d2)
- Fable of trees: a tree tells its kin 'you and I are brothers'; the other is afraid because a stone stronger than it is hurled at it (ETCSL 6.1.08 E.8.e2, ETCSL 6.1.08 E.8.e3)
- Fable or saying in which an object (table, chair, door) speaks or rejoices (ETCSL 6.1.08 E.8.e5)

**Proverbs collection 9, source A: the man in authority, strength and intelligence, lost youth, the fattened pig**
- Saying: ignoramuses are numerous in the palace (ETCSL 6.1.09 A.9.a9)
- Saying: he who knows but does not speak is a fool (is-ḫab2) (ETCSL 6.1.09 A.9.a10)

**Proverbs collection 9, sources B-H: Nanni, the slave as lord, 'Run!' says the king, Utu as judge of the dream, humility**
- Saying on a slave who has taken the role of lord and a slave girl who has taken the role of lady (ETCSL 6.1.09 B.9.b8)
- Prayer: Utu, you are my judge, decide my case; turn the dream I have seen into a favourable one (ETCSL 6.1.09 E.9.e4)
- Saying: let me walk straight, so that I can catch up with my companion (ETCSL 6.1.09 E.9.e5)
- Saying: who can compare with humility (nam-sun5-na)? it is set in goodness (ETCSL 6.1.09 E.9.e7)

**Proverbs collection 11, sources E-K: revenge belongs to Ninurta, the friend's harbour, Adapa, debts to Utu, the scribe, the loving heart**
- Saying: uncleared debts become debts owed to the sun god Utu (ETCSL 6.1.11 I.11.133)
- Saying mocking a scribe who cannot write his own name: shame on you (ETCSL 6.1.11 J.11.146)
- Saying: a loving heart builds houses, a hating heart destroys houses (ETCSL 6.1.11 J.11.147, ETCSL 6.1.11 J.11.148)
- Saying: do not choose a wife during a festival (ETCSL 6.1.11 J.11.150)
- Saying of a scribe boasting of his skill and the prominent place it will win him (ETCSL 6.1.11 K.11.162)

**Proverbs collection 12, source A: master, steward and household**
- Saying: the master knows, the steward does not know (ETCSL 6.1.12 A.12.a4)
- Saying: the man who is always losing things loses them for the man who has to look for them (ETCSL 6.1.12 A.12.a10)

**Proverbs collection 12, sources B-F: changed masters, the damp reed, Nintur and paralysis, the millstone that floats for the righteous**
- Saying: their masters have changed; they are dressed in mourning clothes (ETCSL 6.1.12 B.12.b3)
- Saying: a man who behaves like a damp reed (pliant, servile) towards others does not tell the truth either (ETCSL 6.1.12 B.12.b6)
- Saying: the man whose knees are paralysed has not prayed devoutly to the birth goddess Nintur (illness as neglect of a deity) (ETCSL 6.1.12 B.12.b9)
- Saying: a man who did not tie up his leather sack made his friend angry (ETCSL 6.1.12 C.12.c4)

**Proverbs collection 13, nos. 1-40: thieves and burglars, the crafty, the lame man and his mother**
- Saying: the thief, out of fear of facing a lion, ends up facing a lion cub (ETCSL 6.1.13 13.5)
- A burglar breaks into (digs through, buru3) a house wall and is caught (ETCSL 6.1.13 13.8, ETCSL 6.1.13 13.10)
- A run of sayings on the crafty person (galam): he feasts his neighbour, stirs up the crowd, hangs precious metal on himself (ETCSL 6.1.13 13.13, ETCSL 6.1.13 13.14, ETCSL 6.1.13 13.15, ETCSL 6.1.13 13.16, ETCSL 6.1.13 13.17, ETCSL 6.1.13 13.18, ETCSL 6.1.13 13.20, ETCSL 6.1.13 13.21)
- Sayings and anecdotes about a lame man (kud-ku5-ra2): his mother mocks him, he asks where the runners went, he commands his feet to walk (ETCSL 6.1.13 13.22, ETCSL 6.1.13 13.23, ETCSL 6.1.13 13.24, ETCSL 6.1.13 13.25)

**Proverbs collection 13, nos. 41-59: the ecstatic, the boys in the orchard, the house of debt, the dishonest man, the immigrant**
- Anecdote: an ecstatic (lu2-gub-ba) enters a man's house and a boy is born to the man's wife; the ecstatic announces the birth to the neighbourhood (ETCSL 6.1.13 13.41)
- Anecdote: an ecstatic takes his place at Inana's gate and his daughter tells the crowd that her mother's word is true (ETCSL 6.1.13 13.42)
- Anecdote: gardeners chase boys out of the orchard; the one caught who agrees to come down and bring the others is promised he will not be punished in his father's house (ETCSL 6.1.13 13.48)
- Saying: treating an immigrant (gir5) badly is an abomination (niĝ2-gig) to Ninurta (ETCSL 6.1.13 13.57)

**Proverbs collection 14, source A: repaying favours, the workers' prayer for Enlil's cursed city, the drought**
- Saying-wish: let the favour be repaid to him who repays a favour; may the god grant good to him who speaks well of others (ETCSL 6.1.14 A.14.1, ETCSL 6.1.14 A.14.2)

**Proverbs collection 14, sources B-C: Enlil's temple, the palace, wives and children, the malicious spouse, the stranger leader**
- Saying: the E-babbar that Mesilim built was destroyed by Nanni, a man whose seed was cut off (ETCSL 6.1.14 B.14.16)
- Saying: both the palace and the netherworld (iri11-gal) require obedience from their inhabitants (ETCSL 6.1.14 B.14.19)

**Proverbs collection 15, sources A-B: the well-wisher, the workers' prayer for Enlil's cursed city, Enlil the helper of the lame**
- Saying: the well-wisher is the mother of the refugee; may the people wish you well and your god grant what you agree with (ETCSL 6.1.15 A.15.a5, ETCSL 6.1.15 A.15.a6)
- Saying: do not give a lame man a staff (or weapon); Enlil is his helper (ETCSL 6.1.15 B.15.b6)

**Proverbs collection 15, sources C-F: toughness, oil on the sceptre, the stranger as leader, nothing added to Enlil's temple, the rivers**
- Saying: the things of Enlil's temple are counted; nothing may be added to what has been counted, and the names of those who do are to be destroyed (ETCSL 6.1.15 C.15.c6)
- Saying: the Tigris is a duck, the Euphrates a goose (ETCSL 6.1.15 C.15.c15)

**Proverbs collection 16, sources D-F: friend and colleague, the merchant at the window, the unsound mind, the thief as outcast**
- Saying: he enters through the slave girl's window; he is indeed a merchant (ETCSL 6.1.16 E.16.e3)
- Saying: like a mountain mined for precious metal (full of holes), he is a man whose judgment is unsound (ETCSL 6.1.16 E.16.e7)
- Saying: after becoming a thief one becomes an outcast (ETCSL 6.1.16 E.16.e14)

**Proverbs collection 17: no one reaches heaven, the old man's lament, the poor man and his son, the merchant, the palace**
- Saying: the poor man does not strike his son a single blow; he treasures him forever (ETCSL 6.1.17 B.17.b4)
- Sayings on the poor man (ukur3): he dines on the broth of the breast, he stares into the soup (ETCSL 6.1.17 B.17.b5, ETCSL 6.1.17 B.17.b6)

**Proverbs collection 18: the idler, the talker who got into the palace, the levelling of hills, the lying dream of Agade**
- Saying: the idleness of a good-for-nothing (a-ḫur-rum) causes losses; hire him and fire him after half a day (ETCSL 6.1.18 A.18.4, ETCSL 6.1.18 A.18.5)
- Saying: your worthiness is the result of chance (ĝiš-šub, the lot) (ETCSL 6.1.18 A.18.7)
- Saying: the quick one hid, the strong one fled, the talker (ka tuku) got into the palace (ETCSL 6.1.18 A.18.8)
- Saying: the hills and the depths will be levelled; whenever there is excess, an axe remedies it (ETCSL 6.1.18 A.18.11, ETCSL 6.1.18 A.18.12)
- Saying: a slave entrusted with a burial will be negligent (ETCSL 6.1.18 A.18.13)
- Saying: the whirlwind sent to Agade gave Naram-Suen a lying dream (maš2-ĝi6 lul-la) and provided an interpreter (ETCSL 6.1.18 A.18.15)

**Proverbs collection 19, sources A-C: the old man, the fattened pig, build like a lord, accept your lot, Inana's marriage blessing, a man's goods and kin**
- Saying: build like a lord and you live like a slave; build like a slave and you live like a lord (ETCSL 6.1.19 B.19.b3)
- Wedding wish: marry the wife of your choice; may Inana make a hot-limbed wife lie with you and give you broad-shouldered sons (ETCSL 6.1.19 C.19.c4, ETCSL 6.1.19 C.19.c5)

**Proverbs collection 19, sources D-H: the um bird, the slave girl's banquet, the fool, the river grave, the insatiable glutton, the early-married youth**
- Saying: a great river is a grave (ki-maḫ) (ETCSL 6.1.19 F.19.f2)
- Saying: from the horizon to the heart of heaven the bread is too little for his great stomach; the grain of the whole land is too little for him (ETCSL 6.1.19 F.19.f3)
- Saying: morsels of bread and tasty onions are the food of the school (e2-dub-ba-a) (ETCSL 6.1.19 F.19.f5)
- Saying: the early-working shepherd, the early-working farmer, the young man who married while young: who compares to them? (ETCSL 6.1.19 G.19.g7)

**Proverbs collection 21: the fattened pig, the daughter-in-law, slave girls, the lamentation priest who stole barley**
- Saying: dusk means joy for a daughter-in-law (ETCSL 6.1.21 C.21.c8)
- Anecdote: a lamentation priest (gala) goes into a man's field to steal barley, is caught, and pleads that his beautiful head got confused (ETCSL 6.1.21 D.21.d3)

**Proverbs collection 22, lines 19-101: the husband who picks the fish bones, the younger son driven out, good and evil in the hands, accept your lot**
- Saying: good is in the hands and evil is in the hands; the heart lets go of neither; evil yields no interest to the storehouse - let it sink with the boat (ETCSL 6.1.22 22.ll.62–63, ETCSL 6.1.22 22.ll.64–66, ETCSL 6.1.22 22.l.67, ETCSL 6.1.22 22.l.68, ETCSL 6.1.22 22.l.69)

**Proverbs collection 22, lines 127-202: the stranger eats the bread, raven mongoose and lion, the drought, carry it, the liar with the waterskin, the trades**
- Saying: a feeding belly that becomes bloated is lamentable, a belly made obedient by the prince (ETCSL 6.1.22 22.ll.201–202)

**Proverbs collection 22, lines 203-287: no one reaches heaven, hand at the table, the angry man, the liar, the immigrant, Utu's compassion, the lamentation priest and the lion**
- Saying: his hand is on the table, his tongue in the palace (ETCSL 6.1.22 22.ll.214–215)
- Saying: the man seized by anger pours it out in threats (I will glare, I will destroy your wall), and it means nothing (ETCSL 6.1.22 22.ll.218–223)
- Saying: Utu's glance is prayerful and his heart wide (compassionate); his devotee is holy, and one allotted by Utu for good reaches the quay like a laden ship (ETCSL 6.1.22 22.ll.271–275)
- Saying: a god seizes the man who eats (too much) (ETCSL 6.1.22 22.ll.276–277)
- Anecdote: a lamentation priest is afraid of a lion in the desert; the purification priests ask what his brother is doing in the desert (ETCSL 6.1.22 22.ll.280–283)

**Proverbs collection 25: the drought, the en priest's diet, Unug cursed, Nanni, life better than death, the palace, the king's wealth, the abomination to Suen**
- Saying: although the unhappy days are without number, life is better than death (ETCSL 6.1.25 25.5)
- Saying: into a plague-stricken city one has to be driven like a pack-ass (ETCSL 6.1.25 25.6)
- Saying: the palace is a slippery place where one slips; watch your step when you decide to go home (ETCSL 6.1.25 25.8)

**Proverbs collection 26: the palace, the abominations to Ninurta, Utu and Suen, fear of god and offerings, the curse not returned, the farmer, the unloving beloved**
- Saying: refusing to speak (nu-dug4-ga) is an abomination to Ninurta (ETCSL 6.1.26 A.26.a7)
- Saying: removing something from its place (ki-ta kur2) is an abomination to Ninurta (ETCSL 6.1.26 A.26.a9)
- Saying: when a trustworthy boat sets sail, Utu seeks out a trustworthy harbour for it (ETCSL 6.1.26 A.26.a11)
- Saying: I am not dear to the one I hold dear; he profited from me and filled my hands with dust (ETCSL 6.1.26 C.26.c6, ETCSL 6.1.26 C.26.c7)
- Saying: he did not plough the field in the cool season, and at harvest time he turned to carding wool (ETCSL 6.1.26 D.26.d4)
- Saying: a farmer should not widen his field; a god should not increase the food demands of mankind (ETCSL 6.1.26 D.26.d13)

**Proverbs collection 27: the rich man's sick heart, the light burden, eating and vomiting, cities and men greeting**
- Saying: the rich man's heart is sick, the man with a troubled (over-full) heart is very sick (ETCSL 6.1.27 B.27.b1, ETCSL 6.1.27 B.27.b7)
- Saying: he who carries a light burden can dance (ETCSL 6.1.27 B.27.b3)
- Saying: one city does not greet another, but one man greets another (ETCSL 6.1.27 B.27.b9)

**Proverbs collection 28: the club and the name, the city's name and mine, the mongoose without fear of god, the godless man unburied, man finds and woman loses, the palace a forest**
- Saying: the city may change its name, but let my name stand (ETCSL 6.1.28 A.28.2)
- Saying: the mongoose does not know fear of god (ETCSL 6.1.28 A.28.3)
- Saying: if a man does not treasure his god, he will not be buried, and his heir will not pour water libations for him (ETCSL 6.1.28 A.28.9)
- Saying: when a man walks about he finds something; when a woman walks about she loses something (ETCSL 6.1.28 B.28.21)
- Saying: the palace is a forest; the king, a lion, subdues men with a great net like the goddess Nungal (ETCSL 6.1.28 B.28.24)

**Proverbs from Nibru, segments 1-3: fragments, the exotic animals of distant lands, the courtesan in the street**
- Exotic animals of distant lands (the donkey of Anšan, the bear of Marḫaši, the cat of Meluḫa, the elephant of the east) bite off great trees as if they were leeks (ETCSL 6.2.1 3.A:4-8)
- A proverb about a courtesan (harimtu, kar-kid) who stands in the streets and does not help a fallen man (ETCSL 6.2.1 3.B:6-7)

**Proverbs from Nibru, segments 4-8: Nanni who went down despondent, the cult not to be changed, the destiny in the water, the mill**
- A ruler who captured a city but did not destroy its walls and built a temple only to abandon it never saw mighty kingship and went down despondent to the nether world (ETCSL 6.2.1 4.A:9-12)
- Saying: 'I looked into the water and my destiny was drifting past' (ETCSL 6.2.1 7.A:4)
- Imprecation-saying: let his bread be foul food that no man will eat (ETCSL 6.2.1 4.A:1-4)

**Proverbs from Nibru, segments 9-19: the clown, the vixen, abominations to the god, great and little men**
- A jester who made fun of the city is mocked in turn and weeps (ETCSL 6.2.1 9:8-10)
- Saying: 'my fate is her voice': one's mother can change one's destiny (ETCSL 6.2.1 13.A:4)
- Saying: great men stir up the conflict and lesser men fight it out (ETCSL 6.2.1 17:2-3)

**Proverbs from Nibru, segments 20-44: prayer and life, the just man's hungry son, the widow, Gula, the son before he existed**
- Saying: prayer (sizkur) has given birth to a man's life (ETCSL 6.2.1 21:1)
- Complaint-saying: the son of the just man lies hungry (ETCSL 6.2.1 21:4)
- A widow or junior wife laments that widows can never become principal wives (ETCSL 6.2.1 26:1-3)
- Saying: do not be hostile to the weak and do not weep for the strong (ETCSL 6.2.1 28:1-2)
- A worshipper prostrates himself before his goddess yet feels he has no place to stand (ETCSL 6.2.1 31:1-2)
- Saying: 'Come, you are our son, even from when you did not exist' (ETCSL 6.2.1 33:1-2)
- Saying: talking endlessly is what humankind has most on its mind (ETCSL 6.2.1 39:1)

**Proverbs from Susa: the birds' voices, mouth and hand, the fettered dog, Aratta, the divorcing husband**
- Saying: he who steals from the stores is punished by his god (ETCSL 6.2.2 8:1-3)
- Saying: a husband divorcing his wife claims at least to be taking away his dignity (ETCSL 6.2.2 12:1-2)
- Saying: the water provided for libations was drunk instead (ETCSL 6.2.2 20:1)

**Proverbs from Urim 1-13: justice creates life, Utu not idle, wealth and sleeplessness, bread for the stranger, nowhere to flee**
- Saying: whenever wickedness causes trouble, the sun god (Utu) will not be idle (ETCSL 6.2.3 1:3)

**Proverbs from Urim 14-23: the cult not to be changed, a bitter fate, liars at the gate, scribes and singers, the fox**
- Saying: when liars enter the city gate there is a finger pointing at them in front and behind (ETCSL 6.2.3 16:2-3)
- Proverbs about the scribe: one who does not know his own name, or Sumerian, is a disgrace; one who knows a single line but writes a good hand is a true scribe (ETCSL 6.2.3 17:1-2, ETCSL 6.2.3 18:1-2, ETCSL 6.2.3 20:3, ETCSL 6.2.3 21:1-2)
- Saying: a disgraced scribe becomes an incantation priest, a disgraced singer a flute-player, a disgraced merchant a con-man (ETCSL 6.2.3 17:5-7)

**Proverbs from Urim 24-33: good and evil in the hands, the palace a forest, the unruly tongue, a man's god his shepherd**
- Saying: good is in the hands and evil is also in the hands (a man's deeds are his own) (ETCSL 6.2.3 24:7-8)
- Saying: the palace is a forest and the king a lion who covers men with a great battle-net (ETCSL 6.2.3 26:1-3)
- Saying: the storm god splits the heavens yet does not split the waterskin (ETCSL 6.2.3 30:3)
- Self-address to one's mouth and tongue: the tongue like a runaway donkey does not turn back; the mouth devours everything (ETCSL 6.2.3 31:1-6)

**Proverbs from Urim 34-64: fables of horse, donkey, dog, lion, goat, boar, pig, bear and fox**
- Fable: a dog on the bank promises tears for a donkey floating in the river, calling him 'my own dear father' (ETCSL 6.2.3 36:1-4)
- Fable: a lion catches a goat, which promises a ewe in exchange and tricks the lion about its name (ETCSL 6.2.3 39:1-8)
- Fable: a lion catches a boar: 'your flesh has not filled my mouth but your squeals have deafened my ears' (ETCSL 6.2.3 40:1-4)
- Proverbs about the dog: it understands 'take it' but not 'put it down', it collects bones, a pampered dog becomes a puppy, a rabid dog is flayed (ETCSL 6.2.3 42:1-3, ETCSL 6.2.3 44:1-2, ETCSL 6.2.3 46:1, ETCSL 6.2.3 47:1-2, ETCSL 6.2.3 51:1-5, ETCSL 6.2.3 53:1-3)
- Saying (of a hibernating bear): were the high god not to bestow sleep, creatures would expire (ETCSL 6.2.3 57:1-3)
- Fables of the fox: it boasts, plots treachery, hides under a thorn bush from a dog, frets over its mother (ETCSL 6.2.3 59:1-3, ETCSL 6.2.3 60:1-2, ETCSL 6.2.3 63:1-5, ETCSL 6.2.3 64:1-2)

**Proverbs from Urim 65-81: intelligence and strength, the quick and the strong, abominations to Utu, the slanderer, no child without sin**
- Saying: strength cannot keep pace with intelligence (ETCSL 6.2.3 65:1)
- Saying: do not give the lame man a club for his arm; Enlil will be his help (ETCSL 6.2.3 68:1-2, ETCSL 6.2.3 69:1-2)
- Saying: the slave girl with no authority over her mistress pulls her husband's hair instead (ETCSL 6.2.3 71:1-2, ETCSL 6.2.3 72:1-3)
- Saying: one city does not greet another, but one person greets another (ETCSL 6.2.3 75:1-2)
- The slanderer and liar is pointed at from behind; a goddess crushes his head and the sun god, lover of justice, extirpates wickedness and prolongs righteousness (ETCSL 6.2.3 78:1-10)
- When battle and war arise the plans of the gods are destroyed and the fire god devours the land (ETCSL 6.2.3 79:4-8)
- A wealthy man's fortune is dispersed and he cannot work out why: things change, no one knows what will happen (ETCSL 6.2.3 80:5-9)

**Proverbs from Urim 82-107: the man without a god, honouring elders, the mouse and mongoose, barley and silver, the unburied despiser of god**
- Fable: a mouse fallen from the roof beams tells the solicitous mongoose to keep away (ETCSL 6.2.3 89:1-5)
- Saying: what is in mankind's mouth is as hard to hide as a wall; do not slander the boy of your town (ETCSL 6.2.3 95:1-4)
- Fable: a little mouse says no one saw it go out; its mother answers that whoever saw it will carry it off (ETCSL 6.2.3 96:1-4)
- Saying: 'Although I spoke, what did I gain? I covered up for myself, but what success did it bring me?' (ETCSL 6.2.3 97:1-4)
- Saying: man's intelligence (umuš) comes from god (ETCSL 6.2.3 104:1-3)
- A man who does not value his god is thrown out in the desert unburied, and his heir pours no water for his ghost through the libation pipe (ETCSL 6.2.3 107:1-3)

**Proverbs from Urim 108-151: each tool to its craftsman, sins absolved, the mule, each creature to its hole, the just man's long life, abominations to Utu**
- Saying: the axe belongs to the carpenter, the stone to the smith, the good malt to the brewer (ETCSL 6.2.3 108:1-3)
- Saying: pleasure is created, sins are absolved (nam-tag du8), life is rejuvenated (ETCSL 6.2.3 111:1-3)
- Saying: 'O mule, do you know your sire, do you know your mother?' (ETCSL 6.2.3 117:1-2)
- Wish: let the snake find its deep hole, the scorpion its crevice and the hyena its exit (ETCSL 6.2.3 118:1-2)
- Saying: brotherhood is founded on the words of a quarrel; at the witness box friendship becomes known (ETCSL 6.2.3 128:1-2)
- Saying: by following craftiness one learns to be crafty, by following wisdom one learns to be wise (ETCSL 6.2.3 135:1-2)
- Saying: earth is greater than heaven; who can destroy it? (ETCSL 6.2.3 136:1)
- Saying: adding an inheritance share to an inheritance share is an abomination to Utu (ETCSL 6.2.3 150:1)

**Proverbs from Unug: Enlil holds up the sky, hunger his greatest punishment, the winds**
- Saying: he (Enlil) holds up the sky and lets the earth dangle from his hands (ETCSL 6.2.4 1.B:2)
- Saying: Enlil's greatest punishment is hunger (ETCSL 6.2.4 1.B:3)
- Sayings on the winds: the east wind brings rain and prosperity, the west wind is greater than those who live there (ETCSL 6.2.4 1.B:10-13)

**Proverbs of unknown provenance 1-3: wealth and sleep, the unique warrior, the slave girls, the Dilmun ship, the lion and the nameless plants**
- Saying: the warrior is unique; he alone is the equal of many (ETCSL 6.2.5 1.A:9)
- Saying: a Dilmun ship sank although there was no wind (disaster without visible cause) (ETCSL 6.2.5 2.A:1)
- Fable-saying: to a list of named plants the lion roars 'these have no names' (ETCSL 6.2.5 2.B:2-5)
- Saying: the fool's lot was created by Utu (ETCSL 6.2.5 2.B:6)

**Proverbs of unknown provenance 4-5: eyes lifted to Enlil for the cursed city, revenge belongs to Ninurta, poor and rich**
- Farmer, herdsman, potter and gardener each lift their gaze to Enlil: 'may Enlil look upon the city that he cursed' (ETCSL 6.2.5 4.A:7-14)
- Saying: a palace will fall of its own accord (ETCSL 6.2.5 4.B:2)

**Proverbs of unknown provenance 6-12: righteousness, the fattened pig, what the god destroyed, Enlil's chaff, the snake charmer**
- Saying: what has been destroyed belongs to a god; no one can take it away (ETCSL 6.2.5 7:6-7)
- A snake charmer has a snake and pulls out its tooth (ETCSL 6.2.5 11:3-4)
- Saying: touching a woman's genitals over her clothes is an abomination to the moon god (ETCSL 6.2.5 10.A:1-3)

**Proverbs of unknown provenance 13-43: just decisions, the river ordeal, the man without a god, the city of the lame, the king as scribe, the floating millstone**
- Saying: if the leader is consumed by fire, those behind him do not ask 'where is the leader?' (ETCSL 6.2.5 25:1-2)
- Saying: the king is a scribe; the king is a mighty bond blocking the river (ETCSL 6.2.5 41:1)

**Dumuzid's dream: the shepherd's foreboding lament, his dream, and the call for an interpreter**
- A doomed shepherd god calls on the steppe, the reed-beds, the crabs and frogs of the river and his mother to raise a lament for him (ETCSL 1.4.3 4-11)
- The doomed man tells his mother she will not know the day he dies and asks her to weep for him (ETCSL 1.4.3 12-14)

**Dumuzid's dream: the dream told item by item and Ĝeštinana's interpretation of it as his death**
- A sister, skilled in dreams, interprets her brother's dream item by item as foretelling his capture and death (ETCSL 1.4.3 41-70)
- In an ominous dream a bird of prey seizes a lamb from the sheep-house and a falcon catches a sparrow in the reed fence (ETCSL 1.4.3 35-36, ETCSL 1.4.3 60, ETCSL 1.4.3 62)

**Dumuzid's dream: the sister on the mound sees the demons coming; Dumuzid hides in the grass and binds sister and friend to silence**
- A woman climbs a mound to look out and sees the pursuers coming for her brother (ETCSL 1.4.3 71-89)
- The fugitive binds his helpers by a curse: if you reveal my hiding place, may your own dog devour you (ETCSL 1.4.3 95-97, ETCSL 1.4.3 107-109)

**Dumuzid's dream: the demons described, the sister refuses their gifts, the friend betrays him; Dumuzid is caught**
- Demons come for the victim in pairs from each city in turn (Adab, Akšak, Unug, Urim, Nibru) (ETCSL 1.4.3 119-129)
- Demons offer the sister a river full of water and a field full of grain to reveal her brother's hiding place; she refuses (ETCSL 1.4.3 130-139)
- The victim's friend accepts the demons' gift of water and grain and reveals where he hides (ETCSL 1.4.3 140-150)
- The betrayed man blesses the loyal helper's child and curses the betrayer's child: one shall be kissed in the street, the other not (ETCSL 1.4.3 154-155)

**Dumuzid's dream: refuge in Old Woman Belili's house, recapture, a last plea, flight to the sister's sheepfold**
- The fugitive takes refuge in the house of an old woman (Old Woman Belili), pretending to be a god's spouse and asking for water and flour (ETCSL 1.4.3 205-216)

**Dumuzid's dream: the sister's lament, the demons enter the sheepfold seven times, the dream fulfilled and Dumuzid dead**
- The demons enter the sheepfold one after another (seven times), striking the door, the wood, the churn and the cup, until the god is dead (ETCSL 1.4.3 249-260)

**The marriage of Martu: the city of Inab in former days, the food portions, and Martu's request to his mother for a wife**
- At the distribution of food portions the married man gets two, the man with a child three, the bachelor one (ETCSL 1.7.1 19-25, ETCSL 1.7.1 34-40)
- A young god sees that married men get double food portions and asks his mother to let him take a wife (ETCSL 1.7.1 26-33, ETCSL 1.7.1 41-43)
- The mother answers her son's request for a wife: listen to my word, take a wife where your eyes and heart choose (ETCSL 1.7.1 44-51)

**The marriage of Martu: the festival of Inab, Martu's wrestling victory, his refusal of silver and request for Numušda's daughter, and his marriage gifts**
- At a city festival the hero wrestles (ĝešba) in the great courtyard and fells all comers (ETCSL 1.7.1 53-75)
- The victor refuses silver and precious stones and asks instead for the god's daughter in marriage (ETCSL 1.7.1 76-83)

**The marriage of Martu: gifts to the people of Inab, the friend's warning that Martu is an uncivilised nomad, and Adĝarkidug's answer 'I will marry Martu'**
- The nomad is described as uncivilized: lives in tents in wind and rain, offers no prayer, digs truffles, does not bend the knee, eats raw meat, has no house in life and no burial at death (ETCSL 1.7.1 126-138)
- A friend warns the girl against marrying an uncouth outsider, but she replies 'I will marry Martu' (ETCSL 1.7.1 139-141)

**Ninĝišzida's journey to the nether world: the god boards the barge while his sisters lament at prow and stern**
- The young dying god is addressed by a litany of his names (Damu, Ninĝišzida, Ištaran, Alla, Lugalšud ...) (ETCSL 1.7.3 5-9, ETCSL 1.7.3 19-24)

**Ninĝišzida's journey: the sister asks why the demon takes him; the nether world gives no water, flour or wool; she offers her jewels**
- In the nether world the river gives no water to drink, the field no flour, the sheep no wool (ETCSL 1.7.3 36, ETCSL 1.7.3 37, ETCSL 1.7.3 38)
- The doomed god likens himself to a canal his mother dug that now gives no water, a tamarisk without shade, a date palm whose fruit no one enjoys (ETCSL 1.7.3 32a, ETCSL 1.7.3 33a, ETCSL 1.7.3 34)

**Ninĝišzida's journey: Amašilama pleads with the demon and offers her lapis, the barge sets off, the lament for Urim and its en, and the god's arrival before Ereškigal**
- A sister offers the chief demon her lapis jewels and asks that her brother on his way to the nether world be given bread and water (ETCSL 1.7.3 39-49)
- The lament calls on the city and its shrine 'your house, ah!' as its en priest leaves the ĝipar (ETCSL 1.7.3 58-61, ETCSL 1.7.3 78-87)
- In mourning the king's head is rolled in the dust and his feet trodden in the mire of the street (ETCSL 1.7.3 82-85)
- The god in the nether world is honoured on his throne, eats and drinks and is pleased by the lyre of Ereškigal (ETCSL 1.7.3 76-77, ETCSL 1.7.3 87a-90)

**Kirugu 3: Ningal cannot sleep; she wails day and night for the doom of her city (Lament for Urim 76-135)**
- A grieving goddess finds no sleep or rest in her bedchamber by night because of the coming doom of her city (ETCSL 2.2.2 80, ETCSL 2.2.2 99-100)
- The destroyed house is like a tent or harvest-field shelter torn open and exposed to wind and rain (ETCSL 2.2.2 127-128)

**Kirugu 4: Ningal twice pleads with An and Enlil in the assembly, but their word does not change (Lament for Urim 136-171)**
- A city goddess weeps before the high gods (An, Enlil) and begs them 'let my city not be destroyed, let its people not perish', but they do not change their word (ETCSL 2.2.2 143-148, ETCSL 2.2.2 154-158)

**Kirugu 5: Enlil calls the storm; fire, darkness and the sunless day cover Urim like a cloak (Lament for Urim 172-206)**
- The high god hands the destroying storm over to a divine storm-keeper or enlists the fire god as its helper (ETCSL 2.2.2 176, ETCSL 2.2.2 179)

**Kirugu 6: the city made ruin mounds; corpses in gates and streets; families torn apart; Elam sacks Ekišnuĝal (Lament for Urim 207-253)**
- After the sack corpses lie in the city's great gate, its festival streets and its roads (ETCSL 2.2.2 211-215)
- The bodies of the slain melt away like fat left in the sun (ETCSL 2.2.2 217)
- The slain lie like a gazelle caught in a trap, their mouths biting the dust (ETCSL 2.2.2 219)
- Little children lying in their mothers' laps are carried off like fish by the water (ETCSL 2.2.2 228-229)
- The destroyers value the holy house at a contemptible thirty shekels (ETCSL 2.2.2 243)

**Kirugu 7: Ningal's lament in the first person: An cursed my city, my children are carried off, I am no longer its queen (Lament for Urim 254-330)**
- The goddess's daughters and sons are carried off as captives in boats to a foreign city (ETCSL 2.2.2 283-284)
- A goddess laments that her city no longer exists for her and she is no longer its queen (ETCSL 2.2.2 286-287, ETCSL 2.2.2 302-303)
- The displaced goddess asks where she is to sit and stand: shall another city or house be built for her in place of her own? (ETCSL 2.2.2 288-296, ETCSL 2.2.2 306-308)

**Kirugu 8: 'Lady, how can your heart endure?': priests, festivals and music gone; return to your city (Lament for Urim 331-389)**
- In the ruined land there is no lament-singer left to perform the penitential lament; he has gone to foreign lands (ETCSL 2.2.2 343)
- The bricks of the ruined temple cry out like a person to the departed deity: 'Where are you?' (ETCSL 2.2.2 372)
- The departed deity is begged to return to her city like an ox to its pen, a sheep to its fold, a young child to its chamber (ETCSL 2.2.2 378-380)

**Kirugu 10: the storm that knows no mother or father; may it not return; its account hung on Enlil's peg (Lament for Urim 400-417)**
- The destroying storm knows neither mother nor father, wife nor child, sister, brother nor neighbour (ETCSL 2.2.2 402-406)
- Prayer that the city gates be bolted against the storm as gates are barred at night, so that it never returns (ETCSL 2.2.2 414)
- The account (tally) of the catastrophe is closed and hung on a peg in the high god's house, never to be reopened (ETCSL 2.2.2 415-416)

**Kirugu 11: closing prayer to Nanna: the humble seize your feet; release their sin; restore the city (Lament for Urim 418-438)**
- A man's personal god brings a greeting gift (kadra) to the great god on behalf of the man who prays (ETCSL 2.2.2 427, ETCSL 2.2.2 432A)

**Šulgi as provisioner of E-kur; Urim with its holy chest of the abzu; Enlil's good day for Šulgi's reign (Šulgi G 35-70)**
- A holy chest or box (dub-šen) of the god, kept in the heart of the city or temple, which no eye has seen (ETCSL 2.4.2.07 sa–jara.C:45)

**Fragments of a tigi for Šulgi: the shepherd, the physician, conquest of the rebel land (Šulgi L)**
- The king is praised as a physician (a-zu) who heals (ETCSL 2.4.2.12 sa–gida.A:3, ETCSL 2.4.2.12 sa–gida.A:5)

**A mother's lullaby for a son of Šulgi: come, sleep; a wife and son for you (Šulgi N)**
- A mother sings a lullaby to her son: 'Come, sleep, come to my son; put his restless eyes to sleep' (ETCSL 2.4.2.14 10-18, ETCSL 2.4.2.14 92)
- The lullaby promises the baby a wife and a son of his own, a nursemaid and a happy future (ETCSL 2.4.2.14 27-38, ETCSL 2.4.2.14 57-59)

**Šulgi goes to Eridug, Nibru, Ešumeša, Keš, Urim, Ebabbar, Kulaba and Zabalam, and each god rejoices**
- The king travels in turn to the temple cities of the great gods, and at each the god rejoices at his coming (ETCSL 2.4.2.a 5-36)

**Hymn for Šu-Suen: god of abundance born of Uraš, chosen by Enlil and Ninlil, born for godhood (kirugu 1-4 and fragment)**
- The king is called a hero born for godhood (nam-diŋir), fit for the ornaments of kingship (ETCSL 2.4.4.a :41)

**Išbi-Erra, farmer of Enlil, against Kindattu the Elamite (Išbi-Erra B, fragments)**
- The enemy army is cut off and dies of thirst in the open steppe where ghosts (lil2) howl (ETCSL 2.5.1.2 Seg.E:5-6)

**Adab to Enlil: the Anuna look to Enlil whose word is unalterable; the E-kur's mystery; long reign for Išme-Dagan (Išme-Dagan H)**
- The inside of the god's temple is intricate and tied together, a thing no one knows (ETCSL 2.5.4.08 sa–gida.A:15-17)

**Dedication of a statue: Išme-Dagan the tireless runner sets up his running statue in Eniguru; curse on whoever erases its inscription (Išme-Dagan S)**
- The king sets up a copper statue of himself running in the temple, celebrating his tireless speed as a runner (ETCSL 2.5.4.19 23-25)
- Curse on whoever damages the king's inscription: the gods of rain, grain and herds withdraw abundance from heaven and earth (ETCSL 2.5.4.19 33-34)

**Hymn to Inana for Išme-Dagan: the goddess laments her house; Išme-Dagan restores justice and filial order in Sumer and Akkad**
- A goddess laments in the first person that the fate of her house and city has been cut off, her goods swallowed by the swamp, her mourning garment defiled (ETCSL 2.5.4.a unknown.A:9-13)

**Ur-Ninurta's foes struck down, An's unchangeable fate for him; the Anuna say 'so be it'; Inana, Suen's daughter, and the king go joyfully to the palace (Ur-Ninurta A 44-95)**
- After the high gods have decreed the king's fate, the goddess and the king leave the chief god's presence rejoicing and settle in the palace, a dwelling sweet as honey (ETCSL 2.5.6.1 :74-75)

**Hymn to Nanna for Gungunum: Dilimbabbar, firstborn of Enlil, who fixes the crescent and the months (Gungunum B, fragments)**
- The pair an-šar / ki-šar, 'the whole of heaven and the whole of earth', appears in a hymn (the later primordial pair Anšar and Kišar) (ETCSL 2.6.2.a Seg.B:2)

**Iškur the storm-lord, shade of Larsa and helper in battle; Sîn-iddinam restores Eridug's plans and makes Iškur a great throne with two bulls (Sîn-iddinam E)**
- The king fashions a great throne for the storm god, seats him on it, and sets beside it two great bull figures to gore the king's enemies right and left (ETCSL 2.6.6.5 54-58, ETCSL 2.6.6.5 68-70, ETCSL 2.6.6.5 75-78)

**Hymn to Marduk for a king: 'may you live, be well'; may your lot be life, your dream good, your omen good, your footing safe**
- Blessing on the king: when you lie down may your dream be favourable, when you rise may your chance utterance (omen) be favourable, may the place where you stand be safe (ETCSL 2.8.5.b 11-13, ETCSL 2.8.5.b 26-28)

**Letter-petition of Lugal-nesaĝe to a king radiant as the moon: like an ox without yoke, a cow without calf, a drifting boat; I eat tears in Nibru's street; restore me**
- The sufferer is like a bad tree bearing no fruit, in which no one rejoices (ETCSL 3.3.02 Ver.1:22-23)

**Letter from Ur-Enlila to a governor and temple administrator about canal water: 'It is urgent'**
- A dispute over the share of canal water: one channel each is assigned, but a neighbour's men obstruct the flow and the writer's channel gets no water (ETCSL 3.3.04 3-10)

**Letter from a governor and temple administrator to the king: the Dabta field of Enlil and Ninurta, hoed for lack of plough-teams; 'if my king approves, send a rider'**
- A large field assigned to the gods' temples is reported as partly given out as ration plots to men holding requisitions, and the king is asked to send someone to fix its boundary (ETCSL 3.3.05 Ver.1:3-6)

**Letter-prayer of Inanaka to the healing goddess Nintinuga: twice on my sickbed, friends gone; drive out the Asag demon and I will be your slave, sweeping your courtyard and proclaiming your name**
- The sick petitioner vows that if healed she will be the deity's slave, sweep the temple courtyard, stand before the deity and proclaim the deity's name (ETCSL 3.3.10 23-26)

**Letter from Inim-Inana to Lugal-ibila: do not neglect Sumerian; keep the boy at the scribal school**
- A letter urges that a boy be kept at the scribal school (e2-dub-ba-a) and that his correct Sumerian not be neglected (ETCSL 3.3.12 3-11)

**A hymn to Ḫendursaĝa, segment A 4-41: the night watchman of the streets**
- On the god's estate no inspector seizes the fish, no farmer takes dues, no herdsman counts the sheep for himself: his property is untouchable (ETCSL 4.06.1 Seg.A:31-36)

**A hymn to Ḫendursaĝa, segment A 42-87: the name at night, the priests, and the seven who are neither male nor female**
- A man who takes the god's name (swears or calls on it) is kept safe on the silent street at night (ETCSL 4.06.1 Seg.A:43-45)
- Seven ominous creatures are listed by number (the first is a fox, the second a dog, the third a raven ...), each with its gesture or cry (ETCSL 4.06.1 Seg.A:77-84)
- A band of seven (demons or divine agents) is 'neither female nor male' (ETCSL 4.06.1 Seg.A:85)
- The seven strike the man and bind the woman's arm, laying a weapon at her side (ETCSL 4.06.1 Seg.A:86-87)

**A hymn to Ḫendursaĝa, segment A 89-105: the gods who stand beside him**
- Litany: at each holy place a named deity 'stands beside you' (ša-ra-da-gub) to serve the god (ETCSL 4.06.1 Seg.A:92-93, ETCSL 4.06.1 :81, ETCSL 4.06.1 :83, ETCSL 4.06.1 Seg.A:98-105)

**A hymn to Ḫendursaĝa, segment B: Enki's seven sons and their offerings**
- Enki begets seven sons, who become a band of seven brothers in a god's service (ETCSL 4.06.1 Seg.B:9-13)
- Litany of seven brothers: the first, second, third ... each stands beside the god and brings his due (beer, water, fish, bread, barley, syrup and wine) (ETCSL 4.06.1 Seg.B:14-46)

**A hymn to Ḫendursaĝa, segment C 1-30: the man who has no god and the man whose god is in heaven**
- The storm-wind sinks the boat in the reed-bed and at sea for the man whom no god protects (ETCSL 4.06.1 Seg.C:26-28)

**A hymn to Ḫendursaĝa, segment C 31-57: Utu at the scales, purchases and marriage**
- The sun god takes his stand at the place of the scales (ki ĝiš-erin2), the seat of fair dealing and judgment (ETCSL 4.06.1 Seg.C:31-32, ETCSL 4.06.1 Seg.C:47)
- With the god's consent a man takes a wife, begets children and builds a house; the husband speaks kindly to his wife and she sits amid plenty (ETCSL 4.06.1 Seg.C:48-55)

**A hymn to Inana (ETCSL 4.07.a), fragmentary**
- A goddess wears An's holy crown and garment and holds An's sceptre, sitting in the assembly to decide the great case (ETCSL 4.07.a 4-9)
- The goddess says her spouse (Ama-ušumgal-ana) chose her for marriage (ETCSL 4.07.a 30-34, ETCSL 4.07.a 43)
- The allure of Dumuzid is like a poplar (ildag) standing tall (ETCSL 4.07.a 46-47)

**A balbale to Inana (Dumuzid-Inana O): the litany of blessings may-you-be**
- The lover walks along the bank of the river (Euphrates) (ETCSL 4.08.15 3-7)

**A song of Inana and Dumuzid (Dumuzid-Inana R), main text**
- The girl (Inana) is praised as a speckled grain heap fit for the king and as fragrant oil (ETCSL 4.08.18 sa–gida.A:1-12)

**A song of Inana and Dumuzid (Dumuzid-Inana R), versions 2 and 3**
- The herdsman finds no place in the pen, the ghee and milk are no longer brought: the fold is desolate (ETCSL 4.08.18 Ver.2:5-11)

**A kunĝar to Inana (Dumuzid-Inana T)**
- The goddess finds jewel after jewel and places each on a part of her body (hips, head, nape, hair, ears, eyes, nose, mouth, navel, thighs, vulva, feet) (ETCSL 4.08.20 sa–gida.A:9-22, ETCSL 4.08.20 :23, ETCSL 4.08.20 sa–gida.A:24)

**A song of Inana and Dumuzid (Dumuzid-Inana Y)**
- The beloved's body is praised as the work of craftsmen: beard of lapis, limbs of gold, made by a skilled carpenter and a skilled metal-worker (ETCSL 4.08.25 42-47)
- Blessing that the person's god go with him by night and by day and smooth his road (ETCSL 4.08.25 50a, ETCSL 4.08.25 62-65)

**A balbale to Inana and Dumuzid (ETCSL 4.08.a)**
- The churn of the sheepfold sings for the goddess and her shepherd-husband; she rejoices in the pen (ETCSL 4.08.a 4-12)

**A šir-gida to Martu (Martu A)**
- A god destroys evil and violence and establishes truth (niĝ2-gen6-na) as a just judge (ETCSL 4.12.1 25-27)
- The god of the Amorites (Martu) is given the pure lapis-lazuli mountain, the land of Martu, as his gift (ETCSL 4.12.1 30-32)
- The god destroys for the king the land that does not obey him and is the king's helper in battle (ETCSL 4.12.1 21-23, ETCSL 4.12.1 33)

**An excerpt from a hymn to Nanna (ETCSL 4.13.c)**
- The moon god is born of An and Uraš in Duranki and wears the holy tiara of Urim (ETCSL 4.13.c 3-5)

**A hymn to Nergal (Nergal B)**
- The warrior god (Nergal) is the lord who comes out of the mountains, from the place of the sa-gaz brigands (ETCSL 4.15.2 41)
- A god surpasses others and decrees fates together with the high god (ETCSL 4.15.2 37-39)

**A balbale to Ninazu (Ninazu A)**
- The god is the cowherd or herdsman of a city teeming like cows and sheep (ETCSL 4.17.1 1-5)
- The god receives the staff of en-ship, the sceptre and a golden crown from the moon god or An (ETCSL 4.17.1 13-14, ETCSL 4.17.1 23)
- The god's city and house are set in the 'pure place' of the netherworld (Enegir), his mother is lady of the Kiur (ETCSL 4.17.1 19-22)
- The god's wife stands before him in prayer for his house and city (ETCSL 4.17.1 29-30)

**A balbale to Ninĝišzida (Ninĝišzida A)**
- The god is a great snake (muš-mah) yoked with a dragon (ušumgal) (ETCSL 4.19.1 1-2)
- The god sucked the true milk at the holy breast of his loving mother (ETCSL 4.19.1 4-5)
- The god is the shepherd who knows the number of the black-headed people and goes to seek the ewes and lambs (ETCSL 4.19.1 12-15)

**A hymn to Ninimma (Ninimma A)**
- A goddess holds the lapis measuring line and the measuring rod (ETCSL 4.21.1 Seg.A:8)

**A tigi to Nintur (Nintur A)**
- The mother goddess gives birth to the en priest, the lagar priest and the king on his holy dais (ETCSL 4.26.1 sa–gida.A:8-12)
- The mother goddess calls out like a cow for its calf, seeking with a lament (ETCSL 4.26.1 sa–jara.B:28-33)
- En-ship and kingship are placed in Enlil's hand (ETCSL 4.26.1 sa–jara.B:39, ETCSL 4.26.1 sa–jara.B:43)
- The mother goddess (Nintur, Aruru) of Keš, born on the pure mountain, mother of the lands (ETCSL 4.26.1 sa–gida.A:1-6)

**A balbale to Ninurta (Ninurta F)**
- Litany: for the god's sake the ewe bears the lamb, the goat the kid, the cow the calf, the donkey its foal, mankind children (ETCSL 4.27.06 8-21)
- The god or king is 'named' (mu pad3) by Enlil: true water, true seed (ETCSL 4.27.06 1-7)

**A hymn to Nungal, 1-26: the house of judgment and its gates**
- The goddess's prison-house is described part by part: gate of evening, stair a dragon with open jaws, jambs daggers, foundations scorpions, bolts lions and snakes, arch like a rainbow (ETCSL 4.28.1 12-24)
- The great door does not open for the evildoer but opens for the righteous man (ETCSL 4.28.1 20-21)
- The house of judgment searches out the sinner (lu2 nam-tag-ga kiŋ2-kiŋ2) and separates the just from the evil (ETCSL 4.28.1 9-11)

**A hymn to Nungal, 27-61: the goddess enthroned, the prisoner led in, the ordeal**
- The goddess sits on her great throne to judge cases, knowing true and false, and spreads her net over the land (ETCSL 4.28.1 27-39)
- The prisoner is led in with his eyes covered; acquaintances do not speak to him, brother neglects brother and friends no longer recognise one another (ETCSL 4.28.1 43-54)
- The bricks of the prison crush the wicked and give birth to the righteous man (ETCSL 4.28.1 56)
- In the prison-house hearts are full of tears and laments all day long (ETCSL 4.28.1 55, ETCSL 4.28.1 57)

**A hymn to Nungal, 62-121: the goddess's self-praise; compassion and the prisoner's release**
- The goddess calls herself a compassionate mother who lifts the heavy sin from a man's hand and cools the angry heart (ETCSL 4.28.1 75, ETCSL 4.28.1 79-83)
- The prisoner, cleansed like good silver and rubbed clean of dust, is returned into the kindly hand of his personal god, who praises the goddess (ETCSL 4.28.1 103-111)
- The goddess proclaims herself daughter of An, bride (daughter-in-law) of Enlil and heir of Ereškigal, with a dais in the netherworld (ETCSL 4.28.1 64-69)
- The deity knows the false and the true (lul zid-bi mu-zu) when judging (ETCSL 4.28.1 91, ETCSL 4.28.1 103)

**A hymn to Šul-pa-e (Šul-pa-e A), version 1, 1-40: the hero and lord of the steppe**
- Mankind prays to the god like a frightened bird (ETCSL 4.31.1 Ver.1:20)
- Namtar, the fate demon, has neither hands nor feet and carries men off by night (ETCSL 4.31.1 Ver.1:32-33)
- The god is king of the orchards and gardens and of the four-legged creatures of the broad steppe, given into his hand by An (ETCSL 4.31.1 Ver.1:34-39)
- The god is the beloved husband of the mother goddess Ninḫursaĝa (ETCSL 4.31.1 Ver.1:13-14)

**A hymn to Šul-pa-e (Šul-pa-e A), version 1, 41-85: the man who forgot his god is restored**
- The man who had his grass and water in plenty ate and drank but did not invoke his god's name (ETCSL 4.31.1 Ver.1:41-44)
- A god is the en of Enlil's table (banquet steward) whose laid portions no one may diminish (ETCSL 4.31.1 Ver.1:49-52)
- The god (or king) is 'full of pity' (šag4-la2 sug4) for the lands (ETCSL 4.31.1 Ver.1:83-84)

**A hymn to Utu (Utu B)**
- The sun god is called the great physician (a-zu gal) and father of the black-headed (ETCSL 4.32.2 2)
- The god is like an eagle over the colourful mountains, his eye on the land (ETCSL 4.32.2 30-32)

**The debate between Winter and Summer, 1-79: Enlil begets the seasons and fixes their tasks**
- Enlil couples with the great mountains and begets Summer and Winter, then fixes each one's destiny (ETCSL 5.3.3 11-18)
- Each season is assigned its work: Summer founds houses, cities and harvest; Winter brings the flood, lambs, calves, fish-spawn and fruit (ETCSL 5.3.3 20-24, ETCSL 5.3.3 26-32, ETCSL 5.3.3 50-66)
- Opening of a creation account: An raises his head, a good day comes forth, Enlil sets his foot on the earth and plans abundance (ETCSL 5.3.3 1-10)

**The debate between Winter and Summer, 88-152: Winter's gifts, his envy and the quarrel**
- One brother is filled with envy (ninim) at the other's offering and picks a quarrel with him (ETCSL 5.3.3 107-112)

**The debate between Winter and Summer, 153-258: insults and replies**
- In winter people sit by the oven and the fire; the scribe and the musician do not leave it (ETCSL 5.3.3 158-163)
- The beer goddess Ninkasi is a season's helper and makes the beer sweet (ETCSL 5.3.3 246)
- A named king of Ur (Ibbi-Suen) is praised within a debate poem as recipient of the season's goods (ETCSL 5.3.3 229-240)
- A catalogue of craftsmen and labourers (reed-cutter, builder, potter, weaver, brewer, cook) each named with his work (ETCSL 5.3.3 207-215)

**The debate between Winter and Summer, 259-318: Enlil's verdict and the reconciliation**
- After the verdict the losing brother kneels to the winner; they feast with beer and exchange gold, silver and lapis, and brotherhood is restored (ETCSL 5.3.3 301-315)

**A drinking song (ETCSL 5.5.a)**
- Drinking beer makes the heart happy and the liver joyful (ETCSL 5.5.a 3-4, ETCSL 5.5.a 15, ETCSL 5.5.a 25-29)
- A song lists the brewing vessels one by one (vats, jars, troughs, baskets, pot-stands) (ETCSL 5.5.a 1-9)
- The goddess's heart is restored (šag4 ki-bi ba-ab-gi4) by the drinking and celebration (ETCSL 5.5.a 30-31)

**The farmer's instructions, 1-40: the father's teaching; irrigation, oxen, tools and ploughing**
- Farming rule: watch the dykes and canals; when flooding the field, do not let the water rise too high (ETCSL 5.6.3 2-8)
- Before the work the farmer makes ready his tools: hoes of fixed weight, yoke, whip on its peg, basket (ETCSL 5.6.3 9-22)
- The farmer is given quotas: one plough works 180 iku, you work 144; 18 iku need 3 gur of seed (ETCSL 5.6.3 23-37)
- The farmer is told not to be idle at his work, so that no one has to tell him to work his field (ETCSL 5.6.3 34-40)

**The farmer's instructions, 41-73: sowing, the prayer against pests, watering**
- Precise farming rule: the seed must go two fingers deep, one shekel of barley per rod of furrow (ETCSL 5.6.3 46-51)
- Farming rule: where straight furrows were sown sow slanting ones next, and the reverse; change the share if the seed does not go in (ETCSL 5.6.3 52-62)
- When the seedlings break through, the farmer prays to Ninkilim (lord of field rodents) and drives off the birds (ETCSL 5.6.3 64-66)
- The barley is watered at fixed stages of growth; watering at the wrong time brings blight (ETCSL 5.6.3 67-73)

**The farmer's instructions, 74-111: reaping, gleaners, threshing, winnowing; Ninurta the farmer**
- Reap at the right time, before the grain bends under its own weight (ETCSL 5.6.3 74-78)
- A prayer (sizkur2) is said at each stage of the harvest: over the grain-heap, before winnowing, at evening and night (ETCSL 5.6.3 87-88, ETCSL 5.6.3 103, ETCSL 5.6.3 108)
- Threshing with a sledge whose teeth are fastened with leather and bitumen, drawn by oxen (ETCSL 5.6.3 89-102)
- Two men lift the grain to winnow it; the winnowed grain is laid down like a sceptre (ETCSL 5.6.3 104-109)
- Ninurta is praised as Enlil's true farmer, the source of the farmer's instructions (ETCSL 5.6.3 110-111)

**A man and his god, 28-81: the young man's complaint**
- The sufferer protests that he is wise and his words were true, yet he is bound with the ignorant and his truth is turned into a lie (ETCSL 5.2.4 28-31, ETCSL 5.2.4 44-45)
- Others have their share of food; the sufferer's share is toil and hardship (ETCSL 5.2.4 46-47)
- The sufferer asks his mother, sister and wife to weep and lament his fate before his god (ETCSL 5.2.4 62-68)
- For the land the god's day is bright; for the sufferer the day is dark (ETCSL 5.2.4 69)

**A man and his god, 120-146: the god hears and restores; the young man praises**
- The god hears the tears and pure words of the sufferer, removes his sickness, turns his suffering to joy and sets good spirits to guard him (ETCSL 5.2.4 120-132)
- Subscript naming the composition an eršaĝ-ḫuĝa, a lament 'to soothe the heart' of a god (ETCSL 5.2.4 144-146)

**The old man and the young girl (ETCSL 5.6.6)**
- An old man marries a young girl, and her complaint is brought before the king (ETCSL 5.6.6 1-12)
- An old man describes his failing body in images: his youth fled like a runaway donkey, his black mountain grew white gypsum, his teeth no longer grind, his urine no longer flows (ETCSL 5.6.6 33-37d)
- A wronged woman brings her case to the king, who consults a wise woman and hears both parties before judging (ETCSL 5.6.6 13-41)

**Public announcement of the loss of a seal (ETCSL 5.7.a)**
- A herald announces in the streets that a man's seal is lost, so that no claim may be made against him with it; witnesses are named (ETCSL 5.7.a 1-12)

**Adapa (Middle Babylonian), 1'-38': the broken wing of the South Wind and Ea's instructions**
- The hero's patron god tells him that he will be offered bread and water of death in heaven and must not eat or drink, but must accept garment and oil (Adapa MB –:32'-38')
- The hero's patron god secretly instructs him how to behave before the high god and insists he hold fast to the advice (Adapa MB –:15'-18', Adapa MB –:37'-38')

**Adapa (Middle Babylonian), 39'-78': Adapa before Anu refuses the bread and water of life**
- The high god orders the mortal visitor to be taken back down to his earth (Adapa MB –:77')

**Adapa (Standard Babylonian), a+1-a+24: the sage of Eridu, given wisdom but not eternal life**
- Adapa, the sage (apkallu) of Eridu, was created by Ea in primeval days as a model among men, a sage whose word none could set aside (Adapa SB –:a+5-a+8)
- The sage is pure, of clean hands and anointed, baking bread and setting the god's table daily with his own hands (Adapa SB –:a+9-a+15)
- The sage's boat sails on the wide sea without steering oar or punting pole (Adapa SB –:a+19-a+22)

**Adapa (Standard Babylonian), b+1-c+19: the South Wind, the messenger, Ea's preparation**
- Ea, wide of understanding, knows and examines the hearts of the great gods (Adapa SB –:c+4-c+5, Adapa SB –:c+10)

**Adapa (Standard Babylonian), d+1-f+10: the refusal, Anu's laughter, the view of heaven, the cure for the wind's disease**
- Taken up to heaven, the mortal looks from the horizon (base of heaven) to the heights of heaven and sees its awesomeness (Adapa SB –:e+7-e+8)
- The disease brought by a wind on mankind is to be relieved by the bandages of the healing goddess (Adapa SB –:e+15-e+21)

**Advice to a Prince, 1-15: the king who does not heed justice**
- Conditional warning to the king: if he does not heed justice, his people fall into chaos, his land is devastated and the gods change his fate (AdvPrince SB –:1-6)
- Wisdom or warnings cast in the protasis-apodosis form of omens: 'if the king does X, then Y will happen' (AdvPrince SB –:1-15)

**Advice to a Prince, 35-55: seized oxen and taxed sheep; corrupt officials; the gods leave their shrines**
- The storm god (Adad) withholds water and the king's herds die of starvation as punishment (AdvPrince SB –:36, AdvPrince SB –:38-40)
- The corrupt official dies by the weapon, his place becomes waste, the wind carries away his remains and his works are counted as a puff of air (AdvPrince SB –:41-46)
- Nabu, the scribe of the gods, annuls the contracts of the land of a king who broke his people's contracts (AdvPrince SB –:49-50)

**Anzû (Neo-Assyrian), a+41-a+67: the tidings, the body hung on the Ekur, Ninurta blessed**
- The champion god is one 'who has no rival' (ša gabarê lā iršû) (Anzu NA –:a+61)

**Anzû (Old Babylonian) II 1-35: supremacy stolen; 'who will slay Anzû?'; the gods refuse**
- A monster bird seizes the supreme power (Enlil-ship) and the tablet of destinies; the gods' order collapses and they are struck dumb (Anzu OB II:1-5, Anzu OB II:19-22)
- Champion after champion is offered the greatest name if he will fight the monster, and each refuses (Anzu OB II:11-30)

**Anzû (Old Babylonian) II 36-82: Mami gives her son; the battle orders; the chariot of seven winds**
- The mother goddess, who bore all the gods, offers her son as champion and instructs him for battle (Anzu OB II:36-51)

**Anzû (Old Babylonian) III: the combat, the arrow that turns back, Ea's advice to cut the wings**
- The monster roars at the champion, boasts of the powers it holds and demands that he declare himself (Anzu OB III:3-6)
- The monster cries out to the arrow 'go back!' and the shaft returns without touching him (Anzu OB III:15-17)
- The champion is told to cut off the monster bird's pinions, so that it cries 'wing to wing' and falls (Anzu OB III:a+20-a+22, Anzu OB III:a+35)
- The victorious god is promised daises and shrines founded throughout the four world regions (Anzu OB III:a+27-a+29)

**Lugalirra called from the heaven of Anu at midnight against the catalogue of demons (Bit meseri IT 28-66)**
- The watches of the night and named stars (Pleiades, Yoke, Orion) are called upon as divine helpers in a night ritual (BitMeseri SB IT:45-53, BitMeseri SB IT:60)

**'You know them, I do not': the demons of the house and the gods posted in every room (Bit meseri IT 67-150)**
- Prayer: 'those whom you know but I do not know, whose street and lair you know but I do not' (BitMeseri SB IT:98-101)
- Gods are posted one by one at each part of the house (bedroom, courtyard, window, gate, threshold, back) to guard it (BitMeseri SB IT:126-141)

**The Divine Heptad and the seven primeval sages, the four of human descent and their offences (Bit meseri IT 260-347)**
- One of the primeval sages 'ascended to heaven' (or another descended from heaven) (BitMeseri SB IT:291-292, BitMeseri SB IT:344-345)
- Post-flood sages offend the gods (bringing a goddess down from heaven, enraging the storm god, hanging a seal on a goat-fish, releasing a dragon) and suffer for it (BitMeseri SB IT:297-304)
- A sage enrages the storm god so that there is no rain or green growth in the land for three years (BitMeseri SB IT:299-300)
- After the fish-sages come sages 'of human descent' to whom the wise god gives great wisdom; one is 'two-thirds sage' (BitMeseri SB IT:305-306)

**The watchmen of Ea and Asalluhi and the dogs of four colours at the gate (Bit meseri IT 399-443')**
- Dogs of four colours (white, black, red, brown-green) are drawn or invoked to guard the house, each with its own power (BitMeseri SB IT:412-427)

**The lamp greets Marduk; Nuska, king of the night, drives off Šulak; the Lugalirra figure thrown in the river (Bit meseri IT 473'-525')**
- Litany to a deity entering a house: 'with you may harmony, well-being, life, abundance, peace enter' (BitMeseri SB IT:482'-494')
- A night demon (Šulak) is 'the one who stalks by night, whose touch is death' (BitMeseri SB IT:508'-511')

**Feast for the gods of the watch; Death netted and sent down to Ereškigal, banned from the light and river of the living (Bit meseri IT 526'-B+611')**
- Curse on the banished evil: let him not see the bright light of the upper world, nor drink from the river of the living, nor walk the street of the living (BitMeseri SB IT:B+595'-B+599')

**Figurine list: number, form, attributes, place, recitation and ration of each figure (Bit meseri FI)**
- A figurine of Death himself (made of lead) is placed at the sick man's bed with provisions for his journey (BitMeseri SB FI:30)

**Catalogue of Texts and Authors: works from the mouth of Ea, revealed to Adapa, by sages, kings and scholars (Neo-Assyrian)**
- The core scholarly corpora (exorcism, lamentation, celestial omens, physiognomy) are said to be 'from the mouth of Ea' (CatAuth NA –:1-4)
- A literary work is 'what was revealed to' a named sage or poet and what he then proclaimed (CatAuth NA –:5-6, CatAuth NA –:b+1-b+2)
- A text is said to come 'from before the flood', written down by a primeval sage (CatAuth NA –:d+21-d+22)
- Who dictated and who wrote down a prophet's book (CatAuth NA –:d+21-d+26)

**A sage's counsel to his son: honour parents, beware drink, gossip and disputes, repay evil with good (Counsels of Wisdom 1-54)**
- Advice to a son: father and mother are (like) the gods of the house; honour them and they will bless you (CounsWis SB –:10)
- Saying: the man who loves strong drink will quickly become a pauper and lose friends, god and protective spirit (CounsWis SB –:15-21)
- Do not converse with the gossip or consult the idler, lest you adopt their thinking and leave your own path (CounsWis SB –:22-26, CounsWis SB –:31)
- Do not stand in a crowd or press forward at a dispute: you will be made a witness in a case not your own (CounsWis SB –:32-41)

**Pity the weak, feed the hungry; no slave girl over the house, no prostitute for a wife (Counsels of Wisdom A+1-A+31)**
- Take pity on the weak and helpless, give food to eat and drink to drink: god is pleased and Šamaš repays with favour (CounsWis SB –:A+7-A+16)
- Do not let a slave girl become important in your house and rule it like a wife (CounsWis SB –:A+17-A+22)
- Do not marry a prostitute, a woman dedicated to a goddess, or a temple woman: she will not support you in trouble (CounsWis SB –:A+23-A+31)

**Read from the tablet: no backbiting, daily worship, reverence begets favour, keep your word (Counsels of Wisdom A+63-A+105)**
- Slander or gossip pictured as eating (CounsWis SB –:A+70-A+73)
- For every grain you offer your god, your return will be a talent (CounsWis SB –:A+82-A+84)
- If you have given your word, deliver and do not revoke it; promising and not delivering is abhorrent to the god (CounsWis SB –:A+94-A+97, CounsWis SB –:A+102-A+103)

**Master and servant: palace, dining, hunting, house-building (Dialogue of Pessimism 1-38)**
- Saying: the man who eats well is his own god; the god goes with the one whose hands are washed (DialPess SB –:12-13)
- The roaming man, dog, bird and wild ass are first praised as well fed, then pitied as homeless and broken (DialPess SB –:19-22, DialPess SB –:25-28)
- The man without a house is a fawner and two-thirds a fool who must beg and face his creditor (DialPess SB –:30-36)

**Silence before an adversary, doing something dishonest, loving a woman (Dialogue of Pessimism)**
- The criminal is executed, flayed, blinded, arrested or jailed (DialPess SB –:44-45)
- The man who loves a woman forgets sorrow and care (DialPess SB –:47-48)
- A woman is called a pitfall, a hole, a ditch and a sharp iron dagger that cuts a man's throat (DialPess SB –:51-52)

**Sacrifice to one's god, lending, a good deed for the country (Dialogue of Pessimism 53-78)**
- Sacrifice to one's god is a sound transaction, 'loan upon loan' credited by the god (DialPess SB –:56-57)
- Giving as a loan to God, repaid by him (DialPess SB –:56-57)
- Regular sacrifice trains one's god to follow like a dog, always demanding more rites and figurines (DialPess SB –:60-61)
- Lending is as sweet as falling in love, getting the loan back as painful as giving birth (DialPess SB –:67)
- A good deed done for one's land is laid up in the god's basket (credited by the god) (DialPess SB –:72-73)
- Walk over the ancient ruin mounds and look at the skulls of low and great: who was the evildoer, who the benefactor? (DialPess SB –:76-78)

**What then is good? Death (Dialogue of Pessimism 79-86)**
- Asked what then is good, the answer is death: to have one's neck broken and be thrown into the river (DialPess SB –:80-82)
- The master threatens to kill his servant; the servant retorts that the master will not outlive him by three days (DialPess SB –:85-86)

**When on high: Apsu and Tiamat and the generations of the gods (Enuma elish I 1-20)**
- Things do not yet exist because they have not yet been named; coming into being is being called by name (Ee SB I:1-2, Ee SB I:8, Ee SB I:10)
- Before anything was named, the primeval fresh-water (Apsu) and salt sea (Tiamat) mingle their waters as the parents of all (Ee SB I:3-5)
- Pairs of gods are born generation after generation, each surpassing its parents (theogony) (Ee SB I:9-17)

**Birth and splendour of Marduk (Enuma elish I 79-104)**
- The hero god is born in a holy chamber, suckled by goddesses, a hero from birth, surpassing all in form (Ee SB I:79-88)
- The god has four eyes and four ears, sees in every direction, and fire breaks out when his lips move (Ee SB I:93-98)

**Kakka delivers the message; the gods assemble, feast and decree Marduk's destiny (Enuma elish III 67-138)**
- The gods feast, drink beer until carefree, and then decree the champion's destiny (Ee SB III:129-138)

**Marduk enthroned; the test of his word; 'Marduk is king!' (Enuma elish IV 1-34)**
- To prove the power of his word the god by command destroys a thing and by command makes it whole again (Ee SB IV:19-26)

**Single combat: Marduk slays Tiamat (Enuma elish IV 65-104)**
- When the monster opens her mouth to swallow him, the god drives the winds into it and bloats her, then shoots her through the heart (Ee SB IV:95-102)

**Captives netted, Tablet of Destinies taken, Tiamat split into heaven (Enuma elish IV 105-146)**
- Guards are posted on the sky-hide so that the monster's (upper) waters do not escape (Ee SB IV:139-140)

**Marduk orders stars, year, moon and sun (Enuma elish V 1-46)**
- The creator instructs the moon how to wax, be half on the seventh day, full at mid-month and vanish at month's end (Ee SB V:13-22)

**Trophies, homage, robing and the name Lugaldimmerankia (Enuma elish V 67-116)**
- Images of the defeated monsters are set up at the gate as a sign 'lest they be forgotten' (Ee SB V:73-76)
- Still covered with the dust of battle, the victor is anointed, robed and enthroned with mace and crown (Ee SB V:89-99)

**Humankind made from Qingu's blood to bear the gods' toil (Enuma elish VI 1-38)**
- The assembly is asked who started the rebellion; the guilty god is handed over, bound and executed (Ee SB VI:13-32)

**Gods divided above and below; the gods build Babylon and Esagila and feast (Enuma elish VI 39-81)**
- The supreme god divides the gods into upper and lower, posting 300 in heaven and 300 below (Ee SB VI:39-46)
- The gods themselves mould bricks for a year and build the supreme god's temple and ziggurat as thanks for release from toil (Ee SB VI:49-66)

**The bow set in heaven; oath of allegiance; Marduk to be shepherd of humankind (Enuma elish VI 82-122)**
- The warrior god's bow is laid before the gods, kissed, named, and set in heaven as the 'Bow Star' (Ee SB VI:82-92)
- The god shall do on earth the same as what he did in heaven (Ee SB VI:112)
- Though peoples are divided as to their gods, whatever name is invoked, he (the one god) is our god (Ee SB VI:119-120)

**Names Enbilulu to 'Lord of the Lands' (Enuma elish VII 57-136)**
- The supreme god herds all the gods like sheep (Ee SB VII:130-131)

**Ea gives his own name; epilogue on teaching and writing the names (Enuma elish VII 137-164)**
- The sacred names are to be pondered by the wise, repeated by father to son, and heeded by the shepherd-ruler (Ee SB VII:145-150)

**Hymn to Marduk, provider and absolver (Elevation of Babylon 1-81)**
- The god absolves sin and reconciles the sufferer with his angry personal god (ElevBab SB –:46-47)
- The god's waters are mixed with fire and air (elements of the cosmos) (ElevBab SB –:75-77)

**Gods bless Marduk; Esagil and Eridu-Babylon praised (Elevation of Babylon 82-108)**
- Divine couples and heaven and earth in turn bless the supreme god (litany) (ElevBab SB –:82-85)
- Babylon is identified with Eridu, the primeval sacred city of Ea, gate of the Apsu (ElevBab SB –:93-101)
- The holy city is a carnelian bolt, a treasure chest of obsidian, lapis, agate and jasper (ElevBab SB –:105-108)

**Babylon's abundance, river, wall, king and privileged citizens (Elevation of Babylon 109-134)**
- The holy city is praised as a sea bringing in its yield, a fruit garden, a rolling wave of bounty (ElevBab SB –:109-111)

**Anu begets the Seven and fixes their destructive tasks (Erra I 28-44)**
- The sky god begets on Earth seven warrior gods (the Seven) and gives each a destructive commission (Erra SB I:28-38)

**The Seven goad Erra: the field is better than the city (Erra I 45-91)**
- The open field is praised over city life: city bread cannot compare with a cake baked in embers, the palace with a shepherd's hut (Erra SB I:51-59)
- Neglected weapons: cobwebs on the war gear, the bow too stiff, the arrowhead dull, the sword rusted for lack of slaughter (Erra SB I:88-91)

**Išum pleads; Erra's 'I am' boast and resolve to unseat Marduk (Erra I 92-123)**
- A god praises himself in a litany: in heaven I am a wild bull, on earth a lion, among the gods a fury (Erra SB I:109-118)

**Erra in Esagil; Marduk recalls the flood when he left his throne (Erra I 124-162)**
- After the flood the seven sages (apkallu) and master craftsmen were sent down to the Apsu and never brought up again (Erra SB I:147, Erra SB I:162)

**Marduk warns of chaos if he leaves; Erra offers to govern meanwhile (Erra I 163-191)**
- While the supreme god is away a rival god takes over the government of heaven and earth (Erra SB I:181-189)

**Gods found Kish; no king yet; Ishtar seeks a shepherd (Etana SB I)**
- The gods plan the first city, lay its foundations and build its brickwork (Etana SB I:1-5)
- A goddess comes down to search the land for a shepherd and king (Etana SB I:19-22)

**The eagle seeks the plant; first flight and fall (Etana SB III 1-56)**
- Losing heart on the way to heaven, the rider asks to be set down and plunges toward the earth (Etana SB III:42-51)

**Dream of Ishtar enthroned; second ascent through the gates of heaven (Etana SB III b-c)**
