- The heaven-traveller passes through the gates of Anu, Enlil and Ea, then of Sin, Shamash, Adad and Ishtar, prostrating at each (Etana SB III:b+3-b+6, Etana SB III:b+39-b+43)
- In a dream the visitor opens a sealed house in heaven and finds the goddess enthroned with lions beneath her throne (Etana SB III:b+7-b+14)

**Enkidu, sick, curses the trapper and Šamḫat before Šamaš (MB Ur)**
- The wild man complains that the woman made him weak who had been pure in the wild (Gilg MB Ur:39-40)

**Šamaš answers from heaven; Enkidu turns his curse into a blessing on Šamḫat (MB Ur)**
- The sun god calls from heaven to answer a complainer, reminding him of the good he has received (Gilg MB Ur:41-47)

**Ištar's offer and Gilgameš's catalogue of her lovers (MB Emar 2)**
- A string of insulting similes: a door that keeps out no draught, a waterskin that cuts its carrier, a shoe that bites its wearer's foot (Gilg MB Emar2:13', Gilg MB Emar2:14'–15'a, Gilg MB Emar2:16'b–17'a, Gilg MB Emar2:17'b, Gilg MB Emar2:18')
- The hero lists the goddess's former lovers and the fate each suffered (Dumuzi's yearly wailing, a bird with broken wing, a shepherd turned into a wolf) (Gilg MB Emar2:19', Gilg MB Emar2:24', Gilg MB Emar2:25', Gilg MB Emar2:26', Gilg MB Emar2:27', Gilg MB Emar2:28'a, Gilg MB Emar2:30', Gilg MB Emar2:32', Gilg MB Emar2:33', Gilg MB Emar2:35')

**Enkidu lies sick for days; Gilgameš moans like a dove (MB Megiddo)**
- The friend lies sick in bed, his illness worsening day by day (a first, second, third, fourth day) (Gilg MB Megiddo:a+7'b–a+8'a, Gilg MB Megiddo:8'b–a+9', Gilg MB Megiddo:a+10', Gilg MB Megiddo:a+11')

**The harlot persuades Enkidu, clothes him and leads him to the shepherds, who bow before him as a god (MB private collection)**
- Shepherds prostrate themselves before a newcomer as before a god (Gilg MB Priv1:77, Gilg MB Priv1:79, Gilg MB Priv1:80, Gilg MB Priv1:81, Gilg MB Priv1:82)

**Prologue: he who saw the Deep; the tablet in the cedar box; the wall of Uruk (MB Ugarit)**
- The epic opens by praising its hero as one who saw the Deep, knew all wisdom and brought back knowledge from before the flood (Gilg MB Ug1:1, Gilg MB Ug1:2, Gilg MB Ug1:3, Gilg MB Ug1:4, Gilg MB Ug1:5, Gilg MB Ug1:6, Gilg MB Ug1:9)
- The reader is told to open a cedar box and read the hero's labours from a lapis-lazuli tablet kept in it (Gilg MB Ug1:11, Gilg MB Ug1:22, Gilg MB Ug1:23, Gilg MB Ug1:24)
- The city wall's foundations were laid by the seven sages, and the city's area is measured out (Gilg MB Ug1:20, Gilg MB Ug1:21, Gilg MB Ug1:25, Gilg MB Ug1:26, Gilg MB Ug1:27, Gilg MB Ug1:28)

**Gilgameš oppresses the young men; his giant stature (MB Ugarit)**
- The hero's huge stature is given in cubits (eleven cubits tall, four cubits across the chest) (Gilg MB Ug1:34, Gilg MB Ug1:35, Gilg MB Ug1:36, Gilg MB Ug1:37)

**The wedding guest tells of the king's right to the bride; Enkidu goes to Uruk (OB II)**
- On hearing of an injustice a man's face turns pale with anger (Gilg OB II:165–166)

**Enkidu bars the door of the bride's house; the wrestling; Enkidu hails Gilgameš (OB II)**
- Two equals wrestle at a doorway like bulls, shattering the door jamb and shaking the wall, until one yields (Gilg OB II:200–201, Gilg OB II:202–203, Gilg OB II:212–213, Gilg OB II:214, Gilg OB II:215–216, Gilg OB II:217, Gilg OB II:218–219, Gilg OB II:220–221, Gilg OB II:222–224, Gilg OB II:225–226, Gilg OB II:227–228, Gilg OB II:229–230)
- The high god fixed kingship over the people as the hero's lot (Gilg OB II:239–240)

**Gilgameš addresses the assembly; the elders warn; he laughs; a blessing for the road (OB III)**
- The king shuts the city gates, convenes the assembly and addresses the elders from his throne in the street (Gilg OB III:172, Gilg OB III:173, Gilg OB III:175, Gilg OB III:177, Gilg OB III:179, Gilg OB III:180)

**Gilgameš kneels before Šamaš, weeps and vows a house; arming and departure (OB III)**
- Before a dangerous journey the hero prays to his god for a safe return and vows to build him a house (Gilg OB III:219, Gilg OB III:220, Gilg OB III:221, Gilg OB III:229, Gilg OB III:230, Gilg OB III:231, Gilg OB III:232, Gilg OB III:233, Gilg OB III:234, Gilg OB III:235)

**The elders' advice and blessing; Enkidu takes the lead; the crowd sent home (OB III)**
- The traveller must dig a well at each camp and pour cool water in libation to the sun god (Gilg OB III:266, Gilg OB III:267, Gilg OB III:268, Gilg OB III:269, Gilg OB III:270)

**Enkidu urges the kill; Ḫuwawa slain, his auras escaping; the secret abode of the gods (OB Ishchali)**
- Saying: catch the (mother) bird and where will its chicks go? Deal first with the main foe (Gilg OB Ishchali:15', Gilg OB Ishchali:16', Gilg OB Ishchali:17')
- The slain guardian's blood is carried away by the ravines (Gilg OB Ishchali:25')
- One hero fells the cedars while the other chooses the best timber (Gilg OB Ishchali:39', Gilg OB Ishchali:41', Gilg OB Ishchali:43')

**Gilgameš roams in skins; Šamaš: 'you will not find the life you seek' (OB VA+BM)**
- Before lying in the darkness of death the hero wants his eyes to be sated with the light of the sun (Gilg OB VA+BM:11', Gilg OB VA+BM:12', Gilg OB VA+BM:13', Gilg OB VA+BM:14', Gilg OB VA+BM:15')

**Gilgameš and the ale-wife: Enkidu's death and the counsel to enjoy life (OB VA+BM)**
- The mourner will not give up his dead friend for burial, hoping he will rise at his cry, until a maggot falls from his nose (Gilg OB VA+BM:a+6, Gilg OB VA+BM:a+7, Gilg OB VA+BM:a+8, Gilg OB VA+BM:a+9, Gilg OB VA+BM:a+10)
- When the gods created mankind they allotted death to them and kept life in their own hands (Gilg OB VA+BM:a+18, Gilg OB VA+BM:a+19, Gilg OB VA+BM:a+20)

**Gilgameš smashes the Stone Ones; Sursunabu the boatman and the Waters of Death (OB VA+BM)**
- At a meeting at the edge of the world one asks 'What is your name?' and the other answers with his name, city and journey (Gilg OB VA+BM:b+5, Gilg OB VA+BM:b+6, Gilg OB VA+BM:b+8, Gilg OB VA+BM:b+9, Gilg OB VA+BM:b+10, Gilg OB VA+BM:b+11)

**Prologue: he who saw the Deep; the wall of Uruk and the lapis tablet (Gilgameš SB I)**
- The hero is introduced as the one who saw the Deep (nagbu) and knew the totality of wisdom (Gilg SB I:1-6)
- A sage-hero uncovers secret, hidden things and brings back knowledge from the age before the flood (Gilg SB I:7-8)
- The hero's toils and adventures are inscribed on a stone stele for posterity (Gilg SB I:9-10)

**Hymn to Gilgameš: two-thirds god, eleven cubits tall, the far traveller (Gilgameš SB I)**
- The hero's giant body is measured in cubits (height eleven cubits, chest four cubits, stride six cubits) (Gilg SB I:52-56)
- The hero roams the regions of the world searching for (eternal) life (Gilg SB I:41)
- The hero restores the cult-centres destroyed by the flood and re-establishes the rites for humankind (Gilg SB I:43-44)

**Gilgameš oppresses Uruk; the gods hear and Aruru creates Enkidu from clay (Gilgameš SB I)**
- The oppressed people's complaint about their king reaches the gods, who act on it (Gilg SB I:72, Gilg SB I:76-79, Gilg SB I:91)
- The gods create a rival equal to the overbearing hero, so that they contend and the city may have rest (Gilg SB I:92-96)

**The trapper, his father's counsel and the sending of Šamḫat (Gilgameš SB I)**
- The wild man fills in the hunter's pits, tears up his snares and frees the animals (Gilg SB I:128-131, Gilg SB I:155-158)

**Šamḫat and Enkidu: six days and seven nights, the animals flee, 'you are like a god' (Gilgameš SB I)**
- The wild man couples with the woman for six days and seven nights (Gilg SB I:192)
- After intercourse the animals flee the wild man; he is weakened and slower but has gained reason and understanding (Gilg SB I:195-200)
- The woman tells the man he has become 'like a god' and leads him from the wild to the city (Gilg SB I:205-210)

**Šamḫat describes Uruk and tells Gilgameš's dreams of the star and the axe (Gilgameš SB I)**
- The city is praised as a place of daily festival, drums and comely harlots (Gilg SB I:224-230)
- A dream of a star or rock fallen from the sky that the dreamer cannot lift, and which he loves like a wife (Gilg SB I:244-256)
- Dreams foretell the arrival of a mighty companion who will be the hero's friend and saviour (Gilg SB I:266-270, Gilg SB I:289-295)
- The hero loves his male friend 'like a wife', caressing and embracing him (Gilg SB I:254, Gilg SB I:265, Gilg SB I:269, Gilg SB I:287)

**Enkidu clothed, among the shepherds, taught bread and ale (Gilgameš SB II)**
- The civilised wild man guards the shepherds' flocks at night, driving off wolves and lions (Gilg SB II:59-62)

**Enkidu bars Gilgameš from the wedding house; the heroes wrestle (Gilgameš SB II)**
- The newcomer blocks the door of the wedding house to stop the king entering before the groom, and they wrestle (Gilg SB II:100-102, Gilg SB II:111-114)

**Ninsun on Enkidu's lack of kin; Enkidu weeps; Gilgameš proposes the Cedar Forest (Gilgameš SB II)**
- The hero's friend, born in the wild, has no father, mother, brother or kin (Gilg SB II:175-177)

**Ninsun purifies herself, censes on the roof and prays to Šamaš for her son (Gilgameš SB III)**
- The hero's mother bathes, dresses, climbs to the roof, offers incense to the sun god and raises her arms in prayer (Gilg SB III:37-45)
- A mother complains to the god that he gave her son a restless heart that drives him to danger (Gilg SB III:46-47)
- A hero is promised a place among the gods: sharing heaven with the sun, a sceptre with the moon, or dwelling with the netherworld gods (Gilg SB III:101-106)
- At sunrise the sun god opens the way for the herds to go out and all creatures and gods wait for his light (Gilg SB III:63-73)

**Ninsun adopts Enkidu; rites at the Gate of Cedar (Gilgameš SB III)**
- A foundling is taken in and brought up by temple priestesses and votaries (Gilg SB III:122-126)

**The departure from Uruk: 'judge the cause of the weak'; the officers kiss his feet (Gilgameš SB III)**
- The officials kiss the departing king's feet and the people run after him with blessings (Gilg SB III:212-214)

**The march to Lebanon and the first dream: the mountain falls (Gilgameš SB IV)**
- In a dream a mountain collapses on the travellers (Gilg SB IV:23-25)

**The Cedar Forest: dwelling of the gods, birdsong, resin like rain; terror falls (Gilgameš SB V)**
- The cedar forest on the mountain is the dwelling of the gods and the throne-dais of the goddesses, sweet-shaded and full of delight (Gilg SB V:6-9)
- Resin oozes from the cedars and drizzles down like rain (Gilg SB V:14-16)
- The sacred forest resounds with the song of birds, crickets, doves and monkeys like a band of musicians before its guardian (Gilg SB V:17-26)
- As he enters the sacred place terror falls on the hero, his arms stiffen and his legs tremble (Gilg SB V:27-30)

**'Forget death and seek life': mutual encouragement at the forest's edge (Gilgameš SB V)**
- Exhortation in danger: forget death and seek life; the one tested in battle does not fear death (Gilg SB V:39-47)

**'Two are two'; Šamaš: 'Fear not!'; Ḫumbaba roars and taunts (Gilgameš SB V)**
- The sun god hears the hero's tearful prayer and a voice cries from heaven: 'Fear not, stand against him!' (Gilg SB V:95-98)
- The monster has seven cloaks (auras) of radiance; he is caught wearing only one, the other six shed (Gilg SB V:99-100)
- The monster mocks the hero's companion as a fish's spawn without father or mother's milk, and threatens to feed the hero's flesh to the birds (Gilg SB V:115-124)

**The combat: earth splits, thirteen winds blind Ḫumbaba, the weapons reach him (Gilgameš SB V)**
- In the combat the earth splits under the heroes' heels, mountains are sundered, white cloud turns black and death rains like mist (Gilg SB V:154-158)
- God's control of the wind over ships at sea: raising a storm or stilling it (Gilg SB V:159-163)

**Ḫumbaba begs for his life; Enkidu urges death; Ḫumbaba's curse (Gilgameš SB V)**
- The defeated monster begs for his life, offering to be the hero's slave and keep his timber (Gilg SB V:166-177)
- The companion urges the hero not to listen to the monster's pleas but to kill it before the high god learns of it (Gilg SB V:178-183, Gilg SB V:196-204, Gilg SB V:265-272)
- Saying: catch the (parent) bird, and where will its young go? (destroy the chief and his brood is helpless) (Gilg SB V:250-254)
- The doomed monster curses his captors: may they not grow old, may the companion have no one to bury him but his friend (Gilg SB V:279-280)

**Ḫumbaba slain, the forest laid waste, a cedar door for Enlil's temple (Gilgameš SB V)**
- The monster's seven sons, named after noises and storms, are slain with him (Gilg SB V:307-308)

**Gilgameš washes and is crowned; Ištar proposes marriage (Gilgameš SB VI)**
- A goddess, desiring the hero's beauty, proposes that he be her husband and offers him gifts (Gilg SB VI:6-9)
- The goddess offers a chariot of gold and lapis, kings bowing in tribute, and fertile flocks as marriage gifts (Gilg SB VI:10-21)

**Gilgameš rejects Ištar and lists her ruined lovers (Gilgameš SB VI)**
- The hero refuses the goddess's offer, recounting her faithlessness (Gilg SB VI:24-32)
- The goddess is reviled with a litany of images (a draughty door, pitch that stains, a shoe that bites its owner's foot) (Gilg SB VI:33-41)
- A catalogue of the goddess's former lovers, each ruined by her: Dumuzi wept for yearly, the bird with broken wing, the lion trapped, the horse whipped, the shepherd turned into a wolf, the gardener turned into a dwarf (Gilg SB VI:42-79)
- A goddess's spurned or used lover is turned into an animal (a wolf) and hounded by his own dogs (Gilg SB VI:58-63)
- The gardener refuses the goddess's sexual advances ('did my mother not bake? am I to eat bread of insult?') and is turned into a dwarf (Gilg SB VI:64-78)

**Ištar weeps before Anu, threatens to raise the dead, and obtains the Bull of Heaven (Gilgameš SB VI)**
- The insulted goddess goes weeping to her father and mother in heaven (Gilg SB VI:80-86)
- The father god rebukes his complaining daughter: 'was it not you who provoked him?' (Gilg SB VI:87-91)
- Before sending the Bull of Heaven, the high god demands seven years of chaff and fodder be stored against the famine it will bring (Gilg SB VI:103-111)

**The Bull of Heaven ravages Uruk and is slain; its heart offered to Šamaš (Gilgameš SB VI)**
- At each snort of the Bull of Heaven a pit opens and hundreds of young men fall in (Gilg SB VI:119-124)
- The victors cut out the slain beast's heart and set it before the sun god, prostrating themselves (Gilg SB VI:148-149)

**Ištar's lament, the haunch hurled, the horns dedicated, 'Who is finest among men?'; Enkidu dreams (Gilgameš SB VI)**
- The goddess climbs the city wall, stamps and wails a curse on the hero who killed her beast (Gilg SB VI:151-153)
- The companion tears off the bull's haunch and hurls it at the goddess, threatening her with the same (Gilg SB VI:154-157)
- The goddess assembles the courtesans and harlots and institutes mourning over the bull's haunch (Gilg SB VI:158-159)
- Women of the palace answer in song: 'Who is finest among men? Gilgameš is finest!' (Gilg SB VI:171-175)

**The gods' counsel; Enkidu curses the cedar door (Gilgameš SB VII)**
- The gods take counsel and decree that one of the two heroes must die for killing the guardian and the Bull of Heaven (Gilg SB VII:1)
- The dying hero speaks to the temple door he made, regretting his gift and threatening to tear it down (Gilg SB VII:37-63)

**Gilgameš weeps, vows a golden statue; Enlil's word cannot be rescinded (Gilgameš SB VII)**
- Saying: the dead leave grief and sorrow to the one who survives (Gilg SB VII:75-76)
- The mourner promises to make a statue of his dead friend in gold without limit (Gilg SB VII:82)
- Whether payment may substitute for a life (Gilg SB VII:84)
- People go to their fate before their time (die prematurely) (Gilg SB VII:88-89)

**Enkidu curses the hunter and Šamḫat (Gilgameš SB VII)**
- A detailed curse: no household, the road-junction her seat, ruins her bed, drunkards strike her cheek, thorns flay her feet (Gilg SB VII:102-123)
- Curse: may the god of the house he enters leave by the window (Gilg SB VII:99)

**Šamaš rebukes Enkidu; Enkidu turns his curse into a blessing (Gilgameš SB VII)**
- The god rebukes the curser by recalling the benefits he received (bread fit for a god, beer, clothing, a friend) (Gilg SB VII:134-138)
- The curser's mouth that cursed returns to bless: noblemen will love her and give her gold, a wife of seven will be deserted for her (Gilg SB VII:149-161)

**Enkidu's dream of the House of Dust (Gilgameš SB VII)**
- In a dream a grim man with the face of the Anzû bird, lion paws and eagle talons seizes the dreamer (Gilg SB VII:168-175)
- The dying man is struck and turned into a bird (dove), his arms bound like wings, and led to the netherworld (Gilg SB VII:182-184)
- In the netherworld the crowns of former kings lie heaped away while the kings sit as servants (Gilg SB VII:193-197)
- Before the queen of the netherworld her scribe crouches, reading a tablet aloud; she asks who brought the new arrival (Gilg SB VII:203-208)

**'Remember me'; Enkidu lies sick twelve days, lamenting he does not die in battle (Gilgameš SB VII)**
- The dying hero lies sick day after day, counted from the first to the twelfth (Gilg SB VII:255-260)
- The dying hero laments that he dies on a sickbed, not gloriously in battle where one makes a name (Gilg SB VII:263-267)

**'What sleep has seized you?': Enkidu's heart stops; Gilgameš veils him like a bride (Gilgameš SB VIII)**
- The mourner covers his dead friend's face like a bride's (Gilg SB VIII:59)

**Treasures displayed to Šamaš as gifts for the gods of the Netherworld (Gilgameš SB VIII)**
- Treasures from the king's treasury are displayed to the sun god as gifts for each netherworld deity, that they welcome the dead friend and walk at his side (Gilg SB VIII:94-130, Gilg SB VIII:132-210)
- A netherworld deity is titled 'the scapegoat' (mašhaltappû), the substitute who carries evil away (Gilg SB VIII:181-182)

**'I shall die, and shall I not be like Enkidu?': Gilgameš sets out; lions at night (Gilgameš SB IX)**
- In danger at night the traveller lifts his head and prays to the moon god to keep him safe (Gilg SB IX:8-12, Gilg SB IX:24-26)

**The twin mountains of Māšu and the scorpion-man and his wife (Gilgameš SB IX)**
- Twin cosmic mountains (Māšu) guard the sun's rising and setting, their peaks touching heaven and their roots reaching the netherworld (Gilg SB IX:37-41, Gilg SB IX:45)
- A scorpion-man and his wife, whose glance is death, guard the gate of the mountain of the sun (Gilg SB IX:42-53)
- The far traveller is asked how he crossed the many rivers whose crossing is perilous (Gilg SB IX:56)

**Twelve double-hours of darkness on the path of the sun; the garden of jewel-trees (Gilgameš SB IX)**
- Beyond the darkness lies a garden of the gods whose trees bear fruit and foliage of carnelian, lapis lazuli and other gems (Gilg SB IX:171-194)
- A tree in the divine garden is lovely to look at and bears fruit (Gilg SB IX:174, Gilg SB IX:176)

**Šiduri the ale-wife bars her gate; 'my friend has turned to clay' (Gilgameš SB X)**
- A veiled ale-wife (tavern-keeper) lives in an inn by the shore of the ocean at the edge of the world (Gilg SB X:1-4)
- Seeing the wild-looking stranger, the woman bars her gate and climbs to the roof; he threatens to break the door (Gilg SB X:13-24)

**The way across the ocean and the Waters of Death; Ur-šanabi and the Stone Ones (Gilgameš SB X)**
- No one but the sun god has ever crossed the ocean at the end of the world (Gilg SB X:79-82)
- The Waters of Death lie across the ocean between the living world and the immortal's home; touching them is fatal (Gilg SB X:83-86)
- A boatman with mysterious Stone Ones ferries travellers across the Waters of Death to the immortal flood hero (Gilg SB X:87-91)

**Ur-šanabi's questions; three hundred punting-poles; the crossing; Ūta-napišti watches (Gilgameš SB X)**
- The hero crosses the Waters of Death using poles one by one so his hand never touches the water, then a garment as sail (Gilg SB X:159-183)
- The immortal, watching from the far shore, wonders aloud who the stranger in the boat is (Gilg SB X:184-201)

**Gilgameš meets Ūta-napišti and tells of his toil (Gilgameš SB X)**
- Wish that the gate of sorrow be barred and sealed with pitch and bitumen (Gilg SB X:262-263)

**Ūta-napišti's discourse: the fool's lot, man snapped like a reed, the mayfly, the hidden day of death (Gilgameš SB X)**
- Saying: no one builds a palace or sets a throne in the council for a fool; he gets dregs instead of ghee, bran instead of flour, rags instead of garments (Gilg SB X:270-277)
- Man's name (progeny) is snapped off like a reed in the canebrake; death abducts the comely youth and maiden (Gilg SB X:301-303)
- No one sees death, sees its face or hears its voice, yet savage death cuts man down (Gilg SB X:304-307)
- Litany 'at some time we build a house, at some time we start a family, at some time brothers divide, at some time the river floods' on the transience of all things (Gilg SB X:308-312)
- Image of human life: the mayfly floating on the flood gazes at the sun and is suddenly gone (Gilg SB X:312-315)
- The great gods and the mother of destinies established death and life, but did not reveal the day of death (Gilg SB X:319-322)

**'You are just like me': how did Ūta-napišti find life? (Gilgameš SB XI)**
- The seeker finds that the immortal looks no different from himself, an ordinary man (Gilg SB XI:2-4)

**The sleep test: seven loaves mark seven days asleep (Gilgameš SB XI)**
- The immortal asks the seeker: who will now assemble the gods for you, that you may find life? (Gilg SB XI:207-208)
- The seeker is challenged to stay awake six days and seven nights, but sleep falls on him at once like a fog (Gilg SB XI:209-214)
- Saying: mankind is deceitful and will deceive you (Gilg SB XI:220)
- The immortal's wife bakes a loaf each day the sleeper sleeps and places it by his head, the loaves showing successive staleness as proof of seven days (Gilg SB XI:221-241)
- Death sits in the bedchamber; wherever I turn, there is death (Gilg SB XI:243-246)

**Ur-šanabi banished; Gilgameš washed and robed; the secret plant of rejuvenation (Gilgameš SB XI)**
- The ferryman who brought the seeker is cursed and banished from the quay (Gilg SB XI:247-249)
- The seeker's matted hair is washed, his skins thrown to the sea and he is clothed in a royal robe that will stay new until he reaches home (Gilg SB XI:250-270)
- A secret plant like a thorn-bush, found in the Apsû, restores youth: 'the old man becomes young' (Gilg SB XI:283-286, Gilg SB XI:295-296)
- The hero ties heavy stones to his feet, sinks to the depths and plucks the plant, then cuts the stones loose and is cast ashore (Gilg SB XI:288-293)
- The hero plans to test the plant on an old man in his city before eating it himself (Gilg SB XI:297-300)

**The snake steals the plant and sheds its skin; return to Uruk and its wall (Gilgameš SB XI)**
- While the hero bathes in a pool, a snake smells the plant's fragrance, carries it off and sheds its skin (Gilg SB XI:303-306)
- The snake sloughs its skin, gaining the renewal the man lost (Gilg SB XI:307)
- The hero sits down and weeps: for whom did I toil? I have done a favour to the 'lion of the earth' (Gilg SB XI:308-318)

**Gilgameš appeals to Enlil, Sîn and Ea; Šamaš raises Enkidu's ghost (Gilgameš SB XII)**
- The sun god opens a chink in the earth and brings the dead friend's ghost up like a phantom (zaqīqu) (Gilg SB XII:83, Gilg SB XII:86-87)

**'Tell me the order of the Netherworld': the fates of the dead (Gilgameš SB XII)**
- The living hero embraces and kisses the ghost of his friend and begs: 'tell me the order of the netherworld' (Gilg SB XII:88-91)
- The ghost hesitates: 'I cannot tell you; if I tell you, sit down and weep' (Gilg SB XII:92-95)
- The body once delighted in is devoured by grubs like an old beam and filled with dust like a crack in the ground (Gilg SB XII:96-99)
- The ghost of one whose corpse lies in the open country finds no rest in the netherworld (Gilg SB XII:150-151)

**Chosen as Ninurta's bride; the farmer-god and Gula as Nanše of the field boundary (Gula Hymn 18-43)**
- The warrior god is also the divine farmer who walks behind the ox, holds the plow, heaps grain and resettles abandoned mounds (GulaHymn SB –:26-34)
- A goddess is mistress of seed, plow, ox-driver, measuring cord and rod, and carries a stylus to keep the accounts (GulaHymn SB –:35-43)

**Ninurta's might; 'I am the physician': the healing goddess as Ninigizibara (Gula Hymn 68-91)**
- The healing goddess wears at her waist a satchel of life-saving incantations, carries herbs, scalpel, clean dressing and soft bandage (GulaHymn SB –:80-85)

**Zababa the comely; Bau who has mercy on the weak; Ninurta launcher of the deluge; Šarrat-Nippuri's beauty (Gula Hymn 92-129)**
- The deity has mercy on the weak, enriches the destitute, gives life to whoever reveres her and makes straight the path of whoever seeks her ways (GulaHymn SB –:106-108)

**The husband wears heaven as tiara and earth as sandals; Anu, Antu and Ea endow Gula with the physician's craft (Gula Hymn 130-148)**
- The wise god Ea gives the healing goddess his wisdom, the tablet stylus and the physician's craft, 'a secret of the gods' (GulaHymn SB –:144-146)

**Closing prayer: have mercy on the servant Bullussa-rabi, intercede with your spouse (Gula Hymn 188-200)**
- Prayer that the sufferer may strip off his mourning garment (karru) and put on ordinary clothes again (GulaHymn SB –:194)
- The petitioner promises to kneel or prostrate himself before the deity every day if healed (GulaHymn SB –:200)

**Fragmentary column: the secret place of the gods, divination, and the goddess who removes misdeeds and hears prayer (Syncretistic Gula Hymn A+1-A+50)**
- Where the deity is reconciled, path and way are made straight for the worshipper (GulaSyncr SB –:A+19)

**Her wisdom by leave of each great god; her abodes Esharra, Ekur, Esagil, Duku (Syncretistic Gula Hymn A+51-A+74)**
- Litany 'by leave of DN' (itti DN): by leave of Anshar, Enlil, Ea, Marduk, Nabu, Ninurta the goddess has her wisdom, destinies and rule (GulaSyncr SB –:A+60-A+65)

**City by city, shrine by shrine: the goddess is Ningal in Ur, Aya in Sippar, Ningirimma in Babylon, Ninlil in Hursagkalama ... (Syncretistic Gula Hymn A+75-A+139)**
- Each temple's ceremonial name is matched by what the deity does there (in the House of Life she grants life) (GulaSyncr SB –:A+87-A+90, GulaSyncr SB –:A+113, GulaSyncr SB –:A+120)

**Fragmentary column B: the goddess who cleans away sins in E-dadaglal and Duku (Syncretistic Gula Hymn B+1-B+20)**
- The deity is fierce to the intransigent; the disobedient bear her punishment (GulaSyncr SB –:B+3, GulaSyncr SB –:B+9)

**Fragmentary column C: battle, Erra, the entrance of Ganzir and the princes of the netherworld (Syncretistic Gula Hymn C+1-C+15)**
- Without the deity (ina balīša) the work of farmer and ox-driver, or the ways, are not opened (GulaSyncr SB –:C+8-C+9)

**Ishtar sets her mind on the netherworld, the house none leaves who enters (Ishtar's Descent 1-11a)**
- Dust has gathered on the door and bolt of the netherworld and deathly silence lies over its beam (IshDesc SB –:11-11a)

**At the gate: Ishtar threatens to raise the dead; Ereškigal's dismay and lament for the untimely dead (Ishtar's Descent 12-41)**
- The queen of the dead laments that she must weep for young men torn from their wives, girls torn from lovers and infants taken before their time (IshDesc SB –:32-36)
- The goddess of love and the queen of the netherworld are sisters (IshDesc SB –:26)
- The netherworld is governed by 'age-old rules' (parṣū labīrūtu) applied to every entrant, even a goddess (IshDesc SB –:38)

**The seven gates: Ishtar stripped of crown, earrings, beads, pins, birth-stone girdle, bangles and loincloth; seated above Ereškigal, struck with sixty diseases (Ishtar's Descent 42-75)**
- At each stage the same question ('Why did you take ...?') receives the same fixed answer ('Such are the rules of ...'), repeated as a refrain (IshDesc SB –:43-44)
- The underworld queen has her vizier let loose sixty diseases against the intruding goddess, eye, side, foot, heart and head disease, against all of her (IshDesc SB –:66-75)

**With Ishtar below, no creature mates; Papsukkal mourns before Sîn and Ea; Ea creates Asûšu-namir (Ishtar's Descent 76-99)**
- While the love goddess is in the netherworld, bull does not mount cow, ass does not impregnate jenny, man does not impregnate woman; each sleeps alone (IshDesc SB –:77-80, IshDesc SB –:87-90)
- The wise god creates a being (an assinnu, impersonator) and sends him to the netherworld to make its queen swear by the great gods and to ask for the waterskin of life (IshDesc SB –:92-99)

**Ereškigal curses Asûšu-namir; Namtar sprinkles Ishtar with the water of life (Ishtar's Descent 100-118c)**
- The tricked underworld queen curses the envoy: bread of the city's plowing for food, the sewer for drink, the shadow of the wall and the threshold for home, slapped by drunk and sober (IshDesc SB –:102-108)
- The netherworld gods (Anunnaki) are brought out and seated on golden thrones, the thresholds decorated with cowries, for a judgement or release (IshDesc SB –:111-117)

**Return through the seven gates; the ransom; Tammuz bathed and dressed; Belili's cry; the dead come up to smell the incense (Ishtar's Descent 119-138)**
- Tammuz (Dumuzi) is bathed, anointed and dressed in red; wailing men and women and the lapis flute accompany his annual coming up, and the dead come up to smell the incense (IshDesc SB –:127-130, IshDesc SB –:136-138)

**Praise of Ishtar's might: as great as Anu, rays like Sîn, wings that are the winds (Ishtar 2, 1-56)**
- The goddess is likened in turn to each great god: her command like Anu's, her rays like Sîn's, her ears like Šamaš's, her fighting like Ninurta's, her roar like Adad's (Ishtar2 SB –:10-19)

**A sick man confesses unwitting sins; Ishtar can rescue; description of the afflicted (Ishtar 2, 57-128)**
- The sufferer has no father, no mother and no in-laws to help him (Ishtar2 SB –:92)
- The deity shows terror but knows how to save; her anger is close to reconciliation and after punishing she opens a way of relief (Ishtar2 SB –:83-84, Ishtar2 SB –:90, Ishtar2 SB –:101)

**The sick man mourned while alive, abandoned by friends, driven mad by a god's evil wind; plea 'take his hand' (Ishtar 2, 142-199)**
- The sick man's family already gathers mourners and wails over him while he still lives (Ishtar2 SB –:155-157)
- An evil wind of a god drives the sufferer to madness; he forgets himself and does not know his own mind (Ishtar2 SB –:161)
- Plea that the dream interpreter and diviner not use up the sick man's offerings in vain: let the deity turn to him (Ishtar2 SB –:174-175)
- The penitent says he bears a punishment and pulls a yoke of his negligences (Ishtar2 SB –:195)

**Plea for release: open the doors of heaven, have pity like father and mother; she frees the captive; gods, bow to her; 'Ishtar, have mercy!' (Ishtar 2, 206-247)**
- The petitioner asks the deity to have pity on him like the father who begot him and the mother who bore him (Ishtar2 SB –:218-219)
- The goddess frees the captive, releases the man in bonds and shows light to the one in prison (Ishtar2 SB –:222-223)
- The gods are called to bow down and prostrate themselves before the goddess, who alone is supreme (Ishtar2 SB –:226-227, Ishtar2 SB –:232-233)
- Those who kneel to the goddess receive from her hand offspring and progeny (Ishtar2 SB –:238-239)
- The goddess frees the captive, releases the man in bonds and shows light to the one in prison (Ishtar2 SB –:216-217)

**The god who gathered the share of seven brothers; wings and legs as winds; colophon: secret for experts (IshtarSyncr 26-36)**
- A young deity gathers to himself the shares of his seven brothers (seven cities) (IshtarSyncr SB –:26-27)

**Lipit-Eštar A: the king's self-praise and the gifts of An, Enlil, Ninlil, Nanna, Enki, Inana, Nisaba, Utu (1-42)**
- The king raises his head like a cedar sapling (IsinDyn OB 2.5.5.1_Lipit–Eštar_A:3)

**Lipit-Eštar A: the king as farmer, shepherd and provider, and as humble servant of the gods of Nippur, Kesh, Ur and Eridu (43-66)**
- The king is the farmer who heaps grain, the shepherd who makes cream and milk plentiful, the one who fills the marsh with fish and birds and brings water to the river (IsinDyn OB 2.5.5.1_Lipit–Eštar_A:43-48)
- The king presents himself as one who presses a goat to his chest as offering, puts his hand to his nose in humility and stands in supplication (IsinDyn OB 2.5.5.1_Lipit–Eštar_A:53-57)

**Prologue: 'I will praise the lord of wisdom' - Marduk furious by night, relenting by day, who wounds and heals (Ludlul I 1-40)**
- The god is furious in the night and pacified by day; his anger is a tempest and deluge, his breeze gentle as the morning (Ludlul SB I:1-8)
- None among the gods can comprehend the high god's ways or understand his mind; he alone divines the gods' thoughts (Ludlul SB I:29-32)
- The god pronounces one guilty, but on the day of his justice liability and transgression are absolved (Ludlul SB I:23-24)

**From the day the Lord punished me: god, goddess and protective spirits desert; dignity flees; evil omens and dreams (Ludlul I 41-54)**
- The afflicted man is forced out of his house and wanders outside (Ludlul SB I:50)

**Sighing by day, lament by night; moaning like a dove; tears; 'my sun will shine' (Ludlul I 105-120)**
- The sufferer's supplication is chaotic like a bursting flame, his entreaty discord; honeyed words stick in his mouth (Ludlul SB I:115-118)

**A year passes and it worsens; diviners fail; treated like one who neglected the gods though he was pious; the unknowable will of the gods; human fickleness (Ludlul II 1-48)**
- The sufferer, who was punctilious in prayer, offerings, festivals and teaching reverence, is treated like one who neglected his god and goddess (Ludlul SB II:12-32)
- What is good to oneself may be an offense to a god, and what seems abominable to one's heart may be good to one's god (Ludlul SB II:33-35)
- Who can learn the reasoning of the gods in heaven's depths or fathom their counsel? Where could humans learn the ways of a god? (Ludlul SB II:36-38)
- He who lived yesterday died today; in an instant people go from gloom to song, from hunger like corpses to rivalling their gods (Ludlul SB II:39-47)

**Demons from the netherworld attack; the body broken limb by limb; wallowing in dung; wasting; exorcist baffled; the tomb readied; enemies rejoice (Ludlul II 49-120)**
- The sufferer's diseases come as demons from the ends of heaven, the breast of the netherworld, the Apsu, the mountain: evil vapour, migraine, ghost, Lamashtu, ague (Ludlul SB II:49-58)
- A demon has clothed himself in the sufferer's body as in a garment (Ludlul SB II:71)
- In his illness the sufferer's eyes look but do not see, his ears are open but do not hear (Ludlul SB II:73-74)
- From lack of food the sufferer's flesh wastes, his blood dries, his bones stick out covered only with skin, his features are unrecognisable (Ludlul SB II:90-94)
- The sick man's bed is his confinement, his house his jail, his own flesh his manacle and fetter (Ludlul SB II:95-98)
- The sick man spends the night in his own dung like an ox and wallows in his excrement like a sheep (Ludlul SB II:106-107)
- The sufferer's tomb is opened and his grave goods set out; lamentation for him is complete before he has died (Ludlul SB II:114-116)
- When the sufferer's ill-wisher hears of his plight, his face lights up; the woman who wished him ill is glad (Ludlul SB II:117-118)

**Three dreams: the radiant young man, the exorcist of Nippur with holy water, the fair young woman who says 'Fear not'; Ur-Nintinugga sent by Marduk (Ludlul III 9-50)**
- The sufferer sees three dreams in succession, each with an extraordinary figure (young man, purification priest, fair young woman, bearded exorcist) sent by his god to announce his healing (Ludlul SB III:9-48)
- A radiant figure in a dream says 'Your lord has sent me' (or 'Marduk has sent me') with a message of recovery (Ludlul SB III:15-16, Ludlul SB III:25-26, Ludlul SB III:43-44)
- In a dream a priest sent from a holy city sprinkles the sufferer with consecrated water, casts a spell of life and rubs his body with a tamarisk (Ludlul SB III:23-28)
- A divine figure tells the sufferer 'Fear not!' (la tapallah) and announces mercy: 'he has suffered greatly' (Ludlul SB III:35-36)
- A beautiful young woman, like a goddess and queen among people, enters to the dreamer, sits beside him and speaks mercy (Ludlul SB III:31-34)
- When the visionary tells his attendants what he saw, they fall silent and run away (Ludlul SB III:19-20)
- The divine messenger reveals a favourable sign to the sufferer's people and the illness ends quickly (Ludlul SB III:47-50)

**Marduk's heart is quieted; he disregards the sin and lets the wind carry away the faults (Ludlul III 51-67)**
- The god's heart is quieted; he accepts the entreaties, disregards the sin, removes the punishment and lets the wind carry away the faults (Ludlul SB III:51-61)

**The demons driven back; eyes, ears, nose, lips, mouth, teeth, tongue, throat, lungs, bowels, neck and nails healed (Ludlul III 68-120)**
- The god sends each disease-demon back where it came from: the vapour to the ends of heaven, the ghost to its dwelling, Lamashtu to the mountain, ague to the sea (Ludlul SB III:69-79)
- The sufferer's nails had grown long like an outcast's and are pared when he is restored (Ludlul SB III:118)
- The sagging neck of the sufferer is shored up like a hillside and planted upright like a tree (Ludlul SB III:a+1-a+2)

**Tablet IV fragments: restored body, darkness turned to light, the river ordeal, the slave mark removed, walking Kunush-kadru Street redeemed; let the impious learn from me (Ludlul IV)**
- The restored man slips out (of his sickness) like a snake sloughing its skin (Ludlul SB IV:a+10)
- The restored sufferer passes the river ordeal, the place where people's fates are decided (Ludlul SB IV:b+1)
- The sufferer's forehead is stroked and his slave mark (abbuttu) removed: freed from bondage (Ludlul SB IV:c+10)
- The released man walks along a named street of the city in a state of redemption (pišertu) (Ludlul SB IV:c+16)
- The restored sufferer tells those who sinned against the temple and do not revere their god to learn from his example (Ludlul SB IV:d+4-d+9)

**'My lord granted me relief': taken by the hand, the lion muzzled, the gravedigger's shovel wrested, pulled back from the river of death; 'had it not been for the lord' (Ludlul V 1-36)**
- The god makes the attacker drop his weapon, muzzles the lion, takes the sling from the stalker, the shovel from the gravedigger, the knife from the mourner (Ludlul SB V:12-22)
- 'Had it not been that the lord released me, I would have gone down to the netherworld' as a refrain of thanksgiving (Ludlul SB V:30-36)

**Purified, the redeemed man passes the named gates of Esagila: Gate of Life, Gate of Release from Guilt, Gate of Pure Water ...; kisses Zarpanitu's foot; sacrifices and feasts (Ludlul V 37-68)**
- The restored man washes his matted hair and bathes in an ablution of renewal (Ludlul SB V:37-38)
- The worshipper kisses the feet of the goddess in her temple (Ludlul SB V:53)
- Offerings and libations are made to the temple's protective spirits and to its threshold, bolt socket, bolt and doors (Ludlul SB V:59-63)

**The Babylonians see how Marduk revives: 'Who would have said he would see his sun?'; all who live, praise Marduk; blessing on the sufferer and the king (Ludlul V 69-120)**
- The citizens see how the god restores to life and proclaim: 'Who would have said he would see his sun again? Who but Marduk could revive him?' (Ludlul SB V:69-76)
- All who live, wherever earth and sky extend, sun rises, water runs and wind blows, all humankind formed from clay, are summoned to praise the god (Ludlul SB V:77-90)
- Closing blessing: may whoever has seen suffering have his punishment remitted and his distress relieved (Ludlul SB V:113-118)

**Maqlû I 37-41: 'Netherworld, netherworld' — Gilgameš enforcer of the oath**
- The speaker tells his enemies: whatever you have done I know, whatever I do you do not know (Maqlu SB I:39-40)

**Maqlû I 42-49: 'My city is Zabban' — two gates, water for the gods of heaven**
- The speaker's (mythical) city has two gates, one toward sunrise and one toward sunset (Maqlu SB I:42-45)
- The speaker purifies the gods with water and asks: as I purify you, so purify me (Maqlu SB I:47-49)

**Maqlû I 50-60: 'I have enclosed the ford' — Anu and Antu send the speaker to Bēlet-ṣēri**
- The exorcist encloses (blocks) the ford and the quay, and with them the witchcraft of all the lands (Maqlu SB I:50-51)
- A lock or seal is placed on the mouth of the warlock and witch to silence them (Maqlu SB I:54-55)
- The deity is asked not to answer or listen to the witches when they call, but to answer and listen to the speaker (Maqlu SB I:56-59)

**Maqlû I 61-72: 'I have been sent and I will go' — heaven, netherworld, river and land listen**
- The speaker summons those of heaven and netherworld, river and dry land to pay heed and listen to his speech (Maqlu SB I:63-64)
- The wind and the road are commanded to stand still while the speaker gives his testimony (Maqlu SB I:65-68)

**Maqlû I 73-121: 'O Nuska, these are the figurines of my sorcerer' — the indictment and Girra as judge**
- The god knows the speaker's hidden enemies whom he himself does not know (by name, city, house) (Maqlu SB I:87)

**Maqlû II 77-104: 'O blazing Girra, scion of Anu' — 'you alone are my god'**
- Antithetic series: may they die but I live, may they be bound but I go straight, may they end but I increase, may they weaken but I grow strong (Maqlu SB II:94-97)
- Confession: 'You alone are my god, my lord, my judge, my helper, my avenger' (Maqlu SB II:100-103)

**Maqlû II 105-126: 'O blazing Girra, warlike son of Anu' — burn them; robbers take their goods; the seven sages (dough figurine)**
- Curse: may a strong man take the witch's furnishings, a robber carry off her goods, a plunderer lie in wait at her resting place (Maqlu SB II:119-121)

**Maqlû II 127-135: 'O powerful Girra, wild storm' — justice for the oppressed (clay figurine)**
- The fire god gives right decisions to gods and rulers and justice to the oppressed man and woman (Maqlu SB II:128-129)

**Maqlû II 183-204: 'Whoever you are, O witch, who took clay for me from the river' — the burning oven (clay-and-tallow figurine)**
- The witch takes clay from the river for the victim's figurine and buries it in a dark house, a tomb or grave (Maqlu SB II:183-185)
- Great gods (Sîn, Šamaš, Nergal, Ištar) are sent to collect the seed (offspring) of the witch, as much as there is (Maqlu SB II:193-196)
- The victim protests: I did not bewitch her, she bewitched me; she relies on her witchcraft, I rely on the god (Maqlu SB II:198-201)

**Maqlû III 1-30: 'The witch, she who roams the streets' — her evil eye; fire above and below her city**
- The witch stops traffic in the street and cuts off the victim's trade and business (Maqlu SB III:6-7, Maqlu SB III:14-15)
- By looking at them the witch robs the young man of his virility and vitality and the young woman of her charm (Maqlu SB III:8-12)
- The speaker sets fire above the witch's city, embers beneath it and fire in the house she enters (Maqlu SB III:22-24)

**Maqlû III 77-87: 'The Sutean surrounds me, the Elamite pursues me' (bitumen-and-sulphur figurine)**
- The sufferer is covered by the wave and overwhelmed by the current (Maqlu SB III:78)
- Pure river water is asked to smash the witch's heart and release her witchcraft (Maqlu SB III:85-86)

**Maqlû III 88-101: 'Whoever you are, O witch' — I have seized your mouth; the yellow seal**
- Death stands in the witch's footsteps (Maqlu SB III:91)
- The speaker seizes the witch's mouth, tongue, eyes, feet, knees and arms in turn and ties her arms behind her back (Maqlu SB III:92-97)

**Maqlû III 102-115: 'O you who have performed sorcery against me' — slag and soot on her head**
- Litany addressing the witch: 'O you who have bewitched me, seized me, sealed me, bound me, tied me, defiled me' (Maqlu SB III:102-111)

**Maqlû III 116-124: 'She who has performed sorcery against me ... this be her boat'**
- As this (model) boat turns over, so may the witch's sorcery turn back onto her own head and body (Maqlu SB III:121-123)

**Maqlû III 125-135: Sîn's boat — the witches set adrift to the ocean**
- The moon god's crescent is a boat that carries release from witchcraft between its horns (Maqlu SB III:125-126)

**Maqlû III 136-153: 'O sherd of the streets' — 'I myself am heaven, you cannot defile me'**
- The speaker climbs the roof to cover the witch's window and blocks her tracks on the ground, setting a demon and a pursuing ghost on her path (Maqlu SB III:140-143)
- Self-identification: I am heaven, I am the netherworld, I am a thorn, the sting of the scorpion, a high mountain: your witchcraft cannot touch or come near me (Maqlu SB III:147-153)

**Maqlû III 154-179: 'Hand, hand, strong hand of humankind' — rising like fish from water**
- The speaker is marked with the 'designs of life' (uṣurāt balāṭi) by the goddess who illumines fate (Maqlu SB III:176-177)

**Maqlû IV 1-79: 'Burn, burn, blaze, blaze!' — the great litany of the witch's deeds, 'may Girra release'**
- The witch has handed the victim over to a skull, to the ghost of a kinsman or of a stranger, to a roaming ghost with no one to care for it, to the steppe and the wasteland (Maqlu SB IV:15-23)
- The witch hides the victim's figurines in a wall, under a threshold, in a drain, under a bridge for crowds to trample, or under water in a channel (Maqlu SB IV:30-35)
- The witch feeds the victim's figurines to dogs, pigs and birds and throws them into the river (Maqlu SB IV:40-41)

**Maqlû IV 80-94: 'Whoever you are, O witch ... whether friend or companion' — Night, the veiled bride, breaks their weapon**
- Night is asked to break the witches' weapon and impose sleeplessness on them (Maqlu SB IV:94)

**Maqlû IV 95-106: 'My murderess, my witch' — height of heaven, depth of netherworld (broken)**
- The witch's (or her power's) height is that of heaven and her depth that of the netherworld (Maqlu SB IV:96, Maqlu SB IV:99-100)

**Maqlû IV 107-114: 'Of the Sun, who is his father?' — he is the judge**
- Riddle-genealogy: who is the Sun's father, mother and sister? Sîn, Nikkal, Manzât (the rainbow) — he is the judge who destroys witchcraft (Maqlu SB IV:107-110)

**Maqlû IV 115-122: 'Six are their bindings, seven are my undoings'**
- Foreign women (Gutean, Elamite, Hanigalbatean) and native women tie magical bindings (knots) against the speaker (Maqlu SB IV:116-117)
- Whatever the witches bind by night the speaker releases by day, and what they bind by day he releases at night (Maqlu SB IV:119-120)

**Maqlû IV 123-153: 'My friend is a witch, but I am a releaser' — the seven and seven witches burned; catchline**
- Refrain: 'the witch is a witch (of whatever people or trade), but I am a releaser' (anāku pāširāk) (Maqlu SB IV:123-136)
- May the witches be for the drain, while the speaker sweeps over them like flood water (Maqlu SB IV:150-151)

**Maqlû V 1-10: 'My sorceress ... sits in the shade of a pile of bricks' — thyme and sesame**
- The witch sits in the shade of a pile of bricks working sorcery and forming figurines of the victim (Maqlu SB V:2-3)

**Maqlû V 19-47: 'Strong one, who decides our verdict' — the judge roars; plant-pun curses; the witch driven off like a dog**
- May street and way, cult niche and its socles, and the gods of steppe and city turn against the witch (Maqlu SB V:37-39)
- May the witch be knocked away like a dog with a stick, a lizard with a clod; may passersby frown at her and dogs whirl through her headbands (Maqlu SB V:40-46)

**Maqlû V 48-56: 'Whoever you are, O witch ... three months, ten days' — cord of the qadištu; blown away like chaff**
- The witch has worked sorcery against the victim for a set span: three months, ten days and half a day (Maqlu SB V:48)
- The spell acts by command of Ištar, Dumuzi, Nanaya mistress of love, and Kanisurra mistress of witches (Maqlu SB V:55-56)

**Maqlû V 57-75: 'Hate-magic that you performed against me I perform against you' — smoke an abomination to heaven**
- The smoke of the burning witch is 'an abomination to heaven' (ikkib šamê) (Maqlu SB V:74)

**Maqlû V 89-97: 'The sinews you have bound up Ea has unbound' — pure before Nuska and Girra**
- Ea and Asalluḫi unbind the victim's bound sinews and release his twisted and fettered figurines (Maqlu SB V:89-90)

**Maqlû V 98-111: 'You, Water, that flows over all the lands' — adjured by the seven sages**
- River, Tigris, Euphrates and ocean water, drawn by the sages of the apsû and adjured by the seven sages of Eridu, is sprinkled to cool the witches' hearts and embers (Maqlu SB V:98-110)

**Maqlû V 112-131: 'My sorcerers ... you shall not cross the Tigris and Euphrates to me'**
- The witches are forbidden to cross the Tigris and Euphrates, dyke and canal, wall and battlement, or to enter by the city gate to reach the speaker (Maqlu SB V:125-128)

**Maqlû V 132-141: 'Raging, furious are you' — who but Ea can calm you; my mouth is water, your mouth is fire**
- Antithesis: my mouth is water, your mouth is fire; may the spell of my mouth extinguish the spell of yours (Maqlu SB V:138-141)

**Maqlû VI 1-15: 'Enlil is my head, my face is Ūmu' — gods at the doorway**
- May the enemy's words be like (bad) apples that crumble before god and king (Maqlu SB VI:12)

**Maqlû VI 16-23: 'My sorceress is a qumqummatu' — why do you carry my life to the princes?**
- The witch carries the victim's life off to the infernal 'princes' (malkū) of the netherworld (Maqlu SB VI:20)

**Maqlû VI 24-33: 'Kukru, kukru, inhabitants of the pure, holy mountains'**
- May the witch's sorcery blacken her like ashes and crumble like plaster from a wall; may the knot of her heart be loosened (Maqlu SB VI:31-33)

**Maqlû VI 40-44: 'Ha, my witch, my deceiver' — why is smoke rising from your house?**
- The speaker taunts the witch: why is smoke rising from your house? (Maqlu SB VI:41-42)

**Maqlû VI 45-51: 'Before Ningirsu called out the alāla in the land' — scattering the hailstorm**
- The witch gathers (hail)stones and storm clouds against the victim; he scatters them like the north-west wind (Maqlu SB VI:47-48)

**Maqlû VI 52-64: 'On the day that the witch bewitched me' — she took my shadow from the wall; the kukru twigs**
- The witch 'took my shadow from the wall' and collected the dust of my feet (Maqlu SB VI:55)

**Maqlû VI 65-68: 'You who have performed all kinds of sorcery' — the south wind carries it off**
- May the south wind carry off what (sorcery) is on the witch's right and on her left (Maqlu SB VI:68)

**Maqlû VI 69-77: 'Pure Sulphur, daughter of the great heavens am I'**
- The incantation of Marduk, sage of the gods, is cast upon the speaker's inner hem (Maqlu SB VI:76-77)

**Maqlû VI 78-84: 'Sulphur, Sulphur, daughter of River' — the seven and seven**
- Sulphur, daughter of River, whose witches and enemies are seven and seven, was bewitched yet not bewitched: who can work witchcraft against Sulphur? (Maqlu SB VI:78-82)

**Maqlû VI 106-112: 'O River, I have eaten, I have drunk' — River the door of my gate**
- The speaker tells River that he has eaten, drunk, anointed and clothed himself, and that River is the door of his gate (Maqlu SB VI:106-110)

**Maqlû VI 113-117: 'Ha, my witch ... I know your form' — sulphur, daughter of the great gods**
- The speaker tells the witch: whoever you are, I am watching, I know your form (Maqlu SB VI:113-114)

**Maqlû VII 1-21: 'My hand is the Rainbow, the Scorpion' — the ford and quay asleep, locks on the door**
- The speaker (whose hand is the Rainbow and the Scorpion) shines forth against the witch like the rainbow in the heavens (Maqlu SB VII:1, Maqlu SB VII:3)
- At night the ford, the quay and all the sailors are asleep, locks are set on door and bolt and sealed with an incantation so that sorcery cannot enter the house (Maqlu SB VII:8-13)
- May god, king, noble and prince glower at the witches, and may the witch not escape their grasp (Maqlu SB VII:16-17)

**Maqlû VII 22-28: 'I am impregnating you, my self, my body' — as Šakkan his herd, the plough the earth**
- Fertility analogy: as Šakkan impregnated his herd and the plough the earth, so the speaker casts the spell on himself to 'impregnate' his body and expel the evil (Maqlu SB VII:22-27)

**Maqlû VII 47-54: 'Enlil is my head, Sirius my form' — as tin and iron, sorcery cannot approach**
- As sorcery cannot touch tin and iron (or the shining gods), so it cannot approach the speaker (Maqlu SB VII:51-54)

**Maqlû VII 101-113: 'Your sorcery ... Ea undoes'; 'Your tightly knotted knots' — may your mouth be full of earth**
- May the witch's evil mouth be filled with earth and her evil tongue bound with a gag (Maqlu SB VII:104-105, Maqlu SB VII:111-112)

**Maqlû VII 114-140: 'I wash my hands, I cleanse my body in pure Eridu spring water' — bad dreams, entrails and curses onto the substitute**
- The evil consequences of bad dreams, signs and portents and of ominous entrails seen in extispicy are washed away (Maqlu SB VII:118-122)

**Maqlû VIII 1-16: 'Until you rose, I was awaiting you, my lord, Šamaš' — her witchcraft downstream, I upstream**
- May the witch's witchcraft go downstream, but may I go upstream (Maqlu SB VIII:15-16)

**Maqlû VIII 17-27: 'Šamaš has risen' — the plant of release sent to Šamaš's daughter; unknot the hand that bound**
- The speaker sends the plant of release to the sun god's daughter, his releaser, to unknot the hand that bound a knot (Maqlu SB VIII:20-21)

**Maqlû VIII 28-45: 'When the witch crossed the river' — Ea darkens her face; hands washed over her figurines**
- When the witch crossed the river and sat in the ferry, the sages of the apsû saw her, Ea darkened her face and struck her with epilepsy and trembling, and River cast her own fear upon her (Maqlu SB VIII:28-38)

**Maqlû VIII 54-A+25: 'Now, then, this one: the witch is hostile to me' — removing the witchcraft from her insides (fragmentary)**
- The speaker strikes the witch's stomach, lungs and innards and pulls her witchcraft and spittle up out of her body (Maqlu SB VIII:A+1, Maqlu SB VIII:A+2, Maqlu SB VIII:A+3, Maqlu SB VIII:A+4)

**Maqlû VIII A+38-B+8: 'The sorceress who sets witchcraft in motion' — may Ereškigal refuse her, dog and bitch tear her flesh**
- The witch seizes the forehead, makes the eyes turn, blocks hearing, shuts the ears, wrongs young men and assaults young women (Maqlu SB VIII:A+42, Maqlu SB VIII:A+43, Maqlu SB VIII:A+44, Maqlu SB VIII:A+45)
- Curse: may Ereškigal not let the witch go down to the netherworld; may eagle and vulture prey on her corpse and dog and bitch tear her flesh (Maqlu SB VIII:B+3, Maqlu SB VIII:B+4, Maqlu SB VIII:B+6, Maqlu SB VIII:B+7)

**Maqlû VIII B+9-B+22: 'You are my reflection, you are my vigour' — 'you are mine and I am yours'; colophon**
- The speaker addresses his own reflection, vigour, vitality and virility: do not accept witchcraft or murder; 'you are mine and I am yours' (Maqlu SB VIII:B+9, Maqlu SB VIII:B+10, Maqlu SB VIII:B+11, Maqlu SB VIII:B+12, Maqlu SB VIII:B+18)

**Maqlû Ritual Tablet 1-31': the night rite begins — mouth-washing, the tallow figurine on the torch, prostration, Nuska on the roof**
- A tallow figurine with salt in its mouth is set on a burning torch so that it drips away over a bowl (Maqlu SB RT:8'-11')

**Maqlû Ritual Tablet 138'-180': the morning rites — handwashing over the witch's likeness, bread-figurines for dogs, the face in the water**
- Clay figurines of the witch are set on flour drawings in a washbasin; the patient washes his hands over them and strikes them three times with a cornel stick (Maqlu SB RT:142'-147', Maqlu SB RT:166'-168')
- Dough figurines of the warlock and witch are put inside loaves, raised in the right and left hands and given to a male and a female dog (Maqlu SB RT:170'-174')
- The patient looks at his face reflected in a bowl of water, which is then sprinkled toward sunrise (Maqlu SB RT:175'-177')

**Marduk's Address to the Demons 56-107: 'I am Asalluḫi' (second half) — physician of mankind, releaser of guilt**
- The god purges (sorts) the righteous and the wicked in the river (ordeal) (MardDemons SB –:82)

**Marduk's Address to the Demons 1'-63': 'Or you who ...' — the demons at the invalid's bedside**
- Catalogue of demons that stand, sit and walk by the invalid's bed, eat and drink with him, and butt like an ox, roar like a lion, slither like a snake, bleat like a kid before him (MardDemons SB –:25'-63')

**Marduk's Address to the Demons 64'-99': demons of streets, river and forest; the restless dead with no kin**
- Catalogue of restless dead: those with no guardian on the steppe, killed in battle or by the dagger, impaled, those with no father, mother, kin, son or heir to pour water (MardDemons SB –:85'-99')

**Marduk's Address to the Demons 100'-128': 'May Asalluḫi extirpate you' — handed to the gatekeepers of the netherworld; exorcised by heaven and earth**
- The demons are handed to the gate of the Land of No Return, to the seven gatekeepers of Ereškigal, to Namtar and to the chief gatekeeper, who shuts the gate on them (MardDemons SB –:110'-117')

**Syncretistic Hymn to Marduk 1-17: 'He of insightful thinking' — heaven his tiara, the netherworld his sandals**
- The god's sight is so far-reaching that the whole world is to him no bigger than the impression of a cuneiform wedge (MardSyncr SB –:8-9)

**Syncretistic Hymn to Marduk 18-60: 'Your name is Anšar ... Dagan ... Adad ... Šamaš ... your name is indeed Marduk'**
- Syncretistic litany: each great god (Anšar, Dagan, Adad, Nannar, Šamaš, Erra, Ningirsu) is declared to be a name or aspect of the one supreme god: 'your name is X ... your name is indeed Marduk' (MardSyncr SB –:18, MardSyncr SB –:21-22, MardSyncr SB –:25-26, MardSyncr SB –:29-30, MardSyncr SB –:33-34, MardSyncr SB –:37-38, MardSyncr SB –:41, MardSyncr SB –:44-45, MardSyncr SB –:48-49, MardSyncr SB –:53, MardSyncr SB –:57, MardSyncr SB –:60)

**Great Prayer to Nabû 9-44: 'O Lord ... O Nabû' — anger a dragon, yet heaper of plenty; calm yourself, have pity**
- Prayer in which every couplet is sung twice, first to 'O Lord' and then to the god by name ('O Nabû') (NabuPr SB –:9-44)
- The god's anger is a dragon, his yoke a raging beast, his pitilessness a conflagration, his scowl a dark cloud — yet he heaps up plenty (NabuPr SB –:17-29)

**Great Prayer to Nabû 45-90: 'You are angry with your servant' — cast into the billow and the morass; 'you called my name'**
- The sufferer bellows like a bull slaughtered with the butcher's knife and is cast into the maw of a terrible power (NabuPr SB –:57-58)

**Great Prayer to Nabû 91-116: 'O Forgiver ... without you no forgiveness' — the god cast his servant out; 'How long?'**
- Without the god's consent no forgiveness can occur; unless by him no iniquity or crime can be absolved (NabuPr SB –:91-102)
- The sufferer's body putrefies, his manhood fades, lice torment him, discharge covers his brow, his mind wanders and he craves death (NabuPr SB –:106-115)

**Great Prayer to Nabû 173-225: 'Loose his fetters' — bitter dates turn sweet; leave him a vent to breathe; restore his fields**
- Proverbial consolation: early dates are bitter but later sweet; grain struck by smut in budding still gives full yield at maturity (NabuPr SB –:178-182)
- Plea: if you discipline your servant, leave him a vent to breathe through; turn your face toward him (NabuPr SB –:187-190)
- Prayer that the restored servant regain his fields, prebend shares and sanctuary, build his storehouse and chapel (NabuPr SB –:200-211)

**Cuthaean Legend (MB) A b+1-29: Enmerkar left no stela; the six kings and their host created by Ea**
- A god creates with his own hand an invading horde of supernatural warriors (with the awesomeness of lions) and sends death, famine and high prices with them (NaramSin MB A:b+8, NaramSin MB A:b+9, NaramSin MB A:b+10, NaramSin MB A:b+11, NaramSin MB A:b+12, NaramSin MB A:b+15)
- The gods decree that the destroying host shall not seize the holy city, shall eat no food, drink only water, wander all day and get no sleep at night (NaramSin MB A:b+17, NaramSin MB A:b+18, NaramSin MB A:b+19, NaramSin MB A:b+20, NaramSin MB A:b+21, NaramSin MB A:b+22, NaramSin MB A:b+23, NaramSin MB A:b+24)

**Cuthaean Legend (OB) I a+1-b+22: three armies annihilated — 'What has god brought upon my reign?'**
- The king sends out three successive armies (180,000, 120,000, 60,000) against the enemy and each is annihilated (NaramSin OB I:b+1, NaramSin OB I:b+2, NaramSin OB I:b+3, NaramSin OB I:b+4, NaramSin OB I:b+5, NaramSin OB I:b+6, NaramSin OB I:b+7, NaramSin OB I:b+8)
- The defeated king despairs: 'What has god brought upon my reign? I am a king who brings no well-being to his land, a shepherd who brings none to his people' (NaramSin OB I:b+9, NaramSin OB I:b+10, NaramSin OB I:b+11, NaramSin OB I:b+12, NaramSin OB I:b+13, NaramSin OB I:b+14)

**The gods create the raven-faced host, which sweeps the world (Cuthaean Legend)**
- The great gods create a demonic enemy host with bird-bodies and raven-faces, suckled by Tiamat and raised in the mountains (NaramSin SB –:31-36)
- The invading host is led by seven royal brothers, each named in order, sons of a named king and queen (NaramSin SB –:37-46)

**Blood test, refused oracle, Narām-Sîn's defiance and three lost armies (Cuthaean Legend)**
- A soldier pricks the strange enemy to test whether blood flows: if so they are human, if not they are demons (NaramSin SB –:63-71)
- Rhetorical defiance: what lion ever took omens, what wolf consulted a dream-interpreter? (NaramSin SB –:80-81)
- In three successive years the king sends huge armies and not one man returns alive (NaramSin SB –:84-87)
- The king laments that he is a king who brings no well-being to his land and a shepherd who brings none to his people (NaramSin SB –:88-93)
- A god reminds the divine assembly that, though they ordered humankind destroyed, they also decreed that people should exist forever (NaramSin SB –:97-103)

**New Year rites, favourable omen, Ištar's oracle: spare the enemy (Cuthaean Legend)**
- A goddess forbids the king to destroy the enemy, for a high god will call them to account in future days (NaramSin SB –:128-133)
- Prophecy that a doomed city will be burned and dogs will prowl round it (NaramSin SB –:134)
- Curse or prophecy: the earth will diminish its harvest and the date palm its yield (NaramSin SB –:136)
- The gods themselves remove the enemy as tribute, while the king lays no hand on them (NaramSin SB –:147-148)

**Narām-Sîn's counsel to a future ruler; the stela in Nergal's cella at Cutha (Cuthaean Legend)**
- The king advises his successor to stay inside walls, fill moats, lay down weapons and not go out against the raider (NaramSin SB –:159-169)
- The reader who blesses the author will in turn be blessed by a future reader (NaramSin SB –:175-180)

**Anu sends Kakka down to Ereškigal; Namtar sent up for her portion (Nergal and Ereškigal, SB)**
- A messenger carries greetings of well-being (šulmu) to each of the great gods in turn by name (NergEresh SB –:a+34-a+45)

**Six days of love, Nergal's flight, Ereškigal's lament and threat, the search in heaven (Nergal and Ereškigal, SB)**
- The goddess declares herself made impure (by intercourse) and unable to give judgment until her lover is sent back (NergEresh SB –:d+67-d+68, NergEresh SB –:d+83-d+84)
- After the union the house and attendants are sprinkled with water to purify them (NergEresh SB –:d+39-d+42)

**Nergal storms back down, seizes Ereškigal; Anu grants him to dwell with her forever (Nergal and Ereškigal, SB)**
- The high god decrees that the god shall dwell with the underworld queen forever as her husband (NergEresh SB –:e+43-e+49)

**Ninurta's body as the pantheon (Macranthropic Hymn to Ninurta)**
- Hymn in which each limb of one supreme god (face, eyes, ears, lips, neck, arms, feet) is another god, so that he gathers all the gods in himself (NinurtaMacr SB –:9-32)

**Ninurta's weapons and bow (Macranthropic Hymn to Ninurta)**
- The god's weapon swallows the sea like gruel, melts mountains like tallow, and turns stone mountains to ashes (NinurtaMacr SB –:38-41, NinurtaMacr SB –:47-48)
- The god's weapon is merciless: it accepts no supplication and hears no prayer (NinurtaMacr SB –:42-43)
- The divine bow's upper limb shakes heaven and its lower limb rouses the netherworld; its arrow is a star (NinurtaMacr SB –:49-58)

**Ninurta who reverses fortunes and rescues the helpless (Hymn to Ninurta as Savior)**
- The god frees the bird tied by the fowler, the gazelle from the net and the onager from the enclosure, images of the rescued sufferer (NinurtaSavior SB –:21-26)
- The god in the midst of destruction leaves a remnant (rēhu) and is asked to preserve a city's seed (NinurtaSavior SB –:20, NinurtaSavior SB –:31, NinurtaSavior SB –:53-54)
- The god sends a favourable wind to a skipperless ship swept by storm and brings it on its way (NinurtaSavior SB –:17-18, NinurtaSavior SB –:34-35)
- The learned scholar earns not even chaff while an ordinary accountant set over him earns a mina of gold a day (NinurtaSavior SB –:39-45)

**Prologue: the spring flood brings pasture; Ox's opening speech (Ox and Horse)**
- The spring flood of the rivers and melting snow sweeps down the wadis and turns wasteland into moist pasture (OxHorse SB –:A+9-A+20, OxHorse SB –:A+27-A+32)

**The exchanges of Ox and Horse: war, chariot, labour, the king's stable (Ox and Horse)**
- The horse is mocked as unable to see the track beyond its reins, its eyes staring but seeing nothing (OxHorse SB –:A+16'-A+18')
- The ox is mocked as a beast of burden who with the donkey carries panniers and provisions on the road (OxHorse SB –:B+11-B+12)
- The horse boasts that its stable stands before the king, greenery is chosen for it and its flesh is not eaten (OxHorse SB –:C+10-C+16)
- Someone's tears flow like water from a waterskin (OxHorse SB –:B+9)

**Palm's boast and Vine's reply (Palm and Vine)**
- Date palm and grapevine dispute which is greater: the palm boasts its shade, fruit, beer, timber and rope, the vine its wine for gods and healing (PalmVine SB –:2'-26', PalmVine SB –:33'-50')
- Wine boasts that it heals the feverish, brings back the dying from the netherworld and sweetens the mourner's grief (PalmVine SB –:41'-48')

**Gimil-Ninurta's poverty, his goat and the mayor's insult (Poor Man of Nippur)**
- A destitute man sells the one garment he has, having no change of clothes, to buy an animal (PoorMan SB –:10-15)
- A poor man fears that if he slaughters his one animal his neighbours and kin will be angry at not being fed (PoorMan SB –:16-22)
- A poor man brings a gift to a local official, who keeps it and throws him out with a bone and third-rate beer (PoorMan SB –:23-63)

**The borrowed chariot, the box of birds and the first revenge (Poor Man of Nippur)**
- A poor man goes to the king, prostrates himself, and asks a favour, which the king grants without question (PoorMan SB –:72-84)
- A citizen of the holy city is a protected person (kidinnu) of the god whose blood must not be on one's hands (PoorMan SB –:104-106)

**The false physician and the decoy: second and third revenge (Poor Man of Nippur)**
- The trickster hires a youth to raise a commotion so that the household chases him and the victim is left alone (PoorMan SB –:140-153)
- The beaten oppressor crawls back into town on all fours (PoorMan SB –:159-160)

**Poplar and Ash dispute (Series of the Poplar)**
- Poplar and ash tree dispute: the poplar boasts of shade, gates, boats and rods; the ash of tools that hold joins and dig canals (Poplar SB –:c+6-c+31, Poplar SB –:c+33-c+40, Poplar SB –:d+9-d+24)
- The rod (of a tree's wood) flogs the rebel, strengthens the fool and opens the ears of him who will not listen (Poplar SB –:c+12-c+14)

**Exhortation to worship the Queen of Nippur alone (Hymn to the Queen of Nippur)**
- The worshippers are told not to turn to any other god nor say a prayer to any other goddess, but to bear one deity's yoke alone (QueenNippur SB –:10-13)
- Worshippers are to pray to or remember the deity day and night continually (QueenNippur SB –:9)

**The man who did not bow to Ištar is struck down (Hymn to the Queen of Nippur)**
- A man who brought no offering and did not bow to the goddess is struck: his god and goddess abandon him, he is bent double, his city shuns him, hair falls out and his wife seeks another (QueenNippur SB –:B+6-B+17, QueenNippur SB –:B+25-B+26)
- A female night demon (the owl-demon kilīlu / lilītu) peers into bedrooms and leans through the window to strike a man (QueenNippur SB –:B+18-B+23)
- The narrator of a cautionary tale reveals 'I was that man' who neglected the deity (QueenNippur SB –:B+7)
- Young men and maidens whirl and dance together in a festival (QueenNippur SB –:B+3)

**Litany: no one but she can (Hymn to the Queen of Nippur)**
- Litany refrain 'No one but she can ...' listing the deity's exclusive powers (grant kingship, show mercy, revive the dead, bring back from the grave) (QueenNippur SB –:C+1-C+35)

**Nippur, the Ebaradurgara and the goddess presiding over the gods (Hymn to the Queen of Nippur)**
- The holy city is the bond of heaven and earth and an unscalable mountain that the high god built to dwell in (QueenNippur SB –:D+1-D+4)
- The goddess's temple is a counterpart of the high god's own dwelling, whose light covers the inhabited world (QueenNippur SB –:D+5-D+11)
- Every day the gods assemble around the goddess for counsel, receive their portions and kneel at her feet (QueenNippur SB –:D+16-D+24)
- A hymn ends praying that this song may be pleasing to the deity and never cease before her (QueenNippur SB –:D+41-D+50)

**Feast with the great gods and blessings on the cities (Hymn to the Queen of Nippur)**
- The great gods are seated with the goddess at a feast and told 'drink, drink!' so their hearts rejoice (QueenNippur SB –:E+4-E+16)
- The goddess is asked to decree well-being for a list of cities in turn (Uruk, Akkad, Adab, Badtibira, Kish, Ur) (QueenNippur SB –:E+21-E+32)

**Incantation: the curse, the inviolable drawing of the gods (Saĝba, bilingual)**
- The curse (māmītu) is the gods' inviolable boundary-drawing of heaven and earth, which no god or man may cross or undo (Sagba SB I:1-10)
- A deity is called 'the one god' who does not change or cannot be altered (Sagba SB I:7-8)

**Šamaš illuminator of heaven and earth, shepherd above and below (Great Hymn to Šamaš)**
- Nothing is hidden from the sun god: at his rising people's footprints are revealed and he knows the intentions of all lands of different tongues (ShamashHymn SB –:9-10, ShamashHymn SB –:49-50)
- The sun god is shepherd of the lower regions and herdsman of the upper regions; all creatures Ea created are entrusted to him (ShamashHymn SB –:23-26, ShamashHymn SB –:31-34)
- The sun god crosses heaven, earth and the unfathomed sea every day and returns by night; no other god toils so (ShamashHymn SB –:27-30, ShamashHymn SB –:35-46)
- The gods and the netherworld gods rejoice and assemble at the sun god's rising (ShamashHymn SB –:7-8, ShamashHymn SB –:47)
- Diviners with their oil-bowl and cedar, dream-interpreters, wicked and just all kneel before the sun god (ShamashHymn SB –:53-56)

**Šamaš the judge and rescuer of travellers, captives, the sick and the dead (Great Hymn to Šamaš)**
- The god brings up the one gone down to the depths and rescues the dead from the land of no return (ShamashHymn SB –:70, ShamashHymn SB –:80)

**Šamaš's net for the wicked: adulterer, corrupt judge, usurer, false weigher (Great Hymn to Šamaš)**
- The sun god's net and snare are spread so that no shedder of blood, perjurer or adulterer escapes (ShamashHymn SB –:83-87, ShamashHymn SB –:94)
- The man who covets his neighbour's wife dies before his time, with no father or brother to speak for him at his trial (ShamashHymn SB –:88-93)
- The exploitative lender loses profit and principal, while the honest creditor is blessed with long life, family and seed like a perpetual spring (ShamashHymn SB –:103-106, ShamashHymn SB –:112-121)
- The seed (offspring) of evildoers will not endure (ShamashHymn SB –:121-124)

**All who pray turn to Šamaš; his feast on the twentieth (Great Hymn to Šamaš)**
- The heavens are too small to be the god's divining cup, and all lands too small to be his seer's bowl (ShamashHymn SB –:154-155)
- On his monthly holy day the god rejoices and drinks the beer and libations people pour for him (ShamashHymn SB –:156-161)
- The god opens the understanding (ears) of the whole world and makes omens clear (ShamashHymn SB –:149-153)

**Closing praise: all creatures led before Šamaš; blessings from the gods and Aya (Great Hymn to Šamaš)**
- The god shortens days and lengthens nights and covers the earth with cold, frost, ice and snow (ShamashHymn SB –:180-181)
- The god opens the gate and bolt of heaven, lifting socket, pin, latchkey and bolt (ShamashHymn SB –:182-183)
- The god's bride bids him 'Rest!' in the bedchamber at the end of his day (ShamashHymn SB –:200)

**Lifted-hand prayer to Adad, with Sargon's insertion against an eclipse (šuʾila Adad 1a)**
- At the storm god's roar the people fall silent, meadows are ruined and fields writhe (Shuila Adad SB 1a:17-20)

**Lifted-hand prayer to Adad against enemies and witchcraft, with thunder ritual (šuʾila Adad 1b)**
- The god slaughters the mighty and arrogant and destroys the malevolent and wicked (Shuila Adad SB 1b:9-11)

**Lifted-hand prayer to Anu, releaser of evil dreams (šuʾila Anu 1)**
- If granted mercy the petitioner vows to endow the god's house lavishly and make its door-bolt drip with oil (Shuila Anu SB 1:17)

**Lifted-hand prayer to Bēlet-ilī, creator of the womb (šuʾila Bēlet-ilī 2)**
- The mother goddess is the creator of the womb (bānât šassūri) (Shuila Bēlet-ilī SB 2:2)
- Among all the stars of heaven the goddess's station is the highest (Shuila Bēlet-ilī SB 2:12-13)

**Lifted-hand prayer to Damkina, with Ashurbanipal's insertion (šuʾila Damkina 1)**
- The sufferer asks that the one who does not fear his god may learn from his example (Shuila Damkina SB 1:17-18)

**Lifted-hand prayer to Ea, with Banītu-tēreš's insertion against portents and witchcraft (šuʾila Ea 1a)**
- The god brings the river-flood and abundance, makes the rivers rejoice and creates grain, the life of the people (Shuila Ea SB 1a:6-8)
- The god is addressed as creator of humans and of the womb (Shuila Ea SB 1a:12'-13')

**Lifted-hand prayers to Ea, creator of everything (šuʾila Ea 1b and 2)**
- The god is said to have created the great gods and to render their verdicts (Shuila Ea SB 2:16-17)

**Lifted-hand prayer to Enlil, lord of lords and king of kings, against an eclipse (šuʾila Enlil 1a)**
- The petitioner asks that the one who looks on him with ill will be put to shame and that his own word be heard in the assembly (Shuila Enlil SB 1a:24)

**Lifted-hand prayers to Enlil: personal gods at right and left (šuʾila Enlil 1b and 2)**
- Prayer that the personal god stand at the petitioner's right side and the personal goddess at his left (Shuila Enlil SB 1b:27-30)
- The high god heaps up the mountains and releases heaven and earth (Shuila Enlil SB 2:3-4)

**Lifted-hand prayers to Gula and Baba against illness, eclipse and frightening dreams (šuʾila Gula 1b and 2)**
- The sick man prays that his severe illness be removed so that he may see the light (live) (Shuila Gula SB 1b:10'-15')

**Šuʾila to Ištar 1: 'O valiant Ištar, cherished among the goddesses'**
- Hymnic confidence: how sweet it is to pray to the god, how near is the god's hearing (Shuila Ištar SB 1:21)

**Šuʾila to Ištar 2: 'I beseech you, lady of ladies' (the great prayer to Ištar)**
- The war goddess makes brothers at peace fight each other (Shuila Ištar SB 2:9)
- The love goddess opens the veils of young women (sexuality under her patronage) (Shuila Ištar SB 2:33)
- Litany of 'aḫulap' ('enough!, have mercy'): mercy asked in turn for the sufferer's body, heart, omens, household and feelings (Shuila Ištar SB 2:27-30, Shuila Ištar SB 2:45-50)
- The sufferer tosses like a wave whipped by an evil wind; his heart flutters and flies like a bird of heaven (Shuila Ištar SB 2:62-63)
- The sufferer has seen dark days, gloomy months and years of grief (Shuila Ištar SB 2:72-74)
- Petition for restoration: the dark smoky brazier brightened, the extinguished torch rekindled, the scattered family gathered, the fold enlarged (Shuila Ištar SB 2:87-90)
- Prayer that the deity's mood become calm like the clear water of a river (Shuila Ištar SB 2:96)

**Šuʾila to Ištar 4: a woman's prayer with offerings, for healing and a child**
- The petitioner sets food and drink before the deity: 'eat the pleasing food, drink the sweet drink, let your heart be at ease' (Shuila Ištar SB 4:7'-11')

**Šuʾila to Ištar 13: ritual for a slandered man and the prayer 'I implore you' (an eršahunga)**
- Ritual prescribed for a man beset by slander and sorcery who has lost the favour of god, king and palace (Shuila Ištar SB 13:1-13)
- Image of affliction: a wall has fallen on the sufferer and overwhelmed him (Shuila Ištar SB 13:x+9)

**Šuʾila to Šamaš 5: 'whose yes means yes' (namburbi against an evil portent)**
- The god's 'yes' is yes and his 'no' is no: his affirmation cannot be altered (Shuila Šamaš SB 5:1, Shuila Šamaš SB 5:8-9)

**Šuʾila to Šamaš 6: 'King of heaven and earth', against a curse seizing the chest, with an effigy rite**
- Evil or a curse (māmītu) laid on the sufferer by a friend, brother, sister, slave or kin, someone known or unknown, by hand or mouth, is to be released (Shuila Šamaš SB 6:6-9, Shuila Šamaš SB 6:21-24)
- Wherever the sufferer goes is disagreeable: strife at home, contention in the street, worry pursuing him night and day (Shuila Šamaš SB 6:14-18)

**Series of the Spider: creation in assembly, two creatures named, and their quarrel rebuked**
- After the gods in assembly created heaven, netherworld and all creatures, they distributed sanctuaries and dwellings to every creature (Spider SB –:1-6)
- A creator god makes two small creatures and gives them names that define their nature (Spider SB –:9-12)
- Small creatures boast of their strength and revile one another before the assembly of all animals, and another creature rebukes them for upsetting the order of the gods (Spider SB –:7-8, Spider SB –:13-17, Spider SB –:24-33)
- A creature or demon is called 'master/lord of flies' (bēl zumbī) (Spider SB –:19)

**Babylonian Theodicy, stanzas 1-2: the orphaned sufferer addresses his wise friend; death is the way of the fathers**
- The friend consoles: our fathers all went the way of death and crossed the river of the dead, as ordained of old (Theod SB –:16-17)

**Babylonian Theodicy, stanzas 3-5: poverty of the sufferer; wild ass, lion and rich man prosper without offerings**
- The wise man's heart is a deep wellspring, the swell of the ocean that never diminishes (Theod SB –:23-24)
- The sufferer points out that the wild ass, the lion and the rich man prosper without ever bringing offerings to the gods, while he who offered faithfully suffers (Theod SB –:48-55)
