- A commander stationed for months in Amurru guards the roads and passes, half his chariots by the sea and half at the flank of Mount Lebanon, waiting for the Egyptian king's army (Ugarit RS 20.0033 o:3-20)
- Winter rain fills the cisterns, the cold 'eats' the soldiers, chariots break, horses die and troops are lost (Ugarit RS 20.0033 o:21-30)
- A captive taken in a night skirmish is questioned about the enemy king's plans: 'the king of Egypt is coming out' (Ugarit RS 20.0033 r:4'-15')

**King of Kadesh to the king of Ugarit, 'my brother': my servant Beti-ʾilu says my offerings are in Ugarit; I send goats, donkeys and asafoetida for his sacrifices; let no one bar his way (RS 20.0172)**
- A foreign king sends animals and spices to Ugarit for his offerings (nīqu) there and asks the king to protect his servant on the way (Ugarit RS 20.0172 o:7-r:10)

**'The king' (of Carchemish?) to the king of Ugarit: the king of Ušnatu complains you took his borders and a town; why have you done this? (RS 20.0174,a)**
- A king complains to the overlord that his neighbour has taken his borders and a town ('why have you done this?') (Ugarit RS 20.0174,a o:6-15)

**Rapʾanu to Bin-šipṭi 'my sister': the gods of Baṭruna, of Ugarit and of our father's house sate you with old age; with a second letter of her son, who falls at his mother's feet (RS 20.0178)**
- 'The gods of our father's house' are invoked alongside the gods of the land as the family's protecting gods (Ugarit RS 20.0178 o:7, Ugarit RS 20.0178 o:11)
- A son writing to his mother (often the queen mother) falls at her feet in the letter's greeting (Ugarit RS 20.0178 r:1'-4')

**Letter fragment: Baal and the god of Haballa, city of trust, the gods my helpers, guard you and sate you with good old age before the king your lord for ever (RS 20.0225)**
- The gods are called 'my helpers' (ilānū rēṣīya) and a city 'city of trust' in a letter's blessing (Ugarit RS 20.0225 o:3')
- A letter mentions captivity (šallūtu) of people or of a king in a broken context (Ugarit RS 20.0225 o:8'-l.e:2)

**Madaʾe to the prefect: my oxen stolen by men of Rakba; finish the case and return my oxen, or let the named elders of Rakba enter the house of the god and be cleared (RS 20.0239)**
- Accused men (elders of a town) are to come, enter the house of the god and (by oath there) be cleared (Ugarit RS 20.0239 r:8-l.e:3)

**King of Siyannu to the king of Ugarit, 'my brother': my messenger Šamhu-Rašap; settle the case with the man of Pala on the road; men of Beirut did hostility from Ugarit (RS 21.0183)**
- A king sends his messenger with a letter asking his 'brother' king to watch over him until he departs and to settle his cases with foreigners on the road (Ugarit RS 21.0183 o:6-r:3)

**Urhaʾe to Yabninu: whatever wish I ask, give it, and whatever you ask, I will give; a horse sent as greeting-gift (RS 22.0393)**
- Letter formula: 'whatever wish I ask of you, give it; whatever wish you ask of me, I will give you' (Ugarit RS 22.0393 r:1'-6')

**Lady Aruš-Heba to the prefect, 'my son': while my husband lived you were his good friend; whatever you asked he gave; a sash sent; give bronze for the godhead I make (RS 25.0131)**
- A widow reminds her late husband's friend that while her husband lived they were friends and he gave whatever was asked, and asks the same favour of him (Ugarit RS 25.0131 o:5-8)
- A woman asks for bronze because she is making a divine image (godhead) (Ugarit RS 25.0131 o:11-r:3)

**Deed before the mayor of Ugarit and elders: Rapʾanu takes ʾAbi-malku into brotherhood with 100 shekels; whoever hates the other leaves; the childless one's goods pass to the other; seven witnesses (RS 25.0134)**
- Two men make a contract of brotherhood (aḫḫūtu) before the mayor and elders, with a deposit of silver; whoever 'hates' the other forfeits and leaves, and the childless one's estate passes to his adopted brother (Ugarit RS 25.0134 o:1-b.e:1)
- Legal formula: 'if X hates (zêru) Y' marks the unilateral dissolution of a marriage, adoption or brotherhood, with a fixed penalty (Ugarit RS 25.0134 b.e:2-r:8)
- If a man dies without a son, all his property goes to the man he adopted as brother or son (Ugarit RS 25.0134 r:9-t.e:2)

**Verdict of Ini-Tešub: ʾAmar-Baʿlu v. ʿAbdu, who seized his brother as a replacement and the brother died; ʿAbdu offered the oath, Amar-Baal refuses, ʿAbdu is clear of the blood (RS 27.0052)**
- A man seized by force as a replacement (rību) for another dies in custody; his brother sues, the defendant is offered the oath, and the plaintiff's refusal to swear clears him of the blood (Ugarit RS 27.0052 o:2-11)
- Settlement clause: 'tomorrow or the day after' (urram šēram) neither party may raise a claim against the other (Ugarit RS 27.0052 r:2-4)

**Beya (Bay), chief of the troops of the Great King of Egypt, to ʿAmmurapi of Ugarit: I speak to Amun, Re and Seth, gods of Egypt, that they guard you (RS 86.2230)**
- An Egyptian official writing to the king of Ugarit says he speaks to Amun, Re and Seth, the gods of Egypt, that they may guard him (Ugarit RS 86.2230 o:1-9)

**Letter to Urtenu, 'my brother': when the king of the smiths took from me the table ... (RS 86.2232)**
- A 'king' or chief of the smiths (šar qurqurrī) appears as a guild head in a letter (Ugarit RS 86.2232 o:7-10)

**A 'brother' to Šipiṭ-Baʿlu: the man who fell before you and stayed a month with Ari; speak rightly before the king about Beltaya's words; a talent of wool, silver, fish and turmeric (RS 86.2236)**
- A writer asks a courtier to set his matter right before the king so that the king grants his wish (Ugarit RS 86.2236 r:7-10)

**Urhi-Tešub to Urtenu, Yabninu, Baʿlu-danu, Dananu and the great men and elders of the city: the king of Carchemish has returned from Hatti; troops of help come quickly; guard the city until we arrive (RS 88.2009)**
- The overlord's officer tells a city's notables that relief troops are coming quickly: 'guard the city until we arrive' (Ugarit RS 88.2009 b.e:1-r:7)
- A letter is addressed to named notables and to 'the great men and the elders of the city' (Ugarit RS 88.2009 o:5-6)

**Dagan-bēlu to Urtenu, 'my good brother, whom I love like good oil and the scent of cedar': the gods of Ugarit, Ea lord of the wide sea and the gods of Aštata guard your life; guard your mouth before the king (RS 92.2006)**
- A correspondent is called 'my good brother whom I love like good oil and the scent of cedar' (Ugarit RS 92.2006 o:2-4)
- Advice in a letter: guard your mouth (your words) before the king your lord, that he may honour you (Ugarit RS 92.2006 o:8-10)
- A god is called lord of the (wide) sea in an invocation or greeting (Ugarit RS 92.2006 o:6-7)

**Iṣṣur-Rašap to Urtenu his lord: from afar I fall at my lord's feet; my heart laughs to see my lord; with letters to Adad-dayyan and Tamar-Hebat (twice three times I fall) and to Ziminu (RS 92.2017)**
- A servant writes that his heart laughs (rejoices) greatly at seeing his lord: 'who will see my lord's good face and hear his sweet word?' (Ugarit RS 92.2017 o:8-13, Ugarit RS 92.2017 l.e:1-2)

**King of Amurru to the king of Ugarit, 'my son': the storm god killed some of my troops and great men; search the sea for seven days; release the goods of the troops; if a man loves his wife let him take her by ransom (RS 94.2091)**
- A king reports that the storm god (Baal/Addu) has killed some of his troops and great men, apparently at sea (Ugarit RS 94.2091 o:6-9)
- A search or inspection is to be carried out over seven days (e.g. along the sea) and word sent back (Ugarit RS 94.2091 o:10-r:1)
- If a captured man loves his wife, he may take her back by ransom (ipṭiru) (Ugarit RS 94.2091 r:7-10)

**King of Byblos to the king of Ugarit, 'my brother': the gods of Byblos and of Ugarit guard you; the men of the prison house in your land, the man of Baṭruna; 150 shekels in the house of Šamu-Addu at Raʾšu (RS 94.2182)**
- Men of one kingdom are held in a prison house (bīt kīli) in another king's land (Ugarit RS 94.2182 o:8-12)

**Letter fragment: Yašuta with two men in the land; taking from Ugarit; may the gods give (RS 94.2190)**
- A letter wishes that the gods may grant (give) something to the addressee (Ugarit RS 94.2190 l.e:3-4)

**Hili-Šarruma to the queen his lady: my heart pounds because of the king's illness; send me news about it (RS 94.2277)**
- A courtier writes to the queen that his heart pounds over the king's illness and asks her to send news of it (Ugarit RS 94.2277 o:6-10)

**King of Kadesh to the king of Ugarit, 'my brother': there is no barley in my land; give barley, and I will send sheep for offerings (RS 94.2287)**
- A king writes that there is no barley in his land and asks his 'brother' king to give barley, sending sheep for offerings (Ugarit RS 94.2287 o:11-r:2)

**Kin-[...] to the prefect, 'my brother': why have you not given camp troops and chariots? the Suteans struck their borders; why did your king send no messengers to the crown prince as Kadesh and Amurru did? may the gods of Ugarit know the slanderer (RS 94.2288+)**
- Sutean nomads strike a land's borders, and troops and chariots are sent against them (Ugarit RS 94.2288 + RS 94.2289 o:6-17)
- Letter close: 'may the gods of Ugarit know (judge) whoever speaks an evil word' (Ugarit RS 94.2288 + RS 94.2289 t.e:1-l.e:3)

**Tutu-[...] king of [...] to the king of Ugarit: a chariot overlaid with gold for the Sun; send fine ankle-stones; by the god of Mount Hazzi let us bind a treaty; send the prefect (RS 94.2364)**
- A king promises a chariot overlaid with gold for the Great King (the Sun) and asks for fine stones in return (Ugarit RS 94.2364 b.e:1-r:7)
- A king proposes to bind a treaty under (or by) the god of Mount Hazzi (Ṣapon) (Ugarit RS 94.2364 r:8-12)

**Yapaʿ-Haddu king of Sidon to the king of Ugarit, 'my brother': you know the news of the people of [...] how in all lands, in Hatti, Babylonia and Assyria ... (RS 94.2369)**
- A king tells another of news about peoples moving in all the lands: Hatti, Babylonia and Assyria (Ugarit RS 94.2369 o:5-11)

**Letter to the wife of the king: why have you and the king of Ugarit held back your messengers? my dyers, men of Aleppo, may disturb the palace; let your dyers come with them (RS 94.2374)**
- A king or queen asks another court to send its craftsmen (dyers) or to let its own return (Ugarit RS 94.2374 o:14-r:10)

**A servant to his lord: twice seven times I fall; the gods of the king and Nin-egalla keep you well; bread, flour, fish, oil and the merchants' donkeys sent; the rivers are swollen; do not be sick at heart (RS 94.2387)**
- A messenger cannot travel because the rivers are greatly swollen, and turns back (Ugarit RS 94.2387 r:1-4)
- Letter reassurance: 'my lord, do not let your heart be sick (troubled) about anything' (Ugarit RS 94.2387 r:9-12)

**Ziti-[...] to the king of Ugarit: a two-wheeled chariot and a quartz-studded harness sent; I wrote 'do not take my toll' and he wrote 'I will not take your toll'; but 70 shekels were taken last year (RS 94.2390+)**
- Two kings agree not to take the toll (miksu) on each other's goods or men, and dispute a toll of silver taken the previous year (Ugarit RS 94.2390 + RS 94.2420 r:6'-t.e:3)

**ʾAhi-malku to Uri-Tešub, 'my good brother': the gods of Tyre and of Ugarit sate you with good old age for ever; oil on my ship; your son the apprentice is negligent with his tablet; my runaway man is in a press there; 20 fish as gift (RS 94.2416+)**
- A letter complains that the son, an apprentice (talmīdu), is negligent with his tablets (Ugarit RS 94.2416 + RS 94.2418 r:6-14)
- A runaway servant is reported to be living in a wine or olive press (gt) in another land (Ugarit RS 94.2416 + RS 94.2418 r:15-l.e:1)

**King of Ušnatu to the king of Ugarit, 'my brother': I send the elders of ʾUllamu with ʾIli-malku to stand before you; I appeal: I love these men but my brother hates them (RS 94.2445)**
- One king says 'I love these men, but my brother hates them', setting love against hate (râmu / zêru) in a dispute over persons (Ugarit RS 94.2445 b.e:2-r:9)

**The king of Beirut to the king of Ugarit, his brother: silver of Yadlunu; he sends his servant with his witnesses for judgement (RS 94.2478)**
- A king sends a servant together with his witnesses to another king so that he may judge their case (Ugarit RS 94.2478 r:6-13, Ugarit RS 94.2478 l.e:1-2)

**The king of Ugarit to the king of Sidon: guard my ship going to Tyre; the extispicy for the ship's captain was not good; the ship entrusted to Yabni-ilu (RS 94.2483)**
- Extispicy is performed for a ship's captain before a voyage and the omen is 'not good' (Ugarit RS 94.2483 o:13-b.e:1)

**Ahi-malku to Uri-Teššub his brother: may the gods of Ugarit and Tyre sate you with good old age; the oil for the wool, my ship to Egypt (RS 94.2485)**
- Letter greeting: may the gods sate the addressee with good old age from now to eternity (šībūta damiqta lišbûka ištu inanna adi dārīti) (Ugarit RS 94.2485 o:8-9)

**Uriyanni to Niqmaddu of Ugarit: troops, horses, the troops of Carchemish; Alalakh uninhabited; 'the combat of the Sun will reach you' (RS 94.2511)**
- The Hittite overlord's letter warns the vassal: 'know that the combat of the Sun (the Great King) will reach you' (Ugarit RS 94.2511 b.e:3-r:1, Ugarit RS 94.2511 r:16-18)

**Letter to the prefect: the scatterers with their wives and sons; why do you send me back? my heart is very dark; wheat, milk, cheese, oil (RS 94.2524)**
- A letter writer complains that the addressee sent him back empty and 'my heart is very dark' (ina libbiya ekil danniš): 'you are not good' (Ugarit RS 94.2524 r:14-16)

**Letter on Ušnatu, Amurru and Kadesh: a king would not give troops and chariots; Sutean raiders' captives returned, half to Amurru, half to Kadesh, by oath (RS 94.2559)**
- Men seized by Sutean raiders are returned under oath, half to one king and half to the other, and their fault is said to be another's (Ugarit RS 94.2559 r:10'-19')

**Taʾasi, the king's son, to the prefect: ships from Canaan with provisions; formerly Ugarit lived by Siyannu; send the rest and keep me alive (RS 94.2571)**
- Ships coming down from Canaan (Kinani) are to bring provisions (mānaḫtu) to Ugarit (Ugarit RS 94.2571 o:6-13)
- A letter asks for provisions 'and keep me alive', recalling that the land was formerly kept alive by a neighbour's supplies and promising plenty after the next harvest (Ugarit RS 94.2571 r:1-14)

**The king of Byblos to the king of Ugarit, his brother: my ship's captain; my messengers were not given bread and beer in Ugarit (RS 94.2598)**
- A king protests that his messengers were not given bread and beer in the other king's land, though he never withheld them from the other's messengers (Ugarit RS 94.2598 r:3'-12')

**Palace list: a garment of lapis and red for Iyya-Baʿlu, wool for the singer of ʿAṯtart, a cloak, seven garments, 300 linen (KTU3 4.168)**
- A palace list issues garments, wool and linen to named persons, including the singers (šr) of the goddess ʿAṯtart (Ugarit KTU3 4.168 o:3-4)

**Letter to the king my lord: at my lord's feet from afar seven times and seven times I fall; I spoke to Baal of Ṣapan, to the eternal Sun, ʿAṯtart, ʿAnat and the gods of Alašiya; Nmry the eternal king; ships and merchants (KTU3 2.42)**
- A letter invokes Baal of Ṣapan, the eternal Sun, ʿAṯtart, ʿAnat and 'all the gods of Alašiya (Cyprus)' for the addressee (Ugarit KTU3 2.42 o:6-8)
- A king (the pharaoh) is called 'eternal king' (Ugaritic mlk ʿlm), or the sun deity 'Šapšu of eternity' (Ugarit KTU3 2.42 o:7, Ugarit KTU3 2.42 o:9)

**The king of Beirut to the king of Ugarit: a man of Ashkelon robbed my harbour master's house, fled to Ugarit and went up to Alašiya; seize him and give him to my man (SMEA 42, p. 5-17)**
- A man who stole from an official's house fled through the addressee's land on to another country; the king asks his 'brother' to seize the man and hand him over (Ugarit SMEA 42, p.5-17 o:6-r:8)

**Baal Cycle 1.2 I: Baal curses Yamm; Yamm's envoys come to the assembly on Mount Ll; the gods bow their heads; 'Give up Baal!'; El makes Baal Yamm's slave; Anat and Athtart restrain Baal**
- At the approach of the enemy's envoys the assembled gods lower their heads to their knees; the storm god rebukes them: 'lift up your heads!' (KTU 1.2 I:22-29)
- Divine messengers appear as a blazing fire, their tongue a sharpened sword (KTU 1.2 I:32-33)
- The high god yields to the threat and declares the storm god the enemy's slave and tribute-bearer (KTU 1.2 I:36-38)
- Two goddesses seize the angry god's right and left hands to stop him striking the envoys (KTU 1.2 I:38-41)
- An attack on envoys is rebuked as unthinkable: 'how could you strike the messengers?' (KTU 1.2 I:40-42)

**Baal Cycle 1.2 III: Kothar goes to El at the source of the rivers and is told to build Yamm's palace; Athtar complains he has no house and no wife; Shapsh warns him El will overturn his throne**
- The craftsman god is ordered to build a house and palace for Prince Sea, Judge River (KTU 1.2 III:7-11)
- A god is taunted that he has no wife like the other gods (KTU 1.2 III:22)

**Baal Cycle 1.2 IV: Kothar promises Baal eternal kingship and makes the clubs Yagrush and Ayyamur; they strike Yamm's shoulder, then his skull; Yamm falls; 'Yamm is dead, Baal shall be king'**
- After victory over the enemy the god is told: 'take your eternal kingship, your everlasting dominion' (KTU 1.2 IV:8-10)
- The craftsman god makes two clubs and names them ('Driver', 'Expeller'); each leaps from the storm god's hand like an eagle to strike Sea (KTU 1.2 IV:11-26)
- Acclamation after the combat: 'Sea is dead! Baal shall be king!' (KTU 1.2 IV:32, KTU 1.2 IV:34)
- Curse or boast: 'may the mighty fall to the earth, the strong into the dust' (KTU 1.2 IV:5)

**Baal Cycle 1.3 I: a servant feasts Baal, lord of the earth: brisket carved, a holy cup no woman may see, a thousand jars of wine; a youth sings of Baal on the heights of Ṣapan; Baal looks on his daughters**
- A holy cup of the god that no woman may see, a goblet even the queen-goddess may not look on (KTU 1.3 I:12-15)
- At a feast wine is mixed with spices in vast quantity (a thousand jars, ten thousand mixed) (KTU 1.3 I:15-17)
- A sweet-voiced youth with cymbals sings of the storm god on the heights of his mountain (KTU 1.3 I:18-22)

**Baal Cycle 1.3 II: Anat shuts her house and slaughters the people of the seashore and the sunrise: heads like balls, hands like locusts, knee-deep in blood; she fights tables and chairs, rejoices, washes her hands and bathes in dew of heaven and oil of earth**
- Things or people are likened to locusts or grasshoppers for their number (KTU 1.3 II:10)
- Not yet sated, the goddess sets chairs and tables as warriors in her house and fights among them (KTU 1.3 II:17-22, KTU 1.3 II:29-30)
- A goddess carries a bow and drives captives with its string (KTU 1.3 II:15-16)

**Baal Cycle 1.3 III 1-31: Anat perfumes herself; a song of Baal's love; Baal's message: put war from the earth, hasten to me; the word of tree and stone, of heaven to earth and deeps to stars; 'come, I will reveal it in my mountain, divine Ṣapan, the holy mount of my inheritance'**
- A singer takes the lyre to his breast and sings of the god's love for his brides or daughters (KTU 1.3 III:4-8)

**Baal Cycle 1.3 III 32 - IV 4: Anat trembles at the messengers: what enemy has risen against Baal? 'Did I not smite Yamm, beloved of El, River the great god, muzzle Tunnanu, smite the twisting serpent, Šalyaṭ of seven heads ...'**
- On seeing messengers arrive the goddess's feet shake, her loins break, her face sweats: 'what enemy has risen against Baal?' (KTU 1.3 III:32-38)
- The dragon (Tunnanu, Hebrew tannin) is muzzled (ištbm) and destroyed (KTU 1.3 III:40)
- An enemy drove the storm god from the heights of his mountain like a bird from its nest and from the throne of his kingship (KTU 1.3 III:47-IV:3)

**Baal Cycle 1.3 IV 5-55: the lads repeat Baal's message; Anat agrees to put war from the earth; she crosses a thousand fields to Ṣapan; Baal sends the women away and sets an ox before her; she bathes in dew; lament: Baal has no house like the gods; Anat will make El turn to her**
- The storm god sets his thunderbolt in the heavens and kindles his horns (lightning rays) (KTU 1.3 IV:25-27)

**Baal Cycle 1.3 V: Anat threatens to bloody El's grey beard unless Baal gets a house; she storms into El's tent; El answers from his seven chambers; 'your word is wise; our king is Baal, our judge, none above him'; Shapsh glows, the heavens weak in Mot's hand**
- The high god answers from within his seven chambers, his eight enclosures (KTU 1.3 V:10-11, KTU 1.3 V:25-27)

**Baal Cycle 1.3 VI: a gift for Athirat; Baal sends Gapn and Ugar across sea, mountains and the heights of heaven to Qudšu-Amrur and on to Kothar in Memphis and Caphtor**
- Messengers cross a thousand leagues of sea and rivers, mountains and coasts to the heights of heaven (KTU 1.3 VI:15-21)

**Baal Cycle 1.4 I: Baal has no house; prepare a gift for Athirat; Kothar goes up to the bellows and pours silver and gold into a canopy, couch, throne, footstool, sandals?, a table full of all the beasts of earth's foundations and a bowl with wild bulls**
- The craftsman god works the bellows and casts silver by thousands and gold by ten-thousands into divine furniture: canopy, couch, throne, footstool, table, bowl (KTU 1.4 I:23-37)
- A divine table filled with all the animals of the foundations of the earth, and a bowl with wild bulls by the ten-thousand (KTU 1.4 I:38-43)

**Baal Cycle 1.4 II: Athirat with her spindle washes her garment in the sea; she trembles at the approach of Baal and Anat, 'have they come to slay my sons?', then sees the gleam of silver and gold and rejoices; she calls her fisherman**
- The mother goddess sits by the sea with her spindle, washing her garment in the sea and setting a pot on the fire (KTU 1.4 II:3-9)
- At the sight of approaching gods the mother goddess cries: 'have they come to slay me, to slay my sons?' (KTU 1.4 II:21-26)
- The goddess, fearful at the visitors' coming, rejoices when she sees the gleam of silver and gold (KTU 1.4 II:26-29)
- The sea goddess has a divine fisherman servant who is told to take his net (KTU 1.4 II:29-34)

**Baal Cycle 1.4 III: Baal complains he was mocked and spat on in the assembly of the sons of El; Baal hates three feasts: of shame, of strife and of the handmaids' lewdness; Baal and Anat give gifts to Athirat; feast**
- A god complains that one stood up and mocked him, spat on him in the assembly of the sons of El, and set filth on his table (KTU 1.4 III:10-16)
- Baal hates two feasts, three the Rider of the Clouds: the feast of shame, the feast of strife (or harlotry) and the feast where handmaids act lewdly (KTU 1.4 III:17-22)
- Graded numerical saying: 'two (things) X hates, three ...' (n, n+1) (KTU 1.4 III:17-18)

**Baal Cycle 1.4 IV: Athirat rides a saddled donkey to El at the source of the rivers; El laughs and offers her food, wine or his love; 'our king is Baal'; Baal has no house; El: am I a slave, is Athirat a handmaid, to mould bricks?**
- A servant harnesses a donkey with silver and gold trappings and sets the goddess on its back; one leads, another goes ahead like a star (KTU 1.4 IV:2-19)
- The high god retorts: 'am I a slave, is Athirat a handmaid, to mould bricks? Let him build the house himself' (KTU 1.4 IV:58-62)

**Baal Cycle 1.4 V: El's grey beard instructs him; let Baal give his rain, his voice in the clouds and his lightning; let a caravan bring silver, gold and lapis; Anat brings the good news; Kothar arrives and sits at Baal's right; 'shall I put a window in the house?' - 'No'**
- The goddess praises the high god: 'you are great, you are wise; the grey hair of your beard instructs you' (KTU 1.4 V:3-5)
- With a house the storm god will give the season of his rain, of snow, his voice in the clouds and his lightning flashes to the earth (KTU 1.4 V:6-9)
- A caravan brings silver from the mountains, gold from the hills and gems to build a house of silver, gold and pure lapis lazuli (KTU 1.4 V:13-19, KTU 1.4 V:29-40)
- The craftsman guest is given a throne at the right hand of the storm god and the gods eat and drink (KTU 1.4 V:44-48)
- A scribal note within a poem instructs the reciter to go back and repeat an earlier passage (KTU 1.4 V:42-43)

**Baal Cycle 1.4 VI: 'you will come back to my word'; cedars from Lebanon and Sirion; fire burns in the house six days and on the seventh the silver has become plates and the gold bricks; Baal feasts his brothers, the seventy sons of Athirat**
- The builders go to Lebanon and its trees, to Sirion and its choice cedars, for the god's palace (KTU 1.4 VI:16-21)
- Fire burns in the house for six days; on the seventh it dies down and the silver has turned to plates and the gold to bricks (KTU 1.4 VI:22-35)
- The god celebrates his finished house with a feast for his brothers, the seventy sons of Athirat: rams, ewes, oxen, thrones and jars of wine for gods and goddesses (KTU 1.4 VI:38-59)

**Baal Cycle 1.4 VII: Baal takes sixty-six cities; he orders the window opened, a rift in the clouds; he gives his holy voice, the earth quakes, the mountains tremble, his enemies flee to the forests; 'I alone rule the gods'; messengers to Mot**
- The storm god goes from city to city and seizes sixty-six cities, seventy-seven towns (KTU 1.4 VII:7-12)
- The palace window is opened as a rift in the clouds, through which the god gives his holy voice (KTU 1.4 VII:17-19, KTU 1.4 VII:27-28)
- At the storm god's voice his enemies grasp the forests, his foes the flanks of the mountain (KTU 1.4 VII:35-39)
- A cedar (spear or lightning bolt) leaps from the storm god's right hand at his foes (KTU 1.4 VII:40-41)
- The god challenges: 'shall any king or non-king establish dominion over the earth?' (KTU 1.4 VII:42-44)
- The god declares: 'I alone rule over the gods, I fatten gods and men, I satisfy the multitudes of the earth' (KTU 1.4 VII:45-52)

**Baal Cycle 1.5 I: Mot's message: though you smote Lotan the fleeing serpent, the twisting serpent, Šalyaṭ of seven heads, you shall go down into my throat; my appetite is the lion's of the steppe, the whale's in the sea; you did not invite me to the feast**
- The heavens wither and droop (when the storm god is defeated) (KTU 1.5 I:4)

**Baal Cycle 1.5 II: Mot's lip to earth, lip to heaven, tongue to the stars; Baal fears him and sends word: 'hail, Mot, I am your slave for ever'; Mot rejoices**
- Death opens his jaws, one lip to the earth, one to the heavens, his tongue to the stars (KTU 1.5 II:2-3)
- Submission formula: 'I am your slave, and yours for ever' (ʿbdk an wd ʿlmk) (KTU 1.5 II:12, KTU 1.5 II:19-20)

**Baal Cycle 1.5 V: 'take your clouds, your wind, your rain, your seven lads, your eight boars, Pidray and Tallay, and go down; be counted among those who go down to the earth'; Baal loves a heifer in the field at the shore of death, seventy-seven times; she bears a boy**
- The storm god is told to take his clouds, wind, rain, his seven lads and eight boars and his daughters, and go down into the earth (KTU 1.5 V:6-11)
- The mighty storm god obeys the instruction to go down to death (KTU 1.5 V:17)

**Baal Cycle 1.5 VI: the messengers found Baal fallen in the land of the shore of death: 'mighty Baal is dead'; El comes down from throne to footstool to earth, pours dust on his head, gashes cheek and chin, ploughs his chest: 'Baal is dead, what of the peoples?'; Anat roams every mountain**
- The high god comes down from his throne to the footstool and from the footstool to the ground, pours ashes and dust on his head (KTU 1.5 VI:11-16)
- The mourner covers himself with a loincloth or sackcloth (mizrt) instead of clothing (KTU 1.5 VI:16-17, KTU 1.5 VI:31)

**Baal Cycle 1.6 I 1-31: Anat mourns, drinks her tears like wine; Shapsh lifts Baal onto Anat's shoulder; she carries him up to Ṣapan, weeps and buries him in the pit of the gods of the earth; seventy wild bulls, oxen, sheep, deer, ibex and roebucks are slaughtered**
- The mourning goddess weeps until sated, drinks her tears like wine (KTU 1.6 I:9-10)
- The Sun goddess lifts the dead god onto the goddess's shoulders, who carries him up to his mountain, weeps and buries him (KTU 1.6 I:8-17)
- At the god's burial seventy wild bulls, seventy oxen, seventy sheep, seventy deer, seventy ibex and seventy roebucks are slaughtered (KTU 1.6 I:18-29)

**Baal Cycle 1.6 I 32-67: Anat tells El 'let Athirat rejoice, Baal is dead'; El asks Athirat for one of her sons to make king; Athtar the Terrible ascends Ṣapan, but his feet do not reach the footstool nor his head the top: 'I cannot be king on Ṣapan'; he rules the earth**
- At the storm god's death his rivals (Athirat and her sons) are told they may rejoice (KTU 1.6 I:39-43)
- A god set on the dead king's throne cannot reach the footstool with his feet nor the top with his head, and steps down (KTU 1.6 I:53-65)
- Water is drawn in amphoras and jars (KTU 1.6 I:66-67)

**Baal Cycle 1.6 II: like a cow's heart for her calf, Anat's heart longs for Baal; she seizes Mot by the hem: 'give me my brother'; Mot: 'I put him in my mouth like a lamb'; Anat splits Mot with a blade, winnows, burns, grinds and sows him; birds eat him**
- As the heart of a cow for her calf, the heart of a ewe for her lamb, so is the goddess's heart for the missing god (KTU 1.6 II:6-9, KTU 1.6 II:28-30)
- The goddess seizes Death by the hem of his garment and demands: 'give me my brother!' (KTU 1.6 II:9-12)
- A petitioner or avenger seizes another by the hem or corner of the garment (KTU 1.6 II:9-11)
- The goddess splits Death with a blade, winnows him with a sieve, burns him with fire, grinds him with millstones and sows him in the field; the birds eat his flesh (KTU 1.6 II:30-37)
- The enemy's flesh is eaten by the birds (KTU 1.6 II:35-37)

**Baal Cycle 1.6 III-IV: in El's dream the heavens rain oil and the wadis run with honey; El laughs: 'Baal lives, the prince, lord of the earth, exists'; 'the furrows of the fields are parched, O Shapsh: where is mighty Baal?'; Shapsh will seek him**
- In the high god's dream the heavens rain oil and the wadis run with honey, a sign that the storm god lives (KTU 1.6 III:4-13)
- Joy that the dead god lives again: 'I will sit and rest, for mighty Baal is alive, the prince, lord of the earth, exists' (KTU 1.6 III:2-3, KTU 1.6 III:8-9, KTU 1.6 III:18-21)
- A libation of wine is poured before a deity sets out to search for the lost god (KTU 1.6 IV:18-20)

**Baal Cycle 1.6 V: Baal strikes the sons of Athirat and sits on his throne; in the seventh year Mot returns: 'because of you I suffered shame, winnowing, burning, grinding, sifting, scorching, sowing in the sea; give me one of your brothers to eat'**
- The returning storm god strikes down the sons of Athirat, great and small (KTU 1.6 V:1-4)
- After days, months and years, in the seventh year the defeated adversary returns (KTU 1.6 V:7-10)
- Death recites what he suffered for Baal's sake: shame, winnowing, burning, grinding, sifting, scorching in the fields, sowing in the sea (KTU 1.6 V:11-19)

**Baal Cycle 1.6 VI: Mot eats his own brothers; Baal and Mot fight like wild bulls, serpents, stallions; both fall; Shapsh warns Mot that El will overturn his throne; Mot fears; Baal is enthroned; hymn: Shapsh rules the Rephaim, the dead gods; Kothar drives off Arš and Tunnanu in the sea; colophon**
- Two gods butt like wild bulls, bite like serpents, kick like stallions; both fall, 'Mot is strong, Baal is strong' (KTU 1.6 VI:16-22)
- Invitation to eat the bread of offering (trmmt) and drink the wine of libation (KTU 1.6 VI:42-45)
- Hymn: the Sun rules over the Rephaim, over the divine dead; the dead gods are with her (KTU 1.6 VI:45-48)
- In the sea are Arš and the dragon (tnn); let the craftsman god drive them away (KTU 1.6 VI:51-53)
- An official is 'chief of the priests (khnm), chief of the herdsmen (nqdm)' (KTU 1.6 VI:55-56)

**KTU 1.10 I: fragment: what the sons of El do not know; the assembly of the stars; the circle of heaven; mighty Baal, Rider of the Clouds; Anat**
- The gods are called 'the assembly of the stars' (pḫr kkbm) (KTU 1.10 I:3'-5')

**KTU 1.10 II: Baal is not in his house; he takes his bow and arrows and goes to the marsh of Šamak, full of wild bulls; Anat lifts her wings and flies after him; Baal kneels before her: 'may your life be long; Baal will anoint your horns'; she sees a cow**
- The storm god kneels before his sister and greets her: 'may your life be long' (KTU 1.10 II:13'-20')
- Baal will anoint the horns of the goddess's strength in flight (KTU 1.10 II:21'-23')
- Wish to thrust the god's enemies into the earth, into the dust those who rise against him (KTU 1.10 II:24'-25')
- Narrative formula: 'he lifted his eyes and saw' (KTU 1.10 II:13'-15', KTU 1.10 II:26'-28')

**KTU 1.10 III: the cow bears an ox for Anat; Baal goes up the mountain and sits on his throne; the cow gives birth to a bull for Baal, a wild ox for the Rider of the Clouds, covers it with her udder; Anat climbs Ṣapan with the good news: 'a bull is born to Baal!'; Baal rejoices**
- A deity is called 'our creator', 'the one who established us' (KTU 1.10 III:5'-6')
- The cow embraces her newborn and covers him with her udder (KTU 1.10 III:22'-26')

**KTU 1.11: Baal and Anat grow hot and seize each other; she conceives and bears; the band of the Kotharat (fragment)**
- Storm god and goddess grow hot and seize each other's genitals; she conceives and bears (KTU 1.11 I:1-2)
- The skilful goddesses of birth and conception (the Kotharat) attend a birth (KTU 1.11 I:6)

**KTU 1.12 I: the handmaids complain to El that 'they' devour their liver; El laughs in his heart and sends them into the wilderness to crouch and bear the Devourers and Renders, horned like bulls, with Baal's face; Baal hunts them at the edge of the steppe, burning with desire**
- The gods Dawn (Šaḥar) and Dusk (Šalim) or the East (Qdm) are named (KTU 1.12 I:7'-8')
- The high god laughs in his heart, convulses in his liver (KTU 1.12 I:12'-13')
- The high god sends handmaids into the wilderness to crouch and bear 'the Devourers' and 'the Renders', horned like bulls with Baal's face (KTU 1.12 I:14'-33')
- A woman is sent away into the wilderness, by a sacred tree, to give birth there (KTU 1.12 I:19'-27')
- A sacred oak (or terebinth) at a named place (KTU 1.12 I:19'-20')
- Monstrous offspring have horns like bulls, humps like oxen and the face of a god (KTU 1.12 I:30'-33')

**KTU 1.12 II: Baal approaches the Devourers and seizes them, or is seized; he falls like a bull in the marsh, clothed in his brothers' blood; for seven years, eight cycles, El lets the fields wither; the king ceases to judge, the water-drawers leave the spring, the noise in El's house ceases**
- The storm god falls like a bull, sinks like an ox in the marsh, clothed in the blood of his brothers (KTU 1.12 II:36'-40', KTU 1.12 II:53'-57')
- A god lies clothed in the blood of his brothers as in a garment, of his kin as in a cloak (KTU 1.12 II:46'-49')
- At the god's fall the king ceases to judge, the women drawing water leave the spring, the noise in El's house and the clatter of the craftsman's house cease (KTU 1.12 II:58'-61')
- At a disaster the ordinary sounds cease: water-drawers at the spring, the noise of the house, the clatter of the workshop (KTU 1.12 II:59'-61')

**KTU 1.13: hymn-incantation to Anat: she will kill for two, three, four days; blood for her girdle, heads for her warriors, eagles and birds of prey; a seat promised on the roof of the high heavens where the stars fall like bricks; she bathes and goes up to El her father; the cow of Baal gives birth**
- Eagles and birds of prey gather to the slain (KTU 1.13 I:Vs._8-Vs._9)
- Incantation-hymn: the goddess is promised a seat on the roof of the high heavens, where the stars fall like bricks (KTU 1.13 I:Vs._10-Vs._17)
- A 'messenger of the heavens' is sent (KTU 1.13 II:Rs._4-Rs._7)

**Kirta's house destroyed; his wives and heirs lost; he weeps himself to sleep (Kirta I)**
- The king's house is ruined: his wives die one after another (in health, in sickness, by plague, by the sea, by the weapon) and all his heirs perish (KTU 1.14 I:7-25)
- A man had seven brothers, eight sons of one mother (graded number), all of whom are lost (KTU 1.14 I:8-9)
- The plague god Resheph (Rašpu) gathers in or snatches away members of a family (KTU 1.14 I:18-19)
- The Sea (Yammu) or its lads carry off a man's wife (KTU 1.14 I:19-20)
- The grieving man goes into his inner chamber to weep (KTU 1.14 I:26-27)
- The weeping man falls asleep in his tears and slumber overcomes him, opening onto a divine dream (KTU 1.14 I:31-34)

**El descends in Kirta's dream and asks why he weeps (Kirta I-II)**
- The high god El is called 'Father of Mankind' (ab adm) (KTU 1.14 I:36-37, KTU 1.14 I:43)
- The god appearing to the grieving man asks why he weeps and what he desires (KTU 1.14 I:37-43)
- Offered (or thinking of) silver, gold, slaves and horses, the hero wants none of them, only sons and offspring (KTU 1.14 I:51-52, KTU 1.14 II:1-5)

**At the shrine of Athirat of Tyre Kirta vows silver and gold if he wins Hurriya (Kirta IV)**
- The goddess Athirat is worshipped at her shrine as 'Athirat of Tyre, goddess of Sidon' (KTU 1.14 IV:34-39)
- On the way to his goal the hero vows a gift to a deity at her shrine if he succeeds (KTU 1.14 IV:36-43)

**Siege of Udum; King Pabil offers ransom; Kirta demands Hurriya (Kirta IV-VI)**
- The besieged king calls aloud to his wife to take counsel (KTU 1.14 V:12-15)

**Hurriya is handed over; Udum laments like a cow for her calf (Kirta 1.15 I)**
- The princess used to take the hungry and the thirsty by the hand (her charity mourned when she leaves) (KTU 1.15 I:1'-2')
- The princess is handed over and brought into the conqueror's camp (KTU 1.15 I:3'-4')
- A city laments its departing princess as a cow lows for its calf and children cry for their mothers (KTU 1.15 I:5'-7')

**The assembly of the gods visits Kirta; at Baal's request El blesses him with cup in hand and promises sons (Kirta 1.15 II)**
- The assembly of the gods, named one by one, comes to a mortal king's house (KTU 1.15 II:2'-11')
- Divine blessing: the wife you have taken will bear you seven sons, yes, eight (KTU 1.15 II:21'-25')

**Kirta exalted among the Rephaim; daughters promised, the youngest made firstborn; the children born; Athirat remembers the vow (Kirta 1.15 III)**
- The king is exalted among the Rephaim of the earth, in the gathering of the assembly of Ditanu (royal ancestors) (KTU 1.15 III:2'-4', KTU 1.15 III:13'-15')
- A blessing lists the daughters to be born one after another in a litany ('she will bear the girl ...') (KTU 1.15 III:5'-12')
- The youngest child is formally made the firstborn (KTU 1.15 III:16')
- Having blessed the mortal, the gods go back to their tents, their dwellings (KTU 1.15 III:17'-19')
- A goddess remembers the vow the hero made and did not fulfil, and threatens to annul her favour (KTU 1.15 III:25'-30')

**Hurriya's feasts for the nobles; weeping for the dying Kirta and talk of succession (Kirta 1.15 IV-VI)**
- At the king's order the queen slaughters fat beasts, opens the wine jars and calls the nobles to a feast (KTU 1.15 IV:2'-27', KTU 1.15 VI:3-5)
- The king's nobles are called his seventy 'bulls' and eighty 'gazelles' (KTU 1.15 IV:6'-9', KTU 1.15 IV:17'-20')
- The hostess puts her hand to the dish and the knife to the meat to serve the guests (KTU 1.15 IV:24'-25', KTU 1.15 V:7'-8')
- The guests are told to weep for the dying king like the bellowing of bulls (KTU 1.15 V:12'-16', KTU 1.15 VI:6-7)
- Dying is described as reaching the setting of the sun, joining the high god (KTU 1.15 V:17'-20')
- While the king lies ill the nobles say that when he dies his son will reign over them (KTU 1.15 V:20'-23')

**Ilihau laments over his dying father - 'shall gods die?'; Kirta sends for his daughter Thitmanat (Kirta 1.16 I)**
- Lament: we waste away like a dog in your house, like a cur at your door (KTU 1.16 I:2-3, KTU 1.16 I:15-16)
- The dying father tells his son not to weep or waste the fountain of his eyes, but to call his sister (KTU 1.16 I:24-30)
- A daughter is called to come with tambourine in hand to sing (lament) over her father (KTU 1.16 I:38-45)
- A sister out drawing water sees her brother coming and asks whether their father is ill (KTU 1.16 I:50-62)

**Thitmanat learns the truth and laments her father (Kirta 1.16 II)**
- The mourner sobs and cries out, naked, without garment (KTU 1.16 II:25-31)

**Search for Baal's rain; the ploughmen look up, bread, wine and oil exhausted (Kirta 1.16 III)**
- Messengers are told to roam earth and heaven to its edge, looking for the rain of Baal on the fields (KTU 1.16 III:2'-11')
- Baal's rain is good for the earth and the wheat, like fragrance on the ploughed field, like a garland on the furrow (KTU 1.16 III:7'-11')
- In drought the ploughmen look up: the bread is spent from the jars, the wine from the skins, the oil from the vessels (KTU 1.16 III:12'-16')
- The king's mortal sickness is accompanied by failure of rain and the land's produce (KTU 1.16 III:1'-17')

**El summons Ilish, herald of the gods, and his wife (Kirta 1.16 IV)**
- The high god summons his herald (Ilish) and the herald's wife, herald of the goddesses (KTU 1.16 IV:3'-12')
- The herald is told to climb onto the shoulder of the building, the parapet of the tower, and cry aloud (KTU 1.16 IV:13'-16')

**El asks seven times which god will drive out the sickness; none answers; El fashions Shaatiqat (Kirta 1.16 V)**
- The high god asks the assembled gods seven times who will drive out the king's sickness (KTU 1.16 V:9-22)
- No one among the gods answers the high god's question (KTU 1.16 V:12-13, KTU 1.16 V:16, KTU 1.16 V:19, KTU 1.16 V:22)

**Shaatiqat drives Death from the city and heals Kirta; he eats and returns to his throne (Kirta 1.16 VI)**
- A divine healer drives Death out of the city and the foe out of the town, striking with a staff (KTU 1.16 VI:1-9, KTU 1.16 VI:13-14)
- The healer washes the sick man's sweat and opens his throat so that he can eat again (KTU 1.16 VI:10-12)
- On recovering, the king orders a lamb slaughtered so that he may eat (KTU 1.16 VI:14-21)
- After a day or two the healed king sits again on his royal throne (KTU 1.16 VI:21-24)

**Yassib accuses his father of neglecting justice and demands the throne; Kirta curses him (Kirta 1.16 VI)**
- A son, prompted by his inner voice, demands that his sick father step down from kingship so that he may reign (KTU 1.16 VI:25-38, KTU 1.16 VI:39-53)
- The king is accused of not judging the widow's case, not trying the cause of the wretched, not driving out the oppressor of the poor, not feeding the orphan (KTU 1.16 VI:32-34, KTU 1.16 VI:44-50)
- The sickbed has become the sick king's sister, his couch of illness his companion (KTU 1.16 VI:35-36, KTU 1.16 VI:50-52)
- The father curses the son who sought his throne, calling on gods to break his head and skull (KTU 1.16 VI:54-58)

**Childless Danel feeds the gods for seven days; Baal intercedes; El blesses him with a son who will do a son's duties (Aqhat 1.17 I-II)**
- A list of a son's duties to his father: setting up the ancestral stele, making his smoke rise, silencing his slanderers, supporting him when drunk, offering for him in the temples, plastering his roof and washing his clothes (KTU 1.17 I:25'-33', KTU 1.17 I:42'-47', KTU 1.17 II:1'-8', KTU 1.17 II:14'-23')
- Told he will have a son, the father's face shines; he laughs, rests his feet on the footstool and says his soul is at rest (KTU 1.17 II:8'-15')

**Danel feasts the Kotharat for seven days; he counts the months of pregnancy (Aqhat 1.17 II)**
- The expectant father sits and counts the months of his wife's pregnancy (KTU 1.17 II:43'-46')

**Danel judging at the gate sees Kothar-wa-Hasis approach with a bow; hospitality; the bow given to Aqhat (Aqhat 1.17 V)**
- Lifting his eyes he sees the divine visitor coming from far away (KTU 1.17 V:9'-12')
- The craftsman god brings a bow and arrows for a mortal hero (KTU 1.17 V:12'-13', KTU 1.17 V:25'-28')
- The father strings the bow and gives it to his son, asking for the best of his game (KTU 1.17 V:35'-39')

**At the feast Anat covets Aqhat's bow, offers wealth and then immortality; he refuses and mocks her; she goes to El (Aqhat 1.17 VI)**
- The divine bow's string flashes like lightning, shooting into the deep, and curls like a serpent (KTU 1.17 VI:10'-14')
- A goddess covets the mortal hero's bow and offers silver and gold for it (KTU 1.17 VI:15'-19')
- The hero refuses to give his bow and tells the goddess to bring the materials (wood of Lebanon, sinews, horns) to the craftsman god for her own (KTU 1.17 VI:20'-25')
- A goddess offers the mortal hero life, not-dying, years counted with the gods, in exchange for his weapon (KTU 1.17 VI:25'-33')
- The mortal answers that no one escapes death: at the last glaze is poured on his head, plaster on his crown; he will die the death of all men (KTU 1.17 VI:35'-38')
- The hero taunts the goddess: bows are for warriors; do women now hunt? (KTU 1.17 VI:39'-41')
- The goddess laughs but plots: if she meets him on the path of transgression and pride she will fell him under her feet (KTU 1.17 VI:41'-45')
- The goddess bows at the high god's feet, falls down, prostrates herself and honours him (KTU 1.17 VI:50'-51')
- The goddess slanders the mortal hero before the high god (KTU 1.17 VI:51'-53')

**Anat threatens El and gets leave; she offers Aqhat to be his sister and teach him to hunt (Aqhat 1.18 I)**
- The high god yields to his fierce daughter: 'I know you are implacable; go, do what is in your heart; whoever hinders you will be crushed' (KTU 1.18 I:15-19)
- The goddess invites the hero to go hunting and offers to teach him the hunt (KTU 1.18 I:27-29)

**Anat carries Yatpan as a bird of prey among the eagles; Aqhat is struck down at his meal; Anat weeps (Aqhat 1.18 IV)**
- A goddess enlists a warrior (Yatpan) to kill the mortal she hates (KTU 1.18 IV:5'-16')
- A man is murdered for a possession (his bow) the killer coveted (KTU 1.18 IV:12'-13', KTU 1.18 IV:40'-41')
- The goddess carries the assassin like an eagle in her belt, like a falcon in her sheath, and releases him over the victim (KTU 1.18 IV:17'-22', KTU 1.18 IV:27'-29')
- The killer strikes the victim twice on the skull, three times over the ear (KTU 1.18 IV:22'-23', KTU 1.18 IV:33'-34')
- The killer pours out the victim's blood like a murderer, like a slaughterer, to his knees (KTU 1.18 IV:23'-24', KTU 1.18 IV:34'-35')
- The goddess who had the hero killed weeps over him: 'for your bow I struck you, for your arrows I did not let you live' (KTU 1.18 IV:38'-41')

**The bow is broken and lost; Danel at the gate; Pughat sees the withering; Danel's rain spell; seven years without Baal (Aqhat 1.19 I)**
- The coveted object for which the hero was killed falls into the waters and breaks, so the killer never gets it (KTU 1.19 I:2-17)
- After the hero's death the grain on the threshing floor dries up and the vines wither (KTU 1.19 I:18-19, KTU 1.19 I:29-31)
- The mourner weeps in her heart and sheds tears in her liver (inwardly) (KTU 1.19 I:34-35)
- A garment or cloak is torn in grief at a death or disaster (KTU 1.19 I:36-37, KTU 1.19 I:46-48)
- The righteous man adjures the clouds in the heat of disaster to bring the early rain and the dew on the grapes (KTU 1.19 I:38-42)

**Pughat saddles the donkey; Danel kisses the surviving stalks; messengers bring news of Aqhat's death (Aqhat 1.19 II)**
- The daughter harnesses the donkey with silver and gold trappings, lifts her father and sets him on its back (KTU 1.19 II:3-11)
- In the parched field the father finds a surviving shoot or ear, embraces and kisses it, and wishes that his son's hand may gather it into the granary (KTU 1.19 II:12-25)
- Messengers arrive and announce to the father: your son is dead, the goddess killed him (KTU 1.19 II:27-44)
- Mourners bind (or loose) the locks of their heads and shed tears (KTU 1.19 II:31-34)
- At bad news the hearer's feet shake, his face sweats, his loins break and his back gives way (KTU 1.19 II:44-47)
- Lifting his eyes the father sees eagles in the clouds (KTU 1.19 II:56-57)

**Baal breaks the eagles' wings; Danel searches their entrails, finds Aqhat in Ṣamal, buries him, curses the places near the murder (Aqhat 1.19 III)**
- At a mortal's prayer the storm god breaks the wings of eagles so that they fall at his feet (KTU 1.19 III:1-3, KTU 1.19 III:8-10, KTU 1.19 III:16-17, KTU 1.19 III:22-23, KTU 1.19 III:30-31, KTU 1.19 III:36-37)
- The father splits open the birds' bellies (livers) to look for the fat and bones of his devoured son (KTU 1.19 III:3-6, KTU 1.19 III:10-11, KTU 1.19 III:18-21, KTU 1.19 III:24-25, KTU 1.19 III:32-35, KTU 1.19 III:38-40)
- When the remains are not found the storm god is asked to restore the eagle's wings and it flies away (KTU 1.19 III:12-14, KTU 1.19 III:26-28)
- Named eagles: Hirgab the father of the eagles and Ṣamal the mother of the eagles (KTU 1.19 III:15, KTU 1.19 III:29)
- The dead son is buried in the hole of the gods of the earth (the underworld) (KTU 1.19 III:5-6, KTU 1.19 III:20-21, KTU 1.19 III:34-35, KTU 1.19 III:40-41)
- The father curses any birds that fly over his son's grave and disturb him from his sleep (KTU 1.19 III:42-45)
- The mourner sets down (or takes up) the end of the staff in his hand between curses (KTU 1.19 III:49, KTU 1.19 III:56)

**Abilum cursed with blindness; seven years of mourning with wailing women; mourning ends with sacrifice (Aqhat 1.19 IV)**
- Mourning is ended: the mourning women are sent away, sacrifice is offered and incense rises to the heavens and the stars (KTU 1.19 IV:19-27)

**Pughat asks her father's blessing to avenge her brother; armed under a woman's dress, she plies Yatpan with wine (Aqhat 1.19 IV)**
- The sister asks her father's blessing to go and kill her brother's killer, and he blesses her (KTU 1.19 IV:28-40)
- The avenging woman puts on warrior's garb and a dagger beneath, and a woman's garment over it, and rouges herself (KTU 1.19 IV:41-46)
- The disguised woman avenger serves the killer wine, a second cup of mixed drink, in his tent (KTU 1.19 IV:50-61)
- Drunk, the killer boasts that the hand that slew the hero will slay thousands of enemies (KTU 1.19 IV:57-60)
- The killer is told that 'the one who hired us' (or a hired woman) has come to his tent (KTU 1.19 IV:50-52)
- A rubric at the end of a tablet tells the reciter to return to (the beginning of) the recitation (KTU 1.19 IV:62)

**Liturgical opening of the Gracious Gods - peace to king and queen; Mot-wa-Shar pruned like a vine; songs over fire and basin (KTU 1.23 1-29)**
- Invitation: eat of every bread, drink of every wine (KTU 1.23 I:6)
- Liturgical greeting: peace to the king, peace to the queen, to those who enter and to the guards (KTU 1.23 I:7, KTU 1.23 I:26-27)
- Death (Mot-wa-Šar) sits with the staff of bereavement and widowhood, and the pruners prune him and the binders bind him like a vine (KTU 1.23 I:8-11)
- Death holds in his hand the staff of childlessness and the staff of widowhood (KTU 1.23 I:8-9)
- A rubric prescribes that a text be recited seven times (over the platform, over the fire, over the basin) (KTU 1.23 I:12, KTU 1.23 I:14-15)
- Refrain: the field is the field of the gods, the field of Athirat and Rahmay (KTU 1.23 I:13, KTU 1.23 I:28)

**El takes two women at the shore; they bear Shahar and Shalim and the gracious gods, who are sent to the holy desert for seven years (KTU 1.23 30-76)**
- The high god walks along the shore of the sea, the shore of the deep (KTU 1.23 I:(U.R.)_30)
- The high god sees two women at a basin, takes them into his house and, according to their cry, makes them his wives (not daughters) for ever (KTU 1.23 I:31-49)
- The high god shoots a bird from the sky, plucks it and roasts it on the coals as a sign of his potency (KTU 1.23 I:37-41)
- The high god's wives give birth to Shahar and Shalim, Dawn and Dusk (KTU 1.23 I:51-53)
- Gifts are lifted up to the Sun, the Lady, and to the fixed stars (KTU 1.23 I:54)
- The newborn gods put one lip to the earth and one to the heavens; birds of the sky and fish of the sea enter their mouths, yet they are not sated (KTU 1.23 I:61-64)
- The newborn gods are sent to dwell as strangers among stones and trees in the holy desert for seven full years, eight cycles (KTU 1.23 I:64-67)
- The wanderers from the desert ask the watchman of the sown land to open and give them bread and wine (KTU 1.23 I:68-76)

**Hymn to Nikkal-wa-Ib - the moon god Yarikh woos Nikkal, pays the bride-price, the family weighs it; the Kotharat (KTU 1.24)**
- The moon god burns with desire at sunset and embraces the maiden (KTU 1.24 I:(Vs.)_3-(Vs.)_9)
- The divine suitor sends to the bride's father offering a bride-price of a thousand silver and ten thousand gold and lapis, and to turn her field into vineyards (KTU 1.24 I:(Vs.)_16-(Vs.)_23)
- The bride's father suggests the suitor marry another (more prestigious) girl instead (KTU 1.24 I:(Vs.)_23-(Rs.)_29)
- The suitor refuses the alternative and insists on the bride he chose, and marries her (KTU 1.24 I:(Rs.)_30-(Rs.)_33)
- The bride's father, mother, brother and sister set up the scales and weigh the bride-price (KTU 1.24 I:(Rs.)_33-(Rs.)_37)
- The moon god is called 'the lamp of heaven' (nyr šmm) and asked to shine on the worshipper (KTU 1.24 I:(Vs.)_16, KTU 1.24 I:(Rs.)_31, KTU 1.24 I:(Rs.)_38-(Rs.)_39)
- The singer says the names of the goddesses are in his mouth, their count on his lips, and lists them (KTU 1.24 I:(Rs.)_45-(Rs.)_50)

**The mare, daughter of spring, stone, heaven and deep, sends Shapsh to each god in turn for a spell against snakebite (KTU 1.100 1-60)**
- The mother of stallion and mare is 'daughter of the spring, daughter of the stone, daughter of heaven and the deep' (KTU 1.100 I:(Vs.)_1)
- The sun goddess is asked to carry the petitioner's cry to each god in turn at his own city (KTU 1.100 I:2-3, KTU 1.100 I:8-9, KTU 1.100 I:14-15, KTU 1.100 I:19-20, KTU 1.100 I:25-26, KTU 1.100 I:30-31, KTU 1.100 I:35-36, KTU 1.100 I:40-41, KTU 1.100 I:45-46, KTU 1.100 I:51-52, KTU 1.100 I:57-58)
- Each god petitioned sets out his chair and sits down, without helping (KTU 1.100 I:7, KTU 1.100 I:12-13, KTU 1.100 I:18, KTU 1.100 I:23-24, KTU 1.100 I:29, KTU 1.100 I:34, KTU 1.100 I:39, KTU 1.100 I:(Rs.)_44, KTU 1.100 I:49-50, KTU 1.100 I:55-56)

**Horon expels the venom with the tree of death among tamarisks; the mare asks snakes as her bride-price (KTU 1.100 61-79)**
- The healer god sets his face toward a distant city to fetch the cure (KTU 1.100 I:61-64)
- The god casts the 'tree of death' among tamarisks and date-spathes to neutralise the venom (KTU 1.100 I:64-67)
- The venom grows weak and flows away like a wadi, dispersed like a channel (KTU 1.100 I:68-69)
- The house of the bride is shut against the suitor until he meets her terms (KTU 1.100 I:70-72)
- The bride demands snakes, 'sons of the serpent', as her bride-price, and the god gives them (KTU 1.100 I:73-76)

**Prologue of the Instruction of Amenemope - purpose of the teaching, titles of the author and of his son (Amenemope 1.1-3.7)**
- An instruction presents itself as the teaching for life and the guide to well-being (Amenemope W1:1.1)
- The purpose of instruction: to answer one who speaks and bring back a report to the one who sent you (Amenemope W1:1.1)
- Teaching steers the pupil on the way (path) of life (Amenemope W1:1.1)
- The author of the instruction is a scribe of fields who sets boundary stones and keeps the land register (Amenemope W1:1.13)

**Chapter 1: give your ears, set your heart on the words, keep them in the casket of your belly (Amenemope 3.8-3.17)**
- Opening call of instruction: give your ears, hear the words, set your heart to understand them (Amenemope W1:3.9-3.10)

**Chapter 2: do not rob the wretched; the heated man swept away; leave the evildoer to God and feed him (Amenemope 4.3-5.8)**
- The evildoer is abandoned by the riverbank, carried off by its mud and swept away by the storm; crocodiles await (Amenemope W1:4.12-4.19)

**Chapter 3: do not quarrel with the hot-mouthed; sleep a night before speaking; God knows how to answer him (Amenemope 5.9-5.19)**
- The heated man's anger flares up like fire in straw (Amenemope W1:5.14)

**Chapter 4: the heated man in the temple is a tree that withers and is burned; the silent man is a tree that flourishes with sweet fruit (Amenemope 5.20-6.12)**
- Two trees: the heated man is a tree that withers and ends as firewood; the silent man a tree flourishing in a garden with sweet fruit and pleasant shade (Amenemope W1:6.1-6.12)

**Chapter 5: do not embezzle temple shares; 'today is not like tomorrow' - the flood falls, crocodiles exposed; join the silent (Amenemope 6.13-7.10)**
- When the inundation recedes the crocodiles are exposed, hippopotami stranded, fish gasping, while jackals and birds feast: a sudden reversal of fortunes (Amenemope W1:7.2-7.6)

**Chapter 6: do not move the boundary stone or encroach on the widow's field; one bushel from God is better than five thousand by wrong; riches fly to heaven (Amenemope 7.11-9.8)**
- The moon god catches the perjurer with his lasso (Amenemope W1:7.18)
- The land-grabber's house becomes the town's enemy, his granaries are destroyed and his goods given to another (Amenemope W1:8.1)
- Better a bushel God gives you than five thousand by wrong; better poverty in God's hand than riches in the storehouse (Amenemope W1:8.19-9.7)
- Warning: beware of the Lord of All (God), lest his terror carry you off (Amenemope W1:8.9-8.14)

**Chapter 7: do not set your heart on riches; ill-gotten wealth is swallowed by the earth or flies to heaven like geese; pray to the sun at dawn (Amenemope 9.9-10.15)**
- Do not set your heart on riches, for no one can ignore Fate and Fortune (Amenemope W1:9.10-9.14)
- The ground opens its mouth and swallows ill-gotten wealth into the underworld (Amenemope W1:9.20-10.3)
- Wealth from robbery does not spend the night with you; at daybreak it is gone (Amenemope W1:9.16-9.19/2)
- The great ship of the greedy is left in the mud, while the small boat of the silent man sails on (Amenemope W1:10.10)
- When the sun rises, pray to it: give me well-being and health, and my daily needs (Amenemope W1:10.12-10.14)

**Chapter 8: put your goodness in people's bellies; spit on Apophis; guard your tongue; do not proclaim another's sin (Amenemope 10.16-11.11)**
- Put your goodness into people's bodies and everyone will greet you (Amenemope W1:10.17)
- Guard your tongue from harmful words (Amenemope W1:10.21)
- The virtuous will find his place in the temple, his coffin will hide him and keep him safe (Amenemope W1:11.2-11.4/2)

**Chapter 9: do not befriend the heated man; his portrait - ferryman of words, wolf-cub, crocodile, cloud before the wind; Khnum his potter (Amenemope 11.12-13.9)**
- Do not answer your superior insolently or rashly; consult your equal before answering (Amenemope W1:11.15-11.19)
- The word of an aggrieved man is swifter than the wind (Amenemope W1:12.1)
- The heated man tears down and builds up with his tongue (Amenemope W1:12.3)
- The hypocrite's lips are sweet, his tongue bitter, and fire burns in his belly (Amenemope W1:13.6-13.7)
- The heated man sets one eye against another and makes brothers quarrel (Amenemope W1:12.19-13.1)

**Chapter 10: do not greet the heated man falsely; do not separate your heart from your tongue; God hates falsified words (Amenemope 13.10-14.3)**
- Do not greet your adversary with false words of praise while fear is in your belly (Amenemope W1:13.11-13.13)

**Chapter 11: do not covet the poor man's goods - they choke the throat; the big mouthful swallowed and vomited (Amenemope 14.4-15.7)**
- Do not covet the goods of a poor dependant or hunger for his bread: it chokes the throat (Amenemope W1:14.5-14.8)
- The too-large mouthful (ill-gotten) is swallowed and then vomited up (Amenemope W1:14.17)
- Flattery returns to you as curses, homage as beatings (Amenemope W1:14.15)

**Chapter 12: do not covet an official's property; as steward, avoid his goods (Amenemope 15.8-15.18)**
- One who misbehaves on a mission is not sent again (Amenemope W1:15.17)

**Chapter 13: do not cheat with the pen; remit two-thirds of a poor man's debt; praise better than riches (Amenemope 15.19-16.14)**
- If a poor man owes a large arrear, divide it in three, forgive two parts and let one stand (Amenemope W1:16.5-16.10)

**Chapter 14: do not ingratiate yourself; greet with your mouth (Amenemope 16.15-17.3)**
- Do not push yourself on a man to seek his favour or his gifts (Amenemope W1:16.16-16.20)

**Chapter 15: do good; the beak of the Ibis is the scribe's finger; the baboon's eye roams the Two Lands (Amenemope 17.4-17.16)**
- The son of a scribe who cheats will not be enrolled (Amenemope W1:17.13)
- If you keep these teachings in your heart, your children will see the benefit (Amenemope W1:17.15)

**Chapter 16: do not tamper with the scales or weights; the baboon sits by the balance, his heart the plummet (Amenemope 17.17-18.13)**
- The baboon (Thoth) sits by the balance, his heart the plummet; the god invented weights and measures (Amenemope W1:17.22-18.2)
- Fraudulently gilded metal becomes lead by morning (Amenemope W1:18.12)
- Do not covet copper or fine linen; what use is fine clothing to one who cheats before God? (Amenemope W1:18.8-18.10)

**Chapter 17: do not falsify the corn-measure, the Eye of Re; the threshing-floor's power greater than an oath by the throne (Amenemope 18.14-19.9)**
- The grain measure is the Eye of Re, and its abomination is the thief (Amenemope W1:18.23-19.2)
- Do not exact the harvest tax and then draw up a document against the farmer to harm him (Amenemope W1:19.4-19.6)

**Chapter 18: do not lie awake fearing tomorrow; man's words are one thing, God's deeds another; no one is sinless; the tongue is the rudder, the Lord of All the pilot (Amenemope 19.10-20.6)**
- Man's tongue is the steering oar of the boat, but the Lord of All is its pilot (Amenemope W1:20.4-20.6)

**Chapter 19: in court do not falsify your words or seek a royal oath; speak the truth before the official (Amenemope 20.7-20.19)**
- Do not seek to swear an oath by the lord; speak plainly in court (Amenemope W1:20.12-20.13)
- The high court of 'the Thirty' in the Residence reviews testimony (Amenemope W1:20.18)

**Chapter 20: do not pervert justice, take no bribe from the powerful; truth is God's gift; do not forge oracles (Amenemope 20.20-21.20)**
- In court do not favour the man in bright clothes nor despise the man in rags (Amenemope W1:21.1-21.3)
- Truth (Maat) is a great gift of God, given to whom he loves (Amenemope W1:21.5-21.6)
- Do not falsify an oracle on the scroll or invent divine power for yourself (Amenemope W1:21.13-21.15)
- Return property to its owners and seek your own living (Amenemope W1:21.17-21.19)

**Chapter 22: do not provoke your opponent; let him empty his belly; set yourself in the arms of God (Amenemope 22.19-23.11)**
- Do not provoke your adversary; let him empty his belly and keep calm (Amenemope W1:22.20-23.5)

**Chapter 23: do not eat bread before an official; chew as pretence; look at the cup before you (Amenemope 23.12-23.20)**
- An official great in office is like one with many wells for drawing water (Amenemope W1:23.19)

**Chapter 25: do not laugh at the blind, mock the dwarf, harm the lame; man is clay and straw, God his builder (Amenemope 24.8-24.20)**
- How joyful is he who reaches the West (death) safe in the hand of God (Amenemope W1:24.19)

**Chapter 26: do not sit in the beer-house with a greater man; befriend your equal; give your hand to an old man full of beer (Amenemope 24.21-25.15)**
- Do not sit in the beer-house or join one greater than you there (Amenemope W1:24.22)
- A pilot who looks far ahead does not capsize his ship (Amenemope W1:25.14)

**Chapter 27: do not revile one older than you, for he saw Re before you; let him beat you while your hand is in your lap (Amenemope 25.16-26.7)**
- Do not revile one older than you, for he has seen the sun before you (Amenemope W1:25.17-25.21)
- Let your elder beat you with your hand in your lap, revile you while you are silent (Amenemope W1:26.2-26.4)
- The master's dog does not bark at him who feeds it (Amenemope W1:26.6)

**Chapter 28: do not pounce on a widow gleaning in the field; do not pass the stranger with your oil-jar; God loves him who honours the poor (Amenemope 26.8-26.14)**
- God loves him who honours the poor more than him who respects the noble (Amenemope W1:26.13)

**Chapter 29: do not stop anyone crossing the river; take fare from the rich, waive it for the poor (Amenemope 26.15-27.5)**
- Do not stop a man from crossing the river; take the fare from the rich and let the poor cross free (Amenemope W1:26.16-27.4)
- When an oar is brought to you in midstream, stretch out your arms to take it (Amenemope W1:26.18)

**Chapter 30: 'see these thirty chapters' - they entertain and instruct; colophon (Amenemope 27.6-28.1)**
- An instruction counts itself as 'these thirty chapters' that entertain and instruct (Amenemope W1:27.7-27.10)
- A scribe skilled in his office will be found worthy of being a courtier (Amenemope W1:27.16)
- The teaching makes the ignorant learned and purifies him when it is read to him (Amenemope W1:27.10-27.13)

**Great Hymn to the Aten - titulary of the Aten, Akhenaten and Nefertiti; the sun rises beautiful in the horizon (AtenHymn 1-3/1)**
- The sun god is lord of all the sun disc encircles, lord of heaven and lord of earth (AtenHymn 1)
- The king and his queen are named with full titulary in the hymn to the god (AtenHymn 1/2-1/3)
- The king is 'living on Maat' (truth, right order) (AtenHymn 1/2)
- The god appears beautiful in the horizon and fills every land with his beauty (AtenHymn 2/2-2/5)
- The sun's rays embrace the lands to the limit of all he has made (AtenHymn 2/5, AtenHymn 3)

**Great Hymn to the Aten - night: the land in darkness as in death; lions leave their dens, serpents bite (AtenHymn 3/2-4/3)**
- The god is far away, yet his rays are on earth; he is in people's faces, yet his course is unknown (AtenHymn 3/2-3/3)
- When the sun sets the land lies in darkness as in death: sleepers with covered heads, eye not seeing eye (AtenHymn 3/4-3/7)
- At night goods are stolen from under the sleepers' heads and they do not notice (AtenHymn 3/7)

**Great Hymn to the Aten - day: people wake and work, cattle graze, birds praise, ships sail, fish leap (AtenHymn 4/4-6/2)**
- At sunrise people and birds raise arms and wings in praise of the god (AtenHymn 4/7, AtenHymn 5/5)
- At sunrise all cattle are content with their pasture, trees and plants flourish (AtenHymn 5/2-5/3)
- The fish in the river leap before the sun, whose rays reach into the sea (AtenHymn 6/2)

**Great Hymn to the Aten - the god makes seed grow in women, nurses the child in the womb, gives breath to the chick in the egg; 'O sole god, there is no other' (AtenHymn 6/3-7/7)**
- The god gives breath to keep alive all that he has made (AtenHymn 6/5, AtenHymn 7/2)
- When the child comes forth from the womb the god opens its mouth and supplies its needs (AtenHymn 7)
- The god gives breath to the chick in the egg and sets its time to break out and walk (AtenHymn 7/2-7/5)

**Great Hymn to the Aten - creation alone according to his heart; Syria, Kush and Egypt each in its place, tongues and skins distinguished; the Nile below and the Nile in the sky (AtenHymn 8-10/6)**
- The god created the earth according to his heart when he was alone, with people, cattle and all that walks and flies (AtenHymn 8)
- The god cares for the foreign lands (Syria, Kush) as for Egypt, setting each man in his place (AtenHymn 8/2-8/3, AtenHymn 9/7)
- The god reckons (fixes) each person's lifetime (AtenHymn 8/3)
- The god made the Nile in the underworld for Egypt and a 'Nile in the sky' (rain) for the foreign lands (AtenHymn 9/2-9/8, AtenHymn 10/2-10/3)
- The sun's rays nurse the fields; the god made the seasons, winter to cool and summer heat (AtenHymn 10/4-10/6)

**Great Hymn to the Aten - the sky made to behold creation; millions of forms from the one; 'you are in my heart, none knows you but your son' Akhenaten (AtenHymn 11-13/4)**
- The one god makes millions of forms (cities, fields, roads, rivers) from himself alone (AtenHymn 11/2-11/4)
- Every eye beholds the god above them as the sun of day (AtenHymn 11/5, AtenHymn 12/7)
- When the god rises creatures live, when he sets they die; he is lifetime itself (AtenHymn 12/5-12/6)
- The king says: you are in my heart; no one knows you except your son, the king, whom you have made wise (AtenHymn 12/2-12/3)
- All work is laid down when the sun sets in the west (AtenHymn 13)

**BD 125 (pNu): arrival at the Hall of the Two Truths and the first declaration of innocence**
- Denial: the speaker has not robbed a poor man of his property or made him poorer (BD125 W1:9/2)
- Denial: the speaker has not maligned a servant before his superior (BD125 W1:10)
- Denial: the speaker has not driven small cattle from their pasture or robbed them of fodder (BD125 W1:14/2)
- Denial: the speaker has not trapped birds or caught fish in the gods' marshes and pools (BD125 W1:14/3-15)
- Denial: the speaker has not put out a (sacred) fire at its time (BD125 W1:16)

**BD 125 (pNu): the second declaration of innocence, addressed to the 42 judges**
- Denial: the speaker did no wrong although he saw evil (BD125 W1:53)

**BD 125 (pTurin 1791): the 42 addresses, late version**
- Denial: the speaker has not reviled or complained against his father (BD125 W7:27_2/2)

**BD 125 vignette (pTurin 1791): captions of the weighing of the heart before Osiris**
- After the weighing the justified dead is given back his heart to its place (BD125 W10:Beischrift_zu_Thot-Beischrift_zu_Thot/2)
- Fate (Shai) and the birth goddesses (Renenet, Meskhenet) stand by the balance at the judgment of the dead (BD125 W10:Gottheiten_vor_Thot-Gottheiten_vor_Thot/3)
- Osiris sits in his shrine as ruler of eternity, foremost of the West, before whom the dead is presented (BD125 W10:im_Schrein_des_Osiris)

**The Doomed Prince: a son granted, three fates decreed, the prince shut away and set free**
- Divine birth goddesses (the Hathors) come at a child's birth and pronounce his fate (DoomedPrince 4_3/2-4_4)
- A parent tries to evade a child's foretold death by shutting him in a secluded house, which fails (DoomedPrince 4_5/2)
- A young prince leaves home with chariot, servant and dog to wander abroad as his heart desires, living by hunting (DoomedPrince 4_13-5_2/2)

**The Doomed Prince: the princess in the high window of Naharina**
- A king's only daughter is shut in a house with a window high above the ground; whoever leaps up to it wins her as wife (DoomedPrince 5_3/2-5_5/3, DoomedPrince 6_5-6_6/3)
- A prince abroad passes himself off as the son of a lesser man (a chariot driver) driven out by a stepmother (DoomedPrince 5_11-5_12/2, DoomedPrince 7_3-7_4/2)
- After the mother's death the father takes another wife, who comes to hate her stepson and drives him away (DoomedPrince 5_11/3-5_12/2)
- The bride's father refuses to give his daughter to a fugitive from Egypt and sends men to kill him (DoomedPrince 6_9/2-6_11/3, DoomedPrince 6_14)
- The bride swears by the sun god that she will not eat or drink and will die within the hour if her beloved is taken or killed (DoomedPrince 6_12-6_12/3, DoomedPrince 6_15/2-6_16)

**The Doomed Prince: the wife kills the snake, the dog and the crocodile pursue the prince**
- A wife keeps watch by her sleeping husband, makes the attacking snake drunk with beer and wine, and has it hacked to pieces (DoomedPrince 7_8, DoomedPrince 7_15/2-8_3/4)
- 'Your god has given one of your fates into your hand': a danger overcome is credited to one's god (DoomedPrince 8_5/3-8_5/4)
- Saved from danger, the hero offers to the sun god and praises his power every day (DoomedPrince 8_5/5)
- The fated agent itself speaks: 'I am your fate which has come after you' (DoomedPrince 8_10-8_11)
- A crocodile in a lake and a water-being ('the Strong One') fight each other daily for months, each keeping the other in (DoomedPrince 7_9-7_12/2, DoomedPrince 8_11/2-8_13/2)

**Eloquent Peasant (version R): the journey, the trap on the path and the robbery**
- Before travelling to market the peasant has his wife measure out grain, leaving most for her and the children and taking a little for himself (EloquentPeasant W1:1_1/alt_1-1_6/alt_6/2)

**Eloquent Peasant (version B1): the journey, the trap and the robbery**
- The robbed man appeals to the reputation of the estate's lord as the one who punishes every robber in the land (EloquentPeasant W2:46/alt_15-49/alt_18)
- Proverb thrown at the poor: 'the name of the poor man is spoken only for his master's sake' (EloquentPeasant W2:50/alt_19-52/alt_21)

**Eloquent Peasant (version B1): the second petition (the scales tilt, the officials are inverted)**
- The great man is reminded that he will die with his dependants: will you be a man of eternity? (EloquentPeasant W2:126/alt_95-126/alt_95/2)
- Maat (justice) flees from under the judge, driven from her place (EloquentPeasant W2:128/alt_97)
- The one who should see is blind, the one who should hear is deaf, the guide has become one who leads astray (EloquentPeasant W2:144/alt_113)
- Theft is pardonable in the destitute, but not in the one who lacks nothing and is sated with bread and beer (EloquentPeasant W2:152/alt_121/2-156/alt_125)
- The judge should be a refuge, but his landing place is infested with crocodiles (EloquentPeasant W2:160/alt_129/2-161/alt_130)
- The judge is invoked as the one who brings the drowning to shore and rescues the shipwrecked (EloquentPeasant W2:167/alt_136-169/alt_138)

**Eloquent Peasant (version B1): the third petition (Re and Hapi, the balance of Thoth); the peasant is flogged**
- Does the balance tilt, does the scale lean, is Thoth lenient? Then neither may the judge do wrong (EloquentPeasant W2:179/alt_148-182/alt_151)
- Admonition: do not answer good with evil, do not put one thing in the place of another (EloquentPeasant W2:182/alt_151/2)
- When the hidden truth is found, falsehood is thrown on its back to the ground (EloquentPeasant W2:213/alt_182)
- Do not prepare for tomorrow before it has come: no one knows the trouble it holds (EloquentPeasant W2:214/alt_183-214/alt_183/2)
- The official has the persistent petitioner flogged by guards with whips (EloquentPeasant W2:217/alt_186-217/alt_186/2)
- The negligent ruler's domain is like a town without its mayor, a body without its chief, a ship without its pilot, a troop without its leader (EloquentPeasant W2:220/alt_189)

**Eloquent Peasant (version B1): the fourth petition at the temple of Herishef**
- Goodness is destroyed: the ferry is sunk, so that one must wade the river in sandals; one may no longer travel by night or day or stand up for one's right (EloquentPeasant W2:228/alt_197-232/alt_201/2)
- Saying: pass over a fault and it becomes two (EloquentPeasant W2:246/alt_215-246/alt_215/2)
- Sayings: it is the eater who tastes, the one addressed who answers, the sleeper who sees the dream (EloquentPeasant W2:246/alt_215/3-247/alt_216/2)
- Pleas built on the judge's titles: steersman, let not your ship drift; life-giver, let none die; shade, do not act like sunglare; refuge, let not the crocodile seize (EloquentPeasant W2:252/alt_221-254/alt_223/2)

**Eloquent Peasant (version B1): the fifth petition (the fishermen; the poor man's goods are his breath)**
- The judge was appointed to hear cases, judge between two parties and punish the robber, but he supports the thief (EloquentPeasant W2:265/alt_234-266/alt_235)
- The one appointed as a dyke for the poor has become the flood that sweeps him away (EloquentPeasant W2:268/alt_237-269/alt_238/2)

**Eloquent Peasant (version B1): the seventh petition (colleague of Thoth; the breached dyke)**
- Do not brood over what has not yet come nor rejoice over what has not yet happened (EloquentPeasant W2:302/alt_271-303/alt_272)
- Officials are called 'masters of the good', craftsmen who create what is and rejoin a severed head (EloquentPeasant W2:319/alt_288-320/alt_289)

**Eloquent Peasant (version B1): the eighth petition (Maat goes down to the necropolis with its doer)**
- Greed makes one fall far; the greedy man lacks success and meets only failure (EloquentPeasant W2:321/alt_290-324/alt_293)
- The official whose belly is full and whose grain measure overflows still grasps: is he a robber? (EloquentPeasant W2:325/alt_294-325/alt_294/3, EloquentPeasant W2:331/alt_300-333/alt_302/2)
- The petitioner calls his perfect speech one that comes from the mouth of Re himself (EloquentPeasant W2:349/alt_318)
- The official is addressed as the reed, papyrus and palette of Thoth, and told to keep away from wrong (EloquentPeasant W2:336/alt_305)

**Eloquent Peasant (version B2): the ninth petition, the despairing peasant, the verdict**
- Whoever grows rich by falsehood has no children and no heirs on earth; whoever sails with it never reaches land or harbour (EloquentPeasant W3:98-102)
- Sayings: the sluggard has no yesterday, the one deaf to Maat has no friend, the greedy has no feast day (EloquentPeasant W3:109-110/2)
- Unheard, the petitioner says he will go and petition Anubis (the god of the dead) against the judge (EloquentPeasant W3:113-114/2)
- Death is longed for as the thirsty long for water and the infant for milk (EloquentPeasant W3:119)
- The vindicated petitioner swears he will eat only of his protector's bread and drink only of his beer for ever (EloquentPeasant W3:124-125)
- The petitions are read out from a new papyrus roll and sent to the king, who is delighted and leaves the verdict to his official (EloquentPeasant W3:128-133)
- In the end the oppressor's whole property is inventoried and given to his victim (EloquentPeasant W3:133/2-139)
- Colophon: the text is complete from beginning to end as found in writing (EloquentPeasant W3:142)

**Harper's Song of Neferhotep, first song (TT 50)**
- Re shows himself in the morning and Atum sets in the western mountain; husbands beget, women conceive, every nose breathes (HarpersSongs W3:3/2-5)
- Give bread to him who has no field, so that you gain a good name for ever (HarpersSongs W3:13)
- At the burial the sem priest in a panther skin pours libations, women singers weep and the mummies are set up before Re (HarpersSongs W3:13/2-15)

**Harper's Song of Paser (TT 106)**
- What the god loves is Maat (truth/justice) (HarpersSongs W4:8)

**Harper's Song of Inherkhau (TT 359)**
- Build yourself a house (tomb) in the necropolis so that your name endures in it (HarpersSongs W5:5)
- The Nile flows north and the north wind blows south: each man goes at his hour (HarpersSongs W5:7)
- Do not remember evil, what the god abhors (HarpersSongs W5:13)
- The dead is praised as upright, just, calm, patient, content, cheerful and one who speaks no evil (HarpersSongs W5:13/2)
- Give your heart drunkenness every day until the day of landing (death) comes (HarpersSongs W5:15)

**Harper's Song of Tjanefer, first song (TT 158)**
- The gods of the necropolis are asked to give water to the dead (HarpersSongs W9:10/2-12)

**Harper's Song of Neferhotep, second song (TT 50): against the old songs, praise of the land of eternity**
- The dead man is now a god living for ever, made great in the West (HarpersSongs W11:2)

**Harper's Song of Neferrenpet/Kenro (TT 178)**
- Blessing: may you turn on your right side and on your left and be at ease in your place (HarpersSongs W13:5–6-7)

**Harper's Song of Tjanefer, second song (TT 158)**
