- The blessed dead receives offerings and eats the same as on earth; his heart is glad in the necropolis (HarpersSongs W15:10-10/2)
- All people in the necropolis are given to the dead as his reward (HarpersSongs W15:12)

**Harper's Song of Panniut (TT 331): sweet to dwell in Thebes**
- How sweet it is to dwell in the god's city (Thebes); the heart is in joy every day (HarpersSongs W16:2-2/2)
- The blessed dead rises to heaven like noble vultures or calls like the divine benu bird (HarpersSongs W16:6)

**Harper's Song of Neferhotep, third song (TT 50): the good journey and the name not forgotten**
- Anubis lays his hands on the dead man as the mortuary rites are performed (HarpersSongs W17:9)

**Harper's Song of Piay (TT 263)**
- The dead may hear the petitions of his children at the door of his house (HarpersSongs W18:5)
- The blessed dead joins the followers of Horus and becomes one of them (HarpersSongs W18:8–9-9)

**Transfiguration song of Amenemhet (TT 163)**
- The dead man is summoned to heaven by Re and remembered before the god who awakes unharmed (HarpersSongs W19:3–4)

**Harper's Song of Samut/Kyky (TT 409), fragment**
- The dead endures, abiding for ever in his city (HarpersSongs W20:4)

**Harper's Song of Djehutimes (TT 32)**
- The god has protected the man since he came from the womb until old age and assigns him honour and burial (HarpersSongs W22:4-4/2)

**Harper's Song of Nefersekheru (Zawyet el-Meitin)**
- Blessing: you belong to the morning (tomorrow), not to yesterday; renew yourself like the frog, the 'repeater of life' (HarpersSongs W23:10-13)
- After a life well spent the dead unites with the firmament (HarpersSongs W23:9)

**Harper's Song, unknown owner (private collection), fragment**
- The blessed dead is on the 'island of the just one' (HarpersSongs W26:x+5)

**The aged Re, the plot of mankind, the council of the gods and the Eye sent as Hathor (Heavenly Cow, Seti I)**
- When the sun god has grown old, humankind plots against him (kꜣi̯ md,t r ...) (HeavenlyCow W1:1/3, HeavenlyCow W1:2, HeavenlyCow W1:2/5)
- The aged god's body is described as precious materials: bones of silver, flesh of gold, hair of lapis lazuli (HeavenlyCow W1:2/2-2/4)
- Humankind came into being from the creator's eye (his tears) (HeavenlyCow W1:8/2)
- The sun god sends out his Eye in the form of a goddess (Hathor/Sakhmet) to slay rebellious humankind (HeavenlyCow W1:12/2-13/2, HeavenlyCow W1:14/2)
- The destroying goddess wades in the blood of the slain humans (HeavenlyCow W1:15/2)
- The aged creator wishes to return to the primeval waters (Nun) from which he came into being (HeavenlyCow W1:5/3)

**Red beer, the drunken goddess and the rescue of mankind (Heavenly Cow, Seti I)**
- To stop the destroyer, the god has thousands of jars of beer dyed red like human blood and poured out over the fields (HeavenlyCow W1:16-19, HeavenlyCow W1:21/2-21/3)
- The destroying goddess drinks the red beer, becomes drunk, no longer recognises humans, and the remnant of humankind survives (HeavenlyCow W1:22-23/5)
- An annual festival with an intoxicating drink for a goddess is founded on the day humankind was spared (HeavenlyCow W1:24/4-25)

**Re, weary of men, rides Nut the sky-cow; men fight; the sky, the fields of the hereafter and the stars come into being (Heavenly Cow, Seti I)**
- The creator, weary of living among humans, withdraws from earth to heaven (HeavenlyCow W1:27/2, HeavenlyCow W1:28, HeavenlyCow W1:29)
- The sky goddess turns into a cow and carries the sun god up on her back; she becomes the sky (HeavenlyCow W1:30-31/3, HeavenlyCow W1:32, HeavenlyCow W1:38)
- After the god's withdrawal humans take up bows and clubs against one another: the origin of slaughter among humankind (HeavenlyCow W1:34/2-36/2)
- The god's words name and create the fields of the hereafter (Field of Offerings, Field of Reeds) and the stars (HeavenlyCow W1:39/3-40/3)

**Instructions for drawing the sky-cow with Shu, the Heh-gods and the barques, and its captions (Heavenly Cow, Seti I)**
- The sun god stands in his barque (with steering-oar and shrine) to cross the sky (HeavenlyCow W1:47-47/2)
- A divine utterance reads 'I am (who) I am' (Egyptian jw =j jm =j) (HeavenlyCow W1:49-49/2)
- The stars are set on the belly of the sky goddess (HeavenlyCow W1:45/2)

**Re charges Geb with the serpents of the earth and hands them to Osiris (Heavenly Cow, Seti I)**
- The high god orders the earth god to guard the serpents within the earth and hands them over to the god of the dead (HeavenlyCow W1:56/7-57/4, HeavenlyCow W1:61)
- A written decree is sent to the serpents of every mound, warning them to keep still because the god is present (HeavenlyCow W1:57/4-58/2)
- Warning against magicians who know their spells, for the god of magic himself is with them (HeavenlyCow W1:59/3-60/2)

**Thoth made Re's deputy; the ibis, the moon and the baboon of Thoth (Heavenly Cow, Seti I)**
- The sun god appoints the moon god (Thoth) his deputy and representative to shine in the night (HeavenlyCow W1:63, HeavenlyCow W1:71-71/2, HeavenlyCow W1:72/2-73, HeavenlyCow W1:73/4)
- Gods created by the creator who rebelled are confined in the earth and are to be quelled by his deputy (HeavenlyCow W1:67/2)
- A god is appointed vizier of the high god, and all creatures thank him (HeavenlyCow W1:73/4-74/2)

**Purity rules for reciting the book and the blessings of the reciter (Heavenly Cow, Seti I)**
- Whoever recites the sacred text must be purified: natron in the mouth, new linen, white sandals, bathing in floodwater, a purification of nine days (HeavenlyCow W1:74/3-77, HeavenlyCow W1:78/2-79)
- Whoever performs the rite in the book will have long life, sound eyes and limbs, unfailing affairs and undiminished goods (HeavenlyCow W1:80-83/2)
- Closing formula: 'truly excellent, (proven) a million times' (HeavenlyCow W1:84)

**Spells of the book - Re the creator of heaven, the bas of the gods, the reciter as magician, names Eternity and Everlastingness (Heavenly Cow, Seti I)**
- Asked his names, the blessed dead answers 'Eternity and Everlastingness' (nḥḥ ḥnꜥ ḏt) (HeavenlyCow W1:93/3, HeavenlyCow W1:95/22-95/24)
- Whoever recites the spell will live in the necropolis and be more revered than the living on earth (HeavenlyCow W1:93-93/2)
- The spell or rite is to be recited at the new-moon and half-month festivals (HeavenlyCow W1:92/3)
- The dead king is named 'Osiris NN, justified' (mꜣꜥ-ḫrw) (HeavenlyCow W1:95/25-95/27)

**Frame texts of Nut and Osiris for Tutankhamun on his outer shrine**
- The sky goddess addresses the dead king as her son and wishes him power, justification, a body unharmed and eternal life (HeavenlyCow W3:0/3-0/8)
- Wish that the dead man's corpse endure in the necropolis and his name endure on earth (HeavenlyCow W3:0/10-0/11)

**Heavenly Cow texts on Tutankhamun's outer shrine - the learned scribe in heaven, Mehet-weret welcomes the king**
- Declaration that the speaker has no enemies among men, gods, spirits or the dead in the whole land (HeavenlyCow W4:30)
- The scribe who knows the sacred writings and spells goes up and down to heaven unhindered and no wrongdoing is counted against him (HeavenlyCow W4:33-38/2)

**The lawsuit of Horus and Seth opens before the Lord of All; Ba-neb-Djed counsels writing to Neith (Contendings of Horus and Seth)**
- The son of the dead king sues before the divine tribunal for his father's office, against his father's brother (HorusSeth 1_1/2, HorusSeth 1_11/3, HorusSeth 1_12-1_12/2)
- One claimant proposes to settle the dispute by a trial of strength with his rival before the gods (HorusSeth 1_9-1_10)

**Neith's letter, the insult of Baba, the sulking of Re and Hathor's exposure (Contendings of Horus and Seth)**
- A goddess threatens that if injustice is done she will rage and the sky will fall on the earth (HorusSeth 3_2/2)
- The losing party is to be compensated with the goddesses Anat and Astarte as wives (HorusSeth 3_4-3_4/2)
- The high god mocks the young claimant as weak in body, a boy with bad breath, too small for the office (HorusSeth 3_7/3-3_8)
- Insulted in the assembly, the high god lies on his back in his pavilion, sick at heart, alone for a whole day (HorusSeth 3_9-3_11, HorusSeth 3_13/2)
- A goddess exposes her genitals to the sulking high god, who laughs and returns to the assembly (HorusSeth 4_1-4_3/2)

**Seth's claim of strength, Isis's oath, Seth's threat to kill a god a day (Contendings of Horus and Seth)**
- A goddess swears 'as my mother lives, as (the creator) lives' (HorusSeth 4_10/2-4_11)
- An angry god threatens to take his sceptre and kill one of the gods every day (HorusSeth 5_1/2)
- A litigant swears he will not plead in court as long as a certain goddess is present, and the court is moved to an island (HorusSeth 5_2-5_3)

**The island in the middle, the bribed ferryman, and Isis's parable by which Seth condemns himself (Contendings of Horus and Seth)**
- Barred from the island, the goddess disguised as an old woman bribes the ferryman with a gold ring after he refuses bread (HorusSeth 5_4-5_4/2, HorusSeth 5_6/2-6_2)
- The goddess changes herself into a beautiful young woman (then a kite) to trap her adversary (HorusSeth 6_4/2-6_5, HorusSeth 6_13-6_13/3)
- A widow tells how a stranger threatens to beat her fatherless son and seize his father's cattle (HorusSeth 6_8/2-6_11, HorusSeth 7_4-7_7)
- The ferryman who disobeyed is punished by having the front of his feet cut off (HorusSeth 7_12/3-7_13/2)
- Punished for taking gold, a god forswears gold, which becomes an abomination in his city (HorusSeth 7_13/3-8_1)

**The white crown for Horus, Seth's protest, the hippopotamus contest, Isis's harpoon and the beheading of Isis (Contendings of Horus and Seth)**
- Two rival gods turn into hippopotami and stay under water; whoever surfaces before three months loses (HorusSeth 8_9/3-8_11)
- The mother throws a copper harpoon into the water; it strikes her own son, then her brother, and she releases each when he cries out (HorusSeth 8_11/2-9_7/3)
- The angry son cuts off his mother's head; she becomes a headless flint statue (HorusSeth 9_7/4-9_12)

**Seth tears out Horus's eyes; Hathor heals him with gazelle milk (Contendings of Horus and Seth)**
- The rival tears out the young god's eyes and buries them; they grow into lotus flowers (HorusSeth 10_2-10_4/2)
- The attacker tells the high god he has not found his victim, though he has maimed him (HorusSeth 10_5/2)
- A goddess heals the blinded god by putting gazelle's milk in his eyes (HorusSeth 10_6-10_10/2)

**The feast, Seth's assault, the semen on the lettuce and the golden disk (Contendings of Horus and Seth)**
- The high god orders the quarrelling rivals to eat and drink together and make peace (HorusSeth 10_12-11_1/2)
- At night the rival puts his semen between the young god's thighs, to claim before the court that he has 'done a man's work' on him (HorusSeth 11_1/3-11_4/2, HorusSeth 12_2/5)
- The mother cuts off her son's hands defiled by the rival's semen, throws them in the water and makes him new ones (HorusSeth 11_5/3-11_7)
- The mother puts her son's semen on the lettuce the rival eats; he becomes 'pregnant' and the semen answers from inside him (HorusSeth 11_7/2-11_12)
- The divine scribe calls each god's semen to come out; it answers from where it is, proving the truth before the court (HorusSeth 12_5/2-12_11/3)
- The divine court pronounces 'X is right (mꜣꜥ), Y is wrong (ꜥḏꜣ)' (HorusSeth 13_1/3-13_1/4, HorusSeth 13_2/2-13_2/3)

**The race in stone ships and Horus's appeal to Neith at Sais (Contendings of Horus and Seth)**
- Two rivals race in ships of stone; one secretly plasters a wooden ship, the other's real stone ship sinks (HorusSeth 13_2/4-13_9, HorusSeth 13_9/2-13_10)
- The claimant complains that he has been declared right in hall after hall, a thousand times, yet his opponent ignores the verdict (HorusSeth 14_1/2-14_4/3)

**The letters to and from Osiris - barley and emmer, the messengers of the underworld, all go down to the West (Contendings of Horus and Seth)**
- The god of the dead claims to have created barley and emmer to keep gods and humans ('the small cattle') alive (HorusSeth 14_11)
- The high god retorts that the gift a god boasts of (grain) would have existed even if that god had never been born (HorusSeth 15_2/2-15_2/3)
- The god of the dead complains that justice (Maat) has been allowed to sink into the underworld (HorusSeth 15_3/4)
- The land of the dead is full of fierce-faced messengers who fear no god or goddess and fetch the heart of every evildoer (HorusSeth 15_4/2-15_5)
- The god of the dead reminds the gods that all of them, and nobles and commoners after them, go down to rest in the West where he is (HorusSeth 15_6-15_8)

**Seth brought in fetters; Horus crowned king; Seth becomes Re's thunderer; colophon (Contendings of Horus and Seth)**
- The defeated rival is brought bound in fetters (a yoke) before the high god and concedes the throne (HorusSeth 15_11/3-15_13/3)
- When the rightful heir is crowned the gods hold festival, heaven rejoices, the whole land jubilates and garlands are taken up (HorusSeth 16_2-16_2/4, HorusSeth 16_5/2-16_7/2)
- The defeated rival is taken by the sun god as a son to sit with him and thunder in the sky, feared by all (HorusSeth 16_3/2-16_4/2)

**Broken opening - doorkeepers plunder, the Delta bears shields, a man sees his son as enemy (Admonitions of Ipuwer)**
- In the time of ruin a man sees his own son as his enemy (Ipuwer 1:5/2)
- The present calamity is what the ancestors foretold (Ipuwer 1:10)
- Foreigners have become 'people' (Egyptians) everywhere and foreign bowmen have entered the land (Ipuwer 1:9)

**'O, yet' - the Nile unploughed, women barren, pestilence and blood, the river is blood (Admonitions of Ipuwer)**
- The Nile flood rises but no one ploughs for it (Ipuwer 2:3/3)
- Pestilence (jꜣdt) is throughout the land and blood is everywhere (Ipuwer 2:5/3-2:6/3)
- The many dead are thrown into the river: 'the flood is a grave, the tomb has become a flood' (Ipuwer 2:6/4-2:7)
- The land spins round like a potter's wheel (the world turned upside down) (Ipuwer 2:8/4)
- Crocodiles are glutted because men go to them of their own accord (drown themselves) (Ipuwer 2:12-2:12/2)
- Everyone says 'we do not know what has happened throughout the land' (Ipuwer 2:3/4-2:3/5)

**'O, yet' - foreign bowmen, jewels on maidservants, no ships to Byblos, laughter perished (Admonitions of Ipuwer)**
- The desert has spread throughout the land and the nomes are hacked up (Ipuwer 3:1-3:1/3)
- No one sails to Byblos any more, so there is no cedar for coffins and oil for embalming (Ipuwer 3:6/4-3:8)
- The southern provinces pay no taxes because of strife and the treasury is empty (Ipuwer 3:10-3:12)
- Laughter has perished and is no longer made; mourning mixed with lamentation is throughout the land (Ipuwer 3:13/4-3:14)

**'O, yet' - hair fallen out, endless noise, 'I wish I could die', children dashed against walls, the embalmed cast out (Admonitions of Ipuwer)**
- The son of a well-born man can no longer be distinguished from a have-not (Ipuwer 4:1-4:1/2)

**'O, yet' - 'if I knew where god is', cattle weep, cult is futile, brother strikes brother, end of humankind wished (Admonitions of Ipuwer)**
- A sufferer says: if only I could perceive and know where god is, I would act for him (Ipuwer 5:3-5:3/2)
- Maat (truth) is in the land in name only; wrongdoing is what people do while leaning on it (Ipuwer 5:3/3-5:4)
- Offerings and service to the gods are futile: none can reach the god and giving to him is misery (Ipuwer 5:8-5:9/3)

**'O, yet' - hunger, magic stripped bare, scribes slain and registers destroyed, the poor in the Ennead's place (Admonitions of Ipuwer)**
- In the famine people eat plant fodder and drink water; no flour is found and seed is taken from the pig's mouth (Ipuwer 6:1/2-6:4/2)
- The speaker wishes he had raised his voice at the time, to save himself from the suffering (Ipuwer 6:4/3-6:5)
- Offices are broken open, scribes slain, the land registers and laws thrown out and torn up in the streets (Ipuwer 6:7-6:9/2, Ipuwer 6:9/2-6:10/2)

**'Look' - fire risen, the king carried off by wretches, the pyramid emptied, the Residence fallen in an hour, the inversion of owners (Admonitions of Ipuwer)**
- Something never done before: the king is removed (carried off) by the rabble (Ipuwer 7:1/3, Ipuwer 7:2/3-7:3)
- The royal city has fallen down in a single hour (Ipuwer 7:4-7:4/2)

**'Look' - ladies give children for beds, chiefs flee, offices like a herd without herdsman, a man slain beside his brother (Admonitions of Ipuwer)**
- Rich women give away their children in exchange for beds (necessities) (Ipuwer 8:7/2)
- Rich ladies and the chiefs of the land flee, prostrate with fear of death (Ipuwer 8:13/2-8:14/2)
- A man is slain at his brother's side and the brother flees to save himself (Ipuwer 9:3/2-9:3/4)
- Day does not dawn on the land (darkness persists) (Ipuwer 9:11/2)

**'Destroy the enemies of that august Residence' - the plundered royal estate (Admonitions of Ipuwer)**
- The king's estate and workshop are a free-for-all and without their revenues of grain, fowl, fish, linen and oil (Ipuwer 10:3/2-10:5/2)
- Refrain 'Destroy the enemies of that august Residence!' with a varying epithet each time (Ipuwer 10:6, Ipuwer 10:7/3, Ipuwer 10:8, Ipuwer 10:9/3, Ipuwer 10:10, Ipuwer 10:11/2)

**'Remember' - the lost rites; Re's decree; why does he create? (Admonitions of Ipuwer)**
- Litany 'Remember ...' (sḫꜣ ...) calling to mind the lost temple rites, offerings and purity rules (Ipuwer 10:12, Ipuwer 10:13/2, Ipuwer 11:1, Ipuwer 11:2, Ipuwer 11:3, Ipuwer 11:4, Ipuwer 11:6, Ipuwer 11:6/2)
- The sage asks why the god goes on creating humankind when the fearful cannot be told from the violent (Ipuwer 11:11/3-11:12)
- The god should come and bring coolness upon the heat (of strife) (Ipuwer 11:13)

**The reproach of the creator - shepherd of all, 'is he asleep?', 'is he a shepherd who loves death?' (Admonitions of Ipuwer)**
- The sage reproaches the creator, called 'shepherd of all', for letting his herd perish: he should have known their nature and struck them in the first generation (Ipuwer 12:1-12:2, Ipuwer 12:14/2)
- Had the creator recognised humankind's character in the first generation, he would have stretched out his arm and destroyed the herd and their heirs (Ipuwer 12:2/2-12:2/3)
- Fire (violent passion) belongs to the hearts of humankind (Ipuwer 12:2)
- Authoritative Utterance (Hu), Perception (Sia) and Truth (Maat) are with the creator (Ipuwer 12:12/2-12:12/3)
- Image of insecurity: if three men go on the road, only two are found (Ipuwer 12:13/2-12:14)
- The sage tells the god he has brought this about because he spoke falsehood (Ipuwer 13:1/4-13:2/2)
- The sage wishes the god could taste a little of the misery himself (Ipuwer 13:5/4)

**'Indeed it is good when' - the restored order: ships, pyramids, canals, feasts (Admonitions of Ipuwer)**
- Litany 'Indeed it is good when ...' picturing the restored order (ships sail, canals are dug, people feast) (Ipuwer 13:9, Ipuwer 13:10/3, Ipuwer 13:12/2, Ipuwer 13:13, Ipuwer 13:14, Ipuwer 14:1, Ipuwer 14:3)
- In good times men's hands build pyramids, dig canals and plant trees for the gods (Ipuwer 13:12/2)
- It is good when people are drunk, drink and their hearts are happy, with jubilation in their mouths (Ipuwer 13:13-13:14/2)
- It is good when every man's need is met with a blanket in the shade and the door shut on him who slept in a bush (Ipuwer 14:1)

**Asiatics, Nubians and Libyans; 'Egypt will not be given to the sand' (Admonitions of Ipuwer)**
- Every man fights for his own (his sister) but only protects himself; every man slays his brother (Ipuwer 14:12/2, Ipuwer 14:14/3)
- The sage asks whether the attackers are Nubians or Libyans and laments that Asiatics have learned the governance of Egypt (Ipuwer 14:13-14:14/2, Ipuwer 15:1)
- Popular wisdom says Egypt will not be given over to the sand (desert), for it is strong on its borders (Ipuwer 15:2-15:2/4)

**What Ipuwer said in answer to the Lord of All, and the Lord of All's reply (Admonitions of Ipuwer)**
- Dialogue frame: the sage answers the Lord of All, and the Lord of All answers him (Ipuwer 15:13, Ipuwer 16:10)
- The god has done good and made people live, yet they cover their faces in fear of the morrow (Ipuwer 15:14-15:14/2)
- An old man is carried off by death while his son is still a child without understanding, and the father weeps for him (Ipuwer 16:1-16:2/3)
- If one calls to them, they do not listen (Ipuwer 16:13)

**Empty heading lines and the pAmherst fragments of the Dispute of a Man with his Ba**
- The ba offers to teach the man about the West (ManAndBa pAmherst.3:J–K.2-J–K.3)

**The man complains that his ba drags him to death and appeals to the gods as judges (Dispute of a Man with his Ba)**
- The man complains that his own ba wants to leave him and drag him into death before his time (ManAndBa 7-7/2, ManAndBa 11, ManAndBa 17/2)
- A man argues aloud with his own soul (ba), opening his mouth to answer it (ManAndBa 3/2, ManAndBa 5-6/2)
- The man asks his ba to make the West (the realm of the dead) pleasant for him (ManAndBa 19)
- The 'day of difficulty' (hrw qsnt), the day of misfortune or death (ManAndBa 9, ManAndBa 15)

**The ba replies 'you are no man'; the man promises the ba a well-provided burial (Dispute of a Man with his Ba)**
- The ba mocks the man: 'you are no man; are you even alive? you care for life like a lord of wealth' (ManAndBa 30-32/2)
- When you are dead, only your name lives on (ManAndBa 36/2-36/3)
- The West (realm of the dead) is a mooring place, a resting place for the heart (ManAndBa 37-38)
- The man promises his ba a well-provided burial and shade over his corpse so that other bas will envy it (ManAndBa 39-47, ManAndBa 51)
- If the ba drives the man to death prematurely, it will find no resting place in the West (ManAndBa 49)
- The dying man asks for patience until his heir grows up to make offerings and stand at the tomb on the day of burial (ManAndBa 51)

**The ba: burial is heartbreak; 'follow the beautiful day'; two parables of a peasant (Dispute of a Man with his Ba)**
- The ba argues that burial and tombs are only heartbreak: the builders of pyramids have bare altars like those who died on the riverbank (ManAndBa 56-58)
- The builders of granite pyramids, who became gods, now have altars as bare as those of the unburied dead on the riverbank (ManAndBa 60)
- Exhortation to 'follow the beautiful day and forget care' (šms hrw nfr smḫ mḥ) (ManAndBa 67-68/2)
- Parable: a peasant's wife and children perish in the crocodile-infested water; he mourns the children who died before they lived (ManAndBa 68/3-78)
- Parable: a peasant asks for an early meal, is told it is for supper, goes out and comes back changed, deaf to his wife (ManAndBa 80-84)

**'Behold, my name stinks because of you' (Dispute of a Man with his Ba)**
- Litany 'Behold, my name stinks ...' comparing the speaker's reputation to rotting fish, birds, crocodiles and a slandered wife (ManAndBa 86, ManAndBa 88, ManAndBa 91, ManAndBa 93, ManAndBa 95, ManAndBa 97, ManAndBa 99, ManAndBa 101)
- A wife about whom a lie has been told to her husband (ManAndBa 97)

**'To whom shall I speak today?' (Dispute of a Man with his Ba)**
- Litany 'To whom shall I speak today?' (ḏd =j n m mjn): brothers are evil, friends do not love, hearts are greedy, there is no righteous man (ManAndBa 103, ManAndBa 104/2, ManAndBa 108, ManAndBa 113, ManAndBa 121/2, ManAndBa 127, ManAndBa 129)
- Brothers are evil, friends of today do not love, the former partner has become an enemy, and one turns to strangers for honesty (ManAndBa 103/2-104, ManAndBa 113/2-114, ManAndBa 117-117/2, ManAndBa 118/2-119)
- Hearts are greedy and every man seizes his neighbour's goods (ManAndBa 105-105/2, ManAndBa 112-112/2)
- There is no intimate (confidant) and no man's heart one can lean on (ManAndBa 120/2-121, ManAndBa 123/2-124, ManAndBa 127/2)
- Yesterday is not remembered and no one acts for him who acted (no gratitude) (ManAndBa 115/2-116)
- The wrong that strikes the land has no end (ManAndBa 129/2)

**'Death is before me today' (Dispute of a Man with his Ba)**
- Litany 'Death is before me today like ...' comparing death to recovery from illness, myrrh, lotus, clearing sky, homecoming from captivity (ManAndBa 130, ManAndBa 132, ManAndBa 134, ManAndBa 136, ManAndBa 138, ManAndBa 140)
- Death is like a man coming home from an expedition or longing to see his house after years in captivity (ManAndBa 136, ManAndBa 140)

**'He who is yonder will be a living god' (Dispute of a Man with his Ba)**
- He who is yonder will be a living god, stand in the sun-barque and petition Re as a wise man (ManAndBa 142, ManAndBa 143, ManAndBa 145)
- The blessed dead, as a living god, repels wrong against the one who does it (ManAndBa 142)

**The ba's last word - cling to life, and we shall make a landing place together; colophon (Dispute of a Man with his Ba)**
- The ba finally agrees to stay with the man and make a common landing place with him when he dies (ManAndBa 148-154)

**The rebel, the agitating talker and his followers; mild punishment (Instruction for Merikare)**
- Bend the multitude and drive the heat (unrest) from it (Merikare W1:3_3/2-3_3/3)
- The ruler is told to be mild (gracious) when he punishes (Merikare W1:2_8/2, Merikare W1:3_5/2)
- Justify yourself (make your voice true) at the side of the god (Merikare W1:3_6/2)

**Speech is stronger than fighting; imitate the ancestors; life on earth is short; do Maat (Instruction for Merikare)**
- Be skilful in speech: the tongue is the king's sword and speech is stronger than any fighting (Merikare W1:3_8-3_8/4)
- A good (even) temper is a man's heaven; the rage of the hot-hearted is grievous (Merikare W1:3_7-3_7/2)
- Imitate your fathers and forebears; their words are fixed in writing: unroll and read them (Merikare W1:3_10/2-4_1/2)
- Make your monument endure through the love people bear you (Merikare W1:4_2)
- He who covets what belongs to others is a fool (Merikare W1:4_5-4_5/2)
- Speak and do Maat (justice) while you remain on earth (Merikare W1:4_10/2, Merikare W1:4_11/3)

**Comfort the weeper, oppress no widow; do not kill; the judges of the dead (Instruction for Merikare)**
- God knows the treacherous (crooked-hearted) (Merikare W1:5_3)
- God strikes down with misfortune because of blood(shed) (Merikare W1:5_4)
- Whoever reaches the hereafter without wrongdoing will be there like a god, striding free like the lords of eternity (Merikare W1:5_10-5_10/3)

**Raise the youth, choose men by their deeds, serve the temple; one day gives for eternity (Instruction for Merikare)**
- Every twenty years a new generation of youth comes of age to be recruited (Merikare W1:6_1-6_2/2)
- Do not distinguish the well-born from the commoner: take a man for the work of his hands (Merikare W1:6_4-6_5)
- Build a monument (temple) for the god: it keeps alive the name of him who builds it (Merikare W1:6_6/3-6_6/4, Merikare W1:6_9/2)
- A man should do what benefits his ba: serve as priest, wear white sandals, visit the temple, eat bread in the god's house (Merikare W1:6_6/5)
- A single day of service gives something for eternity, an hour benefits the future (Merikare W1:6_9/3)
- God knows the one who acts for him (Merikare W1:6_10)

**Strife foretold, the tombs of Thinis, peace with the south, do not wreck another's monument (Instruction for Merikare)**
- Generation will attack generation, as the ancestors foretold (Merikare W1:6_11/3)
- Egypt fights even in the necropolis, hacking up the tombs (Merikare W1:6_12-7_1)
- The king is advised to keep peace with the southern realm, renew treaties and receive its goods (Merikare W1:7_2-7_8/2)
- Do not damage another's monument or build your tomb from the ruins of older buildings; quarry your own stone (Merikare W1:7_9-7_9/3)
- The king took a region 'like a cloudburst' (a flood of water) (Merikare W1:7_3/3)

**The pacified Delta and the wretched Asiatic, a crocodile on its bank (Instruction for Merikare)**
- The old king tells how he pacified the west and settled the eastern border with towns of choice people to repel foreigners (Merikare W1:8_2/2-8_8)
- A fortified city with walls, many troops and dykes is 'the door' of the land against foreigners (Merikare W1:9_6/3-9_12/2)
- Because the revenues of the north are in the king's hand, a failure of the Nile flood will not distress him (Merikare W1:8_7/2-8_7/3)

**Build in the Delta; god attacks the temple-rebel; kingship a goodly office; the king's guilt at Thinis (Instruction for Merikare)**
- There is no one who is free of an enemy (Merikare W1:10_9)
- The king is wise from the moment he comes out of the womb, distinguished by god before millions (Merikare W1:10_10-10_11)
- Kingship is a goodly office without son or brother to keep its monuments: each king must restore his predecessor's work so his own is restored after him (Merikare W1:10_11/2-10_12/3, Merikare W1:10_8/4)

**A blow is repaid; the hidden god who knows characters; the upright's loaf preferred to the evildoer's ox (Instruction for Merikare)**
- A blow is repaid with its like: every deed is interlocked with its consequence (Merikare W1:11_3-11_3/2)
- God, who knows the characters of men, has hidden himself while the generations pass (Merikare W1:11_3/3)
- God is worshipped on his processional way in images of stone and copper, one image replacing another like a wave (Merikare W1:11_5)
- No river lets itself be hidden: it breaks the dyke in which it was concealed (Merikare W1:11_6-11_6/2)
- Make your tomb excellent by uprightness and by doing Maat, for that is what the gods rely on (Merikare W1:11_7/2-11_8)
- Act for the god, so that he may act likewise for you (offerings and inscriptions) (Merikare W1:11_9-11_10)

**Hymn to the creator - men the cattle of god, heaven and earth made for their sake, his images from his body; god knows every name (Instruction for Merikare)**
- Humankind is called the well-tended cattle (flock) of god (Merikare W1:11_10/2)
- The creator made plants, cattle, fowl and fish to feed humankind (Merikare W1:12_2/3)
- The creator killed his enemies and destroyed his own children because they plotted rebellion (Merikare W1:12_3, Merikare W1:12_7)
- The sun god sails round the sky to see humankind and has built a shrine around them (Merikare W1:12_4/2-12_4/3)
- The creator gave humans magic as a weapon to ward off the blow of events (Merikare W1:12_6)

**Closing counsel - do not kill your intimate, the king's followers are gods, spread love of yourself; colophon of Khaemwaset (Instruction for Merikare)**
- The father hopes his son will join him in the hereafter with no accuser against him (Merikare W1:12_8/2-12_9)
- Whoever prospers on earth is one of them (the gods); the king's followers are gods (Merikare W1:12_10-12_10/2)
- Spread the love of yourself among all humankind; a good character is remembered after the years have passed (Merikare W1:12_11-12_11/2)
- The ruler's descendants will call him the one who ended the time of suffering, praying 'may he come today' (Merikare W1:13_1)

**Snefru summons Neferti, who chooses to speak of the future (Neferti 1-18)**
- A king, bored, has his courtiers find him a wise man to entertain him with fine words and choice sayings (Neferti 3-4/2, Neferti 5/3, Neferti 13)
- The seer asks the king whether he should speak of what has happened or of what will happen, and the king chooses the future (Neferti 14/2-15/3)
- The king himself takes papyrus and palette and writes down the seer's words as they are spoken (Neferti 15/4-16/2)
- A sage of a past reign foretells a coming age of chaos in the land that ends with the rise of a named saviour king (literary prophecy after the event) (Neferti 1, Neferti 17-18)

**Neferti laments the coming ruin of land and cosmos (Neferti 20-38/2)**
- The prophet addresses his own heart, bidding it stir and weep for the land in which it began (Neferti 20, Neferti 21/2-22)
- Since everything made is as if never made, the creator (Re) is urged to begin the creation over again (Neferti 22/3-22/4)
- The land is utterly destroyed; no remnant is left, not even the black of a fingernail (Neferti 23-23/3)
- The land is ruined, yet no one cares, no one speaks, no one weeps for it (Neferti 24-24/2)
- The sun is veiled by cloud and no longer shines, so that people cannot see or live (Neferti 24/4-25/3)
- Cosmic disorder: the south wind blows against the north wind and the sky no longer has a single wind (Neferti 28-28/2)
- A strange bird breeds in the Delta marshes, having built its nest beside the people, who let it approach (Neferti 29)
- Desert (or foreign) animals drink at the rivers of Egypt with no one to drive them off (Neferti 35/2-36)

**The land in sickness - civil war, social reversal, the sun withdrawn (Neferti 38/3-57/2)**
- In the age of chaos men make weapons of copper and demand bread with blood (Neferti 39/2-40/2)
- No one weeps for the dead or fasts at night for them, mourning customs lapse, because every heart is concerned only with itself (Neferti 41-43)
- A man's possessions are taken from him and given to an outsider; the owner grieves while the stranger is content (Neferti 47-47/2)
- The land is diminished but its rulers are many; it is empty but its taxes are great; grain is scarce but the measure is large (Neferti 50/2-51)
- The sun god separates himself from humankind: his hour cannot be known, his shadow is not seen, he is in the sky only like the moon (Neferti 51/2-53/3)
- The holy city, birthplace of every god (Heliopolis), no longer exists for the land (Neferti 57/2)

**The coming king Ameni restores maat (Neferti 57/3-71)**
- A coming king from the south, son of a woman of the southern land, is named in advance (Ameni) as the one who will restore the land (Neferti 57/3-59)
- The coming king receives the White Crown and wears the Red Crown, uniting the Two Powers and pleasing the Two Lords (Neferti 59/2-61)
- 'Rejoice, people of his time!': those who live in the coming king's days will rejoice (Neferti 61/2-61/3, Neferti 69/2)
- Those who plotted evil and rebellion fall silent for fear of the coming king; rebels belong to his wrath (Neferti 62, Neferti 64)
- The foreign enemies (Asiatics, Libyans) fall before the coming king's slaughter and his flame (Neferti 63)
- The fiery serpent (uraeus) on the king's brow pacifies the rebels (Neferti 65)
- Under the coming king justice (maat) returns to its place and wrong (isfet) is driven out (Neferti 68-69)
- The seer asks that the learned man pour water for him when he sees that what he said has come to pass (Neferti 70)

**Praise of Hapi who comes forth to make Egypt live (Nile Hymn, pSallier II, 11,6-12,9)**
- The flood god creates barley and emmer so that the temples may feast; when offerings to the gods fail, men perish (NileHymn W1:11_10, NileHymn W1:12_1, NileHymn W1:12_4/2)
- The flood god is greeted as king, constant in his laws, coming forth before Upper and Lower Egypt (NileHymn W1:12_8/3-12_9)

**PT 217 (Unas): 'Atum, your son comes to you' - the king announced to the four quarters**
- Pairs of gods are sent to the gods of the south, north, west and east to announce the coming of the transfigured king (PT217 W1:223/4, PT217 W1:226, PT217 W1:228/4, PT217 W1:231/3)

**PT 219: the Osiris litany to the Ennead - 'If he lives, this Unas lives'**
- The dead father's mouth is opened by his son and his limbs counted by the gods (PT219 253/2)

**PT 219: Osiris in his names and cult places; his body is the king's body**
- The dead king is the seed (semen) that came forth from Osiris (PT219 260/3)
- The dead god eats the Eye (of Horus), given him by his son, and lives by it; his belly is round with it (PT219 267-267/2)
- Union formula: 'your body is this king's body, your flesh his flesh, your bones his bones; when you go he goes' (PT219 268/3-268/7)

**Cannibal Hymn (Unas) I: the sky quakes; the king, mightier than Atum, has the gods hunted**
- The king or god is called 'Bull of the sky', fierce of heart (PT273-274 W1:505/2)

**Cannibal Hymn (Unas) II: the gods as meals; the king swallows their wisdom and gains eternity**
- The king is a god older than the eldest; thousands serve him and hundreds offer to him (PT273-274 W1:516-516/4)
- Evildoers will never have power to destroy the king's favoured place among the living for ever (PT273-274 W1:524/2)

**PT 302 (Unas): ascent to Re with Sothis and Upuaut, no accusation against him**
- The king's house in heaven and his throne on earth will never perish, and he will give his throne to no other (PT302 W1:567/2-568, PT302 W1:569/2-569/3)
- The sky goddess Nut uncovers (opens) her arms to receive the ascending king (PT302 W1:568/4)

**PT 600 (Pepi II): Atum-Khepri rose as the hill and the Benben, spat out Shu and Tefnut; protect this pyramid**
- The creator rises as the primeval hill and shines as the Benben stone in the House of the Phoenix in Heliopolis (PT600 N/F/E.inf.17.=:663/2-663/4)
- The creator sneezes or spits out the first gods (Shu and Tefnut), punning on their names (PT600 N/F/E.inf.17.=:663/5)
- The creator puts his arms around his first children as ka-arms so that his life-force is in them (PT600 N/F/E.inf.17.=:663/6, PT600 N/F/E.inf.18.=:664)
- The creator is asked to protect the king and his pyramid for ever as he protected his first children, so that nothing evil happens to it (PT600 N/F/E.inf.18.=:664/3, PT600 N/F/E.inf.20.=:666/2)
- The king's pyramid and his building work are identified with Osiris, and Horus is told not to be far from it (PT600 N/F/E.inf.21.=:667/2-667/3, PT600 N/F/E.inf.22.=:668)
- Horus brings the gods to the dead as reeds (torches?) to light his face in the white chapels (PT600 N/F/E.inf.23.=:669)

**Ptahhotep maxims 5-6: great is maat; human schemes fail, what the god commands happens**
- Wrongdoing may seize wealth, but it never reaches its goal; at the end only justice remains (Ptahhotep W1:6_6-6_7/3)
- Whoever devises a scheme against people is punished by the god in the same manner (Ptahhotep W1:6_8-6_8/2)
- Plan to live in contentment: what the gods give comes of itself (Ptahhotep W1:6_10/2)

**Ptahhotep maxims 7-8: at a great man's table; the faithful messenger**
- Eating bread is under the god's direction; only the ignorant complains about his portion (Ptahhotep W1:7_2/6-7_3)
- Hold fast to justice (maat) and do not swerve from it (Ptahhotep W1:7_4/2-7_4/3)
- Speak ill of no one, great or small; it is an abomination (Ptahhotep W1:7_4/5)

**Ptahhotep maxims 9-10: the god-given harvest, the childless, serving the man who rose from poverty**
- If god gives you a rich harvest, do not boast of it before your neighbours (Ptahhotep W1:7_5/2-7_5/3)
- A man of character who is also rich seizes like a crocodile in the court (Ptahhotep W1:7_5/4)
- Do not be arrogant toward a man without children, for many a father grieves and many a mother is less content than a childless woman (Ptahhotep W1:7_6-7_7)

**Ptahhotep maxim 12: the son who follows your ways, and the son the gods rejected in the womb**
- The son who follows his father's ways and keeps his property is truly his son, begotten of his ka; do everything good for him (Ptahhotep W1:7_10/3-7_11/4)
- He whom the gods guide cannot go astray; he whom they leave boatless cannot find a crossing (Ptahhotep W1:8_1/2-8_1/3)

**Ptahhotep maxims 13-15: in the antechamber, the trusted man, the one who listens to his belly, reporting**
- It is the god who advances a man's position (Ptahhotep W1:8_5)
- The trusted man has a good name without having to speak; he is praised even for what he does not know (Ptahhotep W1:8_8-8_9)
- Report on your commission without negligence and give your counsel in your lord's council (Ptahhotep W1:8_11/2-8_13/3)

**Ptahhotep maxims 16-17: the leader's lasting work; hear the petitioner out**
- No complaint arises amid praise, but when 'the hidden crocodile' emerges, contempt follows (Ptahhotep W1:9_2-9_3)
- A leader should do lasting deeds, thinking of the days that come after (Ptahhotep W1:8_14-9_1)

**Ptahhotep maxim 18: do not approach the women where you are a guest**
- He who lacks desire for it succeeds in every matter (Ptahhotep W1:9_12-9_13)

**Ptahhotep maxims 19-20: beware of greed, the incurable sickness**
- Do not be greedy in the division, nor toward your kin; covet only your own share (Ptahhotep W1:10_5/2-10_7/2)

**Ptahhotep maxim 21: found a household and love your wife - she is a fertile field**
- Keep your wife from power and restrain her, for her eye is her storm (Ptahhotep W1:10_10/3-10_12/3)

**Ptahhotep maxims 22-23: satisfy your dependents; do not repeat slander**
- Satisfy your dependents with what you have; in disaster it is one's own people who are fetched, not strangers (Ptahhotep W1:11_1-11_4/2)
- No one knows what will happen when he thinks of tomorrow (Ptahhotep W1:11_2)

**Ptahhotep maxims 24-27: silence in council; master the hot temper; teach the great**
- The flame of the hot-hearted spreads; master yourself, turn your face away; the gentle man's path is made smooth (Ptahhotep W1:12_1/2-12_3)
- He who is gloomy all day has no happy moment; he who is frivolous all day cannot found a household (Ptahhotep W1:12_4-12_4/2)
- Teach a great man what is useful to him and make him accepted among people; your sustenance depends on his ka (Ptahhotep W1:12_9/3-12_13/2)

**Ptahhotep maxims 28-31: the impartial judge; the man risen from poverty; bow to your superior**
- If you have become great after being poor, do not boast of it or trust your riches: they came to you as a gift of god (Ptahhotep W1:13_6-13_8/3)

**Ptahhotep maxims 32-33: do not rob your neighbour; do not force one who resists**
- Do not have intercourse with a woman or a child when you have seen that he or she resists (Ptahhotep W1:14_4-14_6)

**Ptahhotep maxims 34-37: test a friend alone; be generous; punish rightly; keep a cheerful wife**
- No one escapes the one who fixed his fate; his time will surely come (Ptahhotep W1:14_11/3-14_12)
- Punish promptly and teach thoroughly, but punishment without a real wrong turns the complainant into an enemy (Ptahhotep W1:15_5-15_6)

**Ptahhotep epilogue I: the worth of hearing; the son who hears and the fool who does not**
- Good words pass on to posterity and never perish in the land; teaching a man is teaching him to speak to those who come after (Ptahhotep W1:15_8-15_12/2)
- The fool who will not listen takes knowledge for ignorance and lives on what kills; the officials call him 'a living dead man every day' (Ptahhotep W1:17_4/2-17_9)
- A man's heart is his life, prosperity and health (Ptahhotep W1:16_8)

**Ptahhotep epilogue II: the obedient son, a follower of Horus; 110 years of life; colophon**
- Make justice firm, so that your children may live (Ptahhotep W1:18_1/2)
- Do not take away a word and then bring it back, nor put one thing in place of another (Ptahhotep W1:18_7-18_8)
- Conceal your heart (thoughts) and control your mouth (Ptahhotep W1:18_12-18_12/2)
- The father spoke to (taught) his son while the son was still in the womb (Ptahhotep W1:19_4)

**Ptahhotep in L2: maat, plans, table manners, the disowned son, the petitioner**
- A son who rejects his father's teaching is to be driven away: 'he is not your son, he was not born to you' (Ptahhotep W3:3_15/2-3_17/5)

**Ptahhotep in L2: greed, women, wife, rumour, judge ('partiality is the god's abomination'), friends**
- Partiality in judgment is the abomination of the god (Ptahhotep W3:7_2-7_2–3)

**Shipwrecked Sailor: the expedition returns; the follower urges the anxious prince to speak well (1-21)**
- An expedition returns home without loss: the mooring post is driven in, god is praised and every man embraces his comrade (ShipwreckedSailor 2-11)
- The adviser complains that his listener does as he pleases and that it is wearisome to talk to him (ShipwreckedSailor 20-20/2)

**Shipwrecked Sailor: the storm, the sinking, three days alone, the island of plenty, the burnt offering**
- A ship is described by exact dimensions in cubits (120 by 40) and the number of its crew (120 picked sailors) (ShipwreckedSailor 24-27)
- The expert sailors could foretell a storm before it came and a tempest before it broke (ShipwreckedSailor 28-30–31)
- The sole survivor is cast up on an island by a wave of the sea (ShipwreckedSailor 39)
- The castaway spends three days alone, his heart his only companion, sleeping in the shade of a tree (ShipwreckedSailor 41-42/2)

**Shipwrecked Sailor: the golden serpent appears - 'Who brought you here?' - 'Do not fear'**
- A huge divine serpent appears with thunder, trees breaking and earth quaking; 30 cubits long, bearded, its body overlaid with gold, its brows of lapis lazuli (ShipwreckedSailor 56-66)
- The divine being asks the trembling stranger three times 'Who brought you here?' and threatens to turn him to ashes (ShipwreckedSailor 67-70/2, ShipwreckedSailor 81-84)
- A great serpent takes the man into its mouth, carries him to its resting place and sets him down untouched (ShipwreckedSailor 76-79)
- 'God has let you live and brought you to this island of the ka' (ShipwreckedSailor 113)

**Shipwrecked Sailor: the serpent's own tale - a falling star burned his family of 75**
- How happy is the one who can tell what he has tasted (suffered), once the calamity is past (ShipwreckedSailor 124)
- A star falls from the sky and burns the narrator's whole family (75 serpents) while he is away; he finds them as a single heap of corpses (ShipwreckedSailor 127-131/2)
- Be brave and firm of heart: you will embrace your children, kiss your wife and see your house again (ShipwreckedSailor 132-135/2)

**Shipwrecked Sailor: the promised offerings; the serpent laughs - 'I am the ruler of Punt'; the ship comes**
- The rescued man promises to report his saviour's might to the king and to send incense, oils, burnt offerings and laden ships as to a god (ShipwreckedSailor 139-146)
- The divine being laughs at the mortal's promise of offerings: 'I am the ruler of Punt; the myrrh is mine' (ShipwreckedSailor 149-152)
- Once the visitor leaves, the enchanted island will never be seen again, for it will become water (ShipwreckedSailor 153)
- The divine helper's only request: 'Make my good name known in your city' (ShipwreckedSailor 158/2-159/2)

**Shipwrecked Sailor: the cargo of Punt, the return to the Residence, the promotion, the prince's cynical reply**
- A divine or foreign ruler loads the visitor's ship with exotic goods: myrrh, incense, ivory, giraffe tails, greyhounds, monkeys (ShipwreckedSailor 162-166)
- The returning survivor presents his gifts to the king, who praises god for him before the council and promotes and endows him (ShipwreckedSailor 174-177)
- The listener rejects the consoling tale with a cynical proverb: who gives water to a bird at dawn that will be slaughtered in the morning? (ShipwreckedSailor 183-184)

**Sinuhe (B): Sinuhe made new: bathed, dressed in linen, given a house, and a pyramid tomb among the royal children; colophon**
- The returnee's desert years are taken from his body: he is groomed, his foreign clothes given away, dressed in fine linen, anointed with oil and sleeps in a bed (Sinuhe W1:290/2-294)

**Sinuhe (AOS): the strongman's challenge and the duel**
- After the hero's victory, his foreign host takes him in his arms, kisses and embraces him (Sinuhe W5:55-55/2)

**Two Brothers: Bata prays to Re-Harakhti, who puts a crocodile-filled water between the brothers; the dialogue at dawn**
- The persecuted man prays to the sun god as 'the one who separates the wrongdoer from the righteous', and the god hears all his pleas (TwoBrothers 6_4-6_5/2)
- God makes a great water full of crocodiles appear between the pursuer and the fugitive, so that they stand on opposite sides (TwoBrothers 6_6-6_7)
- The wronged man tells his pursuer to wait until dawn: when the sun disk rises he will plead against him before it, and it will hand over the wrongdoer to the righteous (TwoBrothers 6_8-6_9/2, TwoBrothers 7_2/3)
- The falsely accused hero tells the husband his own account: it was she who propositioned him and she has twisted the story (TwoBrothers 7_3/2-7_6/3)

**Two Brothers: Bata's oath and self-castration; his heart to be placed on the cedar; Anubis kills his wife**
- The falsely accused man swears by the sun god, cuts off his own phallus with a reed knife and throws it into the water, where a catfish swallows it (TwoBrothers 7_8-7_9/3)
- The wronged man reproaches his kinsman: if you remember one bad thing, can you not remember one good thing I did for you? (TwoBrothers 8_2/2)
- A mourner goes home with his hand on his head, which is smeared with dust (earth) (TwoBrothers 8_6/3)
- Convinced of the hero's innocence, the husband goes home, kills his lying wife and throws her to the dogs (TwoBrothers 8_7/2-8_8)

**Two Brothers: Bata alone in the Valley of the Cedar; the Ennead has Khnum fashion him a wife; the Seven Hathors**
- A god (the potter Khnum) is told to fashion a wife for a man 'so that he does not live alone'; she is more beautiful than any woman, the seed of every god in her (TwoBrothers 9_6-9_7)
- The Seven Hathors come to see a newborn (or newly made) being and decree its fate 'with one mouth' (TwoBrothers 9_8-9_9)
- The hero opens his whole heart to his wife, telling her the secret (his heart in the tree) on which his life depends (TwoBrothers 10_1-10_3/2)

**Two Brothers: the Sea steals a lock of hair; Pharaoh's search for its owner; she is brought to Egypt, betrays Bata, the cedar is felled and he dies**
- The Sea (Yam) surges after a woman; the tree gives it a lock of her hair, which the Sea carries to Egypt (TwoBrothers 10_5-10_7/3)
- The fragrance of a lock of hair washed up where the royal laundrymen work perfumes the king's linen; the king quarrels with the launderers until the lock is found and brought to him (TwoBrothers 10_8-11_3/4)
- The king's scribes and wise men declare the lock belongs to a daughter of the sun god in whom is the seed of every god, and advise sending envoys to every land to find her (TwoBrothers 11_4-11_6)
- The king sends messengers and then an army to fetch a beautiful foreign woman; a woman bearing fine jewellery is sent with them to lure her away (TwoBrothers 11_5/2-12_1)
- The hero's wife, now the king's favourite, tells the king to fell the tree that holds her husband's life (TwoBrothers 12_3/2-12_4/2)

**Two Brothers: the bull at Pharaoh's court; Bata reveals himself to his wife; she makes Pharaoh swear and asks for the bull's liver**
- In his new form the hero confronts his betrayer: 'Look, I am still alive! I am Bata'; she is afraid (TwoBrothers 15_7-16_1)
- The wife asks to eat the liver of the sacred bull (her reincarnated husband) so that it will be slaughtered (TwoBrothers 16_4/2-16_5/2)

**Two Brothers: the bull slaughtered; two drops of blood at the palace doorposts become persea trees; the trees felled; the splinter swallowed**
- Two drops of the slaughtered bull's blood fall beside the two doorposts of the king's gate and grow overnight into two great persea trees, hailed as a wonder (TwoBrothers 16_8-17_2)
- The tree in which the hero lives speaks to his betrayer sitting beneath it: 'You liar! I am Bata; I am alive in spite of you' (TwoBrothers 17_3/2-17_8/2)
- A splinter from the felled tree flies into the woman's mouth; she swallows it and conceives at once; the hero is reborn as her son (TwoBrothers 18_2/2-18_5)

**Two Brothers: Bata reborn as the queen's son, crown prince and king; he judges his wife and makes Anubis his heir; colophon**
- The reborn hero is loved by the king, made King's Son of Kush, crown prince, and king when the old king 'flies to heaven' (TwoBrothers 18_6-19_2)
- On becoming king, the hero has his wife brought, pleads against her before the great officials, tells all that happened, and they agree to her condemnation (TwoBrothers 19_3-19_5/3)
- The king makes his loyal brother crown prince; after reigning thirty years he dies and the brother succeeds him (TwoBrothers 19_6-19_7/2)
- Colophon: whoever speaks against this book, Thoth (the scribe god) will be his adversary (TwoBrothers 19_9)

**Truth and Falsehood: the lost dagger; Falsehood has his elder brother Truth blinded and orders him thrown to lions**
- The younger brother, Falsehood, has his elder brother Truth blinded and made doorkeeper of his house (TruthFalsehood 2_1-2_3)
- The wicked younger brother looks upon the excellent character of his elder brother and plots against him (TruthFalsehood 2_3/2-2_4)
- The villain orders servants to throw their master to a fierce lion and lionesses; they spare him and report that the lion devoured him (TruthFalsehood 2_5-3_3)

**Truth and Falsehood: a lady finds the blind Truth, conceives by him; the son mocked as fatherless learns who his father is**
- A lady sees a beautiful man lying abandoned at the foot of a hill, desires him, sleeps with him and conceives a son that night (TruthFalsehood 3_6/2-4_5)
- Schoolmates mock the boy: 'whose son are you? you have no father!'; he asks his mother his father's name (TruthFalsehood 5_3-5_8)

**Truth and Falsehood: the son honours his blind father and goes to avenge him; the ruse of the ox**
- The son seats his blind, despised father on a chair with a footstool and sets food and drink before him (TruthFalsehood 6_2-6_4/3)
- The son learns his blinded father's story and goes out to avenge him (ꜥn wšb, 'seek redress') (TruthFalsehood 6_5-6_7/2)
- The hero leaves a splendid ox in the care of the villain's herdsman; the villain covets it and takes it to eat, giving the owner one of his own instead (TruthFalsehood 7_2-8_4/2)

**Truth and Falsehood: the trial before the Ennead; Falsehood swears his own punishment; Truth found alive; Falsehood blinded**
- The liar swears that if his victim is found alive he himself shall suffer what he did to him; the victim is found alive and the liar receives the punishment he named (TruthFalsehood 10_6-11_3/2)
- An oath formula 'as Amun endures, as the Ruler endures' binding the swearer to a penalty (TruthFalsehood 10_6-10_6/2)

**Westcar: Khafre's tale: Ubaoner's wife and the commoner; the wax crocodile; the adulteress burned**
- A priest's wife takes a commoner as lover; they spend the day drinking in the pavilion of his garden lake and the caretaker reports it to the husband (Westcar 1:23-2:18/2)
- A magician makes a crocodile of wax; thrown into the water after the adulterer it becomes a real crocodile of seven cubits and seizes him; picked up again it is wax (Westcar 2:22/2-3:14, Westcar 4:1/2-4:2/2)
- The magician commands the crocodile to bring up the man from the depths and later the king tells it to take away 'what is yours'; no one knows where it took him (Westcar 3:21/3-3:25/2, Westcar 4:5-4:7)

**Westcar: Baufre's tale: Snefru's rowing maidens; Djadjaemankh folds back the lake to recover the fish pendant**
- A king, restless and bored, goes through every room of his palace seeking diversion and summons a sage to cheer him (Westcar 4:22-5:1)
- A melancholy king is cheered by twenty beautiful young women, clad only in nets, rowing him on the palace lake (Westcar 5:1/3-5:14)
- The magician lays one half of the lake's water upon the other half, finds a lost amulet lying on a shard on the dry bottom, gives it back, and returns the waters (Westcar 6:7/3-6:12/2)
- A cherished object lost in the water is recovered for its owner by a sage's wonder (Westcar 5:15-5:23/2, Westcar 6:10)

**Westcar: Djedefhor tells of the living sage Djedi, aged 110; the prince fetches him**
- A sage commoner of 110 years still eats 500 loaves, half an ox and drinks 100 jars of beer a day (Westcar 7:1-7:2)

**Westcar: Djedi before Khufu: he refuses to use a prisoner and rejoins the severed heads of a goose, a bird and an ox**
- Offered a condemned prisoner for his beheading-and-revival trick, the sage refuses: not on a human being, the noble flock (of god) (Westcar 8:15/2-8:17)

**Westcar: Djedi foretells the three children of Re in the womb of Ruddedet who will rule; Khufu is troubled**
- A seer foretells that a priest's wife is pregnant with three children of the sun god who will become kings, and the reigning king is troubled (Westcar 9:7-9:11)
- The reigning king is dismayed on hearing that children who will become kings are about to be born (Westcar 9:12-9:14)

**Westcar: Ruddedet's hard labour; Isis, Nephthys, Meskhenet, Heqet and Khnum come as musicians and deliver the three kings**
- Birth goddesses disguised as travelling musician-dancers (with Khnum as porter) deliver a woman of divine children, naming each with a pun and declaring 'a king' (Westcar 9:22/2-10:7/2)
- At each birth the midwife goddess addresses the child with a word that puns on his future royal name (Westcar 10:9, Westcar 10:16/2, Westcar 10:23/2)
- Each divine newborn is a cubit long, with firm bones, limbs overlaid with gold and a headdress of true lapis lazuli (Westcar 10:9/2-10:11, Westcar 10:17-10:18/3, Westcar 10:24-10:26)

**Westcar: the goddesses make three crowns and hide them in the sack of barley; the sack sounds with royal music**
- The goddesses hide three royal crowns in a sack of barley left sealed in a room; from it come the sounds of royal singing and jubilation (Westcar 11:10-11:17, Westcar 12:1-12:5)
- After giving birth the mother purifies herself for fourteen days (Westcar 11:18)

**Westcar: the beaten maidservant sets out to betray the royal birth to Khufu and is taken by a crocodile (breaks off)**
- A punished maidservant sets out to betray the birth of the future kings to the reigning king, but is seized by a crocodile on the way (Westcar 12:8/2-12:19, Westcar 12:25/2-12:25/3)

**Anitta (KBo 3.22): Anitta son of Pithana; dear to the Storm-god; the king of Kuššara takes Neša by night and spares it**
- The king's success is grounded in his being 'dear to the Storm-god of Heaven' (CTH 1 W2:obv._2-obv._3)

**Anitta (KBo 3.22): Piyušti of Hatti defeated; the god Šiušummi brought back from Zalpa; Huzziya captured; Hattusa taken by night, sown with weeds and cursed**
- The conqueror brings the defeated enemy king alive to his own capital (CTH 1 W2:obv._43-lo._e._44)
- The conqueror razes the enemy city and sows its site with weeds (ZÀ.AḪ.LI) (CTH 1 W2:rev._48)

**Telipinu Proclamation W2: Ḫantili and Zidanta murder Mursili; the gods seek his blood**
- The murderer of a king, now king himself, laments 'what have I done? I listened to the word of another' (CTH 19 W2:{€1}_obv._I_34', CTH 19 W2:{€1}_obv._I_38'-{€1}_obv._I_40')

**Telipinu Proclamation W2: Ammuna's failures, the murders of Zuru and Taruḫšu, Ḫuzziya, Telipinu spares his rivals**
- A new king spares the rival claimants who plotted against him, gives them houses and says 'let them eat and drink; let no one harm them' (CTH 19 W2:{€1}_obv._II_11-{€1}_obv._II_15)

**Telipinu Proclamation W2: the assembly, the law of succession and the law protecting the royal family**
- The council must tell a king plotting against his kin to read the precedent on the tablet: bloodshed in the past and its divine punishment (CTH 19 W2:{€1}_obv._II_46-{€1}_obv._II_49)

**Telipinu Proclamation, Akkadian version W7: famine, granaries, sumptuary rules, laws on division and sorcery**
- A famine strikes the lands in a king's reign and he orders ploughing, rationing and storage of grain (CTH 19 W7:{€2}_rev._III_9''-{€2}_rev._III_21'')

**Treaty with Paddatiššu of Kizzuwatna (CTH 26): fugitives, envoys, plotters and migrating settlements**
- A fugitive accused of plotting against his lord is returned unless he denies it, in which case notables of the land swear an oath and he is then returned (CTH 26 §1:9-14, CTH 26 §2:23-28)
- If the population of a settlement migrates with its people, goods and herds to the other kingdom, it is seized and returned (CTH 26 §5:41-48)
- A fugitive accused of plotting against his lord is returned unless he denies it, in which case notables of the land swear an oath and he is then returned (CTH 26 §6:49-66)

**Treaty with Paddatiššu (CTH 26): cattle theft by herdsmen, thieves, homicide 'a man like the man'**
- A thief must restore the stolen goods twofold to their owner (and pay a further fine) (CTH 26 §7:67-74, CTH 26 §8:78-85)
- A man who is no herdsman and crosses the border to steal may be killed (CTH 26 §7:75-77, CTH 26 §8:86-88)
- A man who kills (or sells) a man of the other land must give a person in place of the dead ('a man like the man') (CTH 26 §9:89-95, CTH 26 §10:96-102)

**Šunaššura treaty CTH 41.I.2 §61-65: the frontier from the sea, measuring and dividing, the river Šamri not to be crossed**
- The land between two frontier towns is measured out and divided between the two kings (CTH 41.I.2 §61:271-272, CTH 41.I.2 §62:275-276, CTH 41.I.2 §62:280-281, CTH 41.I.2 §62:285-286)

**Treaty of Šuppiluliuma I with Ḫuqqana of Ḫayaša (CTH 42) §1-6: the last dog, the sister given, 'recognize only me', love as your own soul**
- The overlord says he took up the vassal as 'the last dog' and treated him well (CTH 42 §1:1-4)

**Ḫuqqana treaty (CTH 42) §9-26: oath gods destroy the oath-breaker, blessing for the loyal, enemy of the king, no excuse of neutrality**
- Treaty curse: 'these oath gods shall not leave you in peace, shall not release you, shall destroy you' (and whoever you side with) (CTH 42 §10:59-68, CTH 42 §14:100, CTH 42 §18:134-137, CTH 42 §22:175, CTH 42 §26:206-207)

**Ḫuqqana treaty (CTH 42) §29-32: no intercourse with the wife's sisters and kinswomen; avoid palace women; the death of Mariya for a glance**
- A practice permitted in a foreign, uncouth land is declared a capital crime in one's own land ('in Hattusa it is not right') (CTH 42 §29:242-245)
- When a kinswoman of one's wife visits, give her to eat and drink and rejoice, but do not desire to take her (CTH 42 §30:246-256)
- Keep far from the women of the palace: do not approach or speak to one, step well off the road and let her pass (CTH 42 §31:257-268)
- A man is put to death merely for having looked at a palace maid, seen by the king from a window (CTH 42 §32:269-278)

**Šuppiluliuma's decree for his son Šarri-Kušuḫ, king of Karkemiš (CTH 50): borders, the gold tablet, the gods of Karkemiš as witnesses**
- The great king installs his own son as king of a conquered city-state and fixes its borders (CTH 50 §1:2)
- The treaty is written on a tablet of gold (CTH 50 §1:34)

**Šuppiluliuma's treaty with Šattiwazza (CTH 51.I) §1-5: historical prologue, Tušratta's arrogance, the one-year campaign**
- A rival king's arrogance (multarriḫūtu) and boastful words provoke the great king's campaign (CTH 51.I §1:6-17, CTH 51.I §2:27, CTH 51.I §5:83)

**CTH 51.I §6-8: Tušratta killed by his son, the storm god's verdict, not a straw taken, Šattiwazza set on his father's throne and given a daughter**
- The death of a king is read as the god's verdict in a lawsuit between rival claimants ('the storm god decided Artatama's case') (CTH 51.I §6:88-89, CTH 51.I §6:102)

**Šattiwazza's treaty with Šuppiluliuma (CTH 52.I) §1-2: Šuttarna ruins the palace, gives the trophy door to Assyria, blinds and impales the nobles; Šattiwazza escapes**
- A usurper prostrates himself before a king whose ancestors were his fathers' servants and gives him his treasure (CTH 52.I §1:4-12)
- A gold and silver door once taken as a trophy is shamefully handed over to the enemy as tribute (CTH 52.I §2:14-16)
- The fugitive calls on the gods, who lead him on a path of safety to the great king (CTH 52.I §2:32-38)

**CTH 52.I §3-7: Šattiwazza at the great king's feet, adoption as son, the word that does not turn back, the campaign to Irride and Waššukanni**
- A fugitive prince falls at the great king's feet; the king takes him by the hand and rejoices over him (CTH 52.I §3:39-43)
- The great king says to a fugitive prince: 'I take you as my son, I will stand at your side' (CTH 52.I §3:45-49)
- The words that come out of the great king's mouth do not turn back (go unfulfilled) (CTH 52.I §3:50-51)
- The fugitive prince came with three chariots, two attendants and the one garment he wore, and nothing else (CTH 52.I §4:62-63)
- The gods of the great king go before the army on campaign (CTH 52.I §5:79)

**CTH 52.I §11-12: the gods of Mittani; Šattiwazza and the Hurrians curse themselves - tamarisk, water of the gutter, smoke, salt; their blessing in the lord's shade**
- Self-curse: as a felled tree (tamarisk/acacia) puts out no shoot, so may we have no seed (CTH 52.I §11:193-195)
- Self-curse: may we rise like smoke to heaven (CTH 52.I §11:198-199)
- Self-curse: as salt has no seed, so may we have no seed; like a dissolved lump of salt may we not be restored (CTH 52.I §11:200-203)
- The sworn people pray to eat a rich harvest in their lord's shade (ṣillu) while he goes before them (CTH 52.I §11:214-216)
- The vassal asks that the great king love him and his land as he loves his own lands, sons and his own tablet (CTH 52.I §11:219-220)

**Šuppiluliuma rescues Šarrupša of Nuḫašše (CTH 53 §§1-4, historical prologue)**
- A threatened king sends his messenger to the great king: 'I am a servant of the king; save me!', and troops are sent to rescue him (CTH 53 §1:5-8)

**Tribute, audience, friend and enemy, wholehearted war (CTH 53 §§5-7)**
- The vassal must go up every year to the overlord's land to appear before his lord (CTH 53 §5:30)

**The sick heir installed; tribute to Hatti, not Egypt (CTH 62 §§5-7)**
- The overlord installs a vassal's son in his father's place because the father named him before the king while still alive, even though the son is sick (CTH 62 §6:48-55)
- The vassal's fathers paid tribute to Egypt; he must pay it to Hatti instead and 'not turn his eyes to another' (CTH 62 §7:71-73)

**Egypt, secret envoys, the half-hearted ally (CTH 62 §§8-11)**
- The vassal must not secretly send his messenger to a rival great king (Egypt) nor push away the overlord's hand and become that king's vassal (CTH 62 §9:81-87)

**Aid in revolt, feeding troops, captives, evil words and secret orders (CTH 62 §§12-16)**
- If the king secretly orders something that cannot be done, the vassal must protest on the spot 'I cannot do this and I will not do it'; failing to do a feasible order breaks the oath (CTH 62 §16:148-155)

**Manapa-Tarḫunta's flight, the oath gods seize the rebels, his plea for life (CTH 69 §§1-4)**
- While still a child the heir is threatened by his brothers, who try to kill him; he escapes to a foreign people, who shelter him at the great king's word (CTH 69 §1:2-6)
- A rebel vassal falls at the great king's feet and writes 'My lord, let me live, do not destroy me, take me as your servant, protect my person', and is pardoned (CTH 69 §4:42-49)

**The land given; covet nothing of Hatti; past betrayal; revolt (CTH 69 §§5-12)**
- The vassal must not covet a subject or a border district of the overlord's land; coveting them with evil intent breaks the oath (CTH 69 §5:78-80)

**The stolen treaty tablet of Aleppo reissued under seal (CTH 75 §§1-2)**
- A treaty tablet that was stolen is replaced: the great king writes a second tablet, seals it with his own seal and gives it again (CTH 75 §2:2-6)

**Mutual helpers, one house; gods of Hatti and Aleppo; witnesses of the tablet (CTH 75 §§15-17)**
- Two royal houses bound by treaty are to be helpers to each other and to each other's sons: 'we and our house shall be one' (CTH 75 §15:62-69)

**Wiluša's old friendship with Hatti; Muwatalli helps Alakšandu (CTH 76 §§1-5)**
- The king admits that an event of the distant past is beyond his knowledge: 'because the matter is long ago, I do not know (which king it was)' (CTH 76 §1:4-6)

**Alakšandu's chosen son, mutual protection, the fugitive conspirator (CTH 76 §§6-9)**
- If the vassal's brother or kin rebels and seeks the throne, the overlord will recognise only the vassal, not accept the rebel, and destroy the rebel's land (CTH 76 §6:94, CTH 76 §7:95-103)

**Rumours of revolt, 'come alone', no bird oracle, campaigns and the great kings (CTH 76 §§10-14)**
- When summoned to help the king, the vassal must not first take a bird oracle (CTH 76 §10:178)

**The tablet to be read three times a year; the terms are not mutual (CTH 76 §19)**
- The treaty tablet is to be read aloud before the vassal three times every year (CTH 76 §19:291-293)
- The overlord declares that the treaty's words are not mutual (from one side and the other) but come from Hatti (CTH 76 §19:294-297)

**The witness gods, with the gods of Wiluša and Appaliuna (CTH 76 §§20-23)**
- A god [A]ppaliuna (possibly Apollo) is named among the gods of Wiluša (perhaps Troy) invoked as treaty witnesses (CTH 76 §23:304)

**Tiliura deserted since Ḫantili and resettled (CTH 89 §§1-5)**
- A frontier city deserted for generations is rebuilt and resettled with prisoners of war, and later its former inhabitants are brought back to it (CTH 89 §3:4-11)
- Hostile neighbouring peoples take possession of a frontier region and long bar the kings from crossing its river (CTH 89 §5:21-25)

**Rules for the Kaška: not into the city, mixed marriage, slaves, renegades (CTH 89 §§6-20)**
- Armed men and charioteers of a hostile neighbouring people may not go up into the frontier city: they dismount at the gate and go back, and lawsuits are heard outside the city (CTH 89 §6:26-32, CTH 89 §7:33-36)
- An enemy tribesman who marries a woman of the city will betray it; one found sleeping in the city is jailed and fined in cattle and sheep, and one who plots or speaks evil dies (CTH 89 §17:101-111)
- A slave bought from the hostile people must not be brought into the city but kept outside or in the cattle stall; whose slave passes the gate is seized for the offence (CTH 89 §17:112-120)
- A townsman who joins the hostile people forfeits house, field, wives and children to the city, and such a man must be hunted down (CTH 89 §19:127-133)

**Aziru's tablet; Bentešina deposed and restored; royal marriages (CTH 92 §§1-5)**
- Two royal houses intermarry: the great king's daughter becomes queen in the vassal land and the prince takes the vassal's daughter; the daughter's offspring shall rule there (CTH 92 §5:30-33)

**I was a dead man, you brought me back to life: Bentešina asks for a sealed tablet (CTH 92 §§6-9)**
- Curse: the oath gods shall kill the oath-breaker and burn him (CTH 92 §9:61-63)
- As the vassal's own soul, body, wife, children and land are precious to him, so the king's soul and person, wife, children and land must be precious to him (CTH 92 §9:67-68)

**Šauškamuwa taken by the hand; Amurru's history of loyalty and defection (CTH 105 §§1-4)**
- Vassals renounce allegiance: 'of our own free will we were your vassals; now we are your vassals no more', and go over to Egypt (CTH 105 §3:17-22)

**Protect the king's line; do not act like Mašturi; be ready to die (CTH 105 §§5-9)**
- A vassal betrays his benefactor's son, asking 'shall I protect a bastard?', and is held up in a later treaty as a warning (CTH 105 §7:66-67)

**Slander, the great kings, Ahhiyawa erased, embargo on Assyria (CTH 105 §§10-14)**
- The king of Ahhiyawa is written among the great kings of equal rank and then erased from the tablet (CTH 105 §13:111)

**Fragmentary opening of a loyalty oath: life, a new man, blood (CTH 123 §§1-9)**
- Under the oath the sworn man is told to become 'a new man' (LÚ GIBIL) (CTH 123 §4:38-39)

**Niḫriya remembered; 'die for the king; death shall be your limit' (CTH 123 §§10-20)**
- Loyalty formula: when things go hard for the king, the sworn man must die for him; 'death shall be your limit' (CTH 123 §10:82-83, CTH 123 §12:92-97, CTH 123 §13:103, CTH 123 §16:142, CTH 123 §20:166)
- In the king's time of need the sworn man must 'bite the dark earth and hold it' (stand his ground to the death) (CTH 123 §13:98-102)
- The gods are to keep watch on the deed of treason (CTH 123 §15:121)

**The king did not reward me; an engraved word; guardians of the king's life; the king's direst hour (CTH 123 §§21-28)**
- The sworn may not say 'the king has not rewarded me; I will withdraw from these oaths' (CTH 123 §21:167-177)
- Picture of the king's direst hour: no groom left to harness his horses, the charioteer leaping from the chariot, the chamberlain fleeing, not even a gate-dog left nor an arrow to shoot (CTH 123 §27:219-225, CTH 123 §28:226-231)

**Report even father and mother; if a city, a house or one man sins (CTH 133 §§5-12)**
- If a city within the land sins it is killed with its men; if a house within a city sins that house dies with its people; if one man sins, he alone (CTH 133 §10:75-81, CTH 133 §11:82-83)
- The vassal people's troop levy is fixed (from 150 to 60 heavy-armed men) and must be of free men, not servants or hirelings (CTH 133 §11:86-89, CTH 133 §11:91-92, CTH 133 §12:93-96)

**All Išmerika under oath; the named men and their towns; the curse (CTH 133 §§13-19)**
- The leading sworn men of a people are named one by one, each with the town assigned to him in the neighbouring land (CTH 133 §13:105-107, CTH 133 §14:111-125, CTH 133 §15:126-134)

**The Kuruštama treaty: Hatti and Egypt as allies (CTH 134)**
- Hatti and Egypt are to be allies to each other, protect each other and not go to one another with evil words (CTH 134 §11:29-34)

**Treaty with Lab'u and Tunip, opening (CTH 135 §1)**
- The sworn parties are to speak the wording of the oath (the 'word of the oath') aloud (CTH 135 §1:13, CTH 135 §1:27)
- A treaty names the border towns assigned to one party or the other (CTH 135 §1:14-16, CTH 135 §1:31-32)

**Treaty with Tunip, war and booty (CTH 135 §2)**
- A vassal who hides a captured enemy, helps him escape or lets him live instead of handing him over is to die (CTH 135 §2:47-58)
- Treaty rule: cattle, sheep and goods taken by each army belong to that army (CTH 135 §2:65-68, CTH 135 §2:73-76, CTH 135 §2:88-91)
- Named classes of people are declared released (free) from the oath (CTH 135 §2:106-107)

**Treaty with Tunip, messengers, fugitives and evil words (CTH 135 §3)**
- A king's greeting-gift (šulmānu) is mentioned in the relations between rulers (CTH 135 §3:126-128)

**Šuppiluliuma I's treaty with Mukiš, oath gods and duties (CTH 136)**
- The 'primeval' (former) gods (Nara, Namšara, Minki, Alalu, Anu ...) are listed among the oath gods (CTH 136 §1:2)

**Arnuwanda I's oath with the Kaška, hostages and curses (CTH 137.1 §1-11)**
- The overlord tells the sworn party that they have sinned against him before renewing the oath (CTH 137.1 §5:26-31)
- The gods of the enemy people are summoned and set over against the overlord's gods for the oath (CTH 137.1 §8:44, CTH 137.1 §9:49-50)
- Curse: on the day the oath is broken the oath-breakers' gods are to be impure and eat impure bread and drink impure wine and beer (CTH 137.1 §9:51-54)

**Arnuwanda I's oath with the Kaška, the sworn leaders one by one (CTH 137.1 §12-27)**
- An oath record lists leaders one by one, each with his men and his town, and what each swore (CTH 137.1 §14:66-§15:68, CTH 137.1 §21:90-§22:91, CTH 137.1 §24:108-109, CTH 137.1 §25:117-118, CTH 137.1 §26:123-124)
- The number of troops each sworn leader brings is recorded (e.g. 190, 215 men) (CTH 137.1 §17:74-77)
- A named scribe of the capital is recorded as present at or administering the oath (CTH 137.1 §16:72-73)

**Šuppiluliuma II's treaty with Alašija (Cyprus) (CTH 141)**
- Treaty blessing: if the words are kept, eat well, let it flourish, let the flocks bear well, the gods give life (CTH 141 §7:27-36)
- The king boasts that he built a god's temple in silver and gold and made the statue of the storm god (CTH 141 §8:39-40)
- The king boasts that he crossed the sea (on campaign) (CTH 141 §8:42)
- Curse on whoever removes the treaty tablet from before the deity, puts it in a dark place, or fails to read it out year by year (CTH 141 §9:44-47)

**Arnuwanda's oath imposed on the elders of Ura (CTH 144)**
- The king sends a silver rhyton to a local god, from which the god is to be given drink regularly (CTH 144 §1:6-7)
- The sworn must always listen to whatever the king will say in future (CTH 144 §1:11-13)

**The case against Mita of Paḫḫuwa, his oath and its breach (CTH 146 §1-7)**
- The vassal swears to give up the overlord's towns he holds (CTH 146 W2:15-16)
- The faithless vassal takes the enemy's daughter as his wife (CTH 146 W3:33)
- The faithless vassal calls the overlord's subjects to flee to him (CTH 146 W4:34-38)
- Asked to return fugitives, the harbourer hides them and claims he has seen no one and no one has come (CTH 146 W4:39-46)
- A rebel calls out his father's name (claims his father's standing) (CTH 146 W7:81)
- A rebel refuses to hand over towns, saying the former holder was a mere charioteer: 'Am I not also a man?' (CTH 146 W7:83-88)

**The case against Mita, the neighbours' oath and duties (CTH 146 §15-19)**
- The king threatens that whoever does not fight the rebels he will kill first, before attacking the rebel city (CTH 146 W19:193-197)

**The case against Mita, the elders' oath, rules of war, colophon (CTH 146 §20-28)**
- Subjects must protect the king, the queen, the king's sons, grandsons and descendants (CTH 146 W21:202-204)
- Reports must be truthful: do not magnify a small matter nor make light of a weighty one (CTH 146 W22:229-236)
- On campaign no one may violate a man's wife or daughter or steal people, cattle, horses or metals (CTH 146 W23:238-240)

**Instructions for temple personnel: are gods and men of different mind? (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 i 21'-38')**
- The mind of gods and men is said to be no different: the god is to his temple servants as a master to his slave (CTH 264 W15:Vs._I_21'-Vs._I_22')
- The servant stands before his master washed and in clean clothes and gives him food and drink, so the master is at ease (CTH 264 W15:Vs._I_22'-Vs._I_27')
- A master angered by his servant kills him or mutilates his nose, eyes and ears, or punishes his wife, children and kin (CTH 264 W15:Vs._I_28'-Vs._I_32')

**Instructions for temple personnel, the gods' silver and gold (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 ii 25'-51')**
- A temple servant may sell a royal gift only openly before the lords of Ḫatti, with the price recorded on a wooden tablet (CTH 264 W15:Vs._II_38'-Vs._II_44')

**Instructions for temple personnel: festivals at their time, the gods' will not man's (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 ii 52'-72')**
- Temple staff must not hold the spring festival in autumn or the autumn festival in spring (CTH 264 W15:Vs._II_52'-Vs._II_55')
- Do not 'buy death' or 'sell death' (bring capital guilt on yourselves) (CTH 264 W15:Vs._II_72')

**Instructions for temple personnel, sleeping in the temple and the night watch (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 ii 73'-iii 20)**
- All priests and temple servants must spend the night in the temple, not at home (CTH 264 W15:Rs._III_3-Rs._III_6)
- A priest found sleeping at home with his wife instead of in the temple incurs a capital sin (CTH 264 W15:Rs._III_15-Rs._III_16)
- A temple servant at whose watch-post an offence (waštul) happens is to die, without pardon (CTH 264 W15:Rs._III_18-Rs._III_20)

**Instructions for temple personnel, quarrels in the temple and the fire (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 iii 35-54)**
- Whoever starts a quarrel in the temple and disturbs the festival must provide the whole festival again with cattle, sheep, bread and beer (CTH 264 W15:Rs._III_35-Rs._III_43)

**Instructions for temple personnel, the kitchen staff and impurity (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 iii 55-83)**
- One who has been with a woman must tell his superior; if he dares not, he tells a colleague (CTH 264 W15:Rs._III_74-Rs._III_77)

**Instructions for temple personnel, the gods' ploughmen (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 iv 1-33)**
- Gods punish the negligent with a fine of one ox and ten sheep, and treat them as the gods' lords do (CTH 264 W15:Rs._IV_8-Rs._IV_11)
