- Defrauders' grain is all taken and poured into the gods' storehouses (CTH 264 W15:Rs._IV_22-Rs._IV_24)
- A ploughman who sold or ate the god's ox claims it died of leanness, broke its leg, ran off or was gored by a bull (CTH 264 W15:Rs._IV_25-Rs._IV_31)
- In a disputed case the accused goes before the god: if pure, his protective god (is with him); if impure, it is a capital sin (CTH 264 W15:Rs._IV_31-Rs._IV_33)

**Illuyanka, Kella's introduction, the word of the purulli festival (CTH 321 §1)**
- A myth is told as the 'word' (text) of a seasonal festival (the purulli) that is celebrated so the land may grow and prosper (CTH 321 §1:1-7)

**Illuyanka, first version: the storm god's defeat and Inara's trick (CTH 321 §2-10)**
- In the first combat the serpent (dragon) defeats the storm god (CTH 321 §2:8-9)
- The defeated god calls on all the gods to come to his aid (CTH 321 §3:10-11)
- A goddess prepares a feast with vessels full of wine and beer and invites the monster up from its hole to eat and drink (CTH 321 §3:12-§4:15, CTH 321 §8:28-30)
- A mortal agrees to help a goddess on condition that he may sleep with her, and does (CTH 321 §5:16-§7:24)
- The monster and its brood drink every vessel dry and, gorged, cannot go back down into their hole (CTH 321 §9:31-§10:35)
- The gorged monster is tied with a rope by the mortal helper and then killed by the storm god (CTH 321 §8:25-26, CTH 321 §10:36-37)

**Illuyanka: Ḫupašiya forbidden to look out of the window (CTH 321 §11-14)**
- The goddess builds a house on a rock and settles her mortal lover in it (CTH 321 §11:41-42)
- A mortal is forbidden to look out of the window while the goddess is away, lest he see his wife and children (CTH 321 §11:43-47)
- After twenty days the mortal looks out of the window and sees his wife and children (CTH 321 §12:48-50)
- The goddess's mortal lover, having seen his family, laments and begs to be let go home (CTH 321 §13:51-53)
- A mortal is forbidden to look out of the window while the goddess is away, lest he see his wife and children (CTH 321 §14:54-59)

**Illuyanka, the goddess's house given to the king; rain at Nerik (CTH 321 §15-18)**
- The goddess gives her house and the 'river of the flood' into the king's hand (an aetiology of the king's cult) (CTH 321 §15:60-63)
- When rain falls in Nerik the herald brings thick bread; rain is requested from the mountain god Zaliyanu (CTH 321 §16:64-§17:68)

**Illuyanka, second version: the stolen heart and eyes and the storm god's son (CTH 321 §19-24)**
- The victorious serpent takes the storm god's heart and eyes (CTH 321 §19:75-77)
- The disabled god takes the daughter of a poor man as wife and begets a son (CTH 321 §20:78-79)
- The god's son marries the daughter of his father's monstrous enemy (CTH 321 §20:80-81)
- The son, as bridegroom, asks his in-laws for the heart and then the eyes and brings them to his father, who is restored (CTH 321 §21:82-§23:92)
- The son, bound to the house of his in-laws, cries to his father not to spare him, and the storm god kills the serpent and his own son together (CTH 321 §23:96-§24:100)

**Illuyanka, Kella's coda on the gods' ranks, the lot, the land grant and colophon (CTH 321 §25-33)**
- The first gods are made the last and the last the first (a reversal of divine rank) (CTH 321 §26:104-105)
- A local goddess (Zašḫapuna) is declared greater than the storm god (CTH 321 §27:106-107, CTH 321 §30:119)
- A seat of basalt stands over a spring; the priest chosen by lot to hold the god sits on it (CTH 321 §29:112, CTH 321 §29:115-116)
- The king gives back a field, garden, house, threshing floor and servants' houses to a cult, recorded on a tablet (CTH 321 §31:122-§32:124)

**Telipinu and the daughter of the Sea (CTH 322.1)**
- The storm god sends his son Telipinu to the sea to bring back the sun god (CTH 322.1 §2:9-§3:12)
- The Sea sends to the storm god demanding a bride-price for the daughter his son has taken (CTH 322.1 §5:19-27)
- The bride-price is paid 'all by the thousand': a thousand cattle and a thousand sheep (CTH 322.1 §6:28-33)

**The vanished Sun god, trapped by the Sea (CTH 323.1 §1-3)**
- The sun god is shut in a jar sealed with wax and capped with a copper lid (CTH 323.1 §2:14-16, CTH 323.1 §3:20-22)

**The vanished Sun god, Frost seizes the land and the gods (CTH 323.1 §4-8)**
- The storm god challenges: when a man or an ox is killed, do they make him live again? What wonder do your sons do? (CTH 323.1 §4:35-39)
- The storm god praises his son as one who breaks the soil, ploughs, channels water and clears the grain of stones (CTH 323.1 §6:78-84)
- The paralysed storm god's hands stick to his cup and his feet to the ground; he begs Frost not to seize his eyes (CTH 323.1 §7:96-100)

**The vanished Sun god, the annanna-woman's words and the Sun's allotment (CTH 323.1 §9-12)**
- The god's allotment: one to whom the god does good gives nine sheep, a poor man gives one (CTH 323.1 §11:126-133)

**The vanished Sun god, the ritual of the tables and three days of offerings (CTH 323.1 §13-22)**
- The ritual sets out bronze models of the jar and its lid, a door, two windows, a peg, a spade and a hammer for the vanished god (CTH 323.1 §13:135-138, CTH 323.1 §15:141-§16:145)
- For three days the 'lord of the god' burns choice offerings, recites spells and breaks bread, pours libations and lays meat before the gods (CTH 323.1 §17:151-§22:211)

**Telipinu myth, the god hidden in the moor and the dearth (CTH 324.1 §5-6)**
- Mountains, trees, pastures and springs dry up, and famine comes upon the land so that men and gods die of hunger (CTH 324.1 §6:35-41)

**Telipinu myth, the search by eagle, storm god and bee (CTH 324.1 §7-10)**
- The storm god cannot open the gate of his son's city, breaks his hammer and wrapped (in his garment) sits down (CTH 324.1 §8:61-§9:73)

**Telipinu myth, offerings by analogy to sweeten the god (CTH 324.1 §16-23)**
- Fine oil is sprinkled on the god's paths: 'walk on the oiled ways' (CTH 324.1 §23:147-151)

**Telipinu myth, the gods under the hawthorn and the anger shut in bronze vessels below (CTH 324.1 §31-37)**
- The gods sit in assembly under the hawthorn tree (CTH 324.1 §31:196-199)

**Telipinu myth, the god's return and the fleece on the eya-tree (CTH 324.1 §38-40)**
- The god returns to his house, the mist and smoke leave, hearth, fold and stall are freed, mother, ewe and cow accept their young (CTH 324.1 §38:243-253)
- The returned god cares for king and queen and provides them with life, vigour and long future (CTH 324.1 §38:254-§39:256)
- Before the god stands an eya-tree with a sheep's fleece hung on it, in which lie fat, grain, wine, cattle, sheep, long years, progeny and plenty (CTH 324.1 §39:257-§40:267)

**Telipinu myth, second version: the analogies, beer, and the iron vessels below (CTH 324.2 §8-21)**
- As beer makes an angry or anxious man drunk so his anger and care vanish, may it make the god drunk and his anger vanish (CTH 324.2 §15:72-82)

**The Storm god departs; mist, choking, rejected young, barrenness and drought (CTH 325)**
- In the god's absence barley and emmer no longer grow, and cattle, sheep and humans no longer conceive, and the pregnant do not give birth (CTH 325 §7:46-48)
- In the god's absence the mountains, trees, meadows and springs dry up and no shoot comes forth (CTH 325 §8:49-53)

**The father goes down to the fate-goddesses and Hannahanna, who reassures him and sends the bee (CTH 325)**
- The mother goddess reassures: whether it is your sin or not, I will put it right (CTH 325 §13:91-110)

**The house lets the anger go; seven doors and the cauldrons of the dark earth; the Storm god returns and the eya-tree fleece (CTH 325)**
- Each part of the house is told to let the god's anger go: the house, the window, the hinge, the inner court, the door, the gate, the king's road (CTH 325 §31:217-224)
- The doorkeeper opens the seven doors and draws back the seven bolts so that the god's anger may go down into the dark earth (CTH 325 §32:227-228)

**The eye diseases are taken from a child and passed down through palms, fingers and nails to the dark earth, the Sun and the copper cauldrons of the sea (Storm god in Lihzina, CTH 331.1)**
- An illness is passed hand to hand (palms to fingers to nails) down to the dark earth, to the Sun deity and into the sea, where it is laid in copper cauldrons with lead lids (CTH 331.1 §3:16-18, CTH 331.1 §7:31-§8:35)

**The Storm god spends eight years in Lihzina; his sons meet him on the road and ask where he was (CTH 331.1)**
- The Storm god stays eight years in a town, strikes it, harvests it, plants an orchard and fells it, and then returns (CTH 331.1 §12:60-§13:68)
- The returning god meets his sons on the road; they bow and ask 'Father, where were you?' (CTH 331.1 §14:69-75)

**Analogies of flower, fig, nut, raisin and olive; 'incline your ear'; the slanderer of the king; highest of the high (mugawar fragment 3, CTH 332.3)**
- The god is asked to keep his ear inclined and listen to what the king and queen say (CTH 332.3 §6:27-29)
- The god is asked to throw away the bad words like nutshells and take the good words (CTH 332.3 §7:34-§8:38)
- Whoever speaks evil of the king and queen before the god, the god is to give him a sour apple (punish him) (CTH 332.3 §10:42-49)

**Quenching analogy, the shaggy ram, soothing with food, 'highest of the high', purification and the sheep driven out (mugawar fragment 7, CTH 332.7)**
- At the end of the rite a sheep is driven out but not killed (CTH 332.7 §8:44-45)

**The midwife's rite; Anzili and Zukki depart in anger with shoes and veil reversed; household choked (CTH 333)**
- The departing goddess fastens her garment's pins at the back and turns her veil back to front (CTH 333 §6:37-§7:40)
- In the deity's absence mother and son, wife and husband 'choke' (are estranged) as do the herds (CTH 333 §8:49-50)

**Fragrant woods burned; Anzili and Zukki return; the household set right; Anzili eats everything; the salt-lick analogy for the patron's life (CTH 333)**
- Fragrant woods (olive?, šaḫi, parnulli, cedar) are burned in the ritual patron's house to draw the vanished deity back (CTH 333 §10:55-64)
- Analogy: as the salt-lick of the meadow never runs out, so may the life of the ritual patron never run out but be everlasting (CTH 333 §14:91-§15:98)

**Hannahanna invoked; galaktar, parhuena, fig, liti, raisin and olive; 'let go the anger'; pebbles quenched, the cart held back, firewood burned (CTH 334.4)**
- Analogy: as the hot pebbles are quenched with water, so may the deity's anger, wrath, sin and sullenness be quenched (CTH 334.4 §8:42-45)

**The searchers comb forests, roads, currents and springs; the bee, holding honey within, goes through all places and finds the god asleep in a vineyard (CTH 335.2)**
- The vanished god is found lying asleep in a vineyard (or grove) under a plant, gone down toward the dark earth (CTH 335.2 §3:32-43)

**The Storm god's body purged limb by limb; restored, he goes up to heaven; the eagle's wing, the sieve of a thousand holes, Kamrusepa's rams; go to Zalpa by the sea (CTH 335.17)**
- The god's or patient's body is gone through part by part (head, shoulders, brows, eyes, tongue, teeth, lips, throat, liver, lungs, penis, knees) to remove the evil (CTH 335.17 §1:1-§2:3)
- The healed god rises early, becomes again as he was, goes up to heaven and takes his seat again (CTH 335.17 §3:4-7)
- The ritualist takes an eagle's wing and waves it over the deity (or patient) to sweep the evil away (CTH 335.17 §4:8-15)
- The god's or patient's body is gone through part by part (head, shoulders, brows, eyes, tongue, teeth, lips, throat, liver, lungs, penis, knees) to remove the evil (CTH 335.17 §5:16-22)
- The healer takes a sieve with a thousand holes and pours wheat into it as part of the purging rite (CTH 335.17 §7:28-29)

**Hallara's cloud window; the mother goddess brings the souls out of the river into the cloud; Kamrusepa, Telipinu; the oven; Sulinkatti kills a pig; the vessel with lid of lead whence nothing returns; sweet bread (CTH 335.17)**
- The mother goddess goes into the river, brings the souls up out of it and lays them in a cloud (CTH 335.17 §14:67-72)

**Inara myth with ritual for Zababa; Hannahanna's bee; Kamrušepa's words (CTH 336.1)**
- The land is found empty: no one finds a man, cattle or sheep (CTH 336.1 §8:50, CTH 336.1 §9:56)
- A war god kills the ploughmen and drives off the cattle (CTH 336.1 §8:43-45, CTH 336.1 §9:58-60)
- Incantation simile: 'cleanse yourself like a garment' (CTH 336.1 §13:80)
- The ritualist declares 'not my words; they are the words of (a goddess)', ascribing the spell to a deity (CTH 336.1 §14:82-83)
- An 'incantation of life' for when a person's inner self is afraid (CTH 336.1 §15:84-85)

**Hannahanna, the bee, the fleece and the three springs (CTH 336.2)**
- A goddess makes three springs, each marked by a different object (a plant above, a bowl below, a burning fire) (CTH 336.2 §6:25-28)
- A goddess makes three springs, each marked by a different object (a plant above, a bowl below, a burning fire) (CTH 336.2 §8:35-38, CTH 336.2 §10:48, CTH 336.2 §11:52)

**Hannahanna promises Inara a land and a husband; the storm god sends the bee (CTH 336.3)**
- A mother goddess tells a young goddess to sit still and promises her a land and a husband (CTH 336.3 §4:16, CTH 336.3 §5:17-18)
- The storm god is anxious about his missing daughter and sends a searcher (CTH 336.3 §5:19-21, CTH 336.3 §5:25)

**Hannahanna makes a stone a nurse; Zababa sent to war year by year (CTH 336.5)**
- A goddess finds a stone and commands it: 'become a nurse!' (CTH 336.5 §5:22-24)
- The war god is told to go into battle year after year (CTH 336.5 §8:40-44)
- The war god is told to go into battle year after year (CTH 336.5 §10:50-52)

**Weapons grow blunt; the nurse's city destroyed (CTH 336.6)**
- The god's weapons become blunt (CTH 336.6 §3:19-20)
- A god destroys the city of a (divine) nurse (CTH 336.6 §5:43)
- A god destroys the city of a (divine) nurse (CTH 336.6 §1:10-14)

**The Queen of the gods asks who will bring back Pirwa's eagle (CTH 337.1)**
- A goddess asks who will bring back a god's eagle from a far city and promises rich reward (CTH 337.1 §4:5, CTH 337.1 §5:6-7)
- A god's great ones take the road and the assembly and begin to praise a god (CTH 337.1 §7:10-11, CTH 337.1 §8:12-13)

**Ašertu tries to seduce the storm god; he tells Elkunirša (CTH 342.1.1)**
- The goddess whose advances were refused threatens the young god: 'be behind me ... I will press you down with my words, pierce you with my spindle' (CTH 342.1.1 §1:1-5, CTH 342.1.1 §2:19-24)
- The young god goes to the elder god's tent and reports that the elder god's wife tried to seduce him (CTH 342.1.1 §1:6-10, CTH 342.1.1 §2:11-28)
- The elder god tells the young god to go and humiliate his own wife (CTH 342.1.1 §2:32-34)
- The storm god taunts a goddess: 'I killed your 77 children, I killed 88' (CTH 342.1.1 §3:37-38)
- A grieving goddess installs mourners and laments for seven years (CTH 342.1.1 §3:39-43)
- A god takes from a victim the hair of his head, the sight of his eyes and the hearing of his ears (CTH 342.1.1 §10:80-86)

**Elkunirša gives the storm god to Ašertu; Ištar overhears and warns him; purification (CTH 342.1.2)**
- The elder god allows his wife to treat the young god as she wishes (CTH 342.1.2 §1:5-9)
- A goddess turns into a cup in a god's hand and into a bird (owl) on his wall to overhear husband and wife (CTH 342.1.2 §2:10-15)
- A goddess flies like a bird over the desert, finds the endangered god and warns him (CTH 342.1.2 §2:18-22)
- Incantation priests (of Amurru and elsewhere) purify a god from perjury, anger, sacrilege and evil words (CTH 342.1.2 §5:58-59, CTH 342.1.2 §6:60)

**LAMMA's arrows strike Ištar; he takes the storm god's reins (CTH 343.1 §1-3)**
- A god's arrows strike a goddess in her breast (CTH 343.1 §1:12-16)
- A god takes the bridle (donkey halter) out of the storm god's hand (CTH 343.1 §2:27, CTH 343.1 §3:28-31)

**LAMMA king in heaven nine years; a golden age (CTH 343.1 §4-5)**
- Under a divine king there are no storms, wolves or thieves; instead of rain it rains beer, and beer and wine flow in the valleys (CTH 343.1 §5:46-48, CTH 343.1 §5:55-56)

**LAMMA grows hostile, offerings cease, Ea and Kumarbi depose him (CTH 343.1 §6-9)**
- Because the king of heaven is hostile, the lands too become hostile and no one gives the gods bread and libation (CTH 343.1 §6:83-86, CTH 343.1 §9:111-114)
- A high god sends his vizier down into the dark earth with a message to primeval gods (Nara, Napšara) (CTH 343.1 §8:103-108)

**The storm god and Ninurta punish LAMMA (CTH 343.1 §10-17)**
- The deposed god is trampled and cut on his back and shin by the storm god and his vizier (CTH 343.1 §12:140-141, CTH 343.1 §13:142-147)

**Song of Going Forth - the primeval gods called to listen (CTH 344 §1-2)**
- A song opens by calling the primeval gods (Nara, Napšara, Minki, Ammunki, Ellil, Ninlil) to listen (CTH 344 §1:2-5, CTH 344 §2:6-8)

**Alalu, Anu, Kumarbi - nine-year reigns and revolts of the cupbearer (CTH 344 §2-4)**
- The god who bows at the heavenly king's feet and hands him his cup rises against him (CTH 344 §2:11-13, CTH 344 §3:22-24)
- The defeated heavenly king flees down into the dark earth (CTH 344 §3:16-19)
- The fleeing god is seized by the feet and dragged down from heaven (CTH 344 §4:28-34)

**Kumarbi bites off Anu's manhood and is made pregnant with three gods (CTH 344 §5-7)**
- A god bites off his rival's genitals and swallows his manhood (CTH 344 §5:35-37)
- The defeated god tells his victor: do not rejoice; I have placed in you terrible gods who will bring you to grief (CTH 344 §5:40-43, CTH 344 §6:44, CTH 344 §6:49-50)
- The swallower spits out part of what he swallowed and a mountain receives the feared god (CTH 344 §7:54-57)

**Kumarbi's pregnancy; the unborn gods debate how to come out; the storm god's birth from the skull (CTH 344 §8-13)**
- The gods inside the pregnant god speak and debate by which opening to come out (CTH 344 §9:64-66, CTH 344 §12:92-104, CTH 344 §13:105-114)

**Kumarbi demands the son to eat him, breaks his teeth on the diorite; a stone cult is founded (CTH 344 §14-16)**
- The father god demands to be given his son so that he may devour him (CTH 344 §14:124-132)
- The father god begins to eat and a (diorite) stone breaks the teeth in his mouth (CTH 344 §14:142-146)
- A stone is set up and named for worship: the rich shall slaughter cattle and sheep to it, the poor offer meal (CTH 344 §15:153-158, CTH 344 §16:165-166)

**Anu and the storm god plot against Kumarbi; the storm god boasts; Šeri warns (CTH 344 §19-21)**
- The victorious storm god boasts of the gods he has defeated: who will still fight against me? (CTH 344 §20:211-220)

**Ea counts the months; the Earth bears two sons; gifts to the messenger (CTH 344 §27-28)**
- The earth, made pregnant by the gods' seed, goes into labour and bears sons (CTH 344 §28:273-278)

**Ullikummi I - proem; Kumarbi plans a rival and mates with the rock (CTH 345.I.1 §1-3)**
- Proem of a song: 'I sing of (the god)' (CTH 345.I.1 §1:4)

**Impaluri, the Sea's invitation and the feast (CTH 345.I.1 §4-6)**
- Feast formula: they drank once, twice ... seven times (CTH 345.I.1 §6:71-77)

**The stone child is born, named Ullikummi and destined to destroy the storm god; hidden from the gods (CTH 345.I.1 §7-9)**
- The father names his son for the destruction he is to work (Ullikummi, 'destroy Kummiya') (CTH 345.I.1 §8:103-108)

**The Irširra gods carry Ullikummi to Enlil and set him on Upelluri's shoulder; he grows out of the sea to heaven (CTH 345.I.1 §10-18)**
- The monster grows a cubit a day and an acre (IKU) a month (CTH 345.I.1 §13:167-168, CTH 345.I.1 §17:191-194)

**The sun god sees Ullikummi and comes to the storm god; he will not sit, eat or drink (CTH 345.I.1 §19-24)**
- When the guest will not sit, eat or drink, the host asks whether the chamberlain, table servant or cupbearer was at fault (CTH 345.I.1 §23:242-251)

**Ištar sings to the deaf and blind stone; the wave sends her away (CTH 345.I.2 §7-10)**
- A great wave rises from the sea and speaks to the goddess (CTH 345.I.2 §9:93-96)
- Having eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear, said of idols or of people (CTH 345.I.2 §9:97-101)

**The storm god orders his bulls and storm weapons prepared; he arms for battle (CTH 345.I.2 §11-15)**
- The storm god orders rains, winds and the terrible lightning brought out of the bedchamber for battle (CTH 345.I.2 §11:122-130)

**First battle - seventy gods fall into the sea; Ullikummi reaches 9000 miles and shuts in Ḫebat (CTH 345.I.3.1 §1-6)**
- The monster's height and breadth are nine thousand miles (CTH 345.I.3.1 §2:26-33)
- The monster shuts the goddess in her temple so that she hears no word of her husband and the gods (CTH 345.I.3.1 §2:34-37, CTH 345.I.3.1 §3:38-42)

**Ḫebat nearly falls from the roof; 'there will be no king in heaven'; to Ea in Abzuwa (CTH 345.I.3.1 §7-13)**
- The goddess watching from the roof nearly falls; her maids hold her (CTH 345.I.3.1 §7:71-76)
- Visitors bow five times at the outer doors, five at the inner doors and fifteen times before the god himself (CTH 345.I.3.1 §7:93-97, CTH 345.I.3.1 §8:108-112)
- A suppliant kisses a god's knees three times and the soles of his feet four times (CTH 345.I.3.1 §11:131-132)

**Ea, Enlil and Upelluri; the saw that cut heaven from earth (CTH 345.I.3.1 §14-24)**
- The world-bearing giant says: when heaven and earth were built on me, and when they were cut apart, I noticed nothing; now something pains my shoulder (CTH 345.I.3.1 §20:201-202, CTH 345.I.3.1 §22:216-220)

**Ea has seen the dead; the gods bellow; battle with the cut-off Ullikummi and his boast (CTH 345.I.3.1 §25-34)**
- A god is distressed at having seen the dead in the dark earth, standing like dust (CTH 345.I.3.1 §27:247-252)
- All the gods assemble and bellow at the monster like cattle (CTH 345.I.3.1 §28:257-264)

**Kumarbi myth fragment - the merchant, silver and gold, Kumarbi's curse (CTH 346.1)**
- A god curses something so that, like dried wood, it puts forth no branches (CTH 346.1 §7:43-47)

**'The dark earth bore me' - a god's boast of his endowments (CTH 346.2)**
- A god boasts that the dark earth bore him, that he drew earth and heaven seven times, and that he holds Anu's manhood and Nara's wisdom (CTH 346.2 §1:7-13, CTH 346.2 §2:14-18)

**The sun god feasted by the Sea; the Sea weeps, bitten by creatures (CTH 346.4)**
- The weeping Sea complains that creatures, dogs and pigs bite and gnaw its limbs (CTH 346.4 §5:28-35, CTH 346.4 §6:37-39)

**Kumarbi counts the months; Mt Wašitta in labour after a stranger lay with her (CTH 346.5)**
- A mountain that was not fated to bear goes into labour after a stranger lay with it; all the mountains come to look (CTH 346.5 §2:16-29, CTH 346.5 §3:30-32)

**Small Kumarbi fragments - ornaments and a garland; Kumarbi washed; the Sea (CTH 346.6, 346.7, 346.8)**
- A god is washed in a purification rite (CTH 346.7 §2:7-10)

**The Sea's floods rise to the stars; the gods bring tribute to the Sea; Ištar summoned (CTH 346.9)**
- The gods acknowledge the Sea and throw tribute of gems, silver and gold into the water (CTH 346.9 §5:16-20, CTH 346.9 §6:21-25)

**Ḫepat, Takidu and Kutiladu of Šimmurra - a woman gives up her sin (CTH 346.10, 346.12)**
- A woman questioned by a divine messenger gives up her sin and praises the goddess (CTH 346.12 §2:9-18)
- A messenger is told to search the (Mittani) lands for clever people to install in priestly office (CTH 346.12 §1:4-8)

**The gods and the Sea search for the throne; 'made by our fate goddesses' (CTH 346.11)**
- The gods (and the Sea) search for the throne (CTH 346.11 §5:13-16)

**Kumarbi myth fragment with the storm god as king of all mankind (CTH 346.16)**
- A speaker asks where silver and gold come from and whence they are, with divine statues mentioned (CTH 346.16 §4:29-34)

**Kumarbi rises and quotes the saying of the ancients (CTH 346.21)**
- Proverb: the lion's bed begets a hero; if a father begets a heroic son he will stand against a thousand armies (CTH 346.21 §2:7-10)

**Hittite Atramhasis - Hamsha passes Kumarbi's words to his son Atramhasi (CTH 347.1)**
- A father (Hamsha) passes on to his son (Atramhasi) the words of a god and tells him how to act to survive (CTH 347.1 §2:6-9, CTH 347.1 §6:32-35)
- A son is warned that the feast to which a god invites him will mean his death: he will die like a mortal (CTH 347.1 §2:11-15)
- A man's fields are given to another (dameda) in a divine plan or disaster (CTH 347.1 §4:24-27)
- Warning that in this year the ant will eat (the crop), with a plant remedy (hutanu) to take (CTH 347.1 §5:28, CTH 347.1 §6:33-38)
- The hero is told to drive away the carts and bring the grain to another place before disaster (CTH 347.1 §6:39-41, CTH 347.1 §7:49)
- Ditches are dug all around (a field or settlement) as a protective measure (CTH 347.1 §7:44)

**Hittite Atramhasis - the gods face Enlil; Nuska reports (CTH 347.2)**
- According to an oracle the gods and Enlil stand against each other in assembly (CTH 347.2 §2:3)
- A god's vizier hears the words of the divine assembly, returns to his lord and reports that he spoke his master's word before them (CTH 347.2 §3:4-11)

**Song of Hedammu - Ea rebukes the gods for destroying mankind (CTH 348.I.1 §6-7)**
- Without humans the great gods themselves will have to take the plough and grind at the millstone (CTH 348.I.1 §6:60-61)
- A god is asked why he visits mankind with evil when they offer to him gladly in his temple (CTH 348.I.1 §7:62-67)
- The blood and tears of mankind are invoked against a destroying god (CTH 348.I.1 §7:70)

**Song of Hedammu - the monster is reared and devours thousands (CTH 348.I.2-3)**
- A monstrous child is reared on thousands of oxen and horses, countless lambs and kids, and fish (CTH 348.I.2 §1:5-15)

**Song of Hedammu - Ishtar bewitches the waters and shows Hedammu her nakedness (CTH 348.I.4)**
- The goddess pours 'love' and aromatic woods into the waters to bewitch the monster (CTH 348.I.4 §3:10-12)
- Having tasted a potion (beer, love-charm) put into the waters, the monster falls into a sweet sleep like cattle and recognises nothing (CTH 348.I.4 §3:13-17)
- The monster devastates scores of cities and piles up heaps of heads (CTH 348.I.4 §4:27-32)

**Song of Hedammu - a guest refuses chair, table and cup (CTH 348.I.5)**
- A guest refuses to sit on the chair offered, to touch the table or to put his lip to the cup (CTH 348.I.5 §3:15-23)
- Tears flow from someone like canals (CTH 348.I.5 §4:36)

**Song of Hedammu - the Sea offers Kumarbi his daughter Sertapsuruhi (CTH 348.I.6, first tablet)**
- The Sea offers his daughter, a mile long and a mile broad, as wife for the father of the gods to beget a champion (CTH 348.I.6 §2:13-19)

**Song of Hedammu - Ishtar shows herself naked; 'what kind of woman are you?' (CTH 348.I.8)**
- The monster asks the seductive goddess 'what kind of woman are you? which god are you, that you do not fear?' (CTH 348.I.8 §4:21-23, CTH 348.I.8 §5:30-31, CTH 348.I.8 §6:39-40)
- The goddess kneels before the monster and makes him drunk with her words (CTH 348.I.8 §5:32-38)

**Song of Hedammu - Ishtar bathes, anoints herself and calls for music (CTH 348.I.9)**
- After bathing and anointing, the goddess's charms run after her like little puppies (CTH 348.I.9 §2:17)
- The goddess orders her attendants (Ninatta, Kulitta) to play the galgalturi and arkammi on the sea shore (CTH 348.I.9 §3:18-21)

**Song of Hedammu - small fragments (CTH 348.I.10-19)**
- The monster threatens the goddess: I will eat you up (CTH 348.I.11 §2:3-6)

**Song of Hedammu - Kumarbi meets the storm god; the son on Kumarbi's knee (CTH 348.I.20-21)**
- The messenger is honoured seven times and given a golden wreath for his news (CTH 348.I.21 §2:7-10)

**Song of Hedammu - Kumarbi orders sixty youths and sixty maidens of Duddul (CTH 348.I.22)**
- Sixty young men and sixty young women of a city are sent, the maidens with lapis wine vessels (CTH 348.I.22 §1:6-11)

**Song of Hedammu - the storm god, the serpent's head, and asphalt holding the land (CTH 348.I.23-25)**
- The land is held fast by asphalt (bitumen) for seven years (CTH 348.I.25 §2:15-§3:18)

**Song of Hedammu - doors and windows sealed so Ishtar may not hear; the feast prepared (CTH 348.I.26-27)**
- The windows and doors facing Kumme and Nineveh are shut with cloth so that Ishtar may not hear the plan (CTH 348.I.26 §5:25-29, CTH 348.I.27 §1:9-12)
- The vizier prepares food and drink, fills cauldrons and heaps tables as his lord willed, and reports back (CTH 348.I.26 §5:30-31, CTH 348.I.27 §1:13-17, CTH 348.I.27 §2:18-22)

**Teshub cycle fragments - cosmic combat, winds as shoes, dream and vision (CTH 349.1, 349.2.1, 349.2.2)**
- The storm god (or his opponent) grows as high as heaven, mountains on his body, in a cosmic combat (CTH 349.1 §2:3-13)

**Fragment with Ishtar - the Sea sends the wave against the storm god (CTH 350.1)**
- The Sea demands that the living be sent down to the sea, and a sword be sent (CTH 350.1 §1:9-14)
- The Sea sends the wave (hunhuneššar) to fight the storm god; the wave later dries up (CTH 350.1 §1:19-27)

**Fragment with Ishtar - Mount Pishaisha and the sleeping Ishtar (CTH 350.3)**
- A mountain god (Pishaisha) lies with the goddess Ishtar while she sleeps; she wakes in fury asking who has shamed her (CTH 350.3 §2:6-11)
- The offender throws himself at the goddess's knees, 'do not kill me!', and promises to tell her something for his life (CTH 350.3 §2:15-20)

**Fragment with Ea - the beast tells Ea of a new god who will rule heaven and earth (CTH 351.1)**
- Decree: whom he keeps alive let none take back, whom he does not keep alive let none take away; he drives (them) down to the dark earth (CTH 351.1 §5:25-33)
- The new god shall hold the gods and all lands subject by a band (išhiman), the dark earth girded, heaven watching with favour (CTH 351.1 §5:34-48, CTH 351.1 §6:49-57)
- An animal (šuppala, the cattle) reveals to the wise god Ea that a new god is growing who will subdue heaven, earth, mountains and rivers (CTH 351.1 §7:59-64, CTH 351.1 §9:88-93, CTH 351.1 §10:94)
- A deity is to become pregnant with a river (the Aranzah/Tigris) or with a god (Zababa), the seed spat out (CTH 351.1 §14:129, CTH 351.1 §15:130-136)

**Fragments with Huranu - Ishtar, evil words and purification (CTH 352.1, 352.2)**
- A god releases and purifies someone afflicted by anger, sin and 'evil words' or evil sorcery (CTH 352.1 §6:21-28)

**Fragments with the daughter of the Pleiades - 'run from me!' (CTH 353.1, 353.2)**
- Told 'run from me, I will not leave you in peace', a figure flees by night down into a valley, falls and trembles (CTH 353.1 §2:5-12)

**Tale of Appu - the rich childless man, the sun god's promise, and the births of Evil and Righteous (CTH 360.1 §1-16)**
- Opening praise of a god who raises up just men but fells evil men like trees and strikes their skulls (CTH 360.1 §1:2-5)
- A man is the richest in the land, rich in cattle, sheep, silver, gold and lapis, and lacks only one thing: a son or daughter (CTH 360.1 §2:6-11, CTH 360.1 §3:12, CTH 360.1 §4:13-15)
- At the elders' meal each man gives bread and drink to his son; the childless man has no one to give bread to (CTH 360.1 §4:16-19)
- The childless man goes to bed with his boots on and does not lie with his wife (CTH 360.1 §5:20-24, CTH 360.1 §6:25-29)
- The husband answers his wife's question with 'you are a woman of womanly kind and understand nothing' (CTH 360.1 §7:30-37)
- The childless man takes a white lamb and goes to the sun god to plead his case (CTH 360.1 §8:38-40)
- The god tells the childless man: go home, eat and drink, sleep well with your wife; the gods will give you a son (CTH 360.1 §9:53-59)
- Seeing the sun god coming, the storm god asks whether the land has perished, the cities been laid waste, the troops beaten (CTH 360.1 §10:62-68, CTH 360.1 §11:69-74)
- A father names his firstborn 'Evil' because his fathers' gods did not choose the right way for him but kept to the evil way (CTH 360.1 §15:97-100)
- The second son is named 'Righteous' because the fathers' gods took the right way for him (CTH 360.1 §16:101-112)

**Tale of Appu - Evil and Righteous divide the estate; the lawsuit before the sun god and Ishtar (CTH 360.1 §17-30)**
- Grown brothers divide their father's estate and agree to live apart (CTH 360.1 §18:116-120, CTH 360.1 §19:121-123, CTH 360.1 §21:139)
- 'As mountains sit apart and rivers flow apart, as the sun god lives in Sippar, the moon god in Kuzina, the storm god in Kumme, Ishtar in Nineveh, Nanaya in Kissina, Marduk in Babylon, so let us live apart' (CTH 360.1 §19:127-130, CTH 360.1 §20:131-138)
- In the division the evil brother takes the better share (the plough ox) and gives the good brother the worse (the cow) (CTH 360.1 §21:140-142, CTH 360.1 §22:143-147)
- The god looks down from heaven and blesses the poorer share given to the good brother so that it prospers and bears (CTH 360.1 §22:148-150)
- The brothers take their case before the sun god in Sippar, who gives the verdict for the righteous brother (CTH 360.1 §23:154-156)
- The losing party curses the god who judged against him; the god hears the curses (CTH 360.1 §24:157-158)
- The god declines to judge the case again and sends the parties to another deity (Ishtar of Nineveh) (CTH 360.1 §24:159-161, CTH 360.1 §25:162-165)

**Tale of Appu - fragments of Evil's dealings with Righteous (CTH 360.2, 360.3, 360.4)**
- The evil brother speaks repeatedly to the good brother with proposals (ploughing, water) in a scheme against him; the sun god hears (CTH 360.2 §2:3-6, CTH 360.2 §3:7-10, CTH 360.2 §4:12-14)

**Tale of Keshshi the hunter - his beautiful wife, the neglected gods, the hidden game (CTH 361.I.1 §1-7)**
- A man so loves his beautiful wife that he listens only to her and stops giving the gods their bread and libations (CTH 361.I.1 §3:7-13)
- The hunter's mother reproaches him: only your wife is dear to you, you no longer go hunting and bring me nothing (CTH 361.I.1 §4:14-17)
- The gods, angry over neglected offerings, hide all the game from the hunter so that he finds nothing (CTH 361.I.1 §4:18-22)
- The hero's divine father comes down from the mountain and asks the creatures 'why do you devour him?' (CTH 361.I.1 §5:26-28, CTH 361.I.1 §6:29-33)

**Tale of Keshshi - seven dreams in one night and the mother's interpretation (CTH 361.I.1 §8-17)**
- The hero sees a series of seven numbered dreams in one night (a stone from heaven crushes men, the father's gods kindle fire, a yoke on his neck, lions, serpents at the gate) (CTH 361.I.1 §8:35, CTH 361.I.1 §9:38, CTH 361.I.1 §10:42, CTH 361.I.1 §11:45, CTH 361.I.1 §12:47, CTH 361.I.1 §12:50)
- In a dream a heavy stone falls from heaven and crushes servants and a man (CTH 361.I.1 §10:43-44)
- The hero sees a series of seven numbered dreams in one night (a stone from heaven crushes men, the father's gods kindle fire, a yoke on his neck, lions, serpents at the gate) (CTH 361.I.1 §11:46, CTH 361.I.1 §12:48-53)
- At daybreak the sun god comes with a radiant crown (kalmara) and the dreamer rises and tells his mother the night's dreams (CTH 361.I.1 §12:54-57)

**Deeds of Gurparanzah - the hunt, the archery contest at Akkad, the wedding night (CTH 362.1, 362.2, 362.3)**
- At a feast the hero, the king's son-in-law seated at his right, shoots with the bow; his arrow flies like a bird and he defeats sixty men and seventy nobles (CTH 362.1 §3:14-15, CTH 362.1 §4:16-24, CTH 362.2 §2:3-8)
- The king tells his sixty kings and seventy nobles: see, the king of a foreign land took our treasure (hakhari) and our woman (CTH 362.1 §8:50-55)

**Deeds of Gurparanzah - the river Aranzah consoles the weeping hero and visits the mother goddess (CTH 362.4)**
- The river god asks the weeping hero 'why do you lament, why does a stream of tears flow from your pure eyes?' (CTH 362.4 §3:17-21, CTH 362.4 §4:22)
- A guest eats and drinks once, twice, up to seven times (CTH 362.4 §6:37-40)

**The Sun god and the cow - the sun god's desire, the cow's human child and her attempt to devour it (CTH 363.1 §1-10)**
- The sun god looks down from heaven, desires a thriving cow, takes the form of a young man and comes down to her (CTH 363.1 §1:9-15)
- The cow, after ten months, bears a two-legged (human) child, cries 'why have I borne this two-footed one?' and opens her mouth like a lion to devour it (CTH 363.1 §6:49-58)

**The Sun god, the cow and the fisherman - the child guarded by birds, found and adopted by the childless fisherman (CTH 363.1 §11-19, 363.2)**
- A childless fisherman finds the divinely guarded child in the mountains and sees it as a gift of the sun god ('whom the sun god loves he gives bread') (CTH 363.1 §15:114-116, CTH 363.1 §16:125-139)
- The finder tells his wife to take the child to bed and cry out as in labour so the town will say she bore a son and bring gifts of bread, beer and oil (CTH 363.1 §17:140-153, CTH 363.1 §18:159-168)
- Narrator's maxim: a woman's mind is clever, she keeps away from commanding, depends on the god's power, is obedient and does not twist her husband's word (CTH 363.1 §17:154-158)

**Song of Silver - proem (CTH 364.1)**
- The singer opens the song by announcing its subject: 'I sing of ...' (išhamihhi), with praise of the god's wisdom, word and battle (CTH 364.1 §2:7)
- Wise men told the singer of a time when the thing (silver) did not yet exist (CTH 364.1 §2:8-13)

**Song of Silver - the orphan Silver learns his father is Kumarbi and becomes king over the gods (CTH 364.2)**
- A child mocked as fatherless confronts his mother, who answers, 'do not kill me', and names his divine father and his city (CTH 364.2 §5:18-35)
- 'Do not fear any god; fear only the one god' (who raises the low and lowers the high) (CTH 364.2 §5:36-37, CTH 364.2 §5:41-42)
- A god makes those above run down and those below run up, and stirs up enemies and wild beasts in the land (CTH 364.2 §5:38-40)
- The son goes to his father's city but does not find him: the father is roaming the land and the mountains (CTH 364.2 §5:43-48)

**Song of Silver - the orphans' rebuke; the sun and moon bow to Silver (CTH 364.3, 364.4, 364.5, 364.6)**
- A bully who beats orphans is rebuked by an orphan child, 'why do you beat us? you too are an orphan like us', and goes home weeping (CTH 364.4 §2:2-9, CTH 364.4 §2:10-12, CTH 364.4 §3:13-18)
- The usurper pulls the sun and the moon down from heaven; they bow before him and plead 'do not kill us, we are the lights of heaven and earth; without us you would rule dark lands' (CTH 364.5 §2:8-21)

**Myth and ritual of the Euphrates (Mala) - primeval gods, the king son of the sun god, plague (CTH 365)**
- The primeval gods fixed (the earth) and let all the rivers loose, and the rivers of the lands took (water) for the Mala (Euphrates); they purified the land (CTH 365 §1:2-8)
- All the gods take the son of the sun god and make him king of the land (CTH 365 §2:10-11, CTH 365 §4:21)
- A primeval period of 162 years (of strife or rule) is counted (CTH 365 §2:12-13)
- When man was created, a plague (hinkan) arose in the land and lasted years (CTH 365 §3:14-20)
- The myth closes with the rubric of a ritual (of the Mala river) to be performed when plague arises in the land, fixed by oracle (CTH 365 §8:39-45)

**Prayer of the king to the Sun goddess of the Earth and her underworld court (CTH 371.1)**
- The king has made the deity his personal god and kneels on the ground calling on it in person (CTH 371.1 §1:1-2, CTH 371.1 §2:3-9)
- The petitioner asks the god not to listen if his father, mother, brother, sister, in-law or friend slanders him (CTH 371.1 §3:10-19, CTH 371.1 §5:36-37, CTH 371.1 §8:52-53, CTH 371.1 §9:59-60)
- Prayer: lower your kind eyes, lift your thousand eyelashes, look kindly on the king; incline your ears and hear his good word (CTH 371.1 §4:20-24)
- Prayer: take him away from evil and set him in a good place (CTH 371.1 §4:25-27, CTH 371.1 §14:78)

**Vow of praise, enemies, the soothing words of invocation (CTH 372 §20-27)**
- The god is asked to put back into the sufferer the soul he had when he was born from his mother (CTH 372 §26:208-210)

**Kantuzzili's prayer to the Sun god (CTH 373)**
- The sufferer protests that he never swore falsely or broke an oath, never ate what is holy to his god, never parted an ox or sheep from its pen, and never ate his bread or drank his water alone (CTH 373 §3:19-§4:29)
- Life is bound up with death and death with life; a child of mortality does not live forever (CTH 373 §5:34-40)

**Arnuwanda I and Ašmunikal lament the Kaška devastation of the gods' lands (CTH 375.1)**
- The king lays the enemy's deeds before the gods as a legal case for them to judge (CTH 375.1 §10:26-30)
- An enemy people overturns the gods' temples, smashes their statues and divides their silver, gold, vessels and garments among themselves (CTH 375.1 §15:37-§16:41)
- In the lost lands no one calls the gods by name any more or gives their daily, monthly and yearly offerings (CTH 375.1 §19:47-§21:53)

**Duplicate fragment; the royal pair will find out by oracle what the gods lack (CTH 375.4)**
- The king promises to find out by oracle and seeress whatever the gods lack or are angry about and make it good (CTH 375.4 §6:14-16, CTH 375.4 §8:19-§9:23)

**Muršili II's hymn and prayer to the Sun goddess of Arinna in plague and war (CTH 376.1)**
- The deity is told not to let her own name be humbled by the land's defeat (CTH 376.1 §8:118-119)
- The deity is invoked for seven days in each of her cities (CTH 376.1 §13:156-160)

**Muršili II's hymn and prayer to Telipinu, recited daily by the scribe (CTH 377)**
- A scribe recites the king's prayer to the god every day on the king's behalf (CTH 377 §1:1-2, CTH 377 §18:63)

**Muršili II's 'first' plague prayer, on the murder of Tudḫaliya the Younger (CTH 378.1)**
- The king's father, with the princes and nobles, breaks the oath sworn to the reigning king, kills him and takes the throne (CTH 378.1 §2:13-§3:26)
- The murdered king's brothers are seized and sent away to Alašiya (Cyprus) (CTH 378.1 §3:20-22)
- The gods let the guilty king prosper at first and only later avenge his crime on him, his supporters and the land (CTH 378.1 §4:27-50)
- The father and the son each performed a ritual for the bloodshed, but the land did nothing for it (CTH 378.1 §7:79-84)

**Muršili II's 'second' plague prayer, the causes found (CTH 378.2 §1-10)**
- An offering to a river (the Māla, Euphrates) performed by earlier kings has been neglected since the father's days and is found to be a cause of the plague (CTH 378.2 §3:35-38, CTH 378.2 §8:79-80, CTH 378.2 §10:105-109)

**Muršili confesses his father's sin and argues for mercy (CTH 378.2 §11-15)**
- Saying: the father's sin comes upon his son (CTH 378.2 §11:118-120)
- Analogy: when a servant confesses his offence to his master, the master's anger is calmed and he no longer punishes him (CTH 378.2 §12:136-148)
- The petitioner argues that the land has already made restitution for the offence many times over (twentyfold) through the deaths of the plague (CTH 378.2 §12:152-158)
- All the priests are told to sleep in purity so that one may learn the cause of the disaster in a dream (CTH 378.2 §12:159-161, CTH 378.2 §14:169-177)

**Muršili II's 'third' plague prayer to the Sun goddess of Arinna (CTH 378.3)**
- Under the plague a man begets a son and grows to manhood but does not live to be old (CTH 378.3 §2:12-20)

**Muršili II's 'fourth' plague prayer to the assembly of the gods (CTH 378.4)**
- The king and his father before him sought the gods by oracle but could not find them (the oracle gave no answer) (CTH 378.4 §5:38-41)

**Muršili II's plague prayer to the assembly of the gods; the Egyptian affair (CTH 379)**
- The king swears he added no word to the old tablet and took none away, and does not know whether earlier kings did (CTH 379 §9:24-32)
- The king protests that he did not step beyond the borders set by the storm god or left him by his father (CTH 379 §10:33-38)
- The widow of the dead king of Egypt writes to the Hittite king (asking for a husband) (CTH 379 §13:45-§14:51)

**Prayer and substitute ritual for the recovery of Gaššuliyawiya, addressed to Lelwani (CTH 380.1)**
- The deity is invited to eat the fat of the sacrificial animals, eat its fill, drink the blood and quench its thirst (CTH 380.1 §1:8-11, CTH 380.1 §6:41-44)
- A richly dressed woman (or animal) is sent to the angry deity as substitute for the sick person: better, pure, shining and white (CTH 380.1 §2:12-18, CTH 380.1 §3:34-36, CTH 380.1 §6:45-50)
- A queen who saw a goddess in a dream failed to give her an offering, and later her illness is traced to it by oracle (CTH 380.1 §3:27-33)

**Muwatalli II's plea to the assembly of gods, ritual setting and preamble (CTH 381 §1-5)**
- When a matter weighs on a man he makes his plea to the gods: on the roof, facing the sun, he sets up wicker tables with breads, honey, oil and wine and bows to the sun god (CTH 381 §1:2-9)
- The king asks the gods to accept his words, and to let pass unheard any words they do not accept, since they come from a human mouth (CTH 381 §4:22-27)
- The storm god's bull Šeri is asked to convey the king's plea to the gods (CTH 381 §5:28-30)

**Catalogue of the gods of Hatti's cities invoked by Muwatalli (CTH 381 §X1-X59)**
- The prayer calls on the gods named and not named, of the temples the king visits and those he does not, with heaven, earth, clouds, winds, thunder and lightning (CTH 381 §X59:90-95)

**Muwatalli's prayer to the Sun god and the storm god piḫaššašši (CTH 381 §X60-X68)**
- The sun god comes up out of the sea and steps into heaven (CTH 381 §X60:97-98)
- The sun god is asked to stop the gods today and call them from heaven, earth, mountains, rivers, temples and thrones to hear the plea (CTH 381 §X61:100-§X62:103)
- The king says his father begot him but the god took him from his mother, raised him, made him priest and put him on the throne (CTH 381 §X63:105-111)
- The king promises to give the god his bread and libation joyfully, no longer in fear (CTH 381 §X67:143-150)
- The god is asked to shine gently on the king like moonlight and warm him from above like the sun (CTH 381 §X67:151-152)
- The god is asked to walk at the king's right hand and be yoked with him like an ox for pulling (CTH 381 §X68:153-157)

**The bread-breaking offering that accompanies the plea (CTH 381 §6-24)**
- Three white loaves, one of them red, are broken for each god in turn, filled with honey and oil, topped with fat-bread and porridge and a jug of wine poured (CTH 381 §8:164-§18:203, CTH 381 §20:208-§22:216)

**Muwatalli II's plea to the storm god of Kummanni, the cases of offence (CTH 382 §1-7)**
- The king calls one group of gods after another (Ḫebat, the gods of the lands, mountains and rivers, heaven and earth, the sun) and before each 'releases' the storm god's anger (CTH 382 §1:3-17)
- If any god, mountain, river or spring has angered the storm god, the underworld gods (Anunnaki) are asked to reconcile him with it, and he is to look on the land with reconciled eyes (CTH 382 §2:28-29, CTH 382 §3:32-33, CTH 382 §5:70-71)
- The king carries out whatever cult rules he finds on wooden and clay tablets or learns from the great old man, and asks a dream to clarify the rest (CTH 382 §4:44-65, CTH 382 §7:98-103)

**Kummanni prayer, further cases, unknown offences and colophon of Lūrma (CTH 382 §8-13)**
- Since humans know only the words that came out of their mouth, the underworld gods are asked to search out in the dark earth the offences they do not know (CTH 382 §12:132-140)
- The storm god filled the mother's breasts for our good, and as people are sated with cold water so may he grant satiety (CTH 382 §12:142-145)

**Ḫattušili III and Puduḫepa to the Sun goddess of Arinna, disclaiming past offences (CTH 383.1 §1-8)**
- The goddess is she who takes up and who casts off; the king and queen she looks upon succeed through her (CTH 383.1 §1:1-7)
- The deity is asked not to bring up again an old offence against the king and the land in his days, since it would not be right (CTH 383.1 §5:59-62)
- On his brother's death the king installs his brother's son on the throne (CTH 383.1 §6:63-71)

**Ḫattušili's restoration of Nerik as merit against inherited sin (CTH 383.1 §9-12)**
- The king brought the ruined holy city up like a stone out of deep waters, resettled and rebuilt it, which earlier victorious kings had failed to do (CTH 383.1 §9:93-106)
- Deserted by friends who said he would perish, the king said he would rather die for the god's city than give it away; as a mere man he did not seek wealth (CTH 383.1 §9:91-92, CTH 383.1 §10:107-122)
- The gods' sanctuary of favour (daḫanga) is invoked as a place into which the land is enclosed, so that its offences are cast away (CTH 383.1 §11:129-133, CTH 383.1 §12:162)
- As father and mother give the wage of a wet-nurse to one who raises their child, so the gods should reward the king who cared for their son's city (CTH 383.1 §11:134-138)
- If anyone speaks of the evil matter in the assembly of the gods, the gods are asked to weigh the king's merit instead and cast the matter out (CTH 383.1 §12:157-163)

**Puduḫepa to the Sun goddess of Arinna, the story of Nerik and Ḫattušili (CTH 384.1 §1-5)**
- The petitioner says the goddess took one name in one land and another name in another land (Sun goddess of Arinna in Ḫatti, Ḫepat in the land of the cedar) (CTH 384.1 §2:2-5)
- The petitioner calls herself a calf of the deity's cattle-stall and a stone of the deity's foundation (CTH 384.1 §2:6-8)
- A prince is assigned by lot to a god's service as his priest (CTH 384.1 §2:11)
- The petitioner reminds the god that the former kings neglected the god's city and none tried to take it back (CTH 384.1 §2:14-19)

**Puduḫepa's plea, the woman of the birth-stool, and the vow to Lelwani (CTH 384.1 §6-9)**
- The petitioner fears someone has turned the gods against the king by evil words or by giving them a gift for his harm, and asks the deity not to listen and to tread the evil words underfoot (CTH 384.1 §8:102-113)
- A silver statue of the king as large as the king himself, with head, hands and feet of gold, is vowed to a goddess for his life (CTH 384.1 §9:119-120)

**The enemies covet the gods' vessels, servants, temples and fields (CTH 385.8)**
- The enemies covet the gods' silver and gold vessels and their ploughmen, millers and weavers, want to burn the temples and lay waste their fields and gardens (CTH 385.8 §4:14-17)

**Tudḫaliya confesses curtailing the festivals and vows a temple (CTH 385.9)**
- The king confesses he offended the goddess by taking away and curtailing her festivals and promises never to do so again (CTH 385.9 §1:2-5, CTH 385.9 §1:11-12)
- Spring festivals and autumn festivals had been interchanged; the king vows to celebrate spring festivals only in spring and autumn festivals only in autumn (CTH 385.9 §1:13-15)
- The king vows that if he defeats the enemy and returns he will go up the god's mountain, give thousands and build the deity a temple (CTH 385.9 §1:8-10, CTH 385.9 §5:40-47)

**The king's dawn rite and the priest's prayer on the roof of the Sun goddess's temple (CTH 385.10)**
- On a clear, cloudless day the king goes at dawn to a pure place, washes, puts on his festive robe and orders that no one bow or speak (CTH 385.10 §1:2-8, CTH 385.10 §2:9-10)
- Pure water fetched at dawn is poured out three times before the altar and the god and king wash their hands (CTH 385.10 §3:11-15, CTH 385.10 §4:16-19)
- The goddess gives the royal couple a drawn, victorious spear: the surrounding enemy lands shall perish by the hand of the Labarna (CTH 385.10 §9:35-37)
- The land shall graze vigorously in the hand of the king and queen and spread wide (CTH 385.10 §10:38-39, CTH 385.10 §16:59-60)
- The sun god is hailed as one whose radiance is brilliant and whose rays are bright (CTH 385.10 §11:40-42)
- The king and queen are to make the sea their boundary (CTH 385.10 §16:62)
- At dawn the priest goes up on the roof of the sun goddess's temple and recites the prayer facing the sun (CTH 385.10 §18:72-73, CTH 385.10 §19:74-77, CTH 385.10 §22:86)

**Analogic prayer, the soul shall not trickle away; be sweet to the king (CTH 385.11)**
- Analogic prayer: as this bread or beer is sweet and this thing numerous, so may the goddess be sweet to the king and queen and their children be numerous (CTH 385.11 §2:24-29, CTH 385.11 §3:31-33)

**The Storm god of Nerik woken and summoned from all places (CTH 386.1)**
- A goddess is to call a pleasant message like a bird to the god and wake him from his sweet dreams (CTH 386.1 §2:8-10)
- The god is summoned with 'come!' from heaven and earth, sunrise and sunset, a list of mountains, rivers, the sea, lands and the four corners (CTH 386.1 §2:11-13, CTH 386.1 §2:19-21, CTH 386.1 §3:22, CTH 386.1 §4:23-35)
- The king or prince is anointed for the priesthood of a god's beloved cities (CTH 386.1 §2:17)

**Fragment of a prayer, the gods bow before the Storm god of Nerik (CTH 386.7)**
- Three thick breads are set out and a message is sent three times to call the god (CTH 386.7 §3:26-28)

**The thirsty, hungry, wounded gods (CTH 386.8)**
- The gods are described as thirsty, hungry, wounded and weeping, and the god is called away from them (CTH 386.8 §1:2-3, CTH 386.8 §2:4-5)

**Muršili III (Urḫi-Teššub) pleads innocence in his father's quarrels (CTH 387.1)**
- The petitioner says he did not decide the case: 'that was the god's lawsuit' (CTH 387.1 §3:60-67)
- The petitioner says he carried out a deed at another's command, taking nothing from his own mind (CTH 387.1 §3:68-71)

**Muršili III to the deity of Arušna, Tanuḫepa and the gods' silver (CTH 387.5)**
- When silver and gold were given to all the gods, the petitioner's father gave nothing and took it into his own house (CTH 387.5 §3:13-19)

**Ayatarša's ritual for a sick child, sheep for the Sun god of illness, herbs and purification water (CTH 390 §1-21)**
- For a sick child or one whose entrails are 'eaten', a sheep is offered to the Sun god of illness, who is asked to remove the illness from the child (CTH 390 §1:1-4, CTH 390 §2:5, CTH 390 §3:7-10)
- A mash of garden herbs, yeast and beer-wort sprinkled with water of purification is poured into the patient's mouth and over his head and every limb (CTH 390 §8:26, CTH 390 §9:27, CTH 390 §10:28-32, CTH 390 §11:33-37, CTH 390 §12:38-42)
- A bird is waved over the patient and then let go to the Sun god, carrying the evil away (CTH 390 §13:43-45)
- A bowl or vessel is waved over the patient and then smashed (CTH 390 §20:61-64)

**Wattitti's ritual for eaten entrails, bread on the spit, entrails eaten, the bundle under the stars (CTH 390 §22-32)**
- The patient eats an animal's entrails for twice seven days, saying 'entrails overpower entrails' (CTH 390 §22:71, CTH 390 §23:72-77, CTH 390 §24:78-85, CTH 390 §25:86-88)
- A bundle is set on the roof overnight under the stars so that the thousand stars, the gods and the Sun goddess of the Earth conjure it, and then the Sun god at dawn (CTH 390 §26:89-96, CTH 390 §27:97-102, CTH 390 §28:103-109, CTH 390 §29:110-111)
- Analogic healing spell: as the spindle whorl turns, as one arrow-shaft does not hit another, as earth is dug out of a pit, so may the evil turn away from or not reach the patient (CTH 390 §29:112-115, CTH 390 §30:116-118, CTH 390 §31:126-129, CTH 390 §32:132-135)
- A conjured bundle of wool and objects is wound round the patient's body and removed when he recovers (CTH 390 §29:111-112, CTH 390 §31:119-120)

**Against evil tongues, the Old Woman cleans the tongue with honey (CTH 390 §33-35)**
- Against 'evil tongues' the Old Woman smears the victim's tongue with beer-wort and ghee, wipes it with honey and spits into his mouth twice (CTH 390 §33:139-141, CTH 390 §35:159-165)

**The great river bound everything; Kamrušepa conjures and looses it; the child bound and loosed limb by limb (CTH 390 §36-46)**
- A great river binds its flood, the fish, the high mountains, deep valleys, the storm god's meadow, the eagle's wings, eels, the stag under the oak, panther, wolf, lion, wild goat and its milk, and the throne of the protective god (CTH 390 §36:167-174, CTH 390 §37:175-181)
- A word passes from one deity to the next down a chain (Ištar to Maliya, Maliya to Pirwa, Pirwa to Kamrušepa) until the healing goddess acts (CTH 390 §38:182-184)
- The goddess drives to the river and conjures it, and the river, mountains, valleys, animals and throne are loosed (lā- 'to loosen') item by item (CTH 390 §38:185-190, CTH 390 §39:191-196, CTH 390 §40:197-203)
- The patient was 'bound' in each body part, hair, skull, nose, ears, mouth, tongue, throat, chest, lungs, liver, genitals, bladder, anus, knees, hands; each is conjured and loosed (CTH 390 §41:204-220, CTH 390 §42:226-231, CTH 390 §43:232-242, CTH 390 §44:243-249, CTH 390 §45:250-256)

**The eya-tree at the gate, the goat's blood in pots, the evil driven into the enemy land (CTH 391.1 §44-54)**
- On returning home the ritualist drives an eya-tree, leafy above and pointed below, into the ground at the right of the main gate with a pot beneath it (CTH 391.1 §44:194-198, CTH 391.1 §49:225)
- Returning from the rite, the ritualist must not turn round, speak or curse (CTH 391.1 §48:216-220)
- Prayer that the deity keep the petitioner's wife, children and grandchildren alive (CTH 391.1 §49:226-231)
- The evil is driven into the enemy land, into a hole (CTH 391.1 §53:248-251)

**Second version of Ambazzi's ritual for the king, impurity drawn out, the bolt that opens the door (CTH 391.2)**
- Impurity (papratar), taboo-breach (anzellu), sexual abomination (ḫurkil) and the evil of evil men are drawn out of the king's eyes, hands and nine body parts (CTH 391.2 §1:1-5, CTH 391.2 §3:11)

**Anniwiyani's ritual, the virgin at the door, the puppy cut in two at the hawthorn gate (CTH 393 §1-18)**
- Blue and then red wool is bound on the patient's feet, hands, neck, the four bedposts, his chariot, bow and quiver overnight and cut off at dawn (CTH 393 §2:4-6, CTH 393 §3:10-12, CTH 393 §4:13, CTH 393 §5:17-19)
- Clay figures of every oracle bird, with roasted grain, breads and pegs, are set in a basket under the patient's bed overnight (CTH 393 §2:7-9, CTH 393 §4:14-16)
- The rite is carried to an untouched place in the mountains where the plough never comes (CTH 393 §6:26-30)
- A puppy is cut in two and its halves laid either side of a gate of hawthorn; all pass under the gate, the last breaks it, shouts, and they run off (CTH 393 §7:34-37, CTH 393 §8:38-42, CTH 393 §9:43-47, CTH 393 §11:55-60)
- As they go on, the place where the rite was done becomes invisible to them, and they peg the road behind them (CTH 393 §12:61-64)
- The rite is carried to an untouched place in the mountains where the plough never comes (CTH 393 §11:51-54)

**Calling the Lamma of the hunting bag, the lost chaff and the nine pebbles; the colophon (CTH 393 §19-31)**
- The ritualist plucks a tuft of wool from the sheep that has turned its eyes to the sun (CTH 393 §20:100-102)
- Nine dishes are set before the god (meat stew, lentil soup, chickpea soup, barley porridge, fat cake, honeyed porridge, sweet milk) with bread and beer, day after day (CTH 393 §21:103, CTH 393 §26:126-129, CTH 393 §27:132-133, CTH 393 §28:134-135)

**Ašḫella's plague ritual, the rams and the adorned woman sent to the enemy's border (CTH 394 §1-5)**
- In a plague in the army each officer provides a ram; coloured wool and rings are tied on the rams' necks and horns and they are tethered before the tents at night: 'whichever god made this plague, be content with these' (CTH 394 §1:2, CTH 394 §2:5-19)
- An adorned woman is set before the king's tent with beer and bread and is driven out with the substitute animals (CTH 394 §3:22-23, CTH 394 §4:32)
- The plague god is told: these rams are very fat in liver, heart and member; let human flesh be hateful to you, be content with these rams (CTH 394 §4:26-30)
- The officers stretch their hands toward the substitute animals, and bow behind the rams, the king and the adorned woman (CTH 394 §4:24, CTH 394 §4:31-32)
- Rams, woman, bread and beer are driven through the camp and left on the enemy's border, where our people do not go: 'whoever finds them, may that land take this evil plague' (CTH 394 §3:20-21, CTH 394 §5:33-41)

**Ašḫella's ritual, days two to four, eat in a god's way; salt water and two fires; the colophon (CTH 394 §6-9)**
- Animals are slaughtered in the open field: 'O god, eat and drink in a god's way, and leave nothing to man' (CTH 394 §6:42-56)
- While the god is being served, no one sets the god's vessels on the ground or picks them up again: it is not right (CTH 394 §6:59-62)
- Leaving the rite, the participants wash their hands in water with salt, light two fires and walk between them (CTH 394 §7:63-67)
- The god who made the plague is fed and asked to be at peace with the land and army of Ḫatti and turn to them in kindness (CTH 394 §8:74-86)
- A ewe that a ram has not yet gone to is offered (to the Sun god) (CTH 394 §9:87-93)

**Ḫantitaššu's ritual for disturbed years, the table on the roof, 'take the gold, give me back the man' (CTH 395.1 §1-12)**
- As sheep lick salt, so may the Sun god come and lick these incantations (CTH 395.1 §5:23-27)

**Ḫantitaššu's ritual, the piglet in the pit for the old gods, the bolt that opens the dark earth, the sealed bundle (CTH 395.1 §13-25)**
- At nightfall a pit is dug, a piglet is slaughtered in it, its blood let down, food and wine put in, and the primeval gods (karuileš DINGIR.MEŠ) are called up to eat (CTH 395.1 §14:97-101, CTH 395.1 §15:102-112)
- A bolt-wood is anointed with fat and addressed: 'you open again and again; go, open (the dark earth)' (CTH 395.1 §16:114-123, CTH 395.1 §17:124-129)

**Second manuscript of Ḫantitaššu's ritual, 'who of the gods made me a servant again' (CTH 395.2.1)**
- The healed patron asks which of the gods made him a servant again and a master again (CTH 395.2.1 §6:81-82)

**Ḫatiya's ritual for the demoness Wišuriyant at the river (CTH 396.1.1 §1-6)**
- The demoness Wišuriyant (the 'strangler') is brought down to the river, a tent set up, and she is washed with clay of the bank: 'see, I have purified you' (CTH 396.1.1 §1:1-5, CTH 396.1.1 §2:6-12)
- A fish with a cake in its mouth is released into the river to go to the mountain and the river and bring the offering to the demoness (CTH 396.1.1 §3:21-26)
- Three pits are dug before the river bank and breads broken for the fate goddesses and the mother goddess, who are asked for life, health, vigour, long years and sight (CTH 396.1.1 §4:27-31)
- The fish is thrown on the hearth and burned, and there is no smoke (CTH 396.1.1 §5:33-42)

**Ḫatiya's ritual, the sheep for the Sun, the bones burned, the goddess returned to her temple (CTH 396.1.1 §7-12)**
- After the meal the bones are gathered, laid in the hearth and burned (CTH 396.1.1 §10:76-81)
- The ritualist takes the clay and wicker utensils of the rite for herself; the patron takes nothing back (CTH 396.1.1 §11:92-94)

**Ritual naming Wišuriyant, offerings set before the deity (CTH 396.1.2)**
- The trimmed meat of the victim is brought up and carried to the deity (CTH 396.1.2 §2:10-14, CTH 396.1.2 §5:36-37)

**Ritual naming Wišuriyant, address and river disposal (CTH 396.2)**
- The practitioner addresses a deity or demon by name: 'See, (this is) for you' (CTH 396.2 §1:1-4)

**Ritual naming Wišuriyant, eating and drinking (CTH 396.3)**
- The participants say 'we eat, we drink' as part of the rite (CTH 396.3 §1:4-5)

**Ḫepattarakki of Zuḫaruwa releases a bewitched man with dough figures (CTH 397 §1-5)**
- The practitioner 'releases' or 'loosens back' (EGIR-pa la-) a bewitched person from sorcery (CTH 397 §1:2)
- Dog excrement is kneaded into the dough used to treat a bewitched person, and the dog's smell is then driven from him (CTH 397 §1:4-5, CTH 397 §4:22-23)
- The practitioner quenches the fire in the patient's head and makes it burn in the head of the sorcerer instead (CTH 397 §4:20-21)
- Named evil powers are removed and driven out of the patient's head (CTH 397 §4:18-19)

**Ḫepattarakki ritual, fragments and colophon (CTH 397 §6-13)**
- An act of the rite is done at night eight times (CTH 397 §8:49)
- When an evil person has 'spoken against' (bewitched by speech) someone, the practitioner 'speaks him back' with a counter-incantation (CTH 397 §13:78-79)

**The augur Ḫuwarlu against terrible birds, clay birds and roasted seeds (CTH 398 §1-3)**
- Clay models of ominous birds are sealed in oil bowls and seeds are roasted and quenched with water, so that the evil birds and evil words 'go out' like the seeds (CTH 398 §1:2-8, CTH 398 §2:12-14, CTH 398 §3:20-22)
- A donkey of tallow is laid in an oil bowl and the bowl is closed over it (CTH 398 §2:9-11)
- The 'Old Woman' (MUNUS ŠU.GI), a female ritual expert, performs and speaks the rite (CTH 398 §3:15)

**Ḫuwarlu ritual, tallow puppy, binding cords, soap and riverbank clay (CTH 398 §4-9)**
- The four corners of the house, the threshold and the door bolt are treated one by one in the purification (CTH 398 §6:34, CTH 398 §8:50)
- Analogic spell: as soapwort cleans dirty linen and makes it white, so may it clean the bodies of the king, queen and princes and the palace (CTH 398 §8:45-54)
- A ball of riverbank clay that has 'overcome' the evil is to carry it back to the riverbank and the dark earth is to overcome it (CTH 398 §9:57-65)
- The gods see an unlucky matter lurking in the house which neither the house nor the human can overcome (CTH 398 §9:61-62)

**Ḫuwarlu ritual, dough of life, waving and the living puppy as carrier (CTH 398 §10-16)**
- Analogic spell: as grain keeps mankind, cattle, sheep and every beast alive, so may it keep the patients alive apart from the evil (CTH 398 §11:69-71)
- The evil is to go to the place the gods have determined for it (kuwapi DINGIR.MEŠ lamniyan harkanzi) (CTH 398 §14:99-100, CTH 398 §15:109-110)
- The ritual remains that have absorbed the evil are carried out of the house and poured away in the open country (CTH 398 §14:87-89, CTH 398 §16:118-121)
- The Seven gods (Sebettu) are asked to step aside from the deity's road (CTH 398 §16:126)

**Ḫuwarlu ritual, buried head, goat on foliage, gates, washing and prayer to the Sun (CTH 398 §17-27)**
- The earth is dug up and a head of clay is placed in it (CTH 398 §17:127-128)
- Breads and cups are laid out on foliage to the right and to the left for the deity (CTH 398 §19:140-146)
- A he-goat is placed on foliage and cut up, its parts set over the fire for the deity (CTH 398 §20:147-151)
- The patient declares 'Now the gods have set me free' and asks them not to let the evil loose on him again (CTH 398 §26:193-194)
- At the end of the rite bread is offered to the Sun god on a stone and he is told that the evil has been removed (CTH 398 §27:203-212)

**Jarri of Lallupiya against bloodshed and impurity in a house (CTH 399)**
- A ritual is prescribed when bloodshed or some impurity occurs inside a person's house; one and the same rite serves for every impurity (CTH 399 §1:2-5)
- Puppies are listed among the animals required for a purification (CTH 399 §3:8)
- A white ox-hide is laid before the hearth and a red one before the throne in a purification of the house (CTH 399 §5:13)
- The participants repeatedly shout a ritual cry ('ui ui', 'he he') (CTH 399 §5:19)

**Iriya purifies a city of blood, perjury and curse, the riverbank clay and the ancient gods (CTH 400.1 §1-11)**
- A bronze hoe and spade are prepared to dig clay at the riverbank where the potters take it (CTH 400.1 §1:5, CTH 400.1 §7:26, CTH 400.1 §10:46)
- Clay dug from the riverbank is addressed and given to the underground watercourses (CTH 400.1 §7:34-37)
- The ritual clay is smeared with oil and honey and a libation is poured (CTH 400.1 §7:30-32)
- Bloodshed, perjury and curse are treated as a lawsuit (hanneššar) that the gods are asked to judge (CTH 400.1 §8:40, CTH 400.1 §11:53)

**Iriya ritual, the šurašura-bird, the goat burned and buried, eagle and falcon released (CTH 400.1 §14-20)**
- The evil (disease, blood, oath) is told that it has sat on the roof of the palace or of the temple and must now purify them (CTH 400.1 §15:74-76)
- The ritual animals are led through the city out of the gates by which people are taken down to be killed, to the place where people died (CTH 400.1 §17:91-95)

**The augur Banippi when a friend has slandered his companion, the clay tongue (CTH 401.1 §1-4)**
- A friend throws a garment over his companion and hides the gods from him (cuts him off from divine favour) (CTH 401.1 §1:2-3)
- A tongue (EME) is made of clay or wax as the object of a rite against the evil tongue or slander (CTH 401.1 §2:5, CTH 401.1 §2:8)
- The 'tongue of the land' or 'of the multitude' (public slander or curse) is named as the evil to be removed (CTH 401.1 §3:14-15)

**Banippi ritual, the burning of the seven kippa-tents and the bewitched driven off (CTH 401.1 §6-7)**
- The practitioner says 'I make (it) blood-red again and again, white again and again, black again and again' (CTH 401.1 §6:44-46)
- Seven kippa-tents are let down over a man and woman with torches at their heads and are burned; the bewitched man is called by his name (CTH 401.1 §6:47-55, CTH 401.1 §7:56)
- The practitioner calls the patient (ritual patron) by his name during the rite (CTH 401.1 §6:55)
- Stones are thrown and weapons and shields brandished after those who carried out the evil, with the cry 'Go, you bewitched people!' (CTH 401.1 §7:57-62)

**Ritual like CTH 400, the king addresses the mountains about blood, tears and the tongue of the multitude (CTH 401.2 §1-6)**
- The roads are addressed and asked to drive away the gods' oath, the tongue, blood and tears (CTH 401.2 §3:6, CTH 401.2 §4:13)

**Ritual like CTH 400, eagle to heaven and falcon to the pure mountains, the king purified (CTH 401.2 §10-19)**
- The king is purified of oath, the tongue of the multitude and tears (CTH 401.2 §10:58, CTH 401.2 §17:83)
- Possible causes of impurity are named: a man ate fat or his mouth was bloodied (CTH 401.2 §11:65-68)
- A bird used in the rite is carried back to the mountains (CTH 401.2 §12:72)

**Fragment like CTH 400, offerings to the ancient gods, goat burned and bird buried (CTH 401.3)**
- A little of every fruit, seed, malt, wax, fat and porridge is poured out before the gods (CTH 401.3 §1:6-11)
- A bird is offered to the ancient (primeval) gods (CTH 401.3 §1:12)

**Ritual to purify a city of disease and plague, Muršili and the great gate (CTH 401.5)**
- A rite asks that disease and plague (death) leave a city and become well (CTH 401.5 §1:5, CTH 401.5 §1:14)
- A named king (Muršili) and the princes of Hatti appear in a rite against plague (CTH 401.5 §1:3-4, CTH 401.5 §1:12)
- The deity is asked to show mildness (genzu) (CTH 401.5 §1:6)
- At the great city gate woodpiles and pegs are set up on either side and objects buried under the threshold (CTH 401.5 §1:16-23)

**Fragment naming a city, cornel pegs and red wool (CTH 401.6)**
- Another city is treated as an enemy so that the evil may be sent there (CTH 401.6 §1:2-3)
- Nine thick breads are presented in the rite (CTH 401.6 §2:8)

**Alli of Arzawa against sorcery, the clay figurines with tongues and the sorcery handed back (CTH 402 §1-8)**
- The 'Sun god of the hand' (kiššeraš UTU) is called to see the sorcerers and to recognise whether a man or a woman did the bewitching (CTH 402 §4:22, CTH 402 §5:28)
- May the sorcery be the sorceress's headdress, her belt and her shoes: may she put them on and take back what she did (CTH 402 §5:29-35, CTH 402 §6:36-39)

**Alli ritual, coloured threads take off the colours of sorcery, white wool purifies (CTH 402 §9-19)**
- Threads of black, red, yellow-green, blue and white wool take off the patient the blackness, redness, yellowness, 'blue day' and binding of sorcery and are wound round the figurines (CTH 402 §9:56-62, CTH 402 §10:63-68, CTH 402 §11:69-74, CTH 402 §12:75-80, CTH 402 §13:81-86, CTH 402 §14:87-92, CTH 402 §15:93-98)
- Whoever 'bound' the patient by sorcery, the practitioner takes it from all his limbs (CTH 402 §13:83-84)
- The drunkenness caused by sorcery is taken off the patient and the sorcerer made drunk through the figurines (CTH 402 §16:101-104)
- Analogic spell: as white wool appeases fierce hostility, so may it purify the sorcery and impurity and make the person pure before all (CTH 402 §19:111-119)
- Whether someone harmed the patient before the gods or before mortals, the harm is to be removed (CTH 402 §19:115-116)

**Alli ritual, the sorcery buried and pegged, bread for the gods of the roads and the gate (CTH 402 §20-23)**
- Bad dreams are fixed in the earth together with the sorcery (CTH 402 §20:133)
- Flat breads are broken beside the pit for the dark earth, the Sun and other deities, who are to keep the evil fixed (CTH 402 §21:136-147)
- Bread is broken at the right and left of the road and at the crossroads for the gods of the roads, who are to take the evil and not let it come back (CTH 402 §22:148-160)
- The gods of the city gate are asked to speak good things (CTH 402 §23:161-167)

**Alli ritual, the basket under the bed, wax figurines and the hunter who carries off (CTH 402 §24-32)**
- The evils are to be lifted off the patient, off his head and off his bed (CTH 402 §28:196-200)
- Analogic spell: as this dust cleans and this dough heals, so may they clean and heal the person, his house, altar, hearth, spouse and children (CTH 402 §29:205-210, CTH 402 §30:211-215)

**Alli ritual, the bath, the five cups, burial, sacrifice to the Sun and the river (CTH 402 §33-44)**
- Five clay cups are filled with five different liquids for the patient's purification (CTH 402 §33:237-241)
- The patient is bathed (in grain, then in water) in an ablution house and the practitioner says she has removed the evil tongue, defeat and sorcery (CTH 402 §33:242-243, CTH 402 §34:244-249)
- The gods are asked to protect the purified person and not let the evil back into him (CTH 402 §34:248-249)
- The practitioner goes down to the river, spends the night there and breaks bread and sacrifices a sheep to the mother goddess of the riverbank and the river spirits (CTH 402 §42:285-298, CTH 402 §43:299-308)

**Mallidunna's ritual for the Sun god, the three pairs of eyes of the Sun (CTH 403.1)**
- The Sun god has three pairs of eyes: of watching, of appeasement and of governing and judgment (CTH 403.1 §4:12-18)
- Torches are lit as the Sun deity goes down (CTH 403.1 §6:27-28, CTH 403.1 §8:42-45)
- The deity is said to drink her fill (niku-) at the offering (CTH 403.1 §6:29)
- The gods are given offerings one after another in turn (irḫa-) (CTH 403.1 §8:40)

**Mallidunna's ritual to rouse the angry Ḫannaḫanna (CTH 403.2)**
- A mud brick is laid in the inner room and clay objects and vessels of fat and salt with clay lids are set on it to invoke an angry goddess (CTH 403.2 §1:4-6, CTH 403.2 §2:7-9)
- The angry mother goddess (Ḫannaḫanna) has gone back to the riverbank taking the fertility of her womb with her, and is asked why (CTH 403.2 §3:11-14, CTH 403.2 §7:35)
- The deity is said to be angry because of something a human did against her (CTH 403.2 §3:15-20)
- The deity is asked to turn (her face) towards the king and queen (CTH 403.2 §7:34)

**Offerings to the Sun god, 'as the ewe recognises her lamb' (CTH 403.3.1)**
- The Sun god is let into the house through the window (CTH 403.3.1 §2:2)
- The god's image is turned with its eyes toward the king, queen and princes (CTH 403.3.1 §3:14-17)

**Parallel text to the Sun offerings, cheese, liver and recognition (CTH 403.3.2)**
- Analogic spell: as this cheese (food and drink) is pleasant, so may it be pleasant for the king and queen (CTH 403.3.2 §3:5-7)

**Maštigga ritual, the tongues of that day cut, the fish and the tiššatwa thrown into the fire (CTH 404.1.I §6-19)**
- The Sun god is told that the quarrelling tongues are set before him and treated today with his help (CTH 404.1.I §7:24-27)
- Red wool is cut with a knife over the quarrelling pair: the god Andaliya has cut off the tongues of the day of quarrel with a knife (CTH 404.1.I §10:34-39)
- A fish, 'the bull of the sea', is waved over the quarrelling pair: as it was cut off from the sea, so may the tongues and curses be cut off (CTH 404.1.I §11:40-46)
- Each object that has absorbed the curses (cut wool, fish, wool in fat, wax and clay tongues, dough) is thrown into the hearth fire (CTH 404.1.I §10:39, CTH 404.1.I §11:46, CTH 404.1.I §12:55, CTH 404.1.I §14:65, CTH 404.1.I §17:76, CTH 404.1.I §19:92)

**Paškuwatti of Arzawa against impotence, the reed gate, the spindle taken and the bow given (CTH 406 §1-4)**
- A ritual is prescribed for a man who lacks procreative power or 'is not a man' towards a woman (CTH 406 §1:3-4)
- A goddess is invoked (mugai-) for three days with offerings (CTH 406 §2:5-7)
- Small portions of breads, figs, raisins, poppy and drink are set on a large 'soldier bread' carried in the rite (CTH 406 §2:8-10)
- A 'girl of purity' carries the offerings in the procession (CTH 406 §3:11, CTH 406 §3:16)
- The patient has washed before the rite (CTH 406 §3:12-14)
- The rite is performed in open, untrodden (dammeli) country (CTH 406 §3:15)
- The impotent man holds spindle and distaff, passes through a gate, and receives bow and arrows: 'I have taken your womanhood and given you back manhood' (CTH 406 §4:19-28)

**Paškuwatti ritual, the invocation of Uliliyašši to come to the man and be his wife (CTH 406 §5-10)**
- The mortal is described as made of excrement and urine (a child of mortality) (CTH 406 §6:35-37)
- The suppliant has come on his knees and seeks the deity for her divinity, though he did not know her before (CTH 406 §7:38-39, CTH 406 §10:67-69)
- Whether the deity is in the mountain, the meadow or the valley, wherever she is, she is summoned to come (CTH 406 §7:40-45)
- Vow: the man will make the goddess his deity, give her a place, a house, servants, cattle and sheep and votive gifts (CTH 406 §8:46-51)
- The invoked goddess is asked to bring the Moon god, the stars and the Sun goddess of the earth with her (CTH 406 §9:52-55)
- The deity is asked to show her divinity (DINGIR-LIM-tar tekkušnut) so that the man may see it and make her his personal deity (CTH 406 §10:72-75)
- A new table is set up in the house where the goddess is invoked and later becomes her altar (CTH 406 §10:76-81)

**Paškuwatti ritual, three days of invocation, incubation and the goddess in the dream, her image as vessel or stone (CTH 406 §11-20)**
- The patient sleeps on a bed set before the deity's new table, with the garments that lay on the offering bread spread under him (CTH 406 §11:87-89, CTH 406 §17:127-129, CTH 406 §18:130)
- The deity is invoked three times a day, at dawn, midday and evening, with breads broken each time (CTH 406 §12:92-95, CTH 406 §13:96-98)
- In an incubation the patient may see the goddess's body in a dream and she comes and sleeps with him (CTH 406 §18:131-138)
- The patient reports to the practitioner the dreams he sees during the days of invocation (CTH 406 §18:135-136)
- After the goddess has appeared, the man establishes her as a vessel, a standing stone (huwaši) or an image, and the new table becomes her altar (CTH 406 §19:139-146)
- If the sign (dream) does not come, the practitioner keeps on performing the rite (CTH 406 §20:147-149)

**Puliša against plague brought from the enemy, captive and woman in the king's garments, the ringed bull and ewe sent back (CTH 407)**
