- Nature called as witness: Q 99:4 (the earth 'will tell its news' on the Day), 41:20-21 (skins bear witness), 33:72; HB secondary: Deut 32:1, Isa 1:2.

**Destroyed from the dark earth, or protected (CTH 69 §§26-28)** (CTH 69 §26:230-§28:240)
- Twisting the words of the tablet: compare Q 2:75, 4:46, 5:13 (they distort words from their places, taḥrīf) and Q 2:79. The curse 'from the dark earth': compare Q 6:45 ('the last remnant of the wrongdoers was cut off') and 69:8.

**The stolen treaty tablet of Aleppo reissued under seal (CTH 75 §§1-2)** (CTH 75 §1:1-§2:12)
- A covenant tablet lost and written again: compare Moses' tablets broken and replaced, Q 7:145, 7:150, 7:154 ('when his anger subsided he took up the tablets'); HB secondary: Exod 32:19, 34:1 and Deut 10:1-4; also Jer 36:27-32 (the burned scroll rewritten).
- 'Whoever changes it dies': compare Q 2:181 (whoever alters a bequest after hearing it, the sin is on those who alter it) and 69:44-46 (were he to forge sayings against Us, We would cut his aorta); HB secondary: Deut 4:2, Rev 22:18-19.

**The history of Aleppo's kingship and its borders (CTH 75 §§3-14)** (CTH 75 §3:13-§14:50)
- Former great kingship 'filled up' and then destroyed: compare Q 3:26 (God takes kingship from whom He wills) and 17:4-8; the sealed border tablet: compare Q 18:94 and 34:18 (towns set at measured distances). HB secondary: Gen 31:51-52 (boundary heap).

**Mutual helpers, one house; gods of Hatti and Aleppo; witnesses of the tablet (CTH 75 §§15-17)** (CTH 75 §15:61-§17:76)
- 'We and our house shall be one': compare Q 8:72-75 (allies of one another) and 4:33 (those bound to you by oath, give them their share); HB secondary: 1 Kgs 22:4. Named human witnesses at the end of the tablet: compare Q 2:282 (two witnesses, the scribe who writes justly).

**Wiluša's old friendship with Hatti; Muwatalli helps Alakšandu (CTH 76 §§1-5)** (CTH 76 §1:1-§5:66)
- Wiluša (Ilios?) and Alakšandu (Alexandros?) are the much-discussed Trojan names; the Quran has no Trojan story, but the frank 'the matter is long ago, I do not know him' may be compared with Q 20:51-52 (Pharaoh: 'what of the former generations?' Moses: 'their knowledge is with my Lord in a book') and 14:9. HB secondary: Eccl 1:11.

**Alakšandu's chosen son, mutual protection, the fugitive conspirator (CTH 76 §§6-9)** (CTH 76 §6:67-§9:156)
- The overlord accepts a concubine's son as heir if the vassal names him: compare Ishmael and Isaac, Q 37:101-112 and 2:133, and the naming of the heir in 1 Kgs 1; 'I will not abandon you': compare Q 93:3 ('your Lord has not forsaken you') and Deut 31:6.

**Rumours of revolt, 'come alone', no bird oracle, campaigns and the great kings (CTH 76 §§10-14)** (CTH 76 §10:157-§14:210)
- No bird oracle before obeying the summons: compare Q 5:3 and 5:90 (divining by arrows forbidden), 7:131, 27:47 and 36:18-19 (tatayyur, augury of ill omen); HB secondary: Lev 19:26, Deut 18:10.
- 'Do not keep silent about it': compare Q 2:42 and 2:159 (concealing the truth), 4:135 (bear witness even against yourselves).

**Mankind is corrupt; the four kings of Arzawa; borders; fugitives (CTH 76 §§15-18)** (CTH 76 §15:211-§18:290)
- Mankind's corruption makes slander spread: compare Q 12:53 ('the soul commands evil'), 49:6 and 49:12 (avoid suspicion and spying); HB secondary: Gen 8:21 and Jer 17:9.

**The tablet to be read three times a year; the terms are not mutual (CTH 76 §19)** (CTH 76 §19:291-300)
- Periodic public reading of the covenant: compare the recitation and review of the Quran (Q 73:20, 87:6, and the yearly review with Gabriel in hadith) and the command to 'take the tablets with strength', Q 7:145; HB secondary: Deut 31:10-13 (the law read every seventh year at Sukkot) and Neh 8.
- Covenant terms that are not mutual but imposed from above: compare Q 9:1-7 (God's disavowal; 'how can there be a covenant for the idolaters?') and 9:111 (God has bought from the believers their lives).

**The witness gods, with the gods of Wiluša and Appaliuna (CTH 76 §§20-23)** (CTH 76 §20:301-§23:305)
- The sun as 'shepherd of mankind': compare Q 1:2 (rabb al-ʿālamīn) and the Quranic rejection of sun-worship, Q 41:37 ('do not prostrate to the sun or the moon'), 27:24 (Sheba prostrating to the sun), 6:76-79 (Abraham and the heavenly bodies).

**The thousand gods destroy or protect; grow old in the king's hand (CTH 76 §§24-25)** (CTH 76 §24:306-§25:316)
- Long life and old age as covenant blessing: compare Q 16:70 and 36:68 (old age), and the promise of a good life, 16:97; HB secondary: Deut 5:33, 11:21 and Ps 91:16.

**Fragment of a treaty with Annija (CTH 78)** (CTH 78 §1:1-§6:17)
- Compare Q 25:74 ('grant us from our spouses and offspring comfort of eyes') for the offspring formula; too broken for more.

**Tiliura deserted since Ḫantili and resettled (CTH 89 §§1-5)** (CTH 89 §1:1-§5:25)
- A ruined frontier city rebuilt and its exiles brought back: compare Q 2:259 (the town fallen on its roofs, revived after a hundred years) and 17:6; HB secondary: Neh 7:4 and 11:1-2 (Jerusalem repopulated), Ezra 2.

**Rules for the Kaška: not into the city, mixed marriage, slaves, renegades (CTH 89 §§6-20)** (CTH 89 §6:26-§20:138)
- A frontier people kept outside the city, its armed men dismounting at the gate: compare Q 9:28 (the idolaters are impure; let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year) and 9:7-12 on treaties with frontier peoples; HB secondary: Neh 13:16-22 (foreign traders shut out at the gates) and Ezra 9-10.
- Marriage to the hostile people as a route to betrayal: compare Q 2:221 and 60:10-11 (marriage ties with idolaters cut); HB secondary: Deut 7:3-4, Neh 13:23-27.
- The renegade who joins the enemy forfeits his house and family to the town: compare Q 4:89 (if they turn away, seize them) and 5:33; HB secondary: Ezra 10:8 (property forfeited, the man excluded).

**Aziru's tablet; Bentešina deposed and restored; royal marriages (CTH 92 §§1-5)** (CTH 92 §1:1-§5:33)
- A deposed king kept in the great king's land and later restored: compare Joseph raised from prison, Q 12:54-56, and Jehoiachin released, 2 Kgs 25:27-30. Dynastic marriage sealing an alliance: compare 1 Kgs 3:1 (Pharaoh's daughter) and Q 4:23-24 on marriage ties.

**I was a dead man, you brought me back to life: Bentešina asks for a sealed tablet (CTH 92 §§6-9)** (CTH 92 §6:34-§9:71)
- 'I was a dead man and you revived me': compare Q 6:122 and 2:28 ('you were dead and He gave you life'), and the gratitude owed to the one who gives life, 2:152; HB secondary: Ezek 37:1-14 and 2 Sam 9:8 (Mephibosheth: 'a dead dog such as I').
- 'Let the king's life be as dear to you as your own': compare Q 33:6 ('the Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves') and 9:120; HB secondary: 1 Sam 18:1-3 (Jonathan loved David as his own soul).

**Friend and enemy, half-hearted war, mutual aid (CTH 92 §§10-16)** (CTH 92 §10:81-§16:139)
- Compare Q 8:56-58 ('those with whom you made a treaty who break it every time... if you fear treachery, throw it back to them on equal terms') for the treaty-breaking ally; and Q 9:12.

**Kurunta's declaration on his installation in Tarḫuntašša (CTH 96)** (CTH 96 §1:1-§3:22)
- A prince raised by the great king and installed in place of his brother: compare Q 12:21 (Joseph taken into the house of the ʿAzīz, 'perhaps he will benefit us or we adopt him') and 28:9 (Moses in Pharaoh's house).

**Šauškamuwa taken by the hand; Amurru's history of loyalty and defection (CTH 105 §§1-4)** (CTH 105 §1:1-§4:34)
- Allegiance first given 'of our own will' and then withdrawn: compare Q 48:10 and 48:18 (the pledge under the tree), 9:75-77 (those who made a covenant and then broke it), and the apostasy wars after the Prophet's death when tribes said their pledge was to him alone; HB secondary: 1 Kgs 12:16 ('what share have we in David?').
- Hatti and Egypt fighting over Amurru (Qadesh): the Quran's Pharaoh is the archetypal tyrant (Q 28:4); HB secondary: 2 Kgs 23:29 (Necho at Megiddo) for Egypt contesting the Levant.

**Protect the king's line; do not act like Mašturi; be ready to die (CTH 105 §§5-9)** (CTH 105 §5:35-§9:84)
- Loyalty that holds even to the throne of an illegitimate heir: compare Q 4:59 (obey those in authority among you). The vassal ready 'to die with wives and sons' for his lord: compare Q 9:111 (God has bought their lives and wealth), 9:24 (if fathers, sons, wives are dearer to you than God and His Messenger) and 33:23; HB secondary: 2 Sam 15:21 (Ittai: 'whether for death or for life, there will your servant be').

**Slander, the great kings, Ahhiyawa erased, embargo on Assyria (CTH 105 §§10-14)** (CTH 105 §10:85-§14:134)
- An embargo forbidding trade with the enemy: compare the Quraysh trade (Q 106) and the Muslims' blockade of Meccan caravans (Q 8:7, the caravan or the army), and the ban on the idolaters approaching the sanctuary despite loss of trade (Q 9:28); HB secondary: Neh 13:15-22 and Ezek 27 (Tyre's trade).
- 'Be king of Hatti yourself' as the tempter's word: compare Satan's 'shall I lead you to a kingdom that does not decay?' (Q 20:120) and 7:20.

**Ships, fortifying, fragmentary clauses (CTH 105 §§15-20 and §22'''')** (CTH 105 §15:135-§20:167)
- §22'''' (lines 183-192) is a broken fragment placed by the edition after §18; §§19-20 only mention 'the word of My Majesty' and 'you will protect [Hat]ti'. For blockading the enemy's shipping compare Q 2:164 and 30:46 (ships as God's sign) only loosely.

**Witnesses and the curse on whoever alters the tablet (CTH 105 §21)** (CTH 105 §21:168-182)
- Compare Q 2:79 ('woe to those who write the book with their hands and then say: this is from God'), 3:78 and 5:13.

**Šuppiluliuma II's treaty with Talmi-Teššup of Kargamiš, preamble fragments (CTH 122)** (CTH 122 §1:1-§5:10)
- One of the last Hittite treaties; no Quranic parallel beyond the general covenant theme (Q 5:1).

**Fragmentary opening of a loyalty oath: life, a new man, blood (CTH 123 §§1-9)** (CTH 123 §1:1-§9:70)
- 'Become a new man' under oath: compare the convert's new beginning in Q 8:38 (if they desist, what is past is forgiven) and 25:70 (God changes their evil deeds into good); HB secondary: Ezek 18:31 and 36:26 ('a new heart').

**Niḫriya remembered; 'die for the king; death shall be your limit' (CTH 123 §§10-20)** (CTH 123 §10:71-§20:166)
- 'Die beside the king; death shall be your limit' and 'they forced me' are the two poles of Quranic teaching on the faithful and the hypocrite: compare Q 33:23 ('among the believers are men true to what they pledged to God: some have fulfilled their vow by death, some still wait'), 9:111, 3:156-158 and 3:169; for the excuse of compulsion compare Q 16:106 (except one compelled while his heart is firm in faith), 4:97 ('we were oppressed in the land') and 34:31-33 (the weak blame the arrogant). HB secondary: 2 Sam 15:21.
- The king who escaped alone while his man was absent: compare Q 9:25 (Ḥunayn: 'you turned back in retreat') and 3:153 ('when you fled, not looking back at anyone, while the Messenger was calling you from behind').
- 'Bite the dark earth and hold it': compare the believers who stand firm (Q 8:45, 3:200 'be patient, outlast, stand fast').

**The king did not reward me; an engraved word; guardians of the king's life; the king's direst hour (CTH 123 §§21-28)** (CTH 123 §21:167-§28:233)
- 'The king did not reward me, so I withdraw from the oaths': compare Q 9:58 (if given they are pleased, if not they are angry), 9:75-77 (those who vowed and broke it when not enriched) and 22:11 (who worships God on the edge: if good befalls him he is content, if trial, he turns back).
- The king deserted by charioteer, chamberlain and even the gate-dog: compare Q 3:144 (if he dies or is killed will you turn back on your heels?) and 9:38-40 (the two in the cave, 'God is with us'); HB secondary: 2 Sam 15:13-23 (David's flight) and Ps 41:10.
- 'Do not lift your neck': compare Q 26:4 and 17:37 (pride) and 49:2-3 (do not raise your voices above the Prophet's).

**Fragmentary end: frontier service, no hiding of slanderers, oath for the royal seed (CTH 123 §§29-43)** (CTH 123 §29:234-§43:321)
- Report even the lowly man: compare Q 4:135 and 5:8 (justice without partiality); the oath extended to the king's seed: compare Q 2:124 ('My covenant does not include the wrongdoers' among Abraham's seed).

**Late treaty with Kizzuwatna: witnesses and the curse on altering the tablet (CTH 132)** (CTH 132 §1:1-§2:19)
- Compare Q 2:181 and 2:75 on altering what has been heard and written; Deut 4:2.

**Arnuwanda's oath for the men of Išmerika: witnesses and curses (CTH 133 §§1-4)** (CTH 133 §1:1-§4:20)
- Name and seed destroyed: compare Q 19:98 ('do you perceive any of them or hear from them a whisper?') and 69:8; HB secondary: Deut 9:14 and 29:19 ('YHWH will blot out his name from under heaven').

**Report even father and mother; if a city, a house or one man sins (CTH 133 §§5-12)** (CTH 133 §5:21-§12:103)
- Graded punishment by the guilty unit (city, house, single man): compare Abraham's plea for the city, Q 11:74-76 and Gen 18:23-32 ('will you sweep away the righteous with the wicked?'); Q 6:164 and 17:15 ('no bearer bears another's burden'); 17:16 and 28:59 (towns destroyed when their people do wrong); Q 8:25 (a trial that falls not only on the wrongdoers). HB secondary: Deut 13:13-19 (the apostate city put to the sword with its cattle), Josh 7 (Achan and his household), Num 16:22.
- Informing even on father, mother, brother, sister or son: compare Q 58:22 ('you will not find a people who believe ... loving those who oppose God, even if they were their fathers, sons, brothers or kin') and 9:23, 60:4; HB secondary: Deut 13:7-12.

**All Išmerika under oath; the named men and their towns; the curse (CTH 133 §§13-19)** (CTH 133 §13:104-§19:147)
- A whole people sworn with wives and children: compare Q 60:12 (the pledge of the women) and 3:61 (the mubāhala: 'let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women'); HB secondary: Deut 29:9-14 (little ones and wives stand in the covenant) and Neh 10:29.

**The Kuruštama treaty: Hatti and Egypt as allies (CTH 134)** (CTH 134 §1:1-§15:46)
- The Kuruštama people were Hittites who settled in Egyptian territory under a storm-god treaty; compare the Israelites settled in Egypt, Q 12:99-100 and 10:87, and Gen 46-47 as HB secondary. 'Do not go to one another with evil words': compare Q 4:148 and 49:11.

**Treaty with Lab'u and Tunip, opening (CTH 135 §1)** (CTH 135 §1)
- The tablet is Akkadian (the diplomatic language), though listed among the Hittite texts. Compare the treaty frame in Q 9:1-4 (treaties with the polytheists honoured to their term) and Q 8:56.
- Hostage-taking: compare 2 Kgs 14:14.

**Treaty with Tunip, war and booty (CTH 135 §2)** (CTH 135 §2)
- No mercy to kin in battle: compare Q 58:22 (no love for God's enemies 'even if they were their fathers, sons, brothers or kindred') and Q 9:23-24; Deut 13:7-10.
- Booty: contrast Q 8:1 and 8:41 (spoils belong to God and the Messenger, a fifth set aside) with the each-army-keeps-its-own rule here.

**Treaty with Tunip, messengers, fugitives and evil words (CTH 135 §3)** (CTH 135 §3)
- Evil words to be reported: compare Q 4:83 (refer news to the Messenger and those in authority) and Q 49:6 (verify a report brought by a corrupt man).
- Fugitive extradition: contrast Q 60:10 (believing women who emigrate are not to be returned to the unbelievers).

**Šuppiluliuma I's treaty with Mukiš, oath gods and duties (CTH 136)** (CTH 136)
- The primeval gods Alalu and Anu reappear in the Kumarbi cycle; compare the Quran's denial that any former gods share in creation, Q 46:4 and Q 35:40.

**Arnuwanda I's oath with the Kaška, hostages and curses (CTH 137.1 §1-11)** (CTH 137.1 §1:1-§11:61)
- Impure bread as curse: compare Hos 9:3-4 and Ezek 4:13 (Israel eating unclean bread among the nations). The Quran makes idols powerless to feed themselves: Q 22:73, Q 16:73.
- The line LÚ.MEŠ IGI.NU.GÁL 'the blind (men)' (§4:20) in a broken context may refer to blinded captives; compare Judg 16:21.
- Oath-breakers destroyed with their families: contrast Q 6:164 / 35:18 (no bearer bears another's burden).

**Arnuwanda I's oath with the Kaška, the sworn leaders one by one (CTH 137.1 §12-27)** (CTH 137.1 §12:62-§27''':134)
- The Kaška swear tribe by tribe; compare the tribal pledges of Q 48:10, 18 (the pledge under the tree) and the Aqaba pledges.

**Šuppiluliuma II's treaty with Alašija (Cyprus) (CTH 141)** (CTH 141)
- Ruling from sunrise to sunset: compare Dhū l-Qarnayn reaching the setting and the rising of the sun, Q 18:86, 90.
- The tablet read out yearly: compare Deut 31:10-13, 26 (law read every seven years, kept beside the ark); Q 2:63 'hold fast what We gave you and remember what is in it'.
- Blessings for keeping the covenant: Q 7:96 and Q 5:66 (blessings from heaven and earth), Deut 28:4-5.

**Arnuwanda's oath imposed on the elders of Ura (CTH 144)** (CTH 144)
- Not sparing brother or friend: Q 58:22; Deut 13:7-10.
- Iarri is a plague and archer god; compare the plague-arrows of Resheph (Hab 3:5).

**The case against Mita of Paḫḫuwa, his oath and its breach (CTH 146 §1-7)** (CTH 146 W1:1-W7:88)
- Denying having seen the fugitives: compare Cain's 'I do not know; am I my brother's keeper?' (Gen 4:9) and Q 12:17 (the brothers' false account).
- 'Am I not also a man?': compare Pharaoh's 'is not the kingdom of Egypt mine?' (Q 43:51) and Qārūn (Q 28:78).
- Mita of Paḫḫuwa breaks the oath like those who 'break their covenant every time' (Q 8:56) and 'untwist their yarn' (Q 16:92).

**The case against Mita, demands for handing over (CTH 146 §8-14)** (CTH 146 W8:89-W14:123)
- 'Not a thread': Abram refuses from Sodom's king 'not a thread or a sandal-strap' (Gen 14:23); the Quran's 'not wronged by a fatīl (date-stone thread)', Q 4:49, 4:77, 17:71.
- Lines W9-W14 are tiny fragments (Paḫḫuwa, 15 elders, Mita); nothing more can be read.

**The case against Mita, the neighbours' oath and duties (CTH 146 §15-19)** (CTH 146 W15:124-W19:197)
- Fighting those who break their oaths: Q 9:12-13 'fight the leaders of disbelief, for they have no oaths'.

**The case against Mita, the elders' oath, rules of war, colophon (CTH 146 §20-28)** (CTH 146 W20:198-W28:287)
- Truthful report, neither exaggerated nor minimised: Q 49:6, Q 24:15 ('you thought it a small matter, but with God it is great').
- No violation of women or theft after battle: compare Deut 21:10-14 and Deut 20:19; the Quran on the prohibition of ghulūl (embezzling spoils), Q 3:161.

**Instructions for temple personnel, daily bread and the bakers' purity (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 i 1'-20')** (CTH 264 W14:Vs._II_5', CTH 264 W15:Vs._I_1'-Vs._I_20')
- Pig and dog kept from the holy place: compare Isa 66:3, 17 and Q 2:173, 5:3 (swine forbidden). Washed priests in clean garments: Exod 30:17-21, 40:31-32; the Quran's command to purify garments, Q 74:4.

**Instructions for temple personnel: are gods and men of different mind? (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 i 21'-38')** (CTH 264 W15:Vs._I_21'-Vs._I_38')
- The master and slave analogy: Q 30:28 (a parable from yourselves: are your slaves partners in what We provide?), Q 16:71, 16:75-76; and Mal 1:6 ('if I am a master, where is my fear?').
- Family and crops destroyed for one man's offence: Exod 20:5 and Josh 7:24-25 (Achan with sons, daughters, oxen, asses, sheep); rejected in Deut 24:16, Ezek 18:20 and Q 6:164, 35:18, 53:38.

**Instructions for temple personnel, festivals and the god's share (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 i 39'-66')** (CTH 264 W15:Vs._I_39'-Vs._I_66')
- Priests taking the god's portion home: the sons of Eli (1 Sam 2:12-17), Mal 1:12-14; the Quran's charge against those who 'devour people's wealth' in religion, Q 9:34.
- God's portion diverted: Q 6:136 (they assign God a share of crops and cattle, but God's share reaches their partners).

**Instructions for temple personnel: the god says nothing, but does not let go (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 ii 1'-24')** (CTH 264 W15:Vs._II_1'-Vs._II_24')
- Not quick to seize, but never releasing: Q 11:102 ('such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns ... painful, severe'), Q 85:12, Q 35:45 and 16:61 (were God to seize people at once ... but He defers them to a term), Q 3:178 (respite). Also Nah 1:3 ('slow to anger ... will by no means clear the guilty') and Eccl 8:11.
- The silent god who 'does nothing': Zeph 1:12 ('YHWH will not do good, nor will he do evil'), Ps 50:21 ('I kept silent and you thought I was like you'); contrast the idols that do not speak, Q 7:148, 20:89.

**Instructions for temple personnel, the gods' silver and gold (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 ii 25'-51')** (CTH 264 W15:Vs._II_25'-Vs._II_51')
- The temple's metals are holy to God: Josh 6:19 (silver, gold, bronze and iron holy to YHWH), Josh 7 (Achan hides them in his tent and dies with his household). The Quran's ghulūl: Q 3:161.

**Instructions for temple personnel: festivals at their time, the gods' will not man's (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 ii 52'-72')** (CTH 264 W15:Vs._II_52'-Vs._II_72')
- Moving the sacred season: Q 9:36-37 (the postponement, al-nasī', 'an increase in unbelief'); Q 2:189 (new moons are fixed times).
- Excuses of harvest, marriage and journey: Luke 14:18-20 (field, oxen, a wife) and Deut 20:5-7; Q 24:37 (men whom neither trade nor sale diverts from remembering God), Q 62:9-11, 63:9.

**Instructions for temple personnel, sleeping in the temple and the night watch (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 ii 73'-iii 20)** (CTH 264 W15:Vs._II_73'-Rs._III_20)
- Temple guard at night: Num 3:38 and 1 Chr 9:27, 33 (Levites lodge round the house of God at night), Ps 134:1. In the Quran heaven itself is guarded by watchers, Q 72:8-9.
- Bathing after intercourse before approaching the holy: Lev 15:16-18, Exod 19:15, 1 Sam 21:5-6; Q 4:43 and 5:6 (junub must wash before prayer).

**Instructions for temple personnel, the city watch and shame punishment (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 iii 21-34)** (CTH 264 W15:Rs._III_21-Rs._III_34)
- Public shaming by nakedness: Isa 20:2-4, 2 Sam 10:4. The Quran on stripping as shame: Q 7:26-27 (Satan stripped the first pair).

**Instructions for temple personnel, quarrels in the temple and the fire (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 iii 35-54)** (CTH 264 W15:Rs._III_35-Rs._III_54)
- Fire on the altar never to go out (Lev 6:12-13) versus strange fire (Lev 10:1-2); Nadab and Abihu die before YHWH.

**Instructions for temple personnel, the kitchen staff and impurity (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 iii 55-83)** (CTH 264 W15:Rs._III_55-Rs._III_83)
- Impure food and its punishment: Mal 1:7, 12 ('the table of YHWH is polluted') and Mal 2:3 ('I will spread dung on your faces, the dung of your festivals'); Isa 36:12 (eat their own dung, drink their own urine).
- Ritual washing after intercourse: Q 4:43, 5:6; Lev 15:16-18; Lev 22:3-7 (a priest who eats holy food in impurity is cut off).

**Instructions for temple personnel, the gods' ploughmen (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 iv 1-33)** (CTH 264 W15:Rs._IV_1-Rs._IV_33)
- Diverting God's field: Q 6:136 (a share for God and a share for 'partners', and God's share diverted), Q 68:17-33 (the owners of the garden who would give the poor nothing).
- A dead or gored animal sworn before God: Exod 21:28-36, 22:9-12; Gen 31:39 (Jacob bore the loss of the torn).
- First fruits to the house of God before eating the new crop: Exod 23:19, Lev 23:14; compare Q 6:141 ('give its due on the day of its harvest').

**Instructions for temple personnel, the gods' herdsmen, the ordeal and the colophon (CTH 264, KUB 13.4 iv 34-81)** (CTH 264 W15:Rs._IV_34-Rs._IV_81)
- Drinking from the god's vessel as an ordeal: Num 5:11-31 (the water of bitterness) and the golden-calf water, Exod 32:20.
- Exchanging a good animal for a bad: Lev 27:10, 33; Mal 1:8, 13-14 ('cursed is the cheat who has a male in his flock and sacrifices a blemished one'); Q 2:267 ('do not aim at the bad to give from it').

**Illuyanka, Kella's introduction, the word of the purulli festival (CTH 321 §1)** (CTH 321 §1)
- A myth of combat attached to a seasonal festival: compare Enūma eliš at the Babylonian akītu and the 'enthronement' psalms (Ps 93, 74:12-17).

**Illuyanka, first version: the storm god's defeat and Inara's trick (CTH 321 §2-10)** (CTH 321 §2:8-§10:40)
- The storm god and the sea serpent: Isa 27:1 (Leviathan the fleeing, twisting serpent slain), Ps 74:13-14 (the heads of Leviathan crushed), Job 41 (Leviathan drawn out with a hook and cord, 41:1-2), Job 26:12-13, Isa 51:9. The Quran has no divine combat: the great sea creatures are simply created (Q 16:14), and the serpent is Moses' staff, Q 20:20, 7:117.
- Defeat by feasting and drunkenness: Jael and Sisera (Judg 4:19-21, milk then the tent-peg) and Judith 12-13. Compare the unwary feast in Q 5:90-91 (wine as Satan's tool).
- A goddess who takes a mortal to bed for a task: Gilgamesh and Ištar (Gilg SB VI); the angels Hārūt and Mārūt in Q 2:102.

**Illuyanka: Ḫupašiya forbidden to look out of the window (CTH 321 §11-14)** (CTH 321 §11:41-§14:59)
- The look that is forbidden: Lot's wife (Gen 19:17, 26), the Quran's 'let none of you look back' (Q 11:81, 15:65); Orpheus. The single prohibition of Adam in the garden, Q 2:35, 7:19, 20:120-121, and the expulsion after it.
- Remembering wife and children in a divine dwelling: compare Odysseus with Calypso; in the Quran the believers are rejoined with their families in paradise, Q 13:23, 52:21.

**Illuyanka, the goddess's house given to the king; rain at Nerik (CTH 321 §15-18)** (CTH 321 §15:60-§18:73)
- Rain asked of a mountain god: compare Elijah praying for rain on Carmel (1 Kgs 18:41-45) and the Quran's prayer for rain and God who sends rain after despair, Q 71:10-11, 42:28.

**Illuyanka, second version: the stolen heart and eyes and the storm god's son (CTH 321 §19-24)** (CTH 321 §19:74-§24:101)
- The father's son who belongs with the enemy's house and perishes: Noah's son in Q 11:42-46 ('he is not of your family'); the father not sparing his son, Gen 22 / Q 37:102 inverted.
- Heart and eyes taken away: Q 2:7 and 45:23 (God sets a seal on heart and a covering on the eyes); Samson's eyes put out (Judg 16:21).

**Illuyanka, Kella's coda on the gods' ranks, the lot, the land grant and colophon (CTH 321 §25-33)** (CTH 321 §25:102-§33:128)
- First made last and last first: Q 56:3 (the Event 'lowering, raising'), Q 56:10-14; Matt 20:16.
- Lots cast among the divine officiants: Q 3:44 (they cast their pens over who should take charge of Mary), Q 37:141 (Jonah cast lots); Lev 16:8, 1 Chr 24:5.

**Telipinu and the daughter of the Sea (CTH 322.1)** (CTH 322.1)
- The sea that withholds and must be appeased: the Ugaritic Yamm demanding Baal (KTU 1.2 I); God rebuking the sea, Ps 104:6-9, Job 38:8-11. In the Quran the sea is wholly subject to God, Q 45:12, 55:19-20.
- A bride-price paid to the bride's father: Gen 34:12, 1 Sam 18:25; the Quran's mahr owed to the bride herself, Q 4:4.

**Telipinu and the daughter of the Sea, fragment with the anger and hiding (CTH 322.2)** (CTH 322.2)
- As in CTH 324: compare Jonah who 'went off in anger' (dhahaba mughāḍiban), Q 21:87.

**Telipinu and the daughter of the Sea, small fragment (CTH 322.3)** (CTH 322.3)
- Too broken for detailed comparison.

**The vanished Sun god, trapped by the Sea (CTH 323.1 §1-3)** (CTH 323.1 §1:1-§3:28)
- A god or spirit shut in a sealed jar: later Islamic lore of Solomon sealing jinn in bottles (not Quranic); in the Quran Solomon's jinn are 'bound together in fetters', Q 38:37-38. The sun's hiding: Josh 10:12-13 (sun stands still), Amos 8:9.

**The vanished Sun god, Frost seizes the land and the gods (CTH 323.1 §4-8)** (CTH 323.1 §4:29-§8:106)
- Gods sent one after another and failing: compare Enūma eliš II (Ea and Anu turn back) and the angels who cannot bring forth what only God knows, Q 2:31-32.
- Frost and ice as divine weapons: Job 37:9-10, 38:29-30, Ps 147:16-17 ('who can stand before his cold?').
- 'Do they make the dead live again?': Q 2:258 (Abraham and the king: 'my Lord gives life and death'), Q 36:78-79, 22:73.

**The vanished Sun god, the annanna-woman's words and the Sun's allotment (CTH 323.1 §9-12)** (CTH 323.1 §9:107-§12:134)
- Offerings graded by means: Lev 5:7-11, 12:8; Q 65:7 and 2:286 ('God burdens no soul beyond what He has given it').

**The vanished Sun god, the ritual of the tables and three days of offerings (CTH 323.1 §13-22)** (CTH 323.1 §13:135-§22:211)
- Tables set before the god: Exod 25:23-30 (table of the bread of the presence); the table sent down in Q 5:112-115.

**Telipinu myth, first version: the god's anger and departure (CTH 324.1 §1-4)** (CTH 324.1 §1:1-§4:26)
- The god who goes off in anger: Jonah, 'when he went off in anger (idh dhahaba mughāḍiban) and thought We had no power over him', Q 21:87-88; 37:139-144; 68:48 (do not be like the companion of the fish).
- Mothers abandoning their young as the sign of catastrophe: Q 22:2 (every nursing mother forgets her suckling), Q 81:4 (the pregnant camels abandoned); Lam 4:3, 10.

**Telipinu myth, the god hidden in the moor and the dearth (CTH 324.1 §5-6)** (CTH 324.1 §5:27-§6:47)
- Years of drought and dearth as divine withdrawal: Q 7:130 (Pharaoh's people seized with years of famine), Q 12:47-48, Q 2:155; Deut 28:18, 23-24 and Hag 1:6-11 ('you eat but are never satisfied'), Lev 26:26. The Quran's food of hell 'that neither nourishes nor relieves hunger', Q 88:7.
- The hidden god: Isa 45:15, Isa 8:17 ('hiding his face'); Hos 5:15 ('I will return to my place until they seek my face'). Solomon's trial, the body set on his throne in his absence, Q 38:34.

**Telipinu myth, the search by eagle, storm god and bee (CTH 324.1 §7-10)** (CTH 324.1 §7:48-§10:83)
- The bird sent to search and the missing one: the hoopoe found absent and returning with news, Q 27:20-22; the raven sent by God, Q 5:31; Noah's raven and dove, Gen 8:7-12.
- The tiny bee preferred over the mighty: Q 16:68-69 (your Lord inspired the bee); Q 2:26 (God is not ashamed to strike a parable of a gnat).
- The storm god wraps himself and sits down in helplessness: compare 'O you enwrapped' (al-muzzammil, al-muddaththir), Q 73:1, 74:1; Elijah wrapping his face in his mantle, 1 Kgs 19:13.

**Telipinu myth, the god roused in fury and the eagle (CTH 324.1 §11-15)** (CTH 324.1 §11:84-§15:112)
- The wrathful god destroying town and people: compare the ruin of 'Ād and Thamūd, Q 69:6-8, and Jonah's anger at Nineveh's sparing, Jon 4:1-4.

**Telipinu myth, offerings by analogy to sweeten the god (CTH 324.1 §16-23)** (CTH 324.1 §16:113-§23:151)
- Sweetening the angry god: compare the 'soothing aroma' (reaḥ niḥoaḥ) of sacrifice, Gen 8:21, Lev 1:9; in the Quran neither flesh nor blood reaches God, only piety, Q 22:37.
- Oiled paths for the god's return: Isa 40:3 ('prepare the way'), Ps 68:5.

**Telipinu myth, Kamrušepa takes away the god's anger (CTH 324.1 §24-30)** (CTH 324.1 §24:152-§30:195)
- God removes the rage from hearts: Q 9:15 ('and He will remove the rage of their hearts', yudhhib ghayẓa qulūbihim), Q 3:134 (those who restrain anger, al-kāẓimīn al-ghayẓ), Q 7:154 ('when the anger subsided from Moses').
- Asking God to turn back his anger: Ps 85:4-5, Exod 32:11-14 (Moses: 'turn from your burning anger'), Hos 11:9.

**Telipinu myth, the gods under the hawthorn and the anger shut in bronze vessels below (CTH 324.1 §31-37)** (CTH 324.1 §31:196-§37:242)
- Seven gates below: Q 15:44 (Hell has seven gates, to each a portion); Ištar's descent (seven gates).
- What enters does not come out again: Q 23:99-100 (barzakh), Q 32:20 and 22:22 (whenever they wish to leave they are returned); the fire 'closed over them in extended columns', Q 104:8-9, 90:20.
- Vessels of bronze, lead and iron: Q 18:96 (iron and molten copper sealing Gog's barrier), Q 34:12 (the fount of molten copper for Solomon), Q 57:25; Zech 5:7-8 (wickedness shut in a measuring-basket under a lead lid). Solomon's jinn 'bound in fetters', Q 38:37-38.
- God's anger stored up: Deut 32:34 ('laid up in store with me, sealed in my treasuries'), Jer 25:15 (the cup of the wine of wrath).

**Telipinu myth, the god's return and the fleece on the eya-tree (CTH 324.1 §38-40)** (CTH 324.1 §38:243-§40:267)
- The tree of blessing: Q 14:24-25 (the good tree yielding fruit every season), the tree of life (Gen 2:9); the Golden Fleece of Colchis.
- The return of fertility as God's mercy after despair: Q 30:48-50 ('look at the traces of God's mercy, how He revives the earth after its death'), Q 42:28; Hos 2:21-22.

**Telipinu myth, second version: the dearth, the eagle and the bee (CTH 324.2 §1-7)** (CTH 324.2 §1:1-§7:52)
- The bee and its wax/honey as healing: Q 16:68-69 ('from their bellies comes a drink of varied colours in which there is healing for people'). The hoopoe's search, Q 27:20-22.
- The sleeping god roused: Ps 44:23 ('Awake, why do you sleep, O Lord?'), Ps 78:65; contrast Q 2:255 ('neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him').

**Telipinu myth, second version: the analogies, beer, and the iron vessels below (CTH 324.2 §8-21)** (CTH 324.2 §8:53-§21:98)
- Wine that gladdens and makes forget: Prov 31:6-7 ('give strong drink to the one perishing ... let him drink and forget his misery'), Ps 104:15; contrast Q 5:90-91 and the paradisal drink that causes no intoxication, Q 37:47, 56:19.

**The bee is sent, searches and wakes Telipinu (Telipinu myth, third version)** (CTH 324.3 §1:1-§3:19)
- The small creature succeeding where the great gods fail: compare the raven sent to show Cain how to bury (Q 5:31) and the hoopoe who finds what Solomon did not know (Q 27:20-22); the bee itself is honoured as a creature inspired by God (Q 16:68-69).
- The god asleep and roused: contrast Q 2:255 ('neither slumber nor sleep overtakes him') and Ps 121:4; compare the call 'Awake, why do you sleep, O Lord?' (Ps 44:24).

**Woken Telipinu rages and destroys; the gods take counsel and send the eagle (third version)** (CTH 324.3 §4:20-§6:49)
- The awakened god who destroys rivers and cities resembles divine anger let loose on towns overturned (Q 11:82, 'we turned it upside down'; Gen 19:25 'he overthrew those cities').
- The gods' helplessness 'what shall we do?' contrasts with the Quranic God who needs no counsel (Q 2:30-33 is the closest scene of a divine council).

**Anger driven out of Telipinu's limbs; grain, fertility and good rain brought out of the oven (third version)** (CTH 324.3 §7:50-§10:64)
- Rains and winds released from a store (here an oven): compare God's storehouses of rain and wind (Q 15:21-22, 'there is nothing whose storehouses are not with us ... we send the fertilizing winds'; Job 38:22, Jer 10:13).
- The 'evil tongue' and 'envious eyes' removed from the god: compare refuge from the envier (Q 113:5).

**Telipinu returns; house and herds set right; the eya-tree with the fleece (third version)** (CTH 324.3 §11:65-§15:91)
- The fleece hung on the tree that holds long life and progeny: compare Gideon's fleece as a sign (Judg 6:36-40); the tree of blessing beside the god recalls the 'good tree' whose root is firm and branch in heaven (Q 14:24-25).
- Return of the god and restoration of the herds: compare the return of rain and blessing after repentance (Q 71:10-12, 'he will send the sky upon you in showers and help you with wealth and sons'; Joel 2:21-26).

**Offerings and analogic spells to soothe Telipinu (Telipinu myth, fourth version)** (CTH 324.4)
- Eat and drink and be satisfied: compare the formula of eating and drinking in paradise (Q 52:19, 69:24) and the meal set before divine guests (Gen 18:5-8; Q 51:26-27, where the guests do not eat).
- Malt that is not sown: compare the seed that falls and does not sprout in Jesus' parable and the curse 'as malt does not sprout' in Akkadian treaties.

**The gods' counsel over furious Telipinu; the eagle and the sting (CTH 324.7)** (CTH 324.7 §1:1-§6:37)
- The eagle's wings bearing something away: compare 'I bore you on eagles' wings' (Ex 19:4) and Deut 32:11.

**Telipinu's anger sent into the iron vessels of the dark earth; the road of fine oil (CTH 324.7)** (CTH 324.7 §7:38-§9:58)
- Evil sealed below so that it never comes up: compare the sealed pit of the abyss (Rev 20:1-3) and hell whose gates are closed over the damned (Q 90:20, 104:8 'it is closed in upon them'); the lead lid recalls the woman in the ephah shut with a lead cover (Zech 5:7-8).
- What enters the dark earth does not come up: compare 'whoever goes down to Sheol does not come up' (Job 7:9) and Q 23:99-100 (a barrier, barzakh, until the day they are raised).

**Ritual offerings; the god's departure with shoes reversed; the gods' unsatisfying feast and the search (CTH 324.8)** (CTH 324.8)
- A feast at which the guests eat and are not satisfied: compare the covenant curse 'you shall eat and not be satisfied' (Lev 26:26, Hos 4:10, Mic 6:14) and the food of hell that 'neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger' (Q 88:7).

**Fragmentary opening speeches, the iron dagger and the Moon god (Storm god mugawar, CTH 325)** (CTH 325 §1:1-§4:33)
- The old man and old woman (ŠU.GI) as ritual figures: compare the old woman Abraham's wife and old husband told of a son (Q 11:72).

**The Storm god departs; mist, choking, rejected young, barrenness and drought (CTH 325)** (CTH 325 §5:34-§8:53)
- Barrenness of fields, herds and wombs when God withdraws: compare Joel 1:10-20 (grain destroyed, herds of cattle perplexed, the beasts of the field cry to God), Hos 9:11-14 (no birth, no pregnancy, no conception), and Jer 14:5 (the doe abandons her newborn because there is no grass).
- Quranic counterpart: drought and loss of crops and offspring sent as a test or warning (Q 7:130, 'we seized Pharaoh's people with years of drought and shortage of fruits'; Q 2:155); the earth reviving only when God sends rain (Q 30:50).
- The god who departs and is sought: compare Hos 5:15-6:3 ('I will return to my place until they seek my face ... he will come to us like the rain').
- The departure in anger of one on whom the world depends: compare Dhul-Nun (Jonah), 'when he went off in anger' (idh dhahaba mughadiban) and thought We would not constrain him (Q 21:87-88), and Jonah 4:1-9 (Jonah's anger, the withered plant).

**The gods' unsatisfying feast, the eagle's search, and the quarrel over whose sin it was (CTH 325)** (CTH 325 §9:54-§12:90)
- 'My son is not here' and the empty place at the feast: compare the trial of Solomon, on whose throne 'we cast a body (jasad)' until he turned back (Q 38:34), and the god's absence from his seat.
- Searching for the sinner behind a public disaster: compare Jonah's shipmates casting lots to find on whose account the storm came (Jonah 1:7) and Q 37:141; Achan identified by lot (Josh 7).
- 'You alone sinned' / 'I did not sin': the shifting of blame recalls Adam and Eve (Gen 3:12-13), and its Quranic answer that each soul bears its own burden (Q 6:164, 53:38).

**The father goes down to the fate-goddesses and Hannahanna, who reassures him and sends the bee (CTH 325)** (CTH 325 §13:91-§15:130)
- A goddess reassures a frightened petitioner with 'do not fear': compare the angels' 'do not fear' to Abraham (Q 51:28) and to Lot (Q 29:33), and God's to Moses (Q 20:68).

**The Storm god's instructions, the 'water of turning', and the return of thriving to the father's house (CTH 325)** (CTH 325 §16:131-§20:156)
- 'My son has come back!' and the feast in the father's house: compare the father's joy at the return of the lost son (Luke 15:24) and Jacob's revival at news of Joseph (Gen 45:27-28; Q 12:96).

**Kamrusepa takes the anger from the Storm god's body; firewood, fire and the water-pipe analogies; assembly under the hawthorn (CTH 325)** (CTH 325 §21:157-§26:195)
- Anger 'let go' (tarna) and not to flow back: compare the prayer that God's wrath be turned back (Ps 85:4-6; Ex 32:12 'turn from your burning anger') and the Quranic God whose mercy outstrips his wrath (Q 7:156).
- Sin taken off the body and carried away: compare the scapegoat bearing the people's iniquities (Lev 16:21-22).

**A god builds a lasting oven; the golden window of the clouds; soapwort, pebbles and the queen's herbs (CTH 325)** (CTH 325 §27:196-§30:216)
- The golden window of the clouds: compare the 'windows of heaven' opened for rain (Gen 7:11; Mal 3:10) and the gates of the sky opened with pouring water (Q 54:11).

**The house lets the anger go; seven doors and the cauldrons of the dark earth; the Storm god returns and the eya-tree fleece (CTH 325)** (CTH 325 §31:217-§39:274)
- Return and blessing on the house: compare God's 'return' (tawwab) to those who repent and the blessing of rain, sons and gardens (Q 71:10-12).
- The doorkeeper and seven doors of the underworld: compare 'hell has seven gates, for each gate a portion of them' (Q 15:44).

**The Storm god of Queen Asmunikal departs with shoes reversed; mist, smoke and choking (CTH 326)** (CTH 326 §1:1-§3:26)
- A personal god of a queen who withdraws and must be appeased: compare the god who 'turned away' from a ruler (1 Sam 16:14, 28:15-16) and the Quranic reminder that God turns to whom he wills (Q 9:118).

**The Storm god of Asmunikal returns; the lamb's fleece and its mild message; the queen's petition; analogies of firewood and the pot (CTH 326)** (CTH 326 §4:27-§10:75)
- The queen as a 'mild message of the lamb' before her god: compare the offering of a lamb as a 'pleasing odour' (Lev 1:9-10) and the ram that ransomed Abraham's son (Q 37:107).
- The bad cloud that comes and goes: compare the cloud the people of 'Ad took for rain but which bore punishment (Q 46:24).

**The Storm god of Queen Harapsili: choking, invocation, return, lamb's fleece and petition (CTH 327.1)** (CTH 327.1)
- 'Look on your maidservant with good eyes': compare Hannah's 'if you will look on the affliction of your maidservant' (1 Sam 1:11) and Mary's 'he has looked on the lowliness of his servant' (Luke 1:48); in the Quran Zechariah's and Mary's mother's prayers for offspring (Q 3:35-38, 19:4-6).

**The Storm god of the scribe Pirwa departs and returns (CTH 328)** (CTH 328)
- A scribe's personal god who departs and returns to his house: compare the personal relationship with God of the Quranic and biblical petitioner, and the three-day invocation with the three days of Jonah in the fish (Jonah 1:17) or of Zechariah's sign of silence (Q 3:41, 19:10).
- The departure in anger: compare Dhul-Nun (Jonah) 'when he went off in anger' (idh dhahaba mughadiban, Q 21:87) and Jonah fleeing from the presence of the LORD (Jonah 1:3).

**The eye diseases are taken from a child and passed down through palms, fingers and nails to the dark earth, the Sun and the copper cauldrons of the sea (Storm god in Lihzina, CTH 331.1)** (CTH 331.1 §1:1-§11:59)
- Healing of eyes and the body made 'as before': compare Jesus healing the blind (Q 3:49, 5:110: 'you healed the blind and the leper by my permission') and Jacob's sight restored (Q 12:93, 96; Gen 48:10 for his failing eyes).
- Disease cast into the sea: compare the demons sent into the swine that rush into the sea (Mark 5:13) and God casting sins 'into the depths of the sea' (Mic 7:19).

**The Storm god spends eight years in Lihzina; his sons meet him on the road and ask where he was (CTH 331.1)** (CTH 331.1 §12:60-§17:88)
- A long absence that seems short and a question 'where were you?': compare the man who slept a hundred years and is asked 'how long have you stayed?' (Q 2:259) and the sleepers of the cave (Q 18:19).
- Eight years in a foreign town working and harvesting: compare Jacob's years of service for Laban (Gen 31:41) and Moses' eight or ten years in Midian (Q 28:27).

**The queen's Storm god sought by the eagle and then by the bee, who finds him in the grove of Lihzina (mugawar fragment 1, CTH 332.1)** (CTH 332.1)
- The bee's success after the eagle's failure: compare the hoopoe in Q 27:20-22 ('I have encompassed what you have not encompassed').

**The woken Storm god's complaint, washing with the water of turning, the iron sky, and the return to the house (mugawar fragment 2, CTH 332.2)** (CTH 332.2)
- The sky of iron above the god: compare the covenant curse 'your heavens over your head shall be bronze and the earth under you iron' (Deut 28:23; Lev 26:19).

**Analogies of flower, fig, nut, raisin and olive; 'incline your ear'; the slanderer of the king; highest of the high (mugawar fragment 3, CTH 332.3)** (CTH 332.3 §6:24-§17:78)
- Fig and olive side by side as emblems of good held within: compare the oath 'by the fig and the olive' (Q 95:1) and the blessed olive tree whose oil almost glows (Q 24:35); the fig and vine of peace (Mic 4:4).
- 'Incline your ear and hear': compare Ps 17:6, 2 Kgs 19:16, Dan 9:18; and the Quranic God who hears the supplicant (Q 2:186, 3:38 'you are the hearer of prayer').
- Good word versus bad word: compare the parable of the good word like a good tree and the bad word like a bad tree uprooted (Q 14:24-26).
- 'Highest of the high': compare the divine name al-A'la, 'the Most High' (Q 87:1, 92:20) and 'God of gods and Lord of lords' (Deut 10:17).
- The slanderer of the king punished by the god: compare 'do not curse a ruler of your people' (Ex 22:28) and Q 104:1 ('woe to every slanderer and backbiter').

**Fragment: 'as ... is sweet, let the Storm god be sweet' (CTH 332.6)** (CTH 332.6)
- Sweet as honey: compare God's words sweeter than honey (Ps 19:10, 119:103).

**Quenching analogy, the shaggy ram, soothing with food, 'highest of the high', purification and the sheep driven out (mugawar fragment 7, CTH 332.7)** (CTH 332.7)
- A live animal driven out, not slaughtered, at the close of a rite of appeasement: compare the scapegoat sent alive into the wilderness (Lev 16:10, 21-22) and, by contrast, the ransom ram of Abraham, which is slaughtered (Q 37:107).

**The midwife's rite; Anzili and Zukki depart in anger with shoes and veil reversed; household choked (CTH 333)** (CTH 333 §1:1-§9:54)
- The goddess who goes out in anger: compare Dhul-Nun's angry departure (Q 21:87) and Jonah 4:1-5.
- Garments put on wrongly as a sign of disorder: compare the reversal and rending of garments in mourning (Gen 37:34; 2 Sam 13:19).

**Fragrant woods burned; Anzili and Zukki return; the household set right; Anzili eats everything; the salt-lick analogy for the patron's life (CTH 333)** (CTH 333 §10:55-§18:104)
- Salt that never runs out as a figure for lasting life: compare the 'covenant of salt' forever (Num 18:19; 2 Chr 13:5).
- The 'child of mortality' (dandukešnaš DUMU) for a human being: compare 'son of man' (Ps 8:4) and 'every soul shall taste death' (Q 3:185).

**Hannahanna's anger sent to the bronze vessels; the water-pipe and hawthorn analogies; her departure and the choked land; her joyful return (CTH 334.1.1)** (CTH 334.1.1)
- The mother goddess departing in anger and the land's mothers ceasing to care for their young: compare Isa 49:15 ('can a woman forget her nursing child?') and the Hour when 'every nursing mother will forget her suckling' (Q 22:2).
- Hawthorn white in spring and red in summer: compare the colour-change imagery of sins 'scarlet ... white as snow' (Isa 1:18).

**Let the fate goddess be sweet; sons and daughters for king and queen; raisin and olive (CTH 334.1.3)** (CTH 334.1.3)
- The olive among the analogies: compare Q 95:1 and 24:35.

**Hannahanna's anger burned like firewood; Hapantali's soapwort and pebbles; the queen of the spring's pure water and the cloud that drives out the anger (CTH 334.2.1)** (CTH 334.2.1)
- Water poured on hot stones and a cloud that rises: compare the cloud and the water that 'came up from the earth and watered the ground' (Gen 2:6) and God who 'sends the winds that raise clouds' (Q 30:48).

**Hannahanna invoked with bread and libation; laden tables and nine dishes; the eya-tree and the lamb's message (CTH 334.2.2)** (CTH 334.2.2)
- Tables set right and left and a beaker for the god: compare the table of showbread before YHWH (Ex 25:30) and the table sent down from heaven to Jesus' disciples (Q 5:112-115).
- 'Terrible one, become gracious': compare the paired divine attributes of severity and mercy (Q 15:49-50; 40:3 'severe in punishment, possessor of bounty') and Ex 34:6-7.

**Hannahanna invoked; galaktar, parhuena, fig, liti, raisin and olive; 'let go the anger'; pebbles quenched, the cart held back, firewood burned (CTH 334.4)** (CTH 334.4)
- Fig and olive, raisin and wine held within: compare Q 95:1 ('by the fig and the olive') and Q 80:27-31 (grain, grapes, olives, palms among God's provisions).
- Words that hold back divine anger: compare Moses' intercession that turns back God's wrath (Ex 32:11-14; Ps 106:23) and Abraham's pleading for the people of Lot (Q 11:74-76).

**Hannahanna soothed; mother, cow and ewe recognise their young; the deity recognises king and queen; the eya-tree fleece (CTH 334.6)** (CTH 334.6)
- The deity 'recognises' (kaneš-) the king again, as the ewe her lamb: compare God's acknowledging (yada') his chosen (Amos 3:2) and turning in mercy to the repentant (Q 2:37).

**Galaktar, parhuena, fig with a thousand seeds, olive, raisins and samama-fruit set out 'for invocation' of Hannahanna (CTH 334.7)** (CTH 334.7)
- Q 95:1-3 swears by the fig and the olive, Mount Sinai and 'this secure land'; here fig and olive stand for the land of Hatti held securely in the deity's heart.

**The searchers comb forests, roads, currents and springs; the bee, holding honey within, goes through all places and finds the god asleep in a vineyard (CTH 335.2)** (CTH 335.2)
- The god asleep in a vineyard: compare Noah drunk and asleep in his vineyard (Gen 9:20-21); and contrast Q 2:255.
- The bee 'goes through all places' holding honey within: compare Q 16:68-69 ('take your houses in the mountains and trees ... follow the ways of your Lord made easy; from their bellies comes a drink of varying colours').

**The deity's soul glows like fire, quenched with water; dry malt; Hapantali's soapwort and pebbles; pure water, the rising vapour drives out the anger; the hawthorn (CTH 335.4)** (CTH 335.4)
- Anger like burning fire quenched with water: compare 'a soft answer turns away wrath' (Prov 15:1) and the hadith-like Quranic counsel to restrain anger (Q 3:134, 'those who restrain anger and pardon people').

**Fig, raisin, olive, leti and shammamma laid out for the deity; the fleece holding thriving of cattle and sheep, long years, health and the mild lamb (CTH 335.6.1)** (CTH 335.6.1)
- The god holding the king's 'thousands' within like the fig its seeds: compare the promise of countless offspring (Gen 22:17) and the 'thousands' of Israel (Num 10:36).

**Liver and heart on thin bread; cattle and sheep choke; mother, cow and ewe do not care for their young; the deity returns joyfully to Hatti and his temple (CTH 335.7.1)** (CTH 335.7.1)
- Mothers no longer caring for their children: compare the Hour when 'every nursing mother will neglect what she nursed' (Q 22:2) and Lam 4:3-4, 10.

**Invocation; as (the cow takes back) the calf, the deity cares for him again in goodwill, with life and vigour; gold (CTH 335.12)** (CTH 335.12)
- The deity taking back the king as a cow her calf: compare God's compassion like a mother's (Isa 49:15, 66:13) and the divine name al-Rahim from rahim 'womb'.

**The Storm god's body purged limb by limb; restored, he goes up to heaven; the eagle's wing, the sieve of a thousand holes, Kamrusepa's rams; go to Zalpa by the sea (CTH 335.17)** (CTH 335.17 §1:1-§12:64)
- The god restored 'as before' who goes up to heaven and takes his seat: compare God who 'then established himself on the throne' (Q 7:54) and the ascension of Elijah (2 Kgs 2:11) or of Jesus (Q 4:158).
- Evil sent away to the sea: compare Mic 7:19 (sins cast into the depths of the sea).

**Hallara's cloud window; the mother goddess brings the souls out of the river into the cloud; Kamrusepa, Telipinu; the oven; Sulinkatti kills a pig; the vessel with lid of lead whence nothing returns; sweet bread (CTH 335.17)** (CTH 335.17 §13:65-§25:132)
- Souls drawn up out of the river and laid in a cloud: compare God taking the souls (Q 39:42) and the spirit hovering over the waters (Gen 1:2).
- A pig killed in the rite contrasts sharply with the biblical and Quranic prohibition of swine (Lev 11:7; Q 2:173, 5:3, 6:145).

**Inara myth with ritual for Zababa; Hannahanna's bee; Kamrušepa's words (CTH 336.1)** (CTH 336.1)
- The bee as divinely guided creature: compare Q 16:68-69 (your Lord inspired the bee). The bird or insect sent on an errand: compare the hoopoe, Q 27:20-22.
- Ascribing a spell to a deity's words: contrast Q 2:102 (magic taught by devils, not by Solomon) and Q 113-114 (refuge sought with God alone).

**Hannahanna, the bee, the fleece and the three springs (CTH 336.2)** (CTH 336.2)
- Springs made by a deity: compare Q 2:60 (twelve springs from the rock) and Q 19:24-25 (stream under Mary). The fleece: compare Judg 6:36-40.

**Hannahanna promises Inara a land and a husband; the storm god sends the bee (CTH 336.3)** (CTH 336.3)
- A father's anxiety for a lost child: compare Q 12:84-86 (Jacob grieving for Joseph).

**Hannahanna sends the bee; 'take wax' (CTH 336.4)** (CTH 336.4)
- Compare Q 16:69 (from the bees' bellies a drink in which there is healing).

**Hannahanna makes a stone a nurse; Zababa sent to war year by year (CTH 336.5)** (CTH 336.5)
- Kings going out to war at the turn of the year: compare 2 Sam 11:1.

**Weapons grow blunt; the nurse's city destroyed (CTH 336.6)** (CTH 336.6)
- Compare Isa 1:3 (the ox knows its owner).

**The Queen of the gods asks who will bring back Pirwa's eagle (CTH 337.1)** (CTH 337.1)
- A king offering reward to whoever brings what is lost: compare Q 12:72 (a camel-load for whoever returns the king's cup).

**Pirwa grows drowsy (CTH 337.2)** (CTH 337.2)
- Diverges from Q 2:255 (neither slumber nor sleep overtakes Him) and Ps 121:4.

**Ašertu tries to seduce the storm god; he tells Elkunirša (CTH 342.1.1)** (CTH 342.1.1)
- The master's wife and the refused youth: compare Q 12:23-29 and Gen 39:7-20. Here the youth goes to the husband himself, the reverse of Joseph's master hearing the wife's accusation.
- Elkunirša renders West Semitic 'El, creator of earth' (ʾl qn ʾrṣ): compare Gen 14:19, 22. Ašertu = Asherah, cf. 1 Kgs 15:13.

**Elkunirša gives the storm god to Ašertu; Ištar overhears and warns him; purification (CTH 342.1.2)** (CTH 342.1.2)
- The night plot overheard and the victim warned: compare Q 28:20 (a man runs to warn Moses of the plot) and 1 Sam 19:11.

**Ritual offering to Kunirša (CTH 342.1.3)** (CTH 342.1.3)
- Short years versus long life as divine gift: compare Q 35:11 (no one's life is lengthened or shortened but it is in a Book).

**Stars of Ištar and Kumarbi summoned; may all lands incline to the king (CTH 342.2.1)** (CTH 342.2.1)
- Stars as gods who eat and drink: contrast Q 6:76-79 (Abraham and the setting star) and Q 41:37 (prostrate not to sun or moon).

**Washing rite; Zababa; Elkunirša, lord of the dream, son of the dark earth (CTH 342.2.2)** (CTH 342.2.2)
- God as giver of bad dreams and short days: contrast Q 12:43-49 (dreams interpreted by God's gift) and Ps 90:10.

**Stars of Kumarbi, Išḫara and NIN.É.GAL summoned (CTH 342.2.3)** (CTH 342.2.3)
- Compare Q 53:49 (He is the Lord of Sirius) against star-cults.

**Short years; wolf, fox, snake, scorpion held out (CTH 342.2.4)** (CTH 342.2.4)
- Wolf, snake and scorpion as dangers sent: compare Deut 8:15; Q 12:13 (fear the wolf will eat him).

**Stars of all the gods; the charioteers purified of sorcery (CTH 342.2.5)** (CTH 342.2.5)
- Ritual cleansing of the army: compare Num 31:19-24.

**LAMMA's arrows strike Ištar; he takes the storm god's reins (CTH 343.1 §1-3)** (CTH 343.1 §1:1-§3:39)
- Rival gods fighting among themselves: compare Q 23:91 (each god would have taken away what he created, and some would have overcome others).

**LAMMA king in heaven nine years; a golden age (CTH 343.1 §4-5)** (CTH 343.1 §4:40-§5:63)
- Rivers of wine and paradise abundance: compare Q 47:15 (rivers of wine delightful to drinkers) and Joel 4:18 (the mountains drip sweet wine).
- No wolves under the good king: compare Isa 11:6-9 and Isa 65:25.

**LAMMA grows hostile, offerings cease, Ea and Kumarbi depose him (CTH 343.1 §6-9)** (CTH 343.1 §6:64-§9:120)
- A god-king who withholds worship from the gods and is overthrown: compare Q 21:22 (were there gods besides God, heaven and earth would be ruined) and Q 17:42-43.
- Gods deposed for misrule: compare Ps 82:1-7 (the gods judged, to die like men).

**The storm god and Ninurta punish LAMMA (CTH 343.1 §10-17)** (CTH 343.1 §10:121-§17:159)
- The overthrown rebel: compare Isa 14:12-15 and Q 7:13 (Iblis: get down, it is not for you to be arrogant here).

**LAMMA and the elder gods; Ea to Kumarbi (CTH 343.2)** (CTH 343.2)
- Compare Q 21:22.

**Nara rouses; Ištar to LAMMA the king (CTH 343.3.1, 343.3.2)** (CTH 343.3.1, CTH 343.3.2)
- Compare Q 17:42.

**LAMMA fragments - 'let us go up and make a king in heaven' (CTH 343.4-6)** (CTH 343.4, CTH 343.5, CTH 343.6)
- 'Father of the gods' as a title: contrast Q 112:3 and Q 6:101.

**Song of Going Forth - the primeval gods called to listen (CTH 344 §1-2)** (CTH 344 §1:1-§2:8)
- Gods with fathers and mothers: contrast Q 112:3 (He begets not, nor is begotten) and Q 6:101 (how could He have a son when He has no consort?).

**Alalu, Anu, Kumarbi - nine-year reigns and revolts of the cupbearer (CTH 344 §2-4)** (CTH 344 §2:9-§4:34)
- Kingship in heaven seized by violence among gods: compare Q 23:91 (no god with Him, else some would overcome others), Q 17:42-43 (they would seek a way to the Lord of the Throne), Q 21:22.
- Gods cast down into the earth: compare Ps 82:6-7 and Isa 14:12-15.

**Kumarbi bites off Anu's manhood and is made pregnant with three gods (CTH 344 §5-7)** (CTH 344 §5:35-§7:57)
- A god pregnant with gods and gods born of gods: the sharpest contrast to Q 112:3 and Q 19:88-92 (heavens almost burst that they ascribe a son to the Merciful).
- Compare Hesiod's Kronos and Ouranos, and Gen 9:20-25 (a son's offence against his father's nakedness).

**Kumarbi's pregnancy; the unborn gods debate how to come out; the storm god's birth from the skull (CTH 344 §8-13)** (CTH 344 §8:58-§13:118)
- Gods with divided parentage and endowments: contrast Q 6:100-101 (they ascribe to Him sons and daughters without knowledge).
- Wisdom born from a god's head: compare Athena from Zeus; Prov 8:22-25 (Wisdom 'brought forth' before the hills).

**Kumarbi demands the son to eat him, breaks his teeth on the diorite; a stone cult is founded (CTH 344 §14-16)** (CTH 344 §14:119-§16:169)
- A stone set up and given sacrifices: compare Gen 28:18-22 (Bethel stone anointed), Gen 31:45-52, and the Quran's polemic against stones set up for worship (al-anṣāb), Q 5:3, 5:90.
- The idol cannot help its worshippers: Q 22:73, Q 26:72-73.

**The storm god, the Aranzah and Mt Kanzura come out (CTH 344 §17-18)** (CTH 344 §17:170-§18:185)
- A male god giving birth 'like a woman': contrast Q 3:47 and Q 19:20 (Mary: how shall I have a son?), where conception is by God's word alone.

**Anu and the storm god plot against Kumarbi; the storm god boasts; Šeri warns (CTH 344 §19-21)** (CTH 344 §19:186-§21:234)
- A god boasting no one can fight him: compare Q 79:24 (Pharaoh: I am your lord most high) and Q 28:38.

**Ea angered at being cursed; the melting pot; the wagon (CTH 344 §22-26)** (CTH 344 §22:235-§26:257)
- Curses rebounding: compare Ps 109:17-18 and Q 35:43 (the evil plot encompasses only its authors).

**Ea counts the months; the Earth bears two sons; gifts to the messenger (CTH 344 §27-28)** (CTH 344 §27:258-§28:285)
- Gestation counted by months: compare Q 46:15 (thirty months of bearing and weaning) and Q 31:14; Job 39:2.

**Colophon of the Song of Going Forth, tablet one (CTH 344 §29-31)** (CTH 344 §29:286-§31:296)
- Faithful transmission of a worn text: compare Q 15:9 (We sent down the Reminder and We guard it).

**Ullikummi I - proem; Kumarbi plans a rival and mates with the rock (CTH 345.I.1 §1-3)** (CTH 345.I.1 §1:1-§3:33)
- A god begetting a monstrous offspring: compare Gen 6:1-4 (sons of God and the Nephilim) and contrast Q 112:3.
- The father of the gods plotting evil: compare Q 21:26-29 (they say the Merciful has taken a son; glory be to Him).

**Impaluri, the Sea's invitation and the feast (CTH 345.I.1 §4-6)** (CTH 345.I.1 §4:34-§6:87)
- A host's feast for a god: compare Gen 18:1-8; contrast Q 51:24-28.

**The stone child is born, named Ullikummi and destined to destroy the storm god; hidden from the gods (CTH 345.I.1 §7-9)** (CTH 345.I.1 §7:88-§9:128)
- The would-be usurper of heaven: compare Isa 14:13-14 (I will ascend to heaven, above the stars of El) and Q 40:36-37 (Pharaoh's tower to reach the ways of heaven).
- A child hidden from a hostile king: compare Q 28:7 and Exod 2:2-3, reversed.

**The Irširra gods carry Ullikummi to Enlil and set him on Upelluri's shoulder; he grows out of the sea to heaven (CTH 345.I.1 §10-18)** (CTH 345.I.1 §10:129-§18:204)
- Growth reaching heaven: compare Gen 11:4 (a tower with its top in heaven) and Q 40:36-37.
- The giant who bears the world: contrast Q 2:255 (His Throne extends over heavens and earth and guarding them does not weary Him), Q 35:41, Q 13:2 (heavens raised without pillars you can see).

**The sun god sees Ullikummi and comes to the storm god; he will not sit, eat or drink (CTH 345.I.1 §19-24)** (CTH 345.I.1 §19:205-§24:253)
- A heavenly visitor who will not touch the food until his message is out: compare Q 11:69-70 and Q 51:24-28 (Abraham's guests do not eat), Gen 24:33 (I will not eat until I have told my errand).

**The sun god eats and returns to heaven; the storm god takes counsel (CTH 345.I.2 §1-5 to 5:37)** (CTH 345.I.2 §1:1-§5:37)
- Compare Gen 18:8 (the visitors eat) against Q 11:70.

**Ištar meets her brothers; on Mt Ḫazzi the storm god sees the stone and weeps (CTH 345.I.2 §5:38-§6)** (CTH 345.I.2 §5:38-§6:77)
- Mount Ḫazzi is Ṣapanu / Mons Casius: compare Ps 48:3 (Zion, the heights of Zaphon) and Isa 14:13 (the mount of assembly in the far north).

**Ištar sings to the deaf and blind stone; the wave sends her away (CTH 345.I.2 §7-10)** (CTH 345.I.2 §7:78-§10:112)
- The stone that neither hears nor sees: compare Q 7:195-198, Q 19:42 (why worship what neither hears nor sees?), Q 2:18 (deaf, dumb, blind), Ps 115:4-8.
- Ishtar seducing a monster from the sea: the Hedammu song (CTH 348) has the fuller version; it is not in this chunk.

**The storm god orders his bulls and storm weapons prepared; he arms for battle (CTH 345.I.2 §11-15)** (CTH 345.I.2 §11:113-§15:169)
- God riding the storm with lightning as weapon: compare Ps 18:8-16, Ps 104:3-4; Q 13:12-13 (the thunder glorifies Him, He sends thunderbolts).

**First battle - seventy gods fall into the sea; Ullikummi reaches 9000 miles and shuts in Ḫebat (CTH 345.I.3.1 §1-6)** (CTH 345.I.3.1 §1:1-§6:61)
- The heavens torn and rolled up: compare Isa 34:4 and Q 21:104 (We roll up the heaven like a scroll), Q 81:11.
- Seventy gods: compare the seventy sons of Athirat at Ugarit and Deut 32:8 (nations by the number of the sons of God).

**Ḫebat nearly falls from the roof; 'there will be no king in heaven'; to Ea in Abzuwa (CTH 345.I.3.1 §7-13)** (CTH 345.I.3.1 §7:62-§13:149)
- 'No king in heaven' as the outcome of divine rivalry: compare Q 21:22 and Q 23:91; contrast Q 67:1 (Blessed is He in whose hand is the kingship).
- Prostration in graded numbers before a god: compare Gen 33:3 (seven times) and Q 12:100 (they fell down prostrate before him).

**Ea, Enlil and Upelluri; the saw that cut heaven from earth (CTH 345.I.3.1 §14-24)** (CTH 345.I.3.1 §14:150-§24:238)
- Heaven and earth once joined and cut apart: compare Q 21:30 (the heavens and earth were a joined mass, ratq, and We parted them) and Gen 1:6-8.
- Contrast the burdened world-bearer with Q 2:255 (the Kursi encompasses heavens and earth; guarding them does not weary Him), Q 35:41 and Q 22:65 (He holds back the sky from falling).

**Ea has seen the dead; the gods bellow; battle with the cut-off Ullikummi and his boast (CTH 345.I.3.1 §25-34)** (CTH 345.I.3.1 §25:239-§34:301)
- The arrogant one who says 'I will ascend to heaven': Isa 14:13-15 and Q 40:36-37; his fall 'to the depths of the pit' (Isa 14:15). The Hittite end is lost.
- The dead in darkness like dust: compare Q 23:99-100 (a barrier until the Day they are raised) and Job 10:21-22.

**Ullikummi recalls Kumarbi's plan (CTH 345.I.3.2)** (CTH 345.I.3.2)
- Compare Isa 14:13-14.

**Ištar with her instruments goes from Nineveh to the sea (CTH 345.I.4)** (CTH 345.I.4)
- Compare Q 7:195.

**Aštabi, the terrible god (CTH 345.I.5)** (CTH 345.I.5)
- Compare Q 21:22.

**Small Ullikummi fragments - the diorite, Impaluri, spindles of heaven (CTH 345.I.6-10)** (CTH 345.I.6, CTH 345.I.7, CTH 345.I.8, CTH 345.I.9, CTH 345.I.10)
- No further hint: too broken.

**Kumarbi myth fragment - the merchant, silver and gold, Kumarbi's curse (CTH 346.1)** (CTH 346.1)
- A curse like a dried tree: compare Ps 1:3-4 and Q 14:26 (a bad word like a bad tree uprooted).

**'The dark earth bore me' - a god's boast of his endowments (CTH 346.2)** (CTH 346.2)
- 'Father of gods and men' begetting: the exact antithesis of Q 112:3. Compare also Q 72:3 (He has taken neither consort nor son).

**Mukišanu reports; Kumarbi rises; the gods to Mt Šepiša (CTH 346.3)** (CTH 346.3)
- Compare 1 Kgs 22:19 and Q 37:8 (the exalted assembly).

**The sun god feasted by the Sea; the Sea weeps, bitten by creatures (CTH 346.4)** (CTH 346.4)
- The Sea as a person who weeps and is fed by gods: contrast Q 55:19-20 (the two seas with a barrier) and Q 52:6 (the swelling sea) as created signs.

**Kumarbi counts the months; Mt Wašitta in labour after a stranger lay with her (CTH 346.5)** (CTH 346.5)
- Pregnancy unexpected and unfated: compare Q 19:20-21 (Mary: no man has touched me) and Q 11:72 (Sarah: shall I bear, an old woman?).
- Mountains in labour: compare Ps 90:2 (before the mountains were born) and Q 33:72 (the mountains refused the trust).

**Small Kumarbi fragments - ornaments and a garland; Kumarbi washed; the Sea (CTH 346.6, 346.7, 346.8)** (CTH 346.6, CTH 346.7, CTH 346.8)
- No firm hint; compare Q 5:6 on ritual washing only by contrast.

**The Sea's floods rise to the stars; the gods bring tribute to the Sea; Ištar summoned (CTH 346.9)** (CTH 346.9)
- The flood rising toward heaven: compare Gen 7:19-20, Q 11:42-43 (waves like mountains) and Q 54:11-12.
- Gods paying tribute to the Sea: compare Ugaritic Yamm demanding Baal as tribute (KTU 1.2 I) and contrast Ps 93:3-4 and Q 25:53 (God set the two seas).

**Ḫepat, Takidu and Kutiladu of Šimmurra - a woman gives up her sin (CTH 346.10, 346.12)** (CTH 346.10, CTH 346.12)
- A messenger sent to a sinful woman who repents and praises God: compare Q 4:17 and Q 66:8 (sincere repentance); John 4:39 only distantly.

**The gods and the Sea search for the throne; 'made by our fate goddesses' (CTH 346.11)** (CTH 346.11)
- Gods seeking a way to the throne: Q 17:42 (they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne).

**Kumarbi and the lord of the stylus; galgalturi and the city of Kumme (CTH 346.13, 346.14)** (CTH 346.13, CTH 346.14)
- The pen and the tablet of decrees: compare Q 68:1 and Q 85:21-22 (a Preserved Tablet).

**Kumarbi myth, four small fragments (CTH 346.15, 346.17, 346.18, 346.20)** (CTH 346.15, CTH 346.17, CTH 346.18, CTH 346.20)
- Too broken for a parallel; the Kumarbi cycle's succession of divine kings may be set against Q 21:22 (were there gods besides God, heaven and earth would be ruined) and Q 23:91.

**Kumarbi myth fragment with the storm god as king of all mankind (CTH 346.16)** (CTH 346.16)
- 'King of all mankind' for a storm god: compare the Quran's 'malik al-nas' (Q 114:2) and 'Lord of the heavens and the earth' (Q 13:16); divergence: there no rival divine king.
- Divine statues and the question where silver and gold come from: compare Q 20:88 (the calf from the people's ornaments) and Job 28:1.

**Kumarbi myth fragment, 'Which god came to me?' (CTH 346.19)** (CTH 346.19)
- Compare 1 Sam 3:4-10 (who called me?) and Q 20:11-12 (Moses at the fire, 'I am your Lord').

**Kumarbi rises and quotes the saying of the ancients (CTH 346.21)** (CTH 346.21)
- Kumarbi plans to beget a champion against his son the storm god; compare the theme of fathers plotting against sons, and Q 2:170 (following what the forefathers said) for the authority of 'the ancients'.

**Hittite Atramhasis - Hamsha passes Kumarbi's words to his son Atramhasi (CTH 347.1)** (CTH 347.1)
- Hittite reshaping of the Atrahasis flood story inside the Kumarbi cycle: the disaster here is a crop plague (the ant), not yet a flood. Compare Q 11:36-43 (Noah warned, his son lost), Q 71:1-4, and Gen 6:13-22.
- Father warning son, against Q 11:42-43 where Noah calls his son who refuses; here the father warns and the son acts.
- Grain saved from a plague over years: compare Joseph storing grain, Q 12:47-49 and Gen 41:33-36.

**Hittite Atramhasis - the gods face Enlil; Nuska reports (CTH 347.2)** (CTH 347.2)
- The gods' strike against Enlil (Atrahasis I) and the assembly; compare the divine council of Ps 82:1 and, in contrast, Q 2:30-34 where the angels question God's plan for man but submit.

**Song of Hedammu - the serpent in the sea and Ishtar's fear (CTH 348.I.1 §1-5)** (CTH 348.I.1 §1:1-§5:51)
- Sea serpent (illuyanka) devouring in the sea: compare Leviathan (Isa 27:1, Ps 74:13-14) and the Quran's silence on sea monsters; the whale that swallows Jonah (Q 37:142) is God's servant, not a rival.

**Song of Hedammu - Ea rebukes the gods for destroying mankind (CTH 348.I.1 §6-7)** (CTH 348.I.1 §6:52-§7:71)
- Gods who need human offerings and would have to plough and grind for themselves: the sharpest divergence from Q 51:56-57 ('I created jinn and men only to worship me; I want no provision from them nor that they feed me') and Q 6:14 ('He feeds and is not fed'); also Ps 50:12-13 ('if I were hungry I would not tell you').
- A god pleading against the destruction of mankind: compare Abraham pleading for Sodom (Gen 18:23-33, Q 11:74-76) and Ea in Gilgamesh XI 180-188; contrast Q 2:30 where the angels object to man and God answers 'I know what you do not know'.

**Song of Hedammu - Mukisanu summons the Sea to Kumarbi's banquet (CTH 348.I.1 §8-14)** (CTH 348.I.1 §8:72-§14:128)
- A messenger who travels unseen by the sun: compare Q 18:86-90 (the sun's setting and rising places) for the sun as watcher, and Ps 139:7-12 (no hiding from God).
- The head spinning like a potter's wheel; compare Isa 29:16 and Jer 18:3-6 (potter's wheel imagery).

**Song of Hedammu - the monster is reared and devours thousands (CTH 348.I.2-3)** (CTH 348.I.2, CTH 348.I.3)
- A monstrous devourer of cattle and fish: compare Behemoth and Leviathan (Job 40-41), and Gog and Magog who devour the land (Q 18:94, 21:96).

**Song of Hedammu - Ishtar bewitches the waters and shows Hedammu her nakedness (CTH 348.I.4)** (CTH 348.I.4)
- Seduction of the monster by the goddess: compare Shamhat and Enkidu (Gilg SB I) and, inverted, Joseph resisting the master's wife (Q 12:23-24, Gen 39).
- Waters charmed to make the drinker sleep: compare the red beer that makes Sakhmet drunk (Heavenly Cow) and Judith 12-13.

**Song of Hedammu - a guest refuses chair, table and cup (CTH 348.I.5)** (CTH 348.I.5)
- Guest who will not eat: compare Abraham's guests whose hands do not reach the food (Q 11:69-70, 51:26-28) and Gen 18:8 (where they do eat).

**Song of Hedammu - the Sea offers Kumarbi his daughter Sertapsuruhi (CTH 348.I.6, first tablet)** (CTH 348.I.6)
- Kumarbi marrying the Sea's daughter to beget a monster: compare Gen 6:1-4 (divine marriages and giants) and the Quran's denial of divine offspring, Q 6:100-101 ('how can He have a son when He has no consort?') and Q 72:3.

**Song of Hedammu - Kumarbi ponders the assembly, Ea and mankind (CTH 348.I.7)** (CTH 348.I.7)
- A god who fears being struck in the assembly: contrast Q 21:23 ('He is not questioned about what He does, but they are').

**Song of Hedammu - Ishtar shows herself naked; 'what kind of woman are you?' (CTH 348.I.8)** (CTH 348.I.8)
- Compare the 'strange woman' whose smooth words lead to death (Prov 7:21-27) and Delilah (Judg 16).

**Song of Hedammu - Ishtar bathes, anoints herself and calls for music (CTH 348.I.9)** (CTH 348.I.9)
- Toilette of the seductress: compare Esther 2:12 and Ruth 3:3 (wash, anoint, dress) and the Ugaritic Anat's toilette.

**Song of Hedammu - small fragments (CTH 348.I.10-19)** (CTH 348.I.10, CTH 348.I.11, CTH 348.I.12, CTH 348.I.13, CTH 348.I.14, CTH 348.I.15, CTH 348.I.16, CTH 348.I.17, CTH 348.I.18, CTH 348.I.19)
- 'You will die and perish' (akti harakti): compare Q 3:185 ('every soul shall taste death').

**Song of Hedammu - Kumarbi meets the storm god; the son on Kumarbi's knee (CTH 348.I.20-21)** (CTH 348.I.20, CTH 348.I.21)
- Son set on the father's knee: compare Gen 50:23 (born on Joseph's knees) and Gen 30:3; and the Kumarbi-cycle birth of Ullikummi.

**Song of Hedammu - Kumarbi orders sixty youths and sixty maidens of Duddul (CTH 348.I.22)** (CTH 348.I.22)
- Compare the youths and maidens sent as tribute (the Minotaur myth) and Q 18:9-13 for youths, loosely; better HB: Num 31:18.

**Song of Hedammu - the storm god, the serpent's head, and asphalt holding the land (CTH 348.I.23-25)** (CTH 348.I.23, CTH 348.I.24, CTH 348.I.25)
- Seven years of disaster: compare Q 12:47-48 and Gen 41:27-30 (seven years of famine), and 2 Sam 24:13 (seven years of famine offered to David).

**Song of Hedammu - doors and windows sealed so Ishtar may not hear; the feast prepared (CTH 348.I.26-27)** (CTH 348.I.26, CTH 348.I.27)
- A plan hidden from a goddess behind sealed windows: compare the secret council of Joseph's brothers (Q 12:8-10) and, as divergence, Q 58:7 (no secret conference of three but God is the fourth).

**Song of Hedammu - last fragments (CTH 348.I.28-29)** (CTH 348.I.28, CTH 348.I.29)
- The storm god's servitude theme: compare Q 19:93 ('all in the heavens and earth come to the Merciful as servants').

**Teshub cycle fragments - cosmic combat, winds as shoes, dream and vision (CTH 349.1, 349.2.1, 349.2.2)** (CTH 349.1, CTH 349.2.1, CTH 349.2.2)
- God who 'makes the winds his messengers' and rides the clouds: Ps 104:3-4; and Q 21:81 (the wind subjected to Solomon). Dream-and-vision pair: Num 12:6, Job 33:15, Q 12:4-6 (Joseph's dream).

**Fragment with Ishtar - the Sea sends the wave against the storm god (CTH 350.1)** (CTH 350.1)
- Sea fighting the storm god and drying up: compare Yamm and Baal (KTU 1.2), Ps 74:13-15 (dried up rivers), Exod 14:21 and Q 26:63 (the sea split), Q 44:24 (the sea left still).

**Fragment with Ishtar - queen of Nineveh, Mount Hazzi, naked (CTH 350.2)** (CTH 350.2)
- Mount Hazzi is Ugaritic Zaphon: compare Ps 48:3 and Isa 14:13 ('mount of assembly in the far north').

**Fragment with Ishtar - Mount Pishaisha and the sleeping Ishtar (CTH 350.3)** (CTH 350.3)
- Compare Lot's daughters lying with their sleeping father (Gen 19:30-36) and Shukaletuda (ETCSL 1.3.3); the offender buying his life with a secret, as the jinn/Iblis bargain for respite (Q 7:14-15) only loosely.

**Fragments with Ishtar - Mount Pishaisha; 'Ishtar, my sister' (CTH 350.4, 350.5)** (CTH 350.4, CTH 350.5)
- Ishtar as the storm god's sister: compare the sibling pair Baal and Anat (KTU 1.3).

**Fragment with Ea - the beast tells Ea of a new god who will rule heaven and earth (CTH 351.1)** (CTH 351.1)
- 'He gives life and death': compare Q 2:258 (Abraham: 'my Lord gives life and causes death'), Q 3:26 ('You give kingship to whom You will'), and 1 Sam 2:6-7; Deut 32:39.
- An animal that knows what the wise god does not: compare the hoopoe telling Solomon 'I have encompassed what you have not' (Q 27:22) and Balaam's ass (Num 22:28).
- A god's eternal kingship over heaven, earth and sea: Q 2:255 (Throne verse), Q 67:1.

**Fragment with Ea - Ea 'mad'; the storm god angered at the tutelary god's words (CTH 351.2)** (CTH 351.2)
- The storm god angered by the tutelary god LAMMA's claims: see the Song of LAMMA (CTH 343).

**Fragments with Huranu - Ishtar, evil words and purification (CTH 352.1, 352.2)** (CTH 352.1, CTH 352.2)
- Release from the evil word and sorcery: compare Q 113 (refuge from the evil of those who blow on knots) and Q 2:102.

**Fragments with the daughter of the Pleiades - 'run from me!' (CTH 353.1, 353.2)** (CTH 353.1, CTH 353.2)
- The Pleiades: Job 9:9, 38:31, Amos 5:8; the Quran's star oaths (Q 53:1, 86:1-3).

**Tale of Appu - the rich childless man, the sun god's promise, and the births of Evil and Righteous (CTH 360.1 §1-16)** (CTH 360.1 §1:1-§16:112)
- Childless rich man who petitions a god and is promised a son: compare Zakariyya's prayer (Q 19:2-10, Q 21:89-90, Q 3:38-41: 'my Lord, do not leave me alone, You are the best of inheritors') and Abraham's promise (Q 11:69-73, 51:24-30; Gen 15:2-4, 18:1-15).
- A god from heaven who takes the form of a young man: compare the spirit who appears to Mary 'as a well-formed man' (Q 19:17), the angels as men at Abraham's tent (Gen 18:2, Q 51:24) and Manoah's visitor (Judg 13).
- 'What is your sin?': childlessness treated as a fault to be explained; compare Q 42:49-50 (He makes barren whom He wills) and 1 Sam 1:5-18 (Hannah).
- Child named for the father's gods' evil or right way: compare Gen 35:18 (Benoni/Benjamin), 1 Chr 7:23, and Q 3:36 (Mary named by her mother).
- Birth in the tenth (lunar) month: compare Q 46:15 (bearing and weaning thirty months).

**Tale of Appu - Evil and Righteous divide the estate; the lawsuit before the sun god and Ishtar (CTH 360.1 §17-30)** (CTH 360.1 §17:113-§30:174)
- Good and evil brothers and an unequal division: compare Cain and Abel (Q 5:27-31, Gen 4), Jacob and Esau (Gen 25:29-34, 27), Abraham and Lot parting (Gen 13:8-12: 'let us separate'), and the Egyptian Truth and Falsehood.
- God blessing the poorer share of the righteous: compare the owners of the garden (Q 68:17-33) and the two men with gardens (Q 18:32-44), where the proud one's better share is ruined.
- The sun god as judge of a lawsuit between brothers: compare David and Solomon judging the field (Q 21:78-79) and 2 Sam 14:5-11.
- Cursing the judge: compare Exod 22:27 (do not curse God or the ruler) and Q 6:108.

**Tale of Appu - fragments of Evil's dealings with Righteous (CTH 360.2, 360.3, 360.4)** (CTH 360.2, CTH 360.3, CTH 360.4)
- The sun god who 'hears' the evil brother's words: compare Q 58:1 (God has heard the words of her who disputes), Q 20:46 ('I am with you, I hear and see') and Gen 4:10.

**Tale of Keshshi the hunter - his beautiful wife, the neglected gods, the hidden game (CTH 361.I.1 §1-7)** (CTH 361.I.1 §1:1-§7:34)
- A man distracted from God by wife and pleasures: compare Q 64:14-15 (among your wives and children are enemies to you), Q 63:9 (let not wealth and children divert you from remembrance of God) and Solomon's wives turning his heart (1 Kgs 11:4).
- Gods withholding the hunt for neglected offerings: compare Q 68:17-33 (the garden owners who withheld the poor's share) and Hag 1:9-11.

**Tale of Keshshi - seven dreams in one night and the mother's interpretation (CTH 361.I.1 §8-17)** (CTH 361.I.1 §8:35-§17:94)
- Numbered dreams and their interpretation: compare Joseph (Q 12:4-6, 12:36-49; Gen 37, 40-41: Pharaoh's seven cows) and Gilgamesh's dreams of the meteor interpreted by Ninsun (Gilg SB I).
- The neck-yoke in a dream as sign of bondage: compare Jer 27:2 and 28:10-14.

**Tale of Keshshi - his mother's lament, the broken spear; a son born, the seventh year (CTH 361.I.2, 361.I.3)** (CTH 361.I.2, CTH 361.I.3)
- Seven years before a marriage: compare Jacob serving seven years for Rachel (Gen 29:18-20) and Moses' eight or ten years (Q 28:27).

**Tale of Keshshi - fragment with the righteous man, brothers, wives and the mill (CTH 361.I.4)** (CTH 361.I.4)
